About this text

The Chariot That Draws the Jewel of Excellent Explanation, in Tibetan Lekshé Norbu Drenpé Shingta, is a Tibetan notes-commentary on the Pāṇinivyākaraṇa, the Sanskrit grammar of Pāṇini, and it is Toh 4420 in the Tengyur, where it belongs to the section on grammar and the science of language. After opening verses of homage to the guru, to Mañjughoṣa and to the Fifth Dalai Lama as patron, it works through Pāṇini's sūtras one by one, giving each in Sanskrit with a Tibetan rendering, then explaining how affixes, augments and sound changes apply and illustrating them with derived example words. Its closing colophon explains that it was written at Drepung Monastery in the seventeenth century by the young Tibetan scholar Ngawang Phuntsok Lhundrub, at the Fifth Dalai Lama's command, after studying with the Indian paṇḍitas Balabhadra and Gokulanātha Miśra. Taking Rāmacandra's Prakriyākaumudī as its basis, it sets down the meaning, procedures and examples of the root text and its commentary as notes, ending with the derivation of nouns from verbal roots and verses of dedication.

Translation

oṃ svasti prajābhya

With reverence of body, speech and mind, I prostrate to the guru and to the protector Mañjughoṣa.

Into the expanse of the ocean of your surpassing knowledge the hosts of streams of countless knowables all flow down; rich in the wealth of love, your mind is the smile of Vāgīśvara, son of Brahmā; kinsman of the fortunate ocean, Sāgara lord of nāgas, you are the source from which the jewels of virtue and goodness come; all-pervading lord of all families, mighty Vajradhara, protector of the beings of the three realms of existence, to you I bow.

Its root the unfailing vow, its trunk firm, its leaves of compassion stir in a hundred directions;
bearing the fruit of benefit and happiness, rich in nectar, it strives to sustain all beings and the immortals;
sprout of the Victors, wish-fulfilling tree, god who dispels the burning heat of all who endure:
O Guide, embodiment of all secrets, wish-fulfilling jewel, White Lotus, protect us.

From the lap of the moon of whose mind there came a circle of garlands of the light of discernment,
drawing forth thinking beings from the thick darkness of unknowing, the far shore of the waters of learning:
the Protector of the World made manifest, the one called Pāṇini, prophesied by those three without duality,
I praise you alone, become the crown ornament of all the twice-born, the supreme scholars of the noble land.

Not travelling the path of the immortals, free of waxing and waning by day and night,
undriven even by the lifting fan of the wind, in order to dispel the darkness of the world,
they fill the cool-rayed moon with a hundred thousand lights of the five sciences: the paṇḍitas of the noble land,
Balabhadra and his brother. When I think of their kindness, how could the lotus of my hands not bloom at my heart?

The precious treasure transmitted from their lips,
unsullied by the stain of the dust of wrong ways,
the supreme mother of every garland of ornaments of grammar,
the necklace of jewels of fine explanation
that adorns the crown of the graceful lady, the clear mind that seeks the meaning:
merely by entering this supreme chariot that guides,
into the vast and precious isle of treatises hard to traverse,
I delight in this excellent way of entering without hindrance.

Here, moreover, the protector Maitreya says:
If one does not strive in the five fields of learning,
even a supreme noble one will not attain omniscience.
Therefore, in order to refute others and to care for them,
and in order to know everything oneself, one strives in them.

Among those spoken of as the five great fields of knowledge, the field to be studied first is this. As it is said: First, one learned in grammar explains, distinguishing words and their meanings; then one learned in the meaning explains without excess, omission, or error. If one knows grammar one is not confused about the meaning, and this very field of learning is like the first door of entry into all treatises, the basis of all that expresses. As to it, what are known in India, the noble land, as the eight great treatises on grammar are: the Indravyākaraṇa composed by the son of the gods Indra; the Candravyākaraṇa composed by the son of the gods Candra; the Piśalivyākaraṇa composed by the master Piśali; the Śākaṭāyanavyākaraṇa composed by the sage Śākaṭāyana; the Pāṇinivyākaraṇa composed by the sage Pāṇini; the Sumantabhadravyākaraṇa composed by the sage Sumantabhadra; the Patañjalivyākaraṇa composed by the sage Patañjali; and the Manujendravyākaraṇa composed by King Manujendra. These eight are known as the eight great treatises on grammar.

Among them, the one that excels in intelligibility, procedure and the like, in short the one that has become like the mother of all treatises on grammar, is this. Our Teacher, the incomparable Victor of the Śākyas, said in the Root Tantra of Mañjuśrī: The brahmin youth Pāṇini has been prophesied by him to the certain awakening of a śrāvaka. The great being Lokeśvara: that too is the accomplishment of his mantra. And in the Descent into Laṅkā it says, "The grammarian is Pāṇini," and so forth. To the brahmin youth Pāṇini, prophesied in these ways, the noble Lokeśvara (Avalokiteśvara) personally granted the great treatise called the Pāṇinivyākaraṇa, which has two thousand ślokas. On this very treatise there are: the commentary called the Mahābhāṣya, composed by Śeṣa, son of the nāga king Vāsuki, which has a hundred thousand ślokas; this present commentary called the Prakriyā, composed by the master Rāmacandra, which has six thousand ślokas; the Siddhāntakaumudī composed by the master Bhaṭṭoji, which has ten thousand ślokas; and the Kāśikā composed by the master Kāśikara, which has eighteen thousand ślokas. It is said that even now, in the noble land, the stream of their teaching and study has not died out. Among them, taking as my basis the commentary composed by the master Rāmacandra, the Prakriyā, that is, "the Procedure," which is easy to understand and convenient to carry, I shall explain a little of the arrangement of the procedures of the root text and its commentary.

First, the meaning of the title. In the language of India: pāṇinibyākaraṇasūtra. In the language of Tibet: The Sūtra of Pāṇini's Grammar.

Second. At the beginning of the commentary it says: śrīmadiṣṭhalamānamya pāṇinyapāṇinyādimunīnagurūnabrakriyakomudīṅakurma bāṇinīyānusāraṃṇīṃ. In Tibetan, that is: Having bowed to all the gurus, the sage Pāṇini and the rest, and to the glorious Omniscient Ones, following Pāṇini, I shall compose the Procedure in full.

Third, entering the actual text. First, the explanation of the collections of letters, of names, and of technical terms: a i u ṇa ṛḷ ka ai au ca ha ya va ra ṭalaṇ ñi ma ṅa ṇa na ma jha bha ña gha ḍha dhā ṣa ja ba ga ḍa da śa kha pha cha ṭha tha ca ṭa ta ba ka pa ya śa ṣa sa ra ha la. These are the technical terms for the separate collections.

hakārādiṣvakāra ucṭāraṇārtha: in ha and the rest, a is for the sake of pronunciation. When a is placed as the life within the consonants (hal), ha and the rest, it is for ease of pronunciation, because without a vowel they are hard to pronounce.

upadeśe'jnunāsika ita: in the initial teaching, a nasalized vowel (ac) is an it, a marker that goes. In the initial teaching, that is, after the end of roots, affixes and the like, the nasal letters ṅa, ña, ṇa, na and ma without a vowel, and the vowels that have no other letter at their end, are given the name "possessing intent."

tasyalopa: it is elided. Those just explained, the nasals and the rest that are named it, are elided.

halantyaṃ: the final consonant. Not only the nasals and the vowels, but also many other final consonants of affixes and the like are named it.

ādirantyanasahetā: the initial, together with the final it, includes what lies between.

In the arrangement of the collections of letters, a final ṇa named it is attached to a first letter such as a. By something like aṇa, for example, all the letters lying between the first and the last are understood. First, by this aṇa, in which the it-named ṇa is attached to the letter a, the three a, i and u are understood together with their own long kinds. In the same way the kinds go for the others too. Thus the number of collections is forty-one: From one come ṅa, ña, ṇa, ba and ṭa; from two, ṣa; and from three, ka, ṇa and ma; from four, ca and ya; from five, the letter ra; and from six, śa and la: so the collections are explained. So it is said. The letters ṅa, ña, the upper ṇa, ba and ṭa each indicate a single separate collection: by attaching ṅa, eṅa; by attaching ña, yaña; by attaching the upper ṇa, aṇa; by attaching ba, machaba; by attaching ṭa, a. By attaching the letter ṣa, two separate collections are indicated: by attaching it to jha, jhaṣa, and by attaching it to bha, bhaṣa. The letters ka, ṇa and ma each indicate three technical terms for separate collections: by attaching the letter ka, aka, ika and uka; by attaching the lower ṇa, aṇa, iṇa and yaṇa; and by attaching the letter ma, ama, yama and dam. By attaching the letters ca and ya, four technical terms for separate collections are indicated: by attaching ca, aca, ica, eca and aica; and by attaching ya, yaya, maya, jaya and khaya. By attaching the letter ra, five technical terms for separate collections are indicated: yara, jhara, khara, cara and śar. By attaching the letters śa and la, six technical terms for separate collections are indicated: by attaching śa, aśa, haśa, vasā, jaśa, baśa and the rest; and by attaching la, ala, hala, vala, rala, jhala and śala. Thus the forty-one are the technical terms for separate collections.

ū'kālo'jjāsvadvirghapluta: a vowel (ac) with the time of u, ū and prolonged u is short, long and prolonged (pluta). For the first four vowels, as with u, ū and prolonged u, there are three each: the short, the long, and the very long, ending in pluta. Since ḷ has no long form, it has two: the short and the very long. The vowels of the ec group have two each: the long and the very long, ending in pluta. These are a ā a', i ī i', u ū u', ṛ ṝ ṛ', ḷ ḷ ', e ai, and o au. Moreover, each of these is known to have three forms: udātta, anudātta and svarita. The sound pronounced with a high pitch is udātta, that pronounced low is anudātta, and the one in between is svarita.

mukhanāsikācanoñanunāsikā: those pronounced from the mouth and the nose are nasal. The five ṅa, ña, ṇa, na and ma, which must be pronounced from both the mouth and the nose, are named nasal (anunāsika).

anuditsabarṇasyacāpratyaya: aṇ and that which has u as its marker are also similar, but not in an affix. The members of the aṇ collection, such as a and ā, and those marked with u, that is, the classes understood together with u placed in them as their vowel (ku conveying the ka class, cu the ca class, ṭu the ṭa class, tu the ta class, and pu the pa class), are similar in their own nature (prakṛti), but not similar in an affix. For example, where the affix a is to be given, giving ā will not do.

taparastatkālasya: that which has ta after it is of that time. When the letter ta is attached after the end of a vowel, as in at or āt, it conveys a vowel of the very time of the one to which it is attached: if short, just the short; if long, just the long. Saying at does not convey all three, a long, short and so on.

tulyāsyaprayatraṃsabarṇa: those with the same place of origin and of matching kind are similar. Letters with a single place of origin, and those of matching kind that stand within one class, are also named similar (savarṇa); and in some contexts the two letters ra and la are similar as well. The semivowels, the sibilants and the like are not classes.

What are letters with a single place of origin? a, ka, kha, ga, gha, ṅa and the visarga arise from the throat. i, ca, cha, ja, jha, ña and śa arise from the palate. u, pa, pha, ba, bha, ma and the upadhmānīya arise from the lips. ṛ, ṭa, ṭha, ḍa, ḍha, ṇa, ra and ṣa arise from the crown of the head. ḷ, ta, tha, da, dha, na, la and sa arise from the teeth. e and ai arise from the throat and the palate. o and au arise from the throat and the lips. The letter va arises from the lips and the teeth. The jihvāmūlīya arises from the root of the tongue. The nasals arise from the nose. The letter ha drawn above the yaṇ letters, as in hya, hva, hra and hla, and the fifth letters of the classes coming after ha, as in haṅ, haña, haṇa, hana and hama, arise from the chest. These are just a brief summary of the places of origin of the letters.

The names of the letters are explained thus. ṅa, ña, ṇa and ma are called nasal. ya, ra, la and va are named "standing at the boundary" (antaḥstha). śa, ṣa, sa and ha are named "warm" (ūṣman). The sign called ẖka is named "having the root of the tongue" (jihvāmūlīya). The sign called ḫpa is named "having the lips" (upadhmānīya). aṃ is named "after-sound" (anusvāra). aḥ is named "to be cut off" (visarga).

pṛddhirādaica: āt and aic are vṛddhi, increase. āt and aic are both named increase.

adedguṇa: at and eṅ are guṇa, quality. at and eṅ are both named quality.

ikoguṇabṛdbhi: of ik, quality and increase. Those named increase and quality, mentioned above, occur, except for a, within the ik collection. The increase of a is āt; the increase of i is ai; the increase of u is au; and the increase of both ṛ and ḷ is also āt. As for quality, the quality of a is a itself; the quality of i is e; the quality of u is o; and the quality of both ṛ and ḷ is also at.

adarśanaṃloba: non-appearance is elision, being wiped out. Whenever any sūtra says "it is elided," whatever letter that is must be elided so that it is not seen, and that is named "wiped out" (lopa).

bsuvādayodhātaba: bhū and the rest are roots. bhū, "in the sense of existing," and the rest are called roots (dhātu).

upasargakriyāyog: in connection with an action, they are prefixes. pra and the rest, which are joined with words of action, are called prefixes (upasarga). What are pra and the rest? pra, meaning very and supreme; apa, meaning opposed to pra; sam, meaning complete, all around and genuine; anu, meaning after, all and certainly; ava; nir, meaning certainty and negation; dur, meaning bad and difficult; vi, meaning separate and reversed; ā, meaning all; parā, meaning separate; ni; adhi, meaning exceedingly; api; ati; su; ut, meaning very; abhi; prati; pari; and upa. These are the twenty.

virāmoavasānaṃ: cessation, being free of the tip, is final position, having no abode.

Being free of the tip means this: a consonant (hal) without a vowel, at the end of anything at all, whether a root, a noun or the like, is called "having no abode." Relative to others: also; exceedingly past; good; beautiful; happy; well done; very; manifestly; individually; completely; near and beneficial. This is for the sake of what is needed.

paraḥraṃnakarṣaḥsaṃhitā: the utmost proximity of what is beyond is junction. Joining whatever stands in utmost proximity, on this side and the far side, of roots, nouns and the like is called junction (saṃhitā).

suptidantapadaṃ: what ends in sup or in tiṅ is a word. What ends in sup, by attaching sup to a noun, and what ends in tiṅ, by attaching tiṅ to a root, is called a word (pada).

haloanntarā saṃyoga: consonants coming together, not at the end, are a conjunct. Where there is no vowel at the end, consonants without vowels coming together, at the end or in between, stacked two or three high and so on, are called a conjunct (saṃyoga), or a stack.

cādyoasatre: ca and the rest are indeclinable. ca and the rest, which come below, are indeclinable.

prādaya: pra and the rest. Not only ca and the rest, but pra and the rest explained above are also indeclinable.

ādyantauṭakitau: those marked with ṭa and with ka are initial and final. In the contexts of deriving roots and nouns, of junction and so on, an augment (āgama) marked with ṭa is to be placed at the beginning of whatever it is set upon, and one marked with ka at the end.

midaco'nbhātpara: that marked with ma comes after the last vowel. Something marked with ma, such as the augment num, whether affix or added element, is to be understood as given after the last vowel of what is being derived.

anekālśitsarbasya: what has more than one letter, and what is marked with śa, replace the whole. A substitute marked with śa, as when jas and śas are changed into śi, is to be understood as taking the place of the whole, not of a single letter.

dicca: and that marked with ṅa. A substitute marked with ṅa, as when i is changed into anaṅ, also takes the place not of a single letter but of the whole; and that is to be understood as an operation on the end.

skānipadādeśo'nalbidhau: the procedure as for what stands in place, but not in the case of complete substitution. In the context of roots, nouns, words, affixes or anything else, where a single letter is not substituted, as when śas is changed into na, and also in a complete substitution, as when the whole of śas is changed into śi, the procedures apply as though it remained unchanged in place.

itipāṇinibyākaraṇasyasandheḥsūtrādupayogisajhaprakaraṇaṃsamāptāḥ: thus, from the sūtras on junction of the Pāṇinivyākaraṇa, the section on the names used in application is complete.

Second, the explanation of the junction of vowels, that is, of ac, has two parts: the general rule and the special exceptions. First: ikoyaṇaci: ik becomes yaṇ before ac. The letters of the ik collection are changed into the letters of the yaṇ collection when a vowel follows. Into which of the yaṇ collection is each of the ik collection changed? yathāsaṃkhyamanvādeśassamāni: substitutes of equal number follow in order. i and the rest are to be changed, in order, into ya and the rest, of equal number: i becomes vra, ṛ becomes rra, and ḷ becomes lra. For dadhi ānaya, by the two sūtras, earlier and later, i is changed into yra, and dradhrayra ānaya arises.

anacica: and also where there is no vowel. A vowelless letter of the yar collection after a vowel is doubled when a consonant follows: dha is pronounced twice, and dadhudtrayra ānaya arises.

jhalāṃjaśajhaśi: of the jhal letters, jaś before jhaś. The letters of the jhal collection become letters of the jaś collection when letters of the jhaś collection follow. Into which letters of the jaś collection do they change? sthāne'ntaratama: the nearest in place, the middle one. They are changed into whichever, in the middle or within that jaś collection, has the same place of origin and class. dhra is changed into dra, which has the same place of origin and class as itself, giving dadradhrayraānaya. By "and also where there is no vowel," da is again pronounced twice, and dadradraṅhay ānaya arises.

jharojharisabarṇe: of the jhar letters, before a similar jhar. A letter of the jhar collection after a consonant is to be elided when a letter of the jhar collection with the same place of origin as itself follows. By wiping out the middle da: dadradtuy ānaya.

saṃyogītasyasopa: the final of a conjunct is elided. The final of a conjunct, a vowelless consonant at the end of a word, is to be elided. Although by this sūtra the elision of ya would follow, the commentary quotes yaṇalobana: "there is no elision of yaṇ." Since it says, "Even if it is the final of a conjunct, if it is a letter of the yaṇ collection, it is not elided," the y is not elided.

ajjhiṇipareṇasaṃyojyi: what lacks a vowel is joined to what follows. What lacks a vowel, that is, consonants without vowels, are to be drawn up on top of the following letter, whether a vowel or a consonant with a vowel. Drawing them up in order gives batdhyānya. In the same way, for madhuatra there arise madhvatra and maddhvatra; for mūtṛ atraḥla, mātratra; and for ḷākṛti, lṅakṛti.

acorahābhyāṃdve: after a vowel, after ra and ha, two. The letters of the yar collection that come after the letter ra or the letter ha, which themselves come after a vowel, are doubled, except for those that are not letters. (Pen tip here; mchang this; ma this.) For hariarbba, i becomes y: "mother of snakes." By this sūtra ya is pronounced twice: ñaryy arbba. By "after a vowel, after ra and ha, two," the upper ya is pronounced twice again: haryyy artha.

haloyamāṃyamiloṅpa: of the yam letters after a consonant, before a yam letter, elision. The letters of the yam collection that come after a consonant are to be elided when a letter of the yam collection follows. Wiping out the upper ya and drawing them up in order gives haryyarthaḥ, meaning "the sense of the one who carries off." In the same way, for gaurīatra, gauryyatra, "the white lady here"; and for nahiatra, naryyatra and so on, "it is not here."

dīrgdādācāryyaṇāṃ: after a long vowel, according to the teachers. The former teachers explained that the letters of the yar collection after a long vowel are not doubled when a consonant follows: as in dātraṃ, "cutting," and pātraṃ, "vessel," where the ta after the long letter ā is not doubled.

eco'yvvayāvaḥ: ec becomes ay, av, āy and āv.

The letters of the ec collection, when an ac follows, become in order ay, av, āy and āv. Dātra and pātra are formed by adding the suffix tran to dā, "to cut," and pā, "to drink." For example, te āhuḥ becomes tayāhuḥ; go atra becomes gavatra; rai au becomes rāyau; yau iha becomes yāviha, and so on.

vānto yi pratyaye: before a suffix beginning with ya, they end in va. When the suffix ya follows, o and au end in va, that is, they become av and āv. For go yam, "they spoke"; "the cow here," gavyam. For nau yam, nāvyam. "The two possessed of wealth," or "the two of gold." "Which two here."

Cited in the commentary: adhvaparimāṇe ca, also in a measure of road. When a measure of road is expressed, go becomes av before yūti: gavyūtiḥ.

dhātos tannimittasyaiva: only of that which has the root as its cause. Root. The substance of a fire offering. Boat. The o and au that have a root as their cause become, just as was just explained, av and āv when the suffix ya follows. Adding yat to lū, guṇa is made by the rule on sārvadhātuka suffixes and so on. This sūtra changes the o to av, giving lavyam. Two krośas. With avaśya placed before it, lū takes ṇya; by aco ñṇiti, vṛddhi is due before a suffix marked with ñ or ṇ, and this sūtra changes the vowel to āv: avaśyalāvyam.

kṣayyajayyau śakyārthe: kṣayya and jayya in the sense of "able to be." Adding yat to kṣi, "to waste away," and ji, "to conquer," kṣayya, "able to be exhausted," and jayya are irregular forms in the sense of "able to be." To be cut off. It is an irregular form.

krayyas tadarthe: krayya in the sense of "for that." Adding yat to krī gives krayya in the sense of "for that," that is, "to buy." Restricting. When the sense of being for sale is expressed, it is an irregular form: krayyavastraḥ, cloth for sale.

lopaḥ śākalyasya: elision, according to Śākalya. The ancient sage Śākalya taught that the final y and v of the ay and the rest, into which the ec mentioned above were changed, may optionally be elided. For te āhuḥ, the ec is changed to ay, and when this sūtra optionally deletes the ya, the result is ta āhuḥ, ta āhuḥ. Likewise gavatra becomes ga atra; rāyau becomes rā au; yāviha becomes yā iha, and so on.

pūrvatrāsiddham: not established with respect to what precedes. Once the y or v has been deleted, as just explained, sandhi and the like are not applied again, for it is not established with respect to what precedes. "They said": the example has been given. "The cow here." "The two of gold."

ād guṇaḥ: from a, guṇa. "Which two here." When an ac follows a word ending in a, the two together are changed into whatever is the guṇa letter of the latter. For upa indra, upendraḥ; for ramā īśa, rameśaḥ; for gaṅgā udakam, gaṅgodakam; for kṛṣṇa ṛddhi, the a and the ṛ together become a single a.

uraṇ raparaḥ: the aṇ that replaces ṛ also has r after it. By the letter ṛ and by the word "also," guṇa from a applies to the letter ḷ as well. Thus, "near to Indra" is Upendra, "the lord of Ramā" is Rameśa, and "the water of the Gaṅgā." When the aṇ, such as a, is changed into the combined letter, if ṛ follows it one must write ra, and if ḷ follows, la. Writing ra gives kṛṣṇarddhiḥ. Likewise, for tava ḷkāraḥ, tavalkāraḥ. Or else, by anaci ca, doubling where no ac follows, tavalkkāraḥ. Since the commentary says, "the letters of the yay collection are optionally doubled," one may optionally double the ka, giving "the wealth of Kṛṣṇa" and tavalkkāraḥ, "your letter ḷ," or "you who are rich in power," and so on.

vṛddhir eci: vṛddhi before ec. Your letter ḷ, or you, the lord. When an ec follows a word ending in a, the two together become whatever is the vṛddhi letter of the latter. Your letter, or you, the lord. For kṛṣṇa ekatvam, kṛṣṇaikatvam; for gaṅgā oghaḥ, gaṅgaughaḥ, the flood of the Gaṅgā; for deva aiśvaryam, devaiśvaryam, divine lordship; for khaṭvā aupagavaḥ, khaṭvaupagavaḥ, "the bed, and the cow that is near."

etyedhatyūṭhsu: before eti, edhati and ūṭh. Oneness with Kṛṣṇa. When eti, edhati, or a ū that has been changed into ūṭh follows a word ending in a, vṛddhi also takes place. For upa eti, upaiti; for upa edhati, upaidhati. For ūṭh: as when the ū of vāha, being due to become ūṭh, is changed into ūṭh, for prasthā ūhaḥ, prasthauhaḥ.

akṣād ūhinyām: from akṣa, before ūhinī. When ūhinī follows akṣa, the two together become vṛddhi. Goes near; causes to increase near. For akṣa ūhinī, akṣauhiṇī, unbearable to behold as an army.

svād īreriṇyoḥ: from sva, before īra and īriṇī. When īra or īriṇī follows sva, the two together become vṛddhi: for sva īraḥ, svairaḥ. It is the name of a great division of an army, as it is said:

Threefold: chariots and heroes, a hundred thousand;
horses, a million; foot soldiers,
thirty-six koṭis, are enlisted:
this is what is called an akṣauhiṇī.

For sva īriṇī, svairiṇī.

prād ūhoḍhoḍhyeṣaiṣyeṣu: from pra, before ūha, ūḍha, ūḍhi, eṣa and eṣya. Self-willed. When ūha, ūḍha, ūḍhi, eṣa or eṣya follows pra, vṛddhi takes place: prauhaḥ, prauḍhaḥ, prauḍhiḥ, praiṣaḥ, praiṣyaḥ. A self-willed woman, that is, a prostitute. Since the commentary says, "in some cases pra with eṣa also takes guṇa," preṣaḥ.

ṛte ca tṛtīyāsamāse: and before ṛta, in a compound of the third case. Fully carried. Robust in body, or fearless, or steadfast; expansive in mind, or wishing to be steadfast. When ṛta follows a word ending in a, in a compound of the third case, the two together become vṛddhi. Fully desired. For sukhena ṛtaḥ, sukhārtaḥ, and so on.

pravatsataro kambalavasanadaśārṇānām ṛṇe: before ṛṇa, for pra, vatsatara, kambala, vasana, daśa and ṛṇa. When ṛṇa follows pra, vatsatara, kambala, vasana, daśa or ṛṇa, the two together become vṛddhi. Seized by happiness. Prārṇaḥ, a great debt; vatsatarārṇaḥ, a debt of a fine calf; vasanārṇaḥ, a debt of clothing; daśārṇaḥ, a debt of ten; ṛṇārṇaḥ.

upasargād ṛti dhātau: from a prefix, before a root beginning with ṛ. When the initial ṛ of a root follows a prefix ending in a, the two together become vṛddhi. For upa ṛcchati, upārcchati; likewise prārcchati, and so on.

The change of what is called ṛt. A debt of a debt. Nirṛ, in the sense of stopping.

vā supy āpiśaleḥ: optionally before a nominal root, according to Āpiśali. The ancient sage Āpiśali taught that when the initial ṛ of a nominal root follows a prefix such as pra ending in a, vṛddhi also takes place optionally. Goes near. Āpiśali holds. That which goes forth. For upa ṛṣabhīyati, upārṣabhīyati. Since the commentary says, "in some cases the rules taught for ṛ also apply to ḷ," for pra ḷkārīyati, prālkārīyati or pralkārīyati.

eṅi pararūpam: before eṅ, the form of the following. When a root whose first letter belongs to the eṅ collection follows prefixes ending in a, the two together take the form of the following. Acts toward it like a sage. For pra ejati, prejati. Makes one greatly desire ḷ. For upa okhate, upokhate.

eṅādau subdhātau vā: optionally before a nominal root beginning with eṅ. When a nominal root beginning with eṅ follows prefixes ending in a, the change to the form of the following and vṛddhi are both optional. Trembles greatly. For upa eḍakīyati, upaiḍakīyati; burns near; or upeḍakīyati. For pra oghīyati, praughīyati or proghīyati.

Cited in the commentary: śakandhvādiṣu pararūpaṃ vācyam: in śakandhu and the like, the form of the following is to be stated. Śakandhu and the like take the form of the following. Good. Acts near like the body. For śaka andhuḥ, śakandhuḥ, a well that has run dry. Acts greatly like waves. For karka andhu, karkandhu. A great mouth. For kula aṭā, kulaṭā. A nun; a beggar woman of the mountain. For sīman anta, sīmantaḥ, the parting of the hair. For hala īṣā, halīṣā. For lāṅgala īṣā, lāṅgalīṣā. For manas īṣā, manīṣā. For patat añjaliḥ, patañjaliḥ. For sāra aṅga, sāraṅgaḥ.

Cited in the commentary: eve cāniyoge: and before eva when it does not express restriction. When eva follows a word ending in a, and it does not express restriction, the two take the form of the following. Non-attainment; grasping. The pole of a plow. Intelligence. The little one taken up in cupped hands: the sage Patañjali. A black deer. For adya eva, adyeva. If it does express restriction, vṛddhi is made: adyaiva.

otvoṣṭhayoḥ samāse vā: optionally in a compound, before otu and oṣṭha. When otu or oṣṭha follows a word ending in a, in a compound, the two together optionally take the form of the following. Gone into just that. Sthūlotuḥ or sthūlautuḥ; bimboṣṭhaḥ or bimbauṣṭhaḥ. Remains just as it is. If it is not a compound, there is vṛddhi only: for tava oṣṭhaḥ, tavauṣṭhaḥ.

omāṅoś ca: and before om and āṅ. When om or āṅ follows a final a, the two together take the form of the following. A fat cat. Lips like the bimba fruit, that is, very red lips. For buddhāya oṃ namaḥ, buddhāyoṃ namaḥ. Likewise, your lips. For śivāya āyathaḥ, śivāyathaḥ.

avyaktānukaraṇasyāta itau: of the at of a word imitating an indistinct sound, before iti. When iti follows the at of a word imitating an indistinct sound, the two together are changed into the form of the following. Homage to the Buddha. For paṭat iti, paṭiti. From where, destroyed? The commentary explains that even if all those defining conditions are present, if the word has not many vowels but only one, it does not take the form of the following: so for śrat iti, śraditi, and so on.

nāmreḍitasyāntyasya tu vā: not of a repeated word, but optionally of its final t. And this. When iti follows a repeated, that is doubled, word that ends in an at imitating an indistinct sound, the at and the following do not together become the form of the following; but the t alone optionally takes the form of the following. This wind from below. For paṭat paṭat iti, paṭatpaṭeti, or else paṭatpaṭaditi.

akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ: ak, before a similar letter, becomes long. When a letter of the ak collection that is similar follows words ending in a letter of the ak collection, the two together become one long vowel. For daitya ari, daityāriḥ; for śrī īśa, śrīśaḥ; for viṣṇu udayaḥ, viṣṇūdayaḥ, and so on.

Cited in the commentary: ṛti savarṇe ṛ vā: before a similar ṛ, optionally ṛ. When a similar ṛ follows a word ending in ṛ, the two are optionally changed into ṛ, or changed into the long vowel. The enemy of the asuras. The glorious lord. For hotṛ ṛkāraḥ, hotṛkāraḥ, or else hotṝkāraḥ, and so on. The rise of Viṣṇu.

Cited again in the commentary: ḷti ḷ vā: before ḷ, optionally ḷ. When ḷ follows a word ending in ṛ, the two together optionally become ḷ. For hotṛ ḷkāraḥ, hotḷkāraḥ; this too is like hotṝkāraḥ. The ṛ of the fire-offering priest.

nājjhalau: not ac and hal. Even though they have the same place of articulation, an ac and a hal are not lengthened and so on. As in kumārī śete, ī and śa have one and the same place of articulation, yet they are not made long. The ḷ of the fire-offering priest. So it stays just as kumārī śete.

eṅaḥ padāntād ati: from eṅ at the end of a word, before at. When at follows an eṅ that stands at the end of a word, the two together take the form of the preceding. For agne atra, agne'tra; for vāyo atra, vāyo'tra, and so on. Makes the young girl lie down.

sarvatra vibhāṣā goḥ: everywhere optionally for go. When at follows go, changing the two into the form of the preceding and leaving them in their natural state are optional everywhere. O fire, here. O fire, here. For go agram, the best of lands, go'gram or else go agram itself. O wind, here. The best of lands.

avaṅ sphoṭāyanasya: avaṅ, according to Sphoṭāyana. The ancient sage Sphoṭāyana taught that the final of go is optionally changed to avaṅ when an ac follows. For go īśaḥ, gaveśaḥ, or else gavīśaḥ, and so on.

Cited in the commentary: indre ca nityam: and always before indra. By the word "and," when indra or akṣa follows, the final of go always becomes avaṅ. For go indra, gavendraḥ; for go akṣa, gavākṣaḥ.

uñaḥ: from uñ. The lord of cows. This u, when iti follows, is optionally changed to v or left in its natural state: u iti, v iti.

maya uño vo vā: after may, uñ optionally becomes v. When an ac follows the uñ that comes after the may collection, it is optionally changed to v. The lord of others. The eye of a cow, that is, a window. For kim u uktam, kimv uktam or else kim u uktam, and so on.

iko'savarṇe śākalyasya hrasvaś ca: before a dissimilar vowel, the ik, according to Śākalya, is also optionally short. This u. When a dissimilar ac follows a final of the ik collection, it optionally remains in its natural state and, if it is long, is optionally made short; this is the view of the ancient sage Śākalya. What is said? What does he say? For cakrī atra, there are three forms: cakri atra, cakrī atra and cakryatra, and so on.

ṛty akaḥ: before ṛ, of the ak. When ṛ follows, a final ak is joined in sandhi, or not joined, or shortened, and so on, as before. For brahmā ṛṣi: brahma ṛṣiḥ, brahmā ṛṣiḥ, brahmarṣiḥ, and so on.

This king, or this clear one, or this possessor of the wheel. Iti pāṇinivyākaraṇasya sandheḥ sūtrād acsandhayaḥ samāptāḥ: thus, from the sūtras on sandhi of the Pāṇinivyākaraṇa, the vowel sandhis are complete.

Third, the sandhi of remaining in the natural state, the exceptions. A sage of Brahmā.

aco'ntyādi ṭi: that which begins with the last ac is ṭi. In any root, noun or word, the final ac, and the ac together with a final consonant without a vowel, are given the name ṭi for the sake of what is needed.

dūrād dhūte ca: and in calling from afar. The ṭi in calling from afar is given the name pluta.

plutapragṛhyā aci prakṛtyā: pluta and pragṛhya, before an ac, remain in their natural state. When an ac follows an ac that has the name pluta, it remains in its natural state, and no sandhi is made: he devadatta3 atra, he yajñadatta3 atra, he yajñadatta3 idam.

īdūded dvivacanaṃ pragṛhyam: dual words ending in ī, ū or e are pragṛhya. Words that have the dual ending in ī, ū or e do not make sandhi when an ac follows, but remain in their natural state: agnī atra, vāyū iti, gaṅge amū, and so on. O Devadatta, here. O Yajñadatta, here.

maṇīvādīnāṃ na: not so for maṇī iva and the like. Even though they are dual, maṇī and the rest do not remain in their natural state when iva follows, but simply make sandhi: for maṇī iva, the two fires here, the two winds, the two Gaṅgās here, maṇīva. Likewise dampatīva, rodasīva, jambatīva, and so on.

adaso māt: after the m of adas. The final ī and ū after the m into which adas has been changed do not make sandhi when an ac follows: amī īśāḥ, amū āsāte.

nipāta ekāj anāṅ: a particle with a single ac, other than āṅ. Like jewels. This husband and wife, or this eater. This lord of wealth. Particles with a single ac, leaving aside āṅ, which applies in many senses such as "a little" and "pervading up to," do not make sandhi when an ac follows. These are lords; these two stay. A anantaḥ, i indraṃ paśya, ā evam. If it is āṅ, sandhi is made: for ā uttamaḥ, ottamaḥ, and so on.

ot: what ends in o. Particles ending in o also do not make sandhi when an ac follows: aho īśaḥ. From Viṣṇu at the end. Here the lord looked. The lord, the husband of Umā. Just as it is. Atho evam, and so on.

Since the commentary says, "he and hai also do not make sandhi when an ac follows": a little, supreme. He īśa, O lord; hai ume, O Umā. Ah, the lord!

Iti pāṇinivyākaraṇasya sandheḥ sūtrāt prakṛtisandhayaḥ samāptāḥ: thus, from the sūtras on sandhi of the Pāṇinivyākaraṇa, the sandhis of remaining in the natural state are complete. Then, as follows.

The fourth kind of sandhi, consonant sandhi:

stoḥ ścunā ścuḥ: s and the tu, with ś and the cu, become ś and the cu. When ś or the cu, that is, the ca class, follows the letter s or the tu, that is, the ta class, they become ś and the ca class; when ṣ or the ṭu, that is, the ṭa class, follows, they become ṣ and the ṭa class. For rāmas śete, rāmaśśete; for rāmas cinoti, rāmaścinoti; for sat cit, saccit; for bhagavān jayaḥ, bhagavāñjayaḥ, and so on.

ṣṭunā ṣṭuḥ: with ṣ and the ṭu, ṣ and the ṭu. The letter s and the ta class, with the letter ṣ and the ṭu, that is, the ṭa class, become ṣ and the ṭa class. Rāma lies down. Rāma gathers. For rāmas ṣaṣṭhaḥ, rāmaṣṣaṣṭhaḥ. The true mind. For rāmas ṭīkate, rāmaṣṭīkate. The Blessed One, the Victor. For tat ṭīkate, taṭṭīkate; for bhagavān ṭīkate, bhagavāṇṭīkate.

na padāntāṭ ṭor anām: not after a ṭu at the end of a word, except before nām. Rāma the sixth. When the preceding word ends in the ṭa class, and there follows the letter s or the ta class, other than nām, the genitive plural with the augment nuṭ, the tu does not become ṣṭu. Rāma explains, or comments at length. He explains it. The Blessed One explains. For ṣaṭ santaḥ, the s does not become ṣ: ṣaṭsantaḥ. For ṣaṭ te, ṣaṭte. If it is nām, what then? Ṣaṇṇām, of the six.

toḥ ṣi: the tu before ṣ. The word-final ta class does not become the ṭa class when the letter ṣ follows: for bhavān ṣaṣṭhaḥ, bhavānṣaṣṭhaḥ, and so on.

śāt: after ś. The ta class that follows a preceding letter ś does not become the ṭa class. The sixth good one. Those six. For ṣaṭ with ām and nuṭ, this sūtra changes t to ṭ. The yar, before a nasal, optionally becomes a nasal; the ṭ is due to become ṇ. For viśan, viśnaḥ; likewise, for praśan, praśnaḥ. You six.

jhalāṃ jaśo'nte: of the jhal at the end, jaś. The letters of the jhal collection at the end of a word become letters of the jaś collection when the aś collection follows. In the Kalāpa: "The first letters of the classes at the end of a word, going, become the third letters before vowels and voiced letters."

That is the same. For vāk īśaḥ, vāgīśaḥ; for cit rūpaḥ, cidrūpaḥ, and so on.

yaro'nunāsike'nunāsiko vā: the yar, before a nasal, optionally becomes a nasal. The letters of the yar collection at the end of a word optionally become nasals when a nasal follows. This is like the Kalāpa: "Before fifth letters, fifth letters," the lord of speech, "or optionally," body and mind, "they remain third letters." For vāk manaḥ, vāṅmanaḥ or vāgmanaḥ; for ṣaṭ mama, ṣaṇmama or ṣaḍmama.

tor li: the tu, before l. The ta class at the end of a word becomes the letter l when l follows. For tat lunāti, tallunāti.

Cited in the commentary: sānunāsiko niranunāsikatvena yavalā dvidhā: y, v and l are twofold, with nasality and without nasality. Speech and mind. The son of six mothers. Of the four semivowels, the three y, v and l are divided into two, nasal and non-nasal. It cuts. In the nasal kind, before the word-final letter n that is changed into the letter l, the anusvāra that marks the nasal is written. For vidvān likhati, vidvāṃllikhati; likewise, for bhavān likhati, bhavāṃllikhati.

udaḥ sthāstambhoḥ pūrvasya: after ud, of sthā and stambh, the form of the preceding. When sthānam or stambhanam follows ud, its letter takes the form of the preceding. For ut sthānam, utthānam. The learned one writes. Likewise, for ut stambhanam, uttambhanam. You write.

jhayo ho'nyatarasyām: after jhay, h, optionally. The h that follows a word-final letter of the jhal collection optionally becomes the fourth letter of the class of that preceding letter. In the Kalāpa: "After those same letters, the letter h optionally becomes the fourth of the preceding," and it is like that. For vāk hariḥ, vāgghariḥ or vāg hariḥ. You two who carry off. Likewise, for ac halau, ajjhalau or aj halau, the vowels and consonants. For ṣaṭ halāni, ṣaḍḍhalāni or ṣaḍ halāni, six plows, and so on.

khari ca: and before khar, car. The letters of the jhal collection at the end of a word become the car letters of their own class when a letter of the khar collection follows. For tad śivaḥ: by stoḥ ścunā ścuḥ and the rest, d becomes j; by śaś cho'ṭi, ś is due to become ch; and this sūtra changes j to c: tacchivaḥ, and so on.

śaś cho'ṭi: before aṭ, ś becomes ch. The letter ś that follows the jhay collection becomes the letter ch when a letter of the aṭ collection follows. The example has already been given. Since the commentary says, "the letter ś after jhay also becomes ch when the am collection follows," Śiva, for tat ślokaḥ: ś becomes ch, and by stoḥ ścunā ścuḥ and the rest t is changed to c: tacchlokaḥ.

mo'nusvāraḥ: m becomes anusvāra. A word-final letter m becomes anusvāra when a hal follows. For tam hasati, taṃ hasati, and so on.

naś cāpadāntasya jhali: and of n not at the end of a word, before jhal. That verse. Both the n at the end of a word and one not at the end of a word become anusvāra when a letter of the jhal collection follows. For yaśān si, with jas replaced by śi, yaśāṃsi, and so on. You laugh.

anusvārasya yayi parasavarṇaḥ: the anusvāra, before yay, becomes similar to the following. The preceding anusvāra, when a letter of the yay collection follows, becomes whichever letter is similar to it. Fames. For taṃ tanoti, tantanoti; for yaṃ karoti, yaṅkaroti, and so on.

vā padāntasya: optionally at the end of a word. The word-final anusvāra optionally becomes similar to the following when yay follows. For taṃ karoti, taṅkaroti or taṃ karoti. For saṃ yantā, this sūtra optionally changes the anusvāra to y. Hold it! Whatever it does. And since y, v and l are twofold, with nasality and without, one may optionally write the nasal marker: saṃyyantā, sayyantā or saṃyantā, the driver of an elephant. Doing it. Likewise, for saṃ vatsaraḥ, savvatsaraḥ, a year. For yaṃ lokam, yaṃllokam, yallokam or yaṃ lokam, whatever world, and so on.

mo rāji samaḥ kvau: the m of sam, before rāj with kvip. When rāj ending in the suffix kvip follows, the letter m of sam remains m: for sam rāṭ, samrāṭ.

he mapare vā: optionally before h followed by m. The anusvāra optionally becomes m before a letter h that has m after it. For kiṃ hmalayati, kimhmalayati or kiṃ hmalayati.

yavalapare yavalā vā: before h followed by y, v or l, optionally y, v or l. The anusvāra, before a letter h that has any of the three y, v and l after it, optionally becomes those three, y, v or l. Genuinely clear. For kiṃ hyaḥ, kiyhyaḥ or kiṃ hyaḥ. For kiṃ hlādayati, what does he cause to go to? kilhlādayati or kiṃ hlādayati. For kiṃ hvalayati, kivhvalayati or kiṃ hvalayati.

napare naḥ: before n, n. The anusvāra optionally becomes n before a letter h that has n after it. For kiṃ hnute, he went yesterday, kinhnute or kiṃ hnute. Hṇo.

ṅṇoḥ kukṭuk śari: of ṅ and ṇ, kuk and ṭuk, before śar. What is pleasant? After a final letter ṅ or ṇ, when the śar collection follows, the augments kuk and ṭuk optionally occur, in order. What does he cause to go to? The k serves for position, the u for pronunciation. For prāṅ ṣaṣṭhaḥ, optionally adding kuk: prāṅkṣaṣṭhaḥ or prāṅ ṣaṣṭhaḥ. What did he see? Likewise, for sugaṇ ṣaṣṭhaḥ, optionally adding ṭuk: sugaṇṭṣaṣṭhaḥ or sugaṇ ṣaṣṭhaḥ, and so on.

ḍaḥ si dhuṭ: after ḍ, before s, dhuṭ. After a word ending in the letter ḍ, the augment dhuṭ optionally comes before a following s. The ṭ serves for position, the u for pronunciation. For ṣaḍ santaḥ, six who were before, dhuṭ is optionally added, and by khari ca the dh is changed to t, the car letter: ṣaṭtsantaḥ or ṣaṭsantaḥ, six good verses.

naś ca: and after n. After a word ending in n, the augment dhuṭ also optionally comes before a following s. For san saḥ, dhuṭ is optionally added and by khari ca changed to t: santsaḥ, easy giving, or sansaḥ, and so on.

śi tuk: before ś, tuk.

When the letter ś follows, the augment tuk optionally comes to a word ending in n. Not the mother of those six. For san śraddhā, the augment tuk is optionally added; by stoḥ ścunā ścuḥ, s and the tu are due to become ś and the cu, so t becomes c and n becomes ñ; and by śaś cho'ṭi the ś is optionally changed to ch: sañcchraddhā or sañśraddhā.

ṅamo hrasvād aci ṅamuṇ nityam: after a ṅam that follows a short vowel, before an ac, always ṅamuṭ. After a word-final letter of the ṅam collection that has a short penultimate, the augment ṅamuṭ always comes to a following ac. The ṭ serves for position, the u for pronunciation, and the m for the collection. In the Kalāpa: the giving of faith, or the giving for the departed. "ṅ, ṇ and n with a short penultimate are doubled before a vowel": this is one and the same. For pratyaṅ ātmā, pratyaṅṅātmā; likewise, for sugaṇ īśaḥ, sugaṇṇīśaḥ; for bhagavan iti, bhagavanniti, and so on.

pumaḥ khayy ampare: of pum, before khay followed by am. The letter m of pum, before a letter of the khay collection that has a letter of the am collection after it, becomes s. The self, greatly worshipped. The lord of the beautifully adorned, the lord of the good host. The face of the Blessed One. And before it the nasal marker is written, or else the augment anusvāra is given. For pum kokilaḥ, puṃskokilaḥ or puṃskokilaḥ.

samaḥ suṭi: of sam, before suṭ. The letter m of sam, before suṭ, becomes s, and before it the nasal marker is written, or else the augment anusvāra is given. For sam skartā, saṃskartā.

naś chavy apraśān: and of n, before chav, except in praśān. A cuckoo. A word-final n, other than that of praśān, before a letter of the chav collection that has a letter of the am collection after it, becomes ru, and before it the nasal marker is written, or else the augment anusvāra comes. One who accomplishes everything, or one who perfects. For bhavān chindhi, this sūtra changes the n to ru; the u serves for distinction.

kharavasānayor visarjanīyaḥ: before khar and at a pause, visarga is to be made. Where a letter of the khar collection follows, or where there is a pause, that is, at the end of a word, the letter r becomes visarga. Visarga. By visarjanīyasya saḥ, the visarga is due to become s; and by stoḥ ścunā ścuḥ and the rest, the s is changed to ś: bhavāṃś chindhi, you, cut! or bhavāṃś chindhi. Likewise, for cakrin trāhi, cakriṃs trāhi or cakriṃs trāhi. The n of praśān does not become ru: for praśān tanoti, praśāntanoti.

nṝn pe: of nṝn, before p. The letter n of nṝn optionally becomes ru when the letter p follows. When it is changed to ru, the nasal marker before it, or else the augment anusvāra, also comes. O wielder of the wheel, protect! In the case where it is changed to ru, the r becomes visarga, and before ku and pu, the jihvāmūlīya and upadhmānīya are optionally due. Examine minutely and in full. By optionally changing the visarga into the upadhmānīya and so on, the forms are produced: nṝṃḫpāhi, nṝṃḥ pāhi, nṝṃḫpāhi. In the case where it is not changed to ru: nṝn pāhi.

kān āmreḍite: of kān, before its repetition. The letter n of kān, when its repetition follows, becomes ru, and before it the nasal marker, or else the augment anusvāra, also comes. For kān kān, kāṃskān. Protect men! In kaḥ ka and the like, too, it does not become the jihvāmūlīya. Protect men!

kaskādiṣu ca: and in kaska and the like. The visarga of kaḥ ka and the like does not become the jihvāmūlīya and upadhmānīya when ku and pu follow. For kaḥ kaḥ, what? by what? kaskaḥ. Likewise, for tatra kautaḥ kutaḥ, tatrakautaskutaḥ; for sarpiḥ kuṇḍikā, sarpiṣkuṇḍikā, and so on.

che ca: and before ch. A short vowel followed by a word beginning with the letter ch takes the augment tuk; the k serves for position, the u for pronunciation. For śiva chāyā, tuk is added, and by stoḥ ścunā ścuḥ and the rest the t is changed to c: what is bound to it? śivacchāyā.

āṅmāṅoś ca: and of āṅ and māṅ. Fresh butter, coiled. When ch follows, āṅ and māṅ also take the augment tuk. For ā chādayati, ācchādayati; for mā chidat, the drawing of a field? mā cchidat.

dīrghāt: after a long vowel. When ch follows, not only after a short vowel but after a long one too, the augment tuk comes. For me cha, mecchaḥ, a barbarian, one who destroys joy; for hrī cha, hrīcchaḥ, shame, and so on.

padāntād vā: optionally after the end of a word. Covers completely. Do not cut the word. When ch follows a long vowel at the end of a word, the augment tuk optionally comes. For lakṣmī chāyā, lakṣmīcchāyā or lakṣmī chāyā.

Iti pāṇinivyākaraṇasya sandheḥ sūtrād dhalantasandhayaḥ samāptāḥ: thus, from the sūtras on sandhi of the Pāṇinivyākaraṇa, the sandhis of words ending in consonants are complete.

Fifth, the explanation of visarga sandhi in particular:

visarjanīyasya saḥ: of the visarga, s. The shadow of glory. A visarga at the end of the preceding word becomes s when a letter of the khar collection follows. For kaḥ tanoti, kastanoti; buddhas trātā, and so on.

śarpare visarjanīyaḥ: before khar followed by śar, visarga is to be made. A visarga at the end of the preceding word remains visarga before a khar letter that has a letter of the śar collection after it: kaḥ tsaruḥ, and so on.

vā śari: optionally before śar. What does he grind? A visarga at the end of the preceding word, when a letter of the śar collection follows, is optionally changed into the form of the following; otherwise it becomes s. The purifier of the buddhas. For hariḥ śete, hariśśete; for kaḥ ṣaṇḍe, kaṣṣaṇḍe; for kaḥ sādhuḥ, kassādhuḥ, and so on. What is young?

Cited in the commentary: kharpare śari vā visargalopaḥ: before śar followed by khar, visarga is optionally elided.

When a following word begins with a letter of the śar collection that has a khar letter after it, the visarga before it is optionally Hari sleeps. elided. So for hariḥ, What makes into pieces? sphurati, Hari, what is good? sphurati: harissphurati, or hariḥ sphurati.

Cited in the commentary: tadbṛhatoḥ karapatyoś coradevatayoḥ suṭ talopaś ca. Before kara and pati after tat and bṛhat, when thief and god are meant, suṭ, and also elision of t. When kara and pati follow tat and bṛhat respectively, Hari causes to wander, Hari causes to wander, and a thief or a god is meant, the augment suṭ comes in and the final t is elided. So for tat karaḥ, taskaraḥ, a thief; for bṛhat patiḥ, bṛhaspatiḥ, surabu.

kupvoḥ ẖka ḫpau ca: and before ku and pu, also ẖka and ḫpa. A visarga at the end of the preceding word, when ku, the first two letters of the ka class, or pu, the first two letters of the pa class, follow, optionally becomes respectively the ẖka sound before ka and kha, and the ḫpa sound before pa and pha; the ka and the pa are stated only for the sake of pronunciation. For kaḥ karoti, kaẖkaroti, or kaḥ karoti; for namaḥ khagarbhāya, namaẖkhagarbhāya, or namaḥ khagarbhāya; for kaḥ paṭhati, kaḫpaṭhati, or kaḥ paṭhati; for kaḥ phalati, kaḫphalati, or kaḥ phalayati, and so on.

sasajuṣo ruḥ: ru in place of s and of sajuṣ. A word-final s, and the ṣ of sajuṣ, What does he do? become ru. Homage to Ākāśagarbha. For ...as arcya, by this sūtra the s, What makes lightning? becomes ru.

ato ror aplutād aplute: of ru after a non-protracted a, before a non-protracted a. A ru that follows a non-protracted short a What splits the fruit? becomes u when a non-protracted short a follows. Ru becomes u; from a and u comes guṇa; guṇa. Then by the rule eṅaḥ padāntād ati, the a after a word-final e or o takes the form of the preceding, and so we get śivo 'rcaṃ.

haśi ca: and before haś. A ru after a short a also becomes u when a letter of the haś collection follows. For namaḥ buddhāya, namo buddhāya; for namaḥ dharmāya, namo dharmmāya, and so on.

bhobhagoaghoapūrvasya yo 'śi: when bho, bhago, agho or ā precedes, y before aś. Worship Śiva. A ru following bho, bhago, agho or ā becomes y when a letter of the aś collection follows. Homage to the Buddha. For devāḥ iha, by this sūtra the visarga becomes y, and since Śākalya allows its elision, it is optionally dropped: devā yiha, and so on.

vibhāṣā bhavadbhagavadaghavatām oc cāvasya: optionally for bhavat, bhagavat and aghavat, and o for ava. For these three, bhavat and the rest, in the sense of the vocative, the t optionally becomes ru; when it has been changed to ru, va with its vowel and the a, the gods here, become o, and so bhoḥ, bhagoḥ and aghoḥ are formed. For bhoḥ ehi, by the previous sūtra the visarga becomes y, and since Śākalya allows its elision, the y is dropped: bho ehi, "O, come here!"; or else bho yehi.

hali sarveṣām: before hal, according to all. The y that comes from ru after ā and o is elided in every case when a following word begins with a hal letter. For bhagoḥ namaste, the visarga turned y of bho, bhago and the rest is dropped by this sūtra: bhago namaste. Likewise for aghoḥ yāhi, agho yāhi; for devāḥ namaste, devā namaste, and so on.

ro 'supi: r before what is not a sup ending. The n of ahan becomes r when what follows is not a case ending of the sup set. Ahan, ahaḥ, ahar haḥ. Likewise, Homage to the fortunate one. For ahan gaṇaḥ, ahargaṇaḥ. Therefore destroy that sin, and so on. The commentary, Gods, homage to you, says that before rātri, rūpa and rathantara the n of ahan becomes ru; then by haśi ca the ru becomes u. Day, day. By sandhi, ahorātriḥ and ahorathantaraḥ. Also, A collection of days. The commentary says that the visarga of ahaḥ, gīḥ and dhūḥ optionally becomes r before pati, giving aharpatiḥ, gīrpatiḥ or gīpatiḥ, dhūrpatiḥ or dhūpatiḥ.

uṣaso ro budhe: r for uṣas before budha. Day and night. The form of the sun. The chariot of the day. When budha follows, the s of uṣas becomes r. For uṣas buddhaḥ, uṣarbuddhaḥ.

ro ri: of r before r. An r is elided when an r follows. Lord of the day. Lord of speech. Lord of speech. Lord of the earth, that is, a king. For punar ramate, by this sūtra the r is deleted.

ḍhralope pūrvasya dīrgho 'ṇaḥ: when ḍha or ra is elided, lengthening of the preceding aṇ. The vowel before the deleted letter ḍha or ra, Clear from the first, meaning a blazing fire, if it is a short vowel of the aṇ collection, becomes long. By this sūtra it is lengthened; by this sūtra it is changed to a long vowel: punā ramate. Hari. For hariḥ ramyaḥ, by sasajuṣo ruḥ and so on it becomes ru; before r the r is apt to be deleted, and once it is deleted the sūtra lengthens the vowel: harī ramyaḥ, Hari is lovely, and so on.

vipratiṣedhe paraṃ kāryam: in a conflict, the operation of the later rule. A conflict is when two sūtras, Again he plays, both apply. Then the later sūtra's operation has the greater force. For example, by the rule iko yaṇ aci, "ik becomes yaṇ before ac," a change to yaṇ would apply whatever ac follows; yet the operation of the later sūtra, akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ, "ak becomes long before a similar vowel," is the one that applies.

etattadoḥ sulopo 'kor anañsamāse hali: elision of su for etad and tad, when they lack k and are not in a compound with the negative, before hal. For etad and tad, when they are not in a compound with the negative particle and do not have the letter k, the su of the nominative singular is elided before a following word beginning with a hal letter. For eṣaḥ viṣṇuḥ, eṣa viṣṇuḥ; for saḥ hariḥ, sa hariḥ, and so on.

so 'ci lope cet pādapūraṇam: elision of saḥ before ac, if it fills out the line of verse. The visarga of saḥ, the form of tad with su added, is elided before an ac. Although as a general rule no sandhi is made after such an elision, when this completes a line of verse, This is Viṣṇu, this is Hari, sandhi is made. For saḥ eṣa, by this sūtra the visarga is deleted and sandhi is then made again, giving saiṣa. The example verse given in the commentary is:

saiṣa dāśarathī rāmaḥ,
seṣa rājā yudhiṣṭhiraḥ,
saiṣa karṇo mahātyāgī,
saiṣa bhīmo mahābalaḥ.

In Tibetan this is:
This is that Rāma, son of Daśaratha;
this is that king, Yudhiṣṭhira.

This is that Karṇa, the greatly generous;
this is that Bhīma, whose strength is great.

So it is in this verse, where saiṣa occurs at the beginning of the lines.

iti pāṇinivyākaraṇasyasandheḥ sūdrāha pañcasandhayaḥ samābhāḥ: thus, from the sūtras on sandhi of the Pāṇinivyākaraṇa, the five sandhis are complete.

With these, from the work called The Chariot That Draws the Jewel of Excellent Explanation, notes setting out the meaning, the procedures, the examples and so on of the root text and commentary of the great grammatical treatise, the Pāṇinivyākaraṇa, the coarse points of the five sandhis, together with their general rules and exceptions, are for now complete.

Homage to the guru and to the noble Lokeśvara (Avalokiteśvara).

Having thus explained the procedures of sandhi, I shall now explain the chapters on su and the other endings, by which words are formed from nouns.

arthavad adhātur apratyayaḥ prātipadikam: what is not a root, has no suffix, and has meaning is a noun stem. Not a root: that is, something formed, with its changes, by adding a kṛt or other suffix to a root. What has no case-ending suffix of the su set or the ti set, and has meaning, is called a mark, or a name, or a word, or a prātipadika; it is the base to which su and the rest are applied.

pratyayaḥ paraś ca: a suffix, and it comes after. The suffixes sup and the rest are to be added after the noun. The su set is this: su au jas; am auṭ śas; ṭā bhyām bhyas; ṅasi bhyam bhyas; ṅas os ām; ṅi os sup. Of these case endings, the u of the singular of the first, the j of jas, the plural; the ṭ of the dual of the second, the ś of its plural; the ṭ of the singular of the third; the ṅ of the fourth, fifth, sixth and seventh; the i of ṅasi in the fifth; and that of the plural of the seventh, are, each with its purpose, called it.

vibhaktiś ca: and they are case endings. The su set explained above and the ti set that comes below are called case endings. Of these twenty-one, su and the rest: su au jas, the first, express the mere meaning of the noun; am auṭ śas, the second, the object; ṭā bhyām bhis, the third, the agent; ṅe bhyām bhyas, the fourth, that for the sake of which something is done; ṅasi bhyām bhyas, the fifth, the source; ṅas os ām, the sixth, relation; and ṅi os sup, the seventh, the location. Among them, for example, the singular of the first is su, the dual au, and the plural jas; and so all of them stand in threes, singular, dual and plural.

supaḥ: sup. By saying sup, a designation by abbreviation is made: by joining su, the singular of the first, with the final letter of the plural of the seventh, all twenty-one case endings, the seven times three from su to p, are understood.

dvyekayor dvivacanaikavacane: for two and one, the dual and the singular. To eka, the word for one, only the singular of the case endings applies, and to dvi, the word for two, only the dual.

bahuṣu bahuvacanam: for many, the plural. To a word for many, such as bahu, only the plural applies.

I shall now teach the procedures for joining stems with case endings. The stem is of three kinds: masculine, feminine and neuter. Each of these three is found either ending in a vowel or ending in a consonant. First, among the vowel-final masculine stems that end in a short a, the stem or noun rāma will serve as the example.

To rāma, su is added. Its u is an it and is deleted. By the sūtra sasajuṣo ruḥ and so on, the s becomes ru, and by the sūtra kharavasānayor and so on, the r becomes visarga: rāmaḥ.

To rāma, the dual. prathamayoḥ pūrvasavarṇaḥ: before the first two, a long vowel similar to the preceding. When, after a noun ending in a letter of the ak collection, there come endings of the first or second case beginning with a vowel, the preceding vowel at the end of the stem would become long and similar to it. So here too the a would be expected to be lengthened. But there is an exception to this: nādici: not after a before ic. Although a belongs to ak, when ic follows a stem-final a, it does not become long and similar to the preceding, so the a is not lengthened. Then, by vṛddhir eci, since vṛddhi is due before ec, the two together are replaced by a single vṛddhi: rāmau.

To rāma, the plural jas. cuṭū: cu and ṭu. The cu, that is the ca class, and the ṭu, that is the ṭa class, at the beginning of a suffix are called it, so the j is deleted. na vibhaktau tusmāḥ: not tu, s and m in a case ending. The ta class in a case ending, the s as in śas, and the m as in am, are not called it. Rāma and. By prathamayoḥ pūrvasavarṇaḥ the vowel is lengthened; by sasajuṣo ruḥ and so on the s becomes r; and by kharavasānayor and so on it becomes visarga: rāmāḥ.

ekavacane saṃbuddhiḥ: in the singular, saṃbuddhi. The singular of the first case, when used in the sense of address, is given the name saṃbuddhi. To rāma, su in the sense of address. eṅhrasvāt saṃbuddheḥ: after a short vowel or eṅ, the saṃbuddhi. Rāmas. After stems ending in a short vowel or in a letter of the eṅ collection, the following saṃbuddhi is to be elided. Once the saṃbuddhi is deleted, he is placed before it as the sign of a vocative ending: he rāma. The dual and plural are formed as with the first case above: he rāmau, he rāmāḥ.

To rāma, the singular of the second case, am. ami pūrvaḥ: before am, the preceding. If the stem-final is a letter of the ak collection, the a of am, O Rāma, takes the form of the preceding: rāmam. The dual, O two Rāmas, O Rāmas, is formed like the dual of the first case: rāmau.

To rāma, the plural śas. laśakv ataddhite: l, ś and ku, when not in a taddhita. In a case ending that is not a taddhita suffix, and in root formation, the kṛt suffixes and the rest, To Rāma, a letter l, a letter ś or a ku, that is the ka class, standing at the beginning of a suffix, Rāma, Rāma, is called it, so the ś is deleted. By prathamayoḥ pūrvasavarṇaḥ the a is lengthened. tasmāc chaso naḥ puṃsi: after that, n for the s of śas in the masculine. In the masculine, the s of śas after a stem on which the lengthening to a similar vowel has been done becomes n. When the s is changed to n: rāmān.

raṣābhyāṃ no ṇaḥ samānapade: after r and ṣ, ṇ for n in the same word. Within the same word, that is in one and the same word, an n that follows r or ṣ becomes ṇ.

aṭkupvāṅnumvyavāye 'pi: even when aṭ, ku, pu, āṅ or num intervene. To the Rāmas. An n that follows a letter r or ṣ on the near side becomes ṇ even when letters of the aṭ collection, the ka class, the pa class, the preverb āṅ or the augment num stand in between. So, although by the general rule it would become ṇ, there is again an exception to this: na padāntasya: not of a word-final. Even when all the conditions stated above are present, a vowelless n at the end of a word does not become ṇ, and so it remains n.

To rāma, the singular of the third case, ṭā, is added. yasmāt pratyayavidhis tadādi pratyaye 'ṅgam: that after which a suffix is prescribed, together with what begins with it, is the aṅga before that suffix. The base of a suffix, that is, what precedes it, the stem, is given the technical name aṅga because the procedures of the following suffix take place on it.

ṭāṅasiṅasām inātsyāḥ: ina, āt and sya for ṭā, ṅasi and ṅas. After a stem ending in a, designated aṅga, the singular of the third case, ṭā, becomes ina; the singular of the fifth, ṅasi, becomes āt; and the singular of the sixth, ṅas, becomes sya. So ṭā becomes ina; by ād guṇaḥ the vowels become e; and by the sūtra on r and ṣ, n becomes ṇ: rāmeṇa.

To rāma, the bhyām of the third case. supi ca: and before sup. After a stem ending in short a and called aṅga, when a case ending of the sup set beginning with a letter of the yañ collection comes, the final of the stem becomes long: rāmābhyām.

To rāma, the bhis of the third case. ato bhisa ais: ais for bhis after a. A Rāma. After a stem ending in short a and called aṅga, the plural of the third case, bhis, is changed into ais. By vṛddhi before ec, and by sasajuṣo ruḥ and so on: rāmaiḥ.

To rāma, the ṅe of the fourth case. By the two Rāmas. ṅer yaḥ: ya for ṅe. After a stem ending in short a and called aṅga, a following ṅe becomes ya. Once ṅe is changed to ya, by supi ca the vowel is lengthened: rāmāya.

To rāma, the bhyām of the fourth case. By supi ca: rāmābhyām.

To rāma, By the Rāmas, the plural of the fourth case, bhyas. bahuvacane jhaly et: e before jhal in the plural. After a stem ending in short a and called aṅga, whenever a plural case ending beginning with a letter of the jhal collection comes, the stem, For Rāma, changes its final into the letter e, For the two Rāmas: rāmebhyaḥ. The meaning of what is said, "et", is that the letter t marks a vowel of that same length.

To rāma, the ṅasi of the fifth case. By ṭāṅasiṅasām inātsyāḥ, ṅasi becomes āt, and by akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ and so on: rāmāt. To rāma, the bhyām and bhyas of the fifth case, For the Rāmas, are formed as for the fourth case above: rāmābhyām, From the two Rāmas, rāmebhyaḥ, From the Rāmas.

To rāma, the ṅas of the sixth case. By the sūtra ṭāṅasi and so on: rāmasya, Of Rāma.

To rāma, the dual os. From Rāma. osi ca: and before os. When the case ending os follows, the stem called aṅga becomes e. Then come the sūtras eco 'yavāyāvaḥ and sasajuṣo ruḥ and the rest.

To rāma, the ām of the sixth case. hrasvanadyāpo nuṭ: nuṭ after a short vowel, a nadī, or āp. After stems ending in a short vowel, after those called nadī, that is, the feminine endings ī and ū, and after āp, that is, feminine stems ending in long ā, the augment nuṭ is given to the plural of the sixth case, ām. Of the two Rāmas. The ṭ has the purpose it has in ṭit and the like, and the u is there to be pronounced. So: rāma nām. nāmi: before nām. Before nām, whatever vowel ends the stem becomes long. After the stem-final has been lengthened, by the sūtra aṭkupvāṅ and so on, nā becomes ṇā: rāmāṇām.

To rāma, the ṅi of the seventh case. Since ṅ is called it, it is deleted; by ād guṇaḥ: rāme. To rāma, the os of the seventh case: formed as for the sixth case, rāmayoḥ.

To rāma, the plural of the seventh case, sup. Since the p is there for the abbreviation, it is deleted. Of the Rāmas. By bahuvacane jhaly et: rāmesu. ādeśapratyayayoḥ: of a substitute and of a suffix. In Rāma. When on the near side there is a letter of the iṇ collection or of the ka class, In the two Rāmas, a following s that is a substitute, like one already changed into s, or that belongs to a suffix, and is not at the end of a word, becomes ṣ: rāmeṣu. If it is at the end of a word, it does not change. For example, in hari statra, although i, a letter of the iṇ collection, is seen on the near side, the following s does not become ṣ but remains s.

Having thus explained, among the vowel-final masculine stems, the general procedures for those ending in short a, Rāmas, I shall now explain, among those ending in short a, In that Hari, the procedures for the exceptions, sarva and the rest.

sarvādīni sarvanāmāni: sarva and the rest are called sarvanāman. Sarva and the rest are these: sarva, all; viśva, various; ubha, both; ubhaya; ḍatara; ḍatama; itara, one's own or another; anya, other; anyatara, one or the other of two; tvat, you; tva, oneself; nema, law; sama, equal; sima, a portion of ground or a domain; pūrva, par; avara; dakṣiṇa; uttara; apara; adhara; sva; antara; tyad; tad; yad; etad; idam; adas; eka; dvi; yuṣmad; asmad; bhavat; and kim, what. Ḍatara and ḍatama, though not nouns, East, or seven, or before; beyond; other; south; north; another; low, and lip; heaven; interval; that; which; that; this; this; one; two; you; I; being. any noun to which either of those two suffixes is attached is also to be understood as called sarvanāman. These can take all the procedures of the three genders.

To sarva, the su and au of the first case are formed as for rāma, the general short-a stem above: sarvaḥ, sarvau. To sarva, jas. jasaḥ śī: śī for jas. For the stem sarva, ending in short a, the plural of the first case, jas, becomes śī. Since ś is called it, it is deleted, and by the sūtra ād guṇaḥ: sarve. The endings of the second case are as for rāma above: sarvam, sarvau, sarvān. Those of the third case are likewise as above: sarveṇa, sarvābhyām, sarvaiḥ.

To sarva, the ṅe of the fourth case. sarvanāmnaḥ smai: smai after a sarvanāman. For a stem ending in short a and called sarvanāman, that is sarva and the rest, the ṅe of the fourth case becomes smai: sarvasmai. To sarva, the dual and plural of the fourth case are as for rāma above: sarvābhyām.

To sarva, the ṅasi of the fifth case. ṅasiṅyoḥ smātsminau: smāt and smin for ṅasi and ṅi.

For sarva and the rest, the singular of the fifth case, ṅasi, becomes smāt, and the singular of the seventh case, ṅi, becomes smin: sarvasmāt, sarvābhyām, sarvebhyaḥ. To sarva, the ṅas and os of the sixth case are as for rāma above: sarvasya, sarvayoḥ.

To sarva, the plural of the sixth case, ām. āmi sarvanāmnaḥ suṭ: suṭ after a sarvanāman before ām. For sarva and the rest, ending in short a, the augment suṭ enters before ām, the plural of the sixth case: sarvasām. Then by the sūtras "in the plural" and ādeśapratyayayoḥ and so on: sarveṣām.

To sarva, ṅi. By the sūtra "of ṅasi and ṅi": sarvasmin. The dual and plural are like the general rule: sarvayoḥ, sarveṣu.

For those with the sense of address in general: he sarva, he sarvau, he sarve. As in this, the same procedure is to be carried out for viśva and the others called sarvanāman.

Among those called sarvanāman, ubha does not take the seven singulars, su and the rest, nor the seven plurals, jas and the rest; it takes only the seven duals. So in the first case, ubhau; in the second, ubhau; in the third, ubhābhyām; in the fourth, ubhābhyām; in the fifth, ubhābhyām; in the sixth, ubhayoḥ; in the seventh, ubhayoḥ. These are formed with the duals of the case endings alone.

Among those called sarvanāman, for pūrva and the rest, the singular and dual of the first case are as above: pūrvaḥ, pūrvau. With the plural jas there is an option. To pūrva, jas. pūrvaparāvaradakṣiṇottarāparādharāṇi vyavasthāyām asaṃjñāyām: pūrva, para, avara, dakṣiṇa, uttara, apara and adhara, when they denote a fixed relation and are not names. Among the sarva group, pūrva and the rest, that is, from pūrva to adhara, when they denote a fixed relation and are not names, are formed by the procedure of sarvanāman; when they are names, they are formed like rāma, the general short-a stem: pūrve, pūrvāḥ.

Likewise jas with the word sva. svam ajñātidhanākhyāyām: sva, when it does not mean kinsman or wealth. When sva, in the sarva group, is used for kinsmen or wealth, it is not called sarvanāman: jas does not become śī as in the procedure for sarva and the rest, and it is formed solely by the procedure of the general short-a stems: svāḥ, jñātayaḥ.

Jas with antara. antaraṃ bahiryogopasaṃvyānayoḥ: antara, in the senses of connection with the outside and of an undergarment. When the word antara, called sarvanāman, is used in the sense of connection with the outside or of a garment worn, the operations of sarvanāman do not apply and it is formed by the procedure of rāma alone: antarāḥ. And, heaven. When it does not mean the outside or a garment worn, it is formed as one called sarvanāman: antare.

pūrvādibhyo navabhyo vā: optionally after the nine, pūrva and the rest. After the nine, pūrva and the rest, the singular of the fifth case, ṅasi, and the singular of the seventh case, ṅi, are optional: either the procedure of rāma, the general short-a stem, or the procedure of sarvanāman applies. So in the fifth case, pūrvāt or pūrvasmāt; in the seventh, pūrve or pūrvasmin. Likewise parāt or parasmāt in the fifth, and pare or parasmin in the seventh. In this way the same reasoning extends to all of them, from pūrva to antara.

When those called sarvanāman are joined with a preverb, or are names, or when sama has the sense of equal, sva the sense of wealth or kinsman, or antara the sense of outside, they are not called sarvanāman: the procedures of sarvanāman do not apply, and one proceeds as explained for the general short-a stems. For example, in atisarvāḥ, sarva with the preverb ati, jas does not become śī, and the form is made like rāma.

na bahuvrīhau: not in a bahuvrīhi. When sarva and the rest stand in a bahuvrīhi compound, the procedures of sarvanāman do not apply either. For example, to priyasarva, Exceedingly all, ṅe is added; it does not become smai but is changed to ya: priyasarvāya.

tṛtīyāsamāse: in a third-case compound. A third-case compound is a kind of tatpuruṣa compound; whether the third-case ending has been removed by the compounding or, in some instances, not removed, it is the same: for stems called sarvanāman, the sarva operation does not apply, and the procedure for the general short-a stems, For the sake of all joy, is used. For example: māsapūrvāya, māsena pūrvāya.

dvandve ca: and in a dvandva. Even when a stem ending in a and called sarvanāman stands in a dvandva compound, the operations of sarvanāman do not apply, and it is formed by the general procedure. For example, pūrvāparāvarāṇām, Of east, beyond, and other, where suṭ does not enter and nuṭ does. Earlier by an equal.

vibhāṣā jasi: an option with jas. For a sarvanāman standing in a dvandva compound, there is a choice in the first-case jas between the operation of those called sarvanāman and the procedure of the general short-a stems: both the change into śī and the procedure of akaḥ savarṇe apply. For example: varṇāśrametare, varṇāśrametarāḥ.

prathamacaramatayālpārdhakatipayanemāś ca: and prathama, carama, taya, alpa, ardha, katipaya and nema. For prathama and the rest as well, there is a choice: the plural of the first case, jas, both becomes śī as with sarva and the rest and takes the akaḥ savarṇe procedure as with the general short-a stems: prathame, prathamāḥ. First, or at the start; few; half; how many; law. With the suffix tīya added: dvitīye, dvitīye, dvitīyāḥ. For prathama and the rest, all the remaining case endings other than jas are as for rāma.

Cited in the commentary: tīyasya ṅitsu vā sarvanāmatā vācyā. The firsts. Before endings marked with ṅ, it should be stated that what has tīya is optionally sarvanāman. With the suffix tīya, The seconds, before those called ṅit there is a choice between the sarva operation and the rāma operation, so both apply. For the fourth-case ṅe: dvitīyasmai, dvitīyāya; in the fifth: dvitīyasmāt, dvitīyāt; in the seventh: dvitīyasmin, dvitīye. The rest are like rāma.

jarāyā jaras anyatarasyām: jaras optionally for jarā. For the word jarā, before case endings beginning with a vowel, that is, those that do not begin with a hal, a consonant, it is changed into jaras.

With su: nirjaraḥ. Before a vowel it is changed into jaras: nirjarasau, nirjarasaḥ. In the second case: nirjarasam, nirjarasau, nirjarasaḥ.

To nirjara, the ṭā of the third case. Here the commentary quotes from another source: kecid ādāv enātāv ādeśāv icchanti. Old. "Some wish that at first Not old. ena and āt be substituted From every side." Since this is said, the stem nirjara becomes jaras, jaras and jarasna, and three forms arise: nirjarasā, nirjarasena and nirjarasenena. From ṭā onward, every case ending is divided into three forms; and, as the root text itself explains, before endings beginning with a vowel it is changed into jaras, while before those beginning with a hal it remains jarā, and this is optional. The same reasoning extends to all such forms as nirjarase, nirjarasāya and nirjarasenāya.

padannomāshṛnniśasanpūṣandoṣanyakañchakannudannāsañchasprabhṛtiṣu: before śas and the rest, pad, dat, nas, mās, hṛd, niś, asan, pūṣan, doṣan, yakan, śakan, udan and āsan. For pāda and the rest, the three endings of the first case and the singular and dual of the second are as for rāma, the general short-a stem above. Beginning from śas, the plural of the second case, up to sup, the plural of the seventh, whatever case endings come, pāda becomes pad, danta becomes dat, nāsikā becomes nas, māsa becomes mās, hṛdaya becomes hṛd, niśā becomes niś, asṛj becomes asan, pūṣa becomes pūṣan, doṣa becomes doṣan, yakṛt becomes yakan, śakṛt becomes śakan, udaka becomes udan, and āsya becomes āsan. Foot. Bad. Water. Nose. Equal, or similar. And Heart. Not seen. Lineage. Not going. Not given. Pure. Also before the suffix of. Night. Causes to obtain. So: pad ya. Able. Some. Bada ya. Water. Changed into pad, drawn. Seat. Padaḥ is formed. Forming the rest in the same way: padā, padbhyaḥ, padbhiḥ; dataḥ, datā, dadbhyām; nasaḥ, nasā, nobhyām; māsaḥ, māsā, mābhyām; hṛdaḥ, hṛdā, hṛdbhyām; niśaḥ, niśā, niḍbhyām; asnaḥ, asnā, asabhyām; pūṣṇaḥ, pūṣṇā, pūṣabhyām; doṣṇaḥ, doṣṇā, doṣabhyām; yaknaḥ, yaknā, yakabhyām; śaknaḥ, śaknā, śakabhyām; udnaḥ, udnā, udabhyām; āsnā, āsabhyām. The same reasoning extends to all of these. Where they are not changed into hṛd and the rest, they are like rāma.

suḍ anapuṃsakasya: suṭ, of what is not neuter. The five from su, the singular of the first case, to auṭ, the dual of the second, for what is not neuter, that is, for masculine stems and the like, are given the technical name suṭ, as an abbreviation, or the name sarvanāmasthāna, "standing for all," for the sake of a purpose.

svādiṣv asarvanāmasthāne: before su and the rest that are not sarvanāmasthāna. Of the twenty-one, su and the rest, as explained above, the five from su of the first case to auṭ, the dual of the second, are called sarvanāmasthāna, and those beyond the five, from śas up to sup, are given the name non-sarvanāmasthāna, by force of a purpose. The purpose is this: because the preceding noun undergoes modification before śas and the rest that are not sarvanāmasthāna, it is given the name pada. This will come below as appropriate.

yaci bham: bha before y and a vowel. Before the suffix ya, and before the case endings among śas and the rest, which are not sarvanāmasthāna, that begin with a vowel, the preceding noun or stem is given the name bha for the sake of a purpose.

allopo 'naḥ: elision of the a of an. After a stem called bha, such as pūṣan, when a non-sarvanāmasthāna ending beginning with a vowel, such as śas, follows, the a before the vowelless n at the end of the stem is elided. To pūṣan, śas: the a is deleted, and by the sūtra raṣābhyām and so on, n becomes ṇ: pūṣṇaḥ.

To pūṣan, bhyām. nalopaḥ prātipadikāntasya: elision of n at the end of a noun stem. A vowelless n at the end of a noun is elided before case endings beginning with a hal. The n is deleted: pūṣabhyām.

To pūṣan, the ṅi of the seventh case is added. vibhāṣā ṅiśyoḥ: an option before ṅi and śī. Before ṅi of the seventh case and before śī, that is, the au of neuter stems changed into śī, the a standing before the vowelless n at the end of the stem may optionally be elided or not elided: pūṣṇi, pūṣaṇi.

saṃkhyāvisāyapūrvasyāhnasyāhan anyatarasyāṃ ṅau: for ahna preceded by a numeral, by vi or by sāya, ahan optionally before ṅi. The word ahna, when preceded by numerals, by the preverb vi, or by sāya, the word for evening, optionally becomes ahan before ṅi, the singular of the seventh case. With a numeral first: when ṅi is added to dvi ahna: dvyahne, Two days, dvyahani, dvyahni, Two days. With vi placed first: vyahne, vyahani, vyahni. With sāya placed first: sāyāhne, sāyāhani, sāyāhni. Of the three forms that arise in each case, the last ones are formed by "elision of the a of an."

These, then, are the masculine stems ending in short a.
