iti pāṇinibyākarṇasya sūtrāta strīyidga halantāḥ smāpatāḥ That is: the feminine stems ending in consonants, from the sūtras of the Pāṇinivyākaraṇa, are complete.

Thus, from The Chariot That Draws the Jewel of Excellent Explanation, which sets down as notes the meaning, the procedures, the examples and so forth of the root text and commentary of the great treatise on grammar, the Pāṇinivyākaraṇa, the feminine stems ending in consonants, with the general rules and special exceptions of their combination on meeting the case endings, have for now been completed in their broad outlines.

Now I shall explain the neuter stems ending in consonants. Ending in h: for svanaḍuh, su. By caturanaḍuhor ām udāttaḥ, "for catur and anaḍuh, ām, which is udātta": the augment ām. By svamor napuṃsakāt, su and am are elided after a neuter. By vasusraṃsudhvaṃsvanaḍuhāṃ daḥ, "d for vasu, sraṃs, dhvaṃs and anaḍuh": h becomes d. By vāvasāne, optionally at a pause: svanaḍvāt, svanaḍvād. For au: by napuṃsakāc ca, "and after a neuter," au becomes śī: svanaḍuhī. For jas: by jaśśasoḥ śiḥ, "śi for jas and śas": jas, here meaning "having a good ox," becomes śi. By napuṃsakasya jhalacaḥ, num for a neuter ending in jhal or a vowel; and by the rule "when not the vocative," the penultimate is lengthened: svanaḍvāṃhi. For the second case: svanaḍvāt, svanaḍvād, svanaḍuhī, svanaḍvāṃhi. The vocatives are like the first case. From ṭā on, all the remaining case endings are like those explained for the masculine anaḍuh.

Ending in r: for vār, su. By the elision of su and am after a neuter: vāḥ. For au: vārī. For jas: vāri. For the second case too: vāḥ, vārī, vāri. For the vocatives: he vāḥ, he vārī, he vāri. For ṭā: vārā. For bhyām and bhis: vārbhyām, vārbhiḥ. For the fourth case: vāre, vārbhyām, vārbhyaḥ. For the fifth case: vāraḥ, vārbhyām, vārbhyaḥ. For the sixth case: vāraḥ, vāroḥ, vārām. For the seventh case: vāri, vāroḥ, vārṣu.

Ending in r: for catur, jas. By caturanaḍuhor ām udāttaḥ, the augment ām; by jaśśasoḥ śiḥ, śi: catvāri. For śas: catvāri. For bhis: caturbhiḥ. For the two bhyas: caturbhyaḥ. For ām: caturṇām. For sup: caturṣu. For the vocative: he catvāri. Where it does not have the meaning of a number, as in priyacatur, all the case endings occur. For the first case: priyacatuḥ, priyacaturī, priyacaturi. For the second case too: priyacatuḥ, priyacaturī, priyacaturi. For the third case: priyacaturā, priyacaturbhyām, priyacaturbhiḥ. For the fourth case: priyacature, priyacaturbhyām, priyacaturbhyaḥ. For ṅasi: priyacaturaḥ. Bhyām and bhyas are the same. For the sixth case: priyacaturaḥ, priyacaturoḥ, priyacaturām. For the seventh case: priyacaturi, priyacaturoḥ, priyacaturṣu. The vocatives are like the first case.

Ending in m: for kim, su. Since su and am are elided after a neuter, su is dropped: kim. For au: kim becomes ka; au becomes ī: ke. For jas: kāni. For the second case too: kim, ke, kāni. For ṭā and the remaining endings, kim becomes ka, and all its procedures are like those of sarva.

Ending in m: for idam, su. Su and am are elided after a neuter: idam. For au: ime. For jas: imāni. For the second case: idam, ime, imāni. Ṭā and the remaining case endings are like the masculine.

Ending in n: for brahman, su. By nalopaḥ prātipadikāntasya, elision of n at the end of a nominal stem: n is dropped. Su and am are elided after a neuter: brahma. For au: brahmaṇī. For jas: brahmāṇi. For the second case too: brahma, brahmaṇī, brahmāṇi. For ṭā: brahmaṇā. For bhyām and bhis: the n at the end of the stem is dropped: brahmabhyām, brahmabhiḥ. For ṅe: brahmaṇe. Bhyām and bhyas are the same. For ṅasi, the word meaning Brahmā: brahmaṇaḥ. Bhyām and bhyas are the same. For the sixth case: brahmaṇaḥ, brahmaṇoḥ, brahmaṇām. For the seventh case: brahmaṇoḥ, brahmasu. For the vocative, since the commentary says that the elision and non-elision of n are optional: he brahma, he brahman, he brahmaṇī, he brahmāṇi.

Ending in n: for ahan, su. By ahan, r for ahan: the n of ahan, as a neuter stem, becomes r before the letters gathered in jhal and at the end of a word; su is elided: ahaḥ. For au: by vibhāṣā ṅiśyoḥ, optionally before ṅi and śī: ahanī, ahnī. For jas: ahāni. The second case is the same. Ahan means day. For ṭā: by allopo 'naḥ, elision of the a of an, the a of the penultimate is dropped: ahnā. For bhyām and bhis: ahobhyām, ahobhiḥ. For ṅe: ahne. Bhyām and bhyas are the same. For ṅasi: ahnaḥ. Bhyām and bhyas are the same. For the sixth case: ahnaḥ, ahnoḥ, ahnām. For ṅi: ahni, ahani. For os: ahnoḥ. For sup: ahaḥsu. The vocatives are like the first case.

Ending in n: for sudaṇḍin, meaning one with a fine staff, su. The n at the end of the stem is dropped; su and am are elided after a neuter: sudaṇḍi. For au: sudaṇḍinī. For jas: by jaśśasoḥ śiḥ, śi. By inhanpūṣāryamṇāṃ śau, "before śi, for stems in in and han, and for pūṣan and aryaman": the penultimate of these, those ending in in and the rest, is lengthened before the śi that replaces jas and śas: sudaṇḍīni. The second case is the same. For ṭā: sudaṇḍinā. For bhyām and bhis: the n at the end of the stem is dropped: sudaṇḍibhyām, sudaṇḍibhiḥ. For ṅe: sudaṇḍine. Bhyām and bhyas are the same. For ṅasi: sudaṇḍinaḥ. Bhyām and bhyas are the same. For the sixth case: sudaṇḍinaḥ, sudaṇḍinoḥ, sudaṇḍinām. For ṅi: sudaṇḍini. For os: sudaṇḍinoḥ. For sup: sudaṇḍiṣu. The vocatives are like the first case.

Ending in n: for bahuvṛtrahan, su. Su and am are elided after a neuter; the n at the end of the stem is dropped: bahuvṛtraha. For au: bahuvṛtrahaṇī. For jas: by inhan and the rest, the penultimate is lengthened: bahuvṛtrahāṇi. The second case is the same. Ṭā and the rest are like those explained for the masculine vṛtrahan.

Ending in n: for bahvaryaman, su. The n at the end of the stem is dropped; su and am are elided after a neuter: bahvaryama. For au: bahvaryamaṇī. For jas: by inhan and the rest, the penultimate is lengthened: bahvaryamāṇi. The second case too is like the first, in both its forms and its derivation. For ṭā: by allopo 'naḥ, the a of the penultimate is dropped: bahvaryamṇā. For bhyām and bhis: the n at the end of the stem is dropped: bahvaryamabhyām, bahvaryamabhiḥ. For ṅe: bahvaryamṇe. Bhyām and bhyas are the same. For ṅasi: bahvaryamṇaḥ. Bhyām and bhyas are the same. For the sixth case: bahvaryamṇaḥ, bahvaryamṇoḥ, and bahvaryamasu. The vocatives are like the first case.

Ending in n: for bahupūṣan, su. The n at the end of the stem is dropped; su and am are elided: bahupūṣa. For au: bahupūṣaṇī. For jas: by the rule inhan, the penultimate is lengthened: bahupūṣāṇi. The second case is the same. For ṭā: bahupūṣṇā. For bhyām and bhis: the n at the end of the stem is dropped: bahupūṣabhyām, bahupūṣabhiḥ. For ṅe: bahupūṣṇe. Bhyām and bhyas are the same. For ṅasi: bahupūṣṇaḥ. Bhyām and bhyas are the same. For the sixth case: bahupūṣṇaḥ, bahupūṣṇoḥ, bahupūṣṇām. For ṅi: bahupūṣṇi, bahupūṣaṇi. Os is the same. For sup: bahupūṣasu. The vocatives are like the first case.

Ending in j: for asṛj, su. Su and am are elided after a neuter. By the velar for kvin, j becomes g. By vāvasāne, optionally at a pause: asṛk, asṛg. For au: asṛjī. For jas: num: asṛñji. The second case is the same. For ṭā: asṛjā. For bhyām and bhis: the velar for kvin: asṛgbhyām, asṛgbhiḥ. For ṅe: asṛje. Bhyām and bhyas are the same. For ṅasi: asṛjaḥ. Bhyām and bhyas are the same. For the sixth case: asṛjaḥ, asṛjoḥ, asṛjām. For the seventh case: asṛji, asṛjoḥ, asṛkṣu. The vocatives are like the first case.

Ending in j: for ūrj, su. Su and am are elided after a neuter. The velar for kvin. The final of the consonant cluster is not elided. By vāvasāne, optionally at a pause: ūrk, ūrg. For au: ūrjī. For jas and śas, since the commentary explains that num is optional: ūrñji, or else ūrji. The second case is also like what has just been explained. For ṭā: ūrjā. For bhyām and bhis: the velar for kvin: ūrgbhyām, ūrgbhiḥ. For ṅe: ūrje. Bhyām and bhyas are the same. For ṅasi: ūrjaḥ. Bhyām and bhyas are the same. For the sixth case: ūrjaḥ, ūrjoḥ, ūrjām. For the seventh case: ūrji, ūrjoḥ, ūrkṣu. The vocatives are like the first case.

Ending in d: for tyad, su. Su and am are elided after a neuter. By vāvasāne, optionally at a pause: tyat, tyad. For au: au becomes śī. By tyadādi, d becomes a; by ato guṇe, the form of the preceding vowel; by ād guṇaḥ, guṇa after a: tye. For jas: śi; num: tyāni. The second case is also like what has just been explained. Ṭā and the remaining case endings are like the masculine sarva. Likewise tad, yad and etad are also like what has just been explained.

Ending in c: for goac, su. Su is dropped. The velar for a palatal. By vāvasāne, optionally at a pause: goak, goag. For au: by acaḥ, the a is dropped: gocī. For jas: goāñci. The second case is the same. Ṭā and the remaining case endings are like the masculine prāc.

Ending in t: for yakṛt, su. Su and am are elided. By vāvasāne, optionally at a pause: yakṛt, yakṛd. For au: yakṛtī. For jas: yakṛnti. The second case is the same. For ṭā: yakṛtā. For bhyām and bhis: yakṛdbhyām, yakṛdbhiḥ. For ṅe: yakṛte. Bhyām and bhyas are the same. For ṅasi: yakṛtaḥ. Bhyām and bhyas are the same. For the sixth case: yakṛtaḥ, yakṛtoḥ, yakṛtām. For the seventh case: yakṛti, yakṛtoḥ, yakṛtsu. The vocatives are like the first case. All the procedures of śakṛt are like those of yakṛt.

Ending in t: for dadat, su. Su and am are elided. By vāvasāne, optionally at a pause: dadat, dadad. For au: dadatī. For jas: by jaśśasoḥ śiḥ, jas and śas become śi. By vā napuṃsakasya, "optionally for a neuter": for a reduplicated stem ending in the suffix śatṛ, in the neuter, wherever jas and śas become śi, all of which count as strong endings, the augment num is applied optionally: dadanti, dadati. The second case is the same. For ṭā: dadatā. For bhyām and bhis: by jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi, jaś for jhal before jhaś: dadadbhyām, dadadbhiḥ. For ṅe: dadate. Bhyām and bhyas are the same. For ṅasi: dadataḥ. Bhyām and bhyas are the same. For the sixth case: dadataḥ, dadatoḥ, dadatām. For the seventh case: dadati, dadatoḥ, dadatsu. The vocatives are like the first case. Jāgrat, jakṣat and the rest are also like what has just been explained.

Ending in t: for tudat, su. Su and am are dropped. By vāvasāne, optionally at a pause: tudat, tudad. For au: au becomes śī. By āc chīnadyor num, "num before śī and nadī after a": after a root ending in a with the suffix śatṛ, before the śī that replaces au and before what is named nadī, num is applied optionally: tudantī, tudatī. For jas: tudanti. The second case is the same. Ṭā and the rest are like dadat. Bhāt too is like tudat in every respect.

Ending in t: for pacat, su. Su and am are dropped. By vāvasāne and the rest: pacat, pacad. For au: au becomes śī. By śapśyanor nityam, "necessarily after śap and śyan": after a stem ending in long or short a with the suffix śap or śyan, before the śī that replaces au and before what is named nadī, num is given necessarily, never optionally: pacantī. For jas: pacanti. The second case is the same. Ṭā and the rest are like dadat. Dīvyat too is like pacat in all its procedures.

Ending in p: for svap, su. Su and am are dropped. By vāvasāne and the rest: svap, svab. For au: svapī. For jas: svāmpi. The second case is the same. For ṭā: svapā. For bhyām and bhis: by apo bhi, t for the p of ap before bh: svadbhyām, svadbhiḥ. For ṅe: svape. Bhyām and bhyas are the same. For ṅasi: svapaḥ. Bhyām and bhyas are the same. For the sixth case: svapaḥ, svapoḥ, svapām. For the seventh case: svapi, svapoḥ, svapsu. The vocatives are like the first case.

Ending in s: for dhanus, su. Su and am are dropped. By sasajuṣo ruḥ and the rest: dhanuḥ. For au: by the rule for replacements and suffixes, s becomes ṣ: dhanuṣī. For jas: dhanūṃṣi. The second case is the same. For ṭā: dhanuṣā. For bhyām and bhis: by sasajuṣo ruḥ and the rest, s becomes r: dhanurbhyām, dhanurbhiḥ. For ṅe: dhanuṣe. Bhyām and bhyas are the same. Dhanus means a bow. For ṅasi: dhanuṣaḥ. Bhyām and bhyas are the same. For the sixth case: dhanuṣaḥ, dhanuṣoḥ, dhanuṣām. For the seventh case: dhanuṣi, dhanuṣoḥ, dhanuḥṣu. The vocatives are like the first case. Haviṣ, payas and the like are also like dhanus.

Ending in s: for adas, su. Su and am are dropped after a neuter. By sasajuṣo ruḥ, ru: adaḥ. For au: by tyadādi, a; by ād guṇaḥ, guṇa after a: ade. By adaso 'ser dād u do maḥ, u after the d of adas, and m for d as well: amū. For jas: amūni. The second case too is like the first. From ṭā on, all the procedures of the remaining case endings are like those explained for the masculine adas.

iti pāṇinibyāgaraṇasya sūtrādnapuṃsakayiṅga halantāḥ smāpyāḥ That is: the neuter stems ending in consonants, from the sūtras of the Pāṇinivyākaraṇa, are complete.

Thus, from The Chariot That Draws the Jewel of Excellent Explanation, which sets down as notes the meaning, the examples, the procedures and so forth of the root text and commentary of the great treatise on grammar, the Pāṇinivyākaraṇa, the neuter stems ending in consonants, with the general rules and special exceptions of their combination on meeting the case endings, have for now been completed in their broad outlines.

Having thus explained the procedures for forming the six kinds of stems into words, I shall now set out the nipātas, the indeclinable groups, in which a single word shows many meanings. Svarādinipātam avyayam: "svar and the rest, and the nipātas, are indeclinable." Svar and the rest, and the nipātas, are called avyaya, that is, indeclinable.

Svar and the rest are these: svar, antar, prātar, punar, sanutar, uccais, nīcais, śanais, ṛdhak, ṛte, yugapat, both, ārāt, pṛthak, hyas, śvas, divā, rātrau, sāyam, ciram, manāk, īṣat, joṣam, tūṣṇīm, bahis, outside, avas, samayā; heaven; interval; morning or dawn; again; little or small; fainted; high or long; low; slowly; accomplished or holding; abandoned; applying to both the far and the near; separately; having gone; yesterday; the day after; by day; at night; in the evening; much; wisdom; small; joy; silent; in the senses of protecting and of ornament; near; nikaṣā, sva, svayam, vṛthā, naktam, nañ, hetau, iddhā, addhā, sāmi.

Vatpratyayāntaṃ ca: "and what ends in the suffix vat." Stems, whether roots or nominal stems, that end in the suffix vat are also indeclinable: those ending in the suffix vat, such as brāhmaṇavat and kṣatriyavat. And further: sana; near; I, or oneself; false; night; a word of negation; kinsman; unmixed; unmixed; equal or alike; upadhā, sanat, sanāt, tiras, antarā, antareṇa, jyok, kam, śam; happiness or well-being; like a brahmin, or having brahmins; like a kṣatriya, or having them; sahasā, vinā, nānā, svasti; true, or certainly; svadhā, alam, vaṣaṭ, anyat, asti, upāṃśu, kṣamā, dihā; near, or not far; earlier, former, or formerly; flying; between, or interval; clear, and a tiny creature; heaven; like or similar to a brahmin; yasā, doṭā; night; mṛṣā; false; mithyā; together with; abandoned; various; well-being; the sense of the mother; ornament, or full; mantra; other; existing; long; patience; flying in the sky; mudhā; joy; purā; before, or east; connected; mitho, mithas, prāyas, muhus, pravāhukam, āryahalam, abhīkṣṇam; splendor; sākam, sārdham, saha, namas, hiruk, dhik, and the like are also indeclinable.

Tasilādayas taddhitā edhācparyantāḥ: "and the taddhita suffixes from tasil up to edhāc." Those ending in any of the given taddhita suffixes from tasil up to edhāc: in accord; many; again, or also; descending; learned, or teacher; in accord, or companion; together with; mind; multicolored; bad; these are also indeclinable. Those ending in the taddhita suffixes kṛtvasuc, śas, tasi, and cvi and the rest are also indeclinable. Further: atha, ām, pratām, prasān, pratān, mā and māṅ; these belong to svar and the rest.

Ca, vā, ha, aha, eva; this, what, certainty; evam, nūnam, śaśvat, kupat, kuvit, net, cet, caṇ, kaccit, atra; where; neha, hanta, mākim, yāvat, tā; then, auspiciousness; sudden, and illness; not knowing; good; increase; a word of negation; thinking; bat, tvai, dvai, śrai, vauṣaṭ, svāhā; and also; certainty, like "or"; of a word; spoken to fill out a line; thus; certain; fitting; fool; bad; abandoned; exists; fear; in between or at an interval; bondage and suffering; nothing at all; tuma; in water; tvathāhi, lalu, kila, tathā, smā, smi, a, i, u, ṛ, ḷ, e, ai; for its cause; suchness; straight; glory; mantra; settled on its base; the single vowels o, au and so on; āva; a word of negation; the four, a, mā, no and nā; uta, ūñ, ogas, ādat, ātaṅka, velāyām, yathā, kim; what; from; its time, certainty; speech, or a verbal ornament, or certainty; its; existing; yat, yi, hā, hai, he, hyāṭ, yāt, aho, nanu, manye, nahi, utāho, asi, brūhi, natu; boundary, or "thus"; aiti, īva, au, phaṭ, yadi; gives; a knock; house; ash; beggar; time; at what time; ho, ihi, iha, namas; bowing; aho; little, or little; svat, upari; above; which; in which; question; "kye," a word of address; obtained; wonder; a former time; thinking; not; a doubter; exists, and sword; speaking; not; āvām; self; who; thus; at what time; kam; happiness, or heaven; śuka; shame; anukam; following, heaven; exists; this; this; nahikam, satyam, ṛtam, no cet, na cet, jāta, katham, kutaḥ, kutra, śakaṭam, adya, diṣṭyā, paśu, ānuṣak, bhajaka, aṅga, ḍāka, phraan, are, caṭu; flattering advice; cāṭu, hām, kum, mum, khum, lum, ve, bhūyam, aniśam, suṣṭhu, kāmam, purutaḥ, āśu, tarhi, rahas; no heaven; truth; truth; nonexistence, or a word of negation; idly; what, or which; from what; to what; chariot; today; star; animal; pit; a precious thing, or a vessel; body, or form; a word of address to one lesser than oneself, such as "khor"; savadi; calling; a mind of two points; certain; again and again; continually, or always; supreme; desire; now; swiftly; to that; a solitary place; uri, ūrari. These too are indeclinable.

Taddhitaś cāsarvavibhaktiḥ: "and a taddhita after which not all case endings occur." Those with a taddhita suffix after which the case endings do not occur, and which remain in their own nature, are also indeclinable. For example, with a taddhita suffix in the sense of the fifth case, meaning one taken from among many, and with tas and tra attached in the sense of the seventh case: tataḥ, yataḥ, tatra, yatra.

Kṛn mejantaḥ: "a kṛt ending in m or in ec." Stems with a kṛt suffix that end in m, and those ending in the letters gathered in the abbreviation ec, are also indeclinable. For example, smāram, ending in m, and jīvase and pibadhyai, ending in ec. From that, to that, from which, to that, to which: such words too are indeclinable.

Ktvātosunkasunaḥ: "ktvā, tosun and kasun." Words ending in the suffixes ktvā, tosun and kasun are also indeclinable.

For example, ending in the suffix ktvā: kṛtvā, glossed "having remembered"; ending in tosun, glossed "drinking": udeto; ending in the suffix kasun: bisṛpaḥ.

abyayātsupaḥ: "From an indeclinable, sup." After the members of the class of indeclinables, sup, that is, all the case endings beginning with su, are elided. As the commentary says: sadṛśaṃ tṛṣuliṅgeṣu sarbāsu ca bibhaktiṣu bac neṣu ca sarbeṣu yanna byeti tadabya yaṃ In Tibetan, with the gloss "not moving apart," this is: Alike and the same in the three genders, And likewise in all the cases, And likewise in all the numbers: That which does not vary is the indeclinable.

Thus in this class of indeclinables there is not the slightest difference in the endings that mark the distinction of masculine, feminine and neuter; since one and the same form is applied to all, and it changes from nothing into anything else, it is called "the unexhausted" (avyaya). Or again, since a single word expresses various meanings, its meaning is never exhausted, and for that reason too it is called "the unexhausted."

The commentary also says that the ancient sage Bhāguri holds that the a of the two preverbs aba and api is elided, and that ṭāp is given to the three niśa, bācā and diśa.

iti pāṇinibyākaraṇasyatrādabyayāḥsmābyāḥ: thus, from the sūtra of the Pāṇinivyākaraṇa, the indeclinables are complete.

With these, the sections giving a rough presentation of the class of indeclinables, from The Chariot That Draws the Jewel of Excellent Explanation, notes setting out the meaning, the examples, the procedures and so on of the root text and commentary of the great treatise on grammar, the Pāṇinivyākaraṇa, are for now complete.

Now, since one who wishes to identify the three genders wants to know the distinctions of each gender, I shall explain how the feminine suffixes, that is, the suffixes that form the feminine, apply.

ajādyataṣḍāp: "After aja and the rest, and after a, ṭāp." After aja and the rest, and after stems ending in a, the suffix ṭāp that forms the feminine is given. To aja is added ṭāp; the final consonant is deleted as appropriate, by "cuṭū" and the rest the ṭ is deleted, and by the rule that similar vowels of ak become long, the long vowel results as appropriate: ajā. Formed in the same way are eḍakā, a ewe or dam; aśvā, a mare; caṭakā, a hen sparrow; mūikā, a female mouse; bālā, a girl of sixteen; toṭī, a powerful woman; bākā, a measured one; batsā, a heifer calf; mangā, a woman who walks slowly; bila tā, a shameless woman; meṅghā, an intelligent woman; kokilā, a female cuckoo; sarbā, all; and so on. And although they do not end in a, in keeping with Bhāguri's view that ṭāp applies to the three bāc, niśa and diśa, attaching ṭāp gives bācā, speech; niśā, night; diśva, a direction; and so on. Also, the commentary quotes from elsewhere halaṃtādvā, "Or optionally after a stem ending in a consonant"; and because this appears, it is explained that sometimes ṭāp applies not only to stems ending in a but also to stems ending in a consonant.

śūdrāccāmahatpurbājjatiḥ: after the stem śūdrā, when it expresses a caste and is not preceded by mahata, the equivalent of "great," ṭāp applies: śūdrā, a woman of the common caste.

saṃbhajinśaṇapiṇḍebhyaḥplvata: "After saṃ, bhastra, ajina, śaṇa and piṇḍa, from phala." To phala preceded by saṃ, bhastra, ajin, śaṇa or piṇḍa, the feminine suffix ṭāp applies: saṃbalā, she whose fruit is true; bhastraphalā, she whose fruit is the bellows; ajinaphalā, she whose fruit is the hide; śaṇaphalā, she whose fruit is hemp; paṇḍaphala, she whose fruit is the lump. Since the commentary says that sometimes it also occurs when eka precedes, there is ekaphalā, one-fruited. Quoting from elsewhere, the commentary says that ṭāp also applies to buṣpa preceded by sata, prākāṃḍa, prāta, śata or eka; so there are satputpā, she of excellent flowers; prākāṃḍapuṣpā; prāṃtapuṣpā; śatapuṣpā, she of a hundred flowers; and ekapuṣpā, she of one flower. Also, since the commentary says that ṭāp applies to jyeṣṭha, kaniṣṭha and madhyama, and to mūlā preceded by the negative na, there are jyeṣṭhā, the eldest woman; kaniṣṭhā, the youngest woman; madhyamā, the middle one; and amūlā, she who is rootless.

In keeping with what was said above, "After stems in ṛ and n, ṅīp," ṅīp is added; the final consonant is deleted as appropriate; the markers la, śa and ku are removed, and the ṅ is deleted. This gives karttrī, a woman who acts; daṇḍinī, a woman with a staff; rājāvi, a queen; śunī, a bitch; maghonī and maghapatī, the consort of Śakra (Indra); and so on.

ugitaśca: "Also after what has uk as its marker." After stems whose final has as its marker any of the letters gathered in the abbreviation uk, the suffix ṅīp that forms the feminine also applies: biduṣī, a learned woman; śrāmatī, a glorious woman; bhabatī, a fortunate woman; pacantī, a woman who cooks; dibyantī, a woman at play; tudantī, a woman who is ill; bhuntī, a beautiful woman; patyicī and pratyaṃcī, a woman of the west; tirścī, a female animal; and udīcī, a woman of the north.

banoraca: "From van, also r." For a stem ending in n that has va as its penultimate letter, not only does ṅīp apply, but the n also becomes r: to dhiban is added ṅīp, giving dhibarī, an intelligent woman; likewise haridṛśvarī.

The commentary quotes: banonahaśa, "Not for van after haś." Although it was explained above that for stems ending in van ṅīp occurs and the n itself changes, the exception to that is this: if that v is stacked with any of the letters gathered in the abbreviation haś, ṅīp does not apply and the n does not become r. For example, in such words as rājayudhān and sahayudhān, ṅīp does not apply.

Quoting from elsewhere, the commentary gives bahubrīhaubā, "Optionally in a bahuvrīhi." At the end of a compound of the bahuvrīhi type, giving ṅīp and changing n into r is optional: bahuṅhibarī, many intelligent women; or else, without giving ṅīp and forming it as explained above in the section on stems ending in a consonant, bahudhibā.

bādonyatarasyāṃ: "Optionally after pād." After bāda, ṅīp is optional, that is, whether or not it is given is a matter of choice: dībadī, or else bādabata and so on.

ṭābrici: "In the Veda, ṭāp." If pad has the sense of the Veda, the feminine suffix ṭāp applies: dvipadā, she who is two-footed.

manaḥ: "From man." The feminine suffix ṅīp does not apply to stems ending in n that have mā as their penultimate letter. For example, to simna ṅīp does not apply; with su, formed as in the section on stems ending in a consonant above, it becomes simā.

anobahubṝhe: "From an, in a bahuvrīhi." At the end of a bahuvrīhi compound, ṅīp does not apply to a stem ending in an. Since it was explained above that ṅīp is optional at the end of a bahuvrīhi compound, this is the exception to it.

For example, to bahuyajvana ṅīp does not apply; formed as for stems ending in a consonant above, it gives bahuyajvā. It is said, however, that this sūtra applies only to yajvana and not to others.

ḍābuḍhābhyāmanyatarasthaṃ: "For the two, optionally ḍāp." To the two stems bahuyajva and siman at the end of a bahuvrīhi compound, the feminine suffix ḍāp optionally applies. With ḍāp, the final consonant is treated as appropriate, the p is deleted, the ṭi is deleted as appropriate, and the ḍ that stands for the marker is deleted: simā, bahuyajā. Or else, as explained above, bahurājñī.

pratyayasthātkātpūrbasyātaidābyasubaḥ: "Of the a before a k that stands in a suffix, i, before an āp that is not from sup." The a, that is, the letter a, before the k of a suffix that has been given a k, becomes i, that is, the letter i, when there follows the feminine suffix āp, provided it is not the āp that is the abbreviation gathering the case endings of sup from nā up to the plural of the seventh case. For example, to sarbaka and kāraka is added ṭāp, and a becomes i: sarbikā, all; gārikā, māmikā and narikā. If it is not a, it does not become i: naukā, a boatwoman. And the commentary says that even where it is a, in bahuparibrājakā it does not become i.

tyaktyayośca: "Also of tyak and tyap." The taddhita suffixes tyak and tyap also become i when āp follows. For example: dākṣiṇātyikā, glossed "a human female, that is, a woman," ihatyikā and kvatyṛkā.

nayāsyoḥ: "Not of ya and sa." Even when it precedes k, the a of ya and sa, that is, of the two yad and tad, does not become i. For example, they remain yakā and sakā and do not become yikā and sikā.

The commentary says, "Not of tyakana," so the ending of the taddhita suffix tyakan does not become i; for example, adhityakā and upatyakā remain just as they are.

The commentary also quotes, "Not of vun in a benediction." When the suffix vun has the sense of a benediction, a does not become i, as in jībakā, "may she live," and bhabakā: this follows the change of vun into ākā. It does not change in respect of the later member of a word, as in debadattikā, a woman named Devadatta, and yajñikā, a woman named Yajñadatta. The commentary also says, "Not after kṣipakā and the rest"; accordingly, in kṣipkā, she who casts off; caṭakā, a hen sparrow; dhrubakā, she who is firm; and tārkā, she who rescues, a also does not become i. In parṇakā, if it has the sense of thread, a thread's colour, a becomes i, and if it has another sense, it changes. As for parttakā, the commentary says that the eastern paṇḍitas hold that it remains just so, while the northern paṇḍitas hold that a becomes i, as in bartikā, glossed "a coloured one" and "a torma." In aṣṭakā, if it has the sense of the gods and the ancestors, a does not become i, while in another sense a becomes i, giving aṣṭikā, a girl of eight years.

The commentary also quotes from elsewhere, "Optional for sūtakā and the rest." Hence sūtakā, the name for a woman more than ten days after she has given birth, and sūtekā; putikā, a daughter; brindārkā, a gathering of many women, or bṛndārikā; she is also called a woman of a ravaged land.

udīcāmātasanelakapūrbāyāḥ: "Of the northerners, in the place of ā, where ya or ka precedes." The northern paṇḍitas hold that, when there follows an āp with the letter ya or the letter ka in the place where ā was deleted, the change of a into i is optional, either happening or not: āryyakā and āryyikā, a noble woman; caṭakakā and caṭakikā, a hen sparrow. The commentary also says, "ākāśyakā and the rest always become i"; hence sāṃkāśyikā, a woman of Kāśī; aśīkā, a wild woman; śubhayikā, a beautiful woman; sunayikā, a very beautiful woman; supākikā, a woman who cooks well. For these the option does not apply.

bhastrai ṣājājñādvāsvānañapūrbāṇāmapi: "Of bhastra, eṣa, aja, jña, dva and sva, optionally, even when nañ precedes." For those words, bhastrā and the rest, whether nañ precedes them or not, the change of a into i is optional, either happening or not: bhastrakā, bhastrikā; eṣakā, eṣikā; ajakā, ajikā; jñakā, jñikā, she who knows; dvakā, dvikā, the two; sakā, sikā; abhastrikā, bhastrikā; and so on. The commentary also says that among these, eṣakā preceded by nañ does not become i, so it remains just aneṣakā. The commentary further notes that when a preverb precedes bhastrakā, becoming i or not is also optional: nirbhastrakā, nirbhastrikā.

abhāṣitapuṃskācca: "Also optionally for what is not stated as masculine." For those not stated earlier in the section on the masculine gender, the change of a into i is likewise to be treated as optional: gagakā, gaṃgikā; agaṃgakā; baramagagakā, parmagaṃgikā. For those stated in the section on the masculine gender, only the change of a into i is made, and the option is not taken, as in śubhrikā.

bahubrīhautunityaṃ: "But in a bahuvrīhi, necessarily." For a stem just explained in the earlier section on the masculine gender that forms a bahuvrīhi compound, the option is not taken, and only the change of a into i is made, as in akhaṭrikā.

ādācāryyāṇāṃ: "Of ā, in the view of the teachers." Some earlier teachers also hold that the long finals of stems not stated in the earlier section on the masculine gender are changed into short ones when a k with ṭāp follows. For example, gaṃgākā becomes gaṃgakā.

ṭiḍhyaṇañadvayasajadaghnañmātracatayapaṭhakaṭhañakañakārapabūnāṃ: "Of ṭi, ḍhi, aṇ, añ, dvayasaj, daghnañ, mātrac, tayap, ṭhak, ṭhañ, kañ, kvarap and khyun." At the end of suffixes that have ṭ as marker, those that have ḍh as marker, aṇ, and the rest of these, the suffix ṅīp that expresses the feminine also applies. For example, at the end of a suffix with ṭ as marker: kurucarī, she who moves about in the land of the Kurus, and nadī, she who has a current, that is, a river, and so on. With ḍh as marker: sauparṇeyī. With aṇ: andrī. With añ: autsāṃdṛ. With dvayasaj: urudvayasī. With daghnañ: urudagni. With mātrac: urumātrī. With tayap: pañcatāyī. With ṭhak: vakṣikī. With ṭhañ: lāvaṇikī. With kañ: yādṛśī. With kvarap: itvarī. With khūn: ādyaṃ karaṇī, glossed "an eye," and so on.

Also, since the commentary says that, as an exception to aṇ, ṅīp does not apply to pahukurucara and daṇḍa but ṭāp does, we get such forms as bahukurucarā and daṇḍā.

nañasnañi kaktaruṇatalunānāṃca: "Also of nañ, snañ, īkak, taruṇa and taluna." To the suffixes nañ, snañ and īkak, and to the stems taruṇa and the rest, ṅīp also applies. For example, with nañ: staiṇī. With snañ: pauṃsnī. With īkak: yāṣṭīkī, a woman bearing a staff, and śaktīkī. Then taruṇī, taluni, and so on.

prācāṃṣgatadrhitaḥśar: "For the easterners, ṣpha, a taddhita." After a stem ending in yañ, the teachers of eastern India apply ṣka, a suffix that forms the feminine, and they give it the technical designation taddhita, that is, a noun of the "derived" type. To gārgya is added ṣka.

ṣaḥpratyayasya: "The ṣ of a suffix." The letter ṣ at the beginning of a suffix such as ṣka bears the name "marker"; so ṣ is deleted. By the rule "In the original teaching, a vowel that is nasalized is a marker," the a is deleted; the final consonant is treated as appropriate, and the k is deleted: gārgya.

yañaścaḥ: "Also from yañ." After a stem ending in the suffix yañ, the suffix ṅīp that forms the feminine also applies. To gārgya is added ṅīp, and by the rule "also before ī," the a at the end of the stem is deleted.

halastaddhitvasya: "Of a taddhita after a consonant." The y of a taddhita suffix that follows a consonant is to be elided; so y is deleted: gargī.

āyaneyīnīyiyāḥphḍhalachagāṃ: "Of pha, ḍha, kha, cha and gha: āyan, eyan, īn, īya and iya." Each pha of a taddhita suffix becomes āyana, each ḍha becomes eya, each kha becomes īn, each cha becomes īya, and each gha becomes iya. To gārgya is added phañ, glossed "the wife of the sage Gārga"; pha is changed into āyana: gārgāyaṇa.

ṣidgaurādibhyaśca: "Also after what has ṣ as marker, and after gaura and the rest." To suffixes that have ṣ as marker, and to gaura and the rest, the suffix ṅīṣ that expresses the feminine applies. Since gārgyuyaṇa is a member of the group of gaura and the rest, ṅīṣ is added; the final consonant is treated as appropriate; ṣ is deleted; by "la, śa, ku" the ṅ is deleted; and by "also before ī," the a at the end of the stem is deleted: gārgyāyaṇī; nartakī, a dancing woman; gaurī, a fair woman.

bayasiprathame: "In the first stage of life." The first stage of life means the age up to ten years. To stems ending in the letter a whose sense expresses that age, ṅīṣ also applies: kumārī, a maiden; kiśvarī. Since the commentary says that ṅīṣ applies not only up to ten years but also to the bloom of youth that is not yet old age, there is ciraṭī. If she is old, ṅīp does not occur but ṭāp applies, so bṛddhā, an old woman. If the stem does not end in a, it does not change even for the first stage of life; for example, ṅīṣ does not apply to śiśu, a young girl. Even when the stem ends in a, ṅīṣ does not apply to kanyā but ṭāp does: kanyā, a maiden.

dvigoḥ: "After a dvigu." To stems ending in a that form a dvigu compound, one of the kinds of compound, the suffix ṅīp that expresses the feminine applies: pañcamūlī, she of five roots. Although it is a dvigu, ṅīp does not apply to triphala, but ṭāp does: triphalā, she of three fruits.

aparimāṇabistācitakambalyebhyonataddhitaluki: "Not after what is not a measure, nor after bista, ācita and kambalya, when the taddhita is elided." For bista and the rest of these, where the taddhita suffix has been elided by the dvigu compound, and for words that are not terms of measure, ṅīp does not apply; ṭāp applies: bañcaśva, five mares; dvibarṣā, two years old; dvibistā, of two spans; dvyacitā, of two ācitas; dvikambalyā, of two blankets. If it is a measure, ṅīp applies: dvyāḍaki, of two measures.

kāṇḍāṃtātakṣetre: "After what ends in kāṇḍa, for a field." When kāṇḍa is preceded by a numeral and has the sense of expressing a field, and the taddhita suffix has been elided, ṅīp does not apply: dvikāṇḍākṣetrabhaktiḥ. If it is not a field, ṅīp occurs: dvikāṇḍī rajjuḥ, a rope of two kāṇḍas.

rjuḥpuruṣātpramāṇenyatarasyāṃ: "After puruṣa, for a measure, optionally." When a taddhita after a numeral has been elided, ṅīp is optional after puruṣa in the sense of a measure: dvipura ṣīyaṣciḥ, a post two men high, or dvipuruṣā.

ūdhasonar: "Of ūdhas, anaṅ." The ṭi of ūṅhas, if it is not before a suffix expressing the feminine, does not become anaṅ. The ṭi is changed into anaṅ; the final consonant is treated as appropriate; the ṅ is deleted, and the a of n is treated as the sense requires: ūṅdhana.

bahubrīherūṅhasorīṣa: "After ūdhas in a bahuvrīhi, ṅīṣ." To ūṅhas ending a bahuvrīhi compound, the suffix ṅīṣ that expresses the feminine is added; the a of n is elided as appropriate, the a of the penultimate letter is deleted: pīnoṅhni, she whose udder is full of milk. If it is not before a suffix expressing the feminine, the ṭi does not become anaṅ.

dāmahrāyanāṃtāccha: "Also after dāman and hāyana." After dāman and hāyana preceded by a numeral, ṅīṣ occurs with respect to age: dīrāmni, dvihāyanī, two years old. Since the commentary also says that ṅīṣ occurs after hāyana with respect to age, and that if tri or catur precedes, n too becomes ṇ, there are trihāyaṇī, three years old, and catuḍhāyaṇī, a female four years old. If it does not concern age, ṅīṣ does not occur: trihāyanāśālva, a hall three years old.

andarbatpatirnuk: "After antarvat and pativat, nuk." To antarvat and pativat, when a suffix expressing the feminine follows, the augment nuk is added: antarbapmī, a pregnant woman; patibatnī, a woman who has a lord, that is, a wife.

tyārnoyajñasaṃyige: "Of pati, n, in connection with a sacrifice." From the word pati, when it means connected with a sacrifice, that is, possessed of a lord, the ṭi becomes n and ṅīṣ applies: patnī, she who has a lord.

bighāṣāsadūrbasya: "Optionally, with what precedes." For the word pati together with another noun preceding it, the change into n and ṅīṣ are optional: dṛbhapatnī or dṛbhapatiḥni.

ni hnyādiṣa: "Always in sapatnī and the rest." For the word pati following samāna and the rest, n and ṅīṣ always occur: sapātnī, ekapatnī, and so on.

būtakratorce: "Also ai, of pūtakratu." The word pūtakratu becomes ai, and ṅīṣ applies: pūtakātāyī, glossed "the lady of the teaching" and "the lord of the teaching."

bṛṣākādyagnikusitakusīdāmudāttaḥ: "Of vṛṣākapi, agni, kusita and kusīda, the udātta."

For vṛṣākapi and the rest of these, in the sense of "connected with a male," ṅīṣ occurs and the final also becomes ai; this is said to bear the name udātta. bāṛṣāḥ, glossed "the sacrifice of the pure"; kapāyī, a she-monkey like a jackal; agnāyī, the goddess of fire; kusitāyī, a wicked woman; kusīdāyī, a lazy woman.

manorauvā: "After manu, optionally au." After manu, in the sense of "connected with a male," ṅīṣ is optional; that is, the final becomes au, or else it becomes au: manāvī, a woman; manāyī, a woman; manuḥ, a man.

barṇādanudāttāttopadhāttonaḥ: "From a vowel that is anudātta, of the penultimate t, n." Where the final vowel is anudātta, that is, pronounced with a low pitch of voice, the letter t that is the penultimate of a short a becomes the letter n when ṅīṣ follows: enī, or else atā. If the final is not the letter a, then even if it is anudātta, the t does not become n, as in śitī.

The commentary quotes: "Also from paśaṃg." Since it says that the suffix ṅīṣ expressing the feminine also occurs for paśaṃg, there is piśaṃgṣi. The commentary also says that for asita and palita ṅīṣ does not apply and ṭāp occurs instead; hence aśitā and balitā, a white woman. Also, for those with the suffix kna ṅīṣ occurs: aśignī, balignī.

sūryatiṣyāgskyamatsyānāṃyaupabhāyāḥ: "Of sūrya, tiṣya, agastya and matsya, the y of the penultimate." For sūrya and the rest of these, ṅīṣ occurs and the y of the penultimate is elided: sdurī, the sun's; tiṣī; agastī, a very old woman; matsī, a female fish. Since the commentary says that the y of puṣya is also elided, there is buṣī, glossed with the Tibetan name of the lunar mansion Puṣya.

jānpadkuṇḍagoṇamṭhākabhājanāgalālanīlakuśakāmukakaḍarāṛddratyaṃnatrābaṃpanākṛttimāśrāṇāsṭhaulyabarṇānāchādanāyobaikāramaithunechākeśabeśeṣu: "From jānapada, kuṇḍa, goṇa, sthala, bhāja, nāga, kāla, nīla, kuśa, kāmuka and kabara, for a livelihood, a vessel, a load, the natural, a leaf, thickness, colour, what is not a covering, an iron thing, the desire for intercourse, and a hairdress." For those eleven, jānapada and the rest, ṅīṣ applies when they express, in order, the eleven senses beginning with livelihood: jānapadī, the livelihood of one's native land; kuṇḍī, a vessel; goṇī, an ox's load; sthālī, natural; bhājṣi, a leaf; nāgī, thick or rich; kālī, black; nīlī, blue; kuśī, an iron house; kāmukī, a woman desiring intercourse; kabarī, a topknot. For other senses ṭāp applies, so there are jānapadā and so on up to kabarā. The commentary quotes from elsewhere: "From nīla, optionally, for living beings and for herbs." Hence nīlībaḍabā, a blue mare, and nīmīoṣadhiḥ, a blue herb.

The commentary also says that the eastern paṇḍitas hold that ṅīṣ optionally applies to śoṇa; hence śoṇī and śoṇā.

uṅaṃtāṅguṇabacanāta: "From what ends in u and expresses a quality." For a stem ending in u that expresses a quality, ṅīṣ is optional: mridvī, mriduḥ, soft; paṭvī, paṭuḥ, skilled. If it does not end in u, then even though it expresses a quality, ṅīṣ does not occur: śruciḥsbī, a red woman. And even if it ends in u, ṅīṣ does not apply if it does not express a quality: ākhuḥ, a mouse. The commentary quotes: "If it is kharu, or there is a stacked penultimate, ṅīṣ does not occur." Hence kharuḥ and pāṇḍuḥ.

bahvādibhyaśca: "Also optionally from bahu and the rest." For bahu and the rest, whether ṅīṣ applies or not is optional: bahvī and bahuḥ, many; paddhatī and paddhatiḥ, a path.

itāḥ prātyāṃgāta: "From i, from a limb of a living being." For a stem ending in i that expresses a limb of the body of a living being, ṅīṣ is optional: aṃgulī, aṃguliḥ, a finger.

kṛdikārādaktinaḥ: "From a kṛt with the letter i, not from ktin." For kṛt and the other suffixes ending in i that are not ktin, ṅīṣ is optional: rājī, rājiḥ, ājiḥ. With ktin: buddhiḥ, matiḥ.

puṃyobādākhyāyāṃ: "For a name connected with a male." For a name connected with a male, ṅīṣ occurs: gopī, a herdswoman; anaḍuhī and anaḍvahī, a cow; matāmahī, a mother's mother; pitāmahī, a father's mother. Since the commentary says that ṅīṣ does not occur for gobālikā and the like, a woman who yokes oxen, there is gosālikā.

sūryāddebatāyāṃcāya: "From sūrya, for a deity, cāp." In connection with a male, that is, from sūrya when it expresses the wife of the sun, cāp occurs: the final consonant as appropriate, p is deleted; by "cuṭū" and the rest, c is deleted: sūryā. Or else, by "sūryatiṣya" and the rest, sūrī, a lady of the sun.

indrabaruṇabhabaśarbarudramṛḍahimārṇyayabayabanamātulṅacāryāṇāmānuka: "Of indra, varuṇa, bhava, śarva, rudra, mṛḍa, hima, araṇya, yava, yavana, mātula and ācārya, ānuk." For indra and the rest of these, in connection with a male, ṅīṣ occurs and the augment ānuk is also added: indāṇī, the consort of Indra; basudharandrāṇī, the Indra-consort who upholds wealth; baruṇāṇī, the lady of the waters; bhabānī, the lady of becoming; śarbāṇī, the lady who harms; rudvāṇī, the fierce lady; mṛḍānī, the lady of bliss; himānī, the lady of snow; araṇyānī, the lady of the wilds; yabānī, barley; yabanānī, the mixed; mātulānī, the wife of a maternal uncle; ācāryāṇī, the wife of a teacher. Since the commentary says that after brahma, ānuk and ṅīṣ are optional, there is brahmaṇī, the consort of Brahmā. Since the commentary explains that for the two, mātula and upādhyāya, it is optional, there are mātulānī and mātuli, the wife of a maternal uncle; and upābhyāyānī and upādhyāyi, a preceptress. Since the commentary says that for the two, ārya and kṣatriya, it is optional, there are āryāṇī, a lady or a noble woman, and āryā; kṣatriyāṇī, a woman of the kṣatriya caste, and kṣatriyā. Or else, when ṅīṣ occurs and ānuk is not given: āryī, kṣatriyī. For sūrya, too, ānuk may in some instances apply: sūryāṇī.

krītātkaraṇadūrbāta: "From krīta preceded by an instrument."

After krīta whose prior member is a word of instrument, ṅīṣ occurs: bastrakrītā. Since the commentary says that in some cases ṅīṣ does not occur with a prior member that is a word of instrument, there is dhanakrītā, a woman bought with wealth.

ktādavākhyāyāṃ: "From kta, in expressing smallness." After a stem ending in kta with a prior member of instrument, ṅīṣ occurs when smallness is expressed: abhrabilibhī, she who is not covered by clouds.

bahubrīheścāṃtodāttāta: "Also at the end of a bahuvrīhi, from what is udātta." After a stem ending in kta at the end of a bahuvrīhi compound that is udātta, ṅīṣ also occurs: ūrubhinnī. Since the commentary says that ṅīṣ does not occur after jāta, there is dantajātā, she whose teeth have grown.

pahunañasukālasukhādipārbāccani: "And not when bahu, nañ, su, kāla, sukha and the rest precede." Where bahu and the rest of these stand before it, ṅīṣ does not occur at the end either: bahukṛtā, she who does much; akṛtā, she who does not act; sukṛtā, she who does well; kālakṛtā, she who acts in time; sukhakṛtā, she who brings happiness; and so on.

Since the commentary says that after pāṇigṛhīta ṅīṣ occurs in the sense of a bride, there is pāṇagṛtītī, she who has been taken by the hand, that is, a bride; in other senses, pāṇigṛhītā, she who holds the hand.

asāṃgapārbabarādvā: "Optionally, from a prior member that is not one's own limb." After a stem ending in kta whose prior member is not a limb of one's own body, ṅīṣ is optional: surāpītā and surāpītā, a woman who drinks liquor.

svāgāccopasrjanādasaṃyogobadhāta: "Also from a limb of one's own, from a subordinate member, from what has no conjunct penultimate." After a word for a limb of one's own body with a prior member, where the penultimate is not a conjunct, that is, not stacked, ṅīṣ is optional: sumukhā and sumukhī, a woman with a beautiful face; atikeśā and atikeśī, a woman with fine hair. If the penultimate is a conjunct, ṅīṣ does not occur: suguvā, a woman with beautiful ankles. Since the commentary says that for aṅga, gātra and kaṇṭha ṅīṣ is optional, there are svaṃgī and svaṃgā, a woman of beautiful form; sugātrī and sugātrā, a woman of beautiful body; sukaṇṣī and sukaṇṭhā, a woman with a beautiful throat. Since the commentary also says that ṅīṣ does not apply to bahusveda and the rest, there are bahusedā, a woman from whose body much sweat drips; sujvānā, a woman of excellent wisdom; and susopā, a woman with a fine house. Since the commentary also says that ṅīṣ is optional for what is not a living being, there are sustanī and sustanā, a woman with beautiful breasts.

nāsikodarauṣṭhajighādantākartaśrāgācca: "Also from nāsika, udara, oṣṭha, jaṅgha, danta, karṇa and śṛṅga." For nāsika and the rest of these, ṅīṣ is optional: sunāsikī, a woman with a beautiful nose; sriṣodarī and pṛṣodarā, a woman with a full belly, or with a belly like a deer's; bimdaṣṣā and bambaṣṭhā, a woman with lips like the bimba fruit; sujighṅe and sujaṃghā, a woman with beautiful calves; sudantī and sudantā, a woman with beautiful teeth; sukarṇī and sukarṇā; suśṛṅgī and suśṛṅgā, a woman with beautiful horns. Since the commentary says that after supuccha ṅīṣ is optional, there are supucchī and supucchā, a woman with a beautiful tail. The commentary also says that after puccha preceded by kabara, maṇi, viṣa and śara, ṅīṣ always occurs and the option is not taken: kabara puccī, a slender tail; maṇipucchī, a jewelled tail; śarpucchā, a poisoned tail.

ubamānātpakṣapucchābhaṃ: "After a comparison, from pakṣa and puccha." After a comparison, ṅīṣ is optional for pakṣa and puccha: śyenapakṣī and śyenapakṣā, a woman like a hawk's feather; ulūkapucchī and ulūkapucchā, a woman like an owl's tail.

nakroḍādibahbṛcaḥ: "Not from kroḍa and the rest, nor from what has many vowels." After kroḍa and the rest, and after words with many vowels, ṅīṣ does not occur: sukroḍā, sujaghanā, bahbṛcā.

sahanañīdyamānapūrbāccha: "Also from what is preceded by saha, nañ and vidyamāna." When saha and the rest of these precede a word for one's own limb, ṅīṣ does not occur: sākeśā, a woman with hair; anāsikā, a woman without a nose; bidyamānodarā. Since the commentary says that after nakha and mukha ṅīṣ does not occur in a name, there are sūrbanakhā, and gauramukhā, she of the white face. If it is not a name: ṣāmanakhī, a woman with copper nails; cārumukhī, a woman with a lovely face.

bāhaḥ: "From vāha." After a stem ending in vāha, ṅīṣ also occurs: bhārohī, a woman who carries a load.

sakhyaśiśvībhāṣāyāṃ: "In speaking of sakhi and aśiśvi." With ṅīṣ attached to sakhi and aśiśvi, the two words sakhī, a woman friend, and aśiśvī, a barren woman, are the terms for expressing a woman.

jātirastībiṣayādayopadhāta: "From a word of class, not confined to females, with no y as penultimate." From a word common to a class whose penultimate is not the letter y and which is not confined to the female domain, ṅīṣ occurs: mṛgā, a doe; haṃsī, a goose; dhaṭī, a balance; kukkuṭī, a hen; sukarī, a sow. If it is not a word of class, ṅīṣ does not occur: muṃḍna. If it is confined to the female domain, ṅīṣ does not occur: balṅakā, a strong woman. If the letter y is the penultimate: kṣatriyā, a woman of the kṣatriya caste. Since the commentary says that even where the letter y is the penultimate, ṅīṣ occurs if it is not confined to that domain, there are gapayī, a female wild ass; hayī, a mare; mukāyī, a female frog; matsyī; manuṣṭā, a human female, that is, a woman.

pākakarṇaparṇapuṣpaphalamūlabālottarpadācca: "Also from pāka, karṇa, parṇa, puṣpa, phala, mūla and vāla as later members." For pāka and the rest as the later member of a word that expresses a class, ṅīṣ occurs: danapākī, śaṃkukarṇī, śālabarṇī, śaṃṣapuṣpī, dāsaphalī, darbhamūlā, gobālī.

itomanuṣyajāteḥ: "From i, for a human class." From a stem in i, that is, ending in the letter i, that expresses a human class, ṅīṣ occurs: ababtī, dākṣī, kuntī.

ūdutaḥ: "From u, ūṅ."

[Glosses on the preceding examples:] she who cooks rice; she with broad ears; she of the leaves; she of the conch flower; the round berry; she of the kuśa root; the young cow.

From a stem ending in the letter u, the suffix ūṅ, which expresses the feminine, occurs: kurūḥ, brahmabandūḥ, dhribanhūḥ. [Glosses:] she who guards the body; the daughter or bride of Brahmā; she who bears a lance.

Since the commentary states that ūṅ does not occur from a stem that has the letter y as its penultimate, we have aṅharyuḥ, glossed "a female sacrificer."

The commentary says that ūṅ occurs from words that do not denote living beings, and from those that do, except for rajju and the rest. [Glosses:] a woman of the land of the Kurus; a kinswoman of Brahmā; a kinswoman of the intellect. Therefore: alābūḥ, glossed "su nga"; yavāgūḥ, glossed "gruel." If it denotes a living being: dhenuḥ. For rajju and the rest: rajjuḥ, hanuḥ, tanūḥ.

The commentary cites: pigu śvaśru, "Also from paṅgu and śvaśru." From paṃgu and śvaśru as well, the suffix ūṅ expressing the feminine occurs: paṃgūḥ, śvaśruḥ. These words are formed to express the feminine.

ārāttarapadādaupamye, "From ūru as a later member, in the sense of comparison." [Glosses:] destroyer of desire; rope; jaw; body. If the word ūru is the later member, ūṅ occurs in expressing a feminine that carries the sense of comparison. [Glosses:] the ptarmigan hen; the mother-in-law. Thus karabhorūḥ. If it is not a comparison: vṛtoruḥ.

saṃhitaśaphalakṣaṇavāmādeśca, "Also from saṃhita, śapha, lakṣaṇa, vāma and the rest." When ūru is preceded by these, saṃhita and the rest, ūṅ occurs: saṃhitorūḥ, śaphorūḥ, lakṣaṇorūḥ, vāmorāḥ. [Glosses:] she with beautiful thighs; she whose thighs are like an elephant's trunk.

sahitasahābhyāṃca, "Also from sahita and saha." [Gloss:] she with even thighs. When ūru is preceded by sahita or saha, ūṅ also occurs: sahitorāḥ, sahorūḥ.

[Glosses:] she with thighs, that is, with very stout thighs; the hair of the thigh; she with perfect thighs, or with thighs bearing the marks. Since the commentary explains that ūṅ occurs optionally for tanu and the rest, we have tanūḥ and tanuḥ, cañcuḥ and cañcuḥ.

śārṅgaravādyaño ṅīn, "From śārṅgarava and the rest, and from aÑ, ṅīn." For śārṅgarava and the rest, and for stems ending in the suffix aÑ, the suffix ṅīn expressing the feminine occurs: śārṅgaravī, baidī.

nṛnarayorvṛddhiśca, "From nṛ and nara, and also strengthening." [Glosses:] form; water. From nṛ and nara the suffix ṅīn expressing the feminine occurs, and there is also strengthening (vṛddhi): nārī.

yaṅaścāp, "From yaṅ, cāp." After a stem ending in yaṅ, the suffix cāp expressing the feminine occurs. The c marks its kind, and its purpose is to exclude ṭāp. [Glosses:] she whose voice is like a wild animal's; she of the Veda. Thus kārīṣagandhyā, "she with the smell of urine"; kaumudagandhyā, "she with the fragrance of the kumuda lotus"; vārāhyā, "the sow." [Gloss:] woman. Since the commentary says, "Also for yañ following ṣa," we have pauñimāṣcā, glossed "she of pure earth and sky."

yūnastiḥ, "From yuvan, ti." From the word yuvan the suffix ti expressing the feminine occurs, and the n at the end of the stem is to be elided. With the n removed: yubtiḥ, glossed "the full-grown one."

iti bāṇinivyūkaraṇasya trāta striyo batsan pratyayās samābhāḥ. Thus, in the sūtra of Pāṇini's grammar, the suffixes expressing the feminine are complete.

From The Chariot That Draws the Jewel of Excellent Explanation, notes setting out the meaning, procedures, examples and so on of the root text and commentary of the great treatise on grammar, Pāṇini's Vyākaraṇa: the identification of the suffixes that express the feminine, their domains of application, and their procedures, the general rules together with the exceptions, are each complete.

Now I shall explain the chapter on the kārakas. This chapter shows in detail the domains in which the case endings explained above apply.

prātipadikāchāliṅgabarimāṇāmatre brathama, "For expressing merely the meaning of the nominal stem, its gender and measure, the first." To express merely the meaning of a noun that has the characteristic of being able to take any one of the three genders, the first case endings occur: uccaiḥ, nīcaiḥ, kṛṣṇaḥ, śrīḥ, jñānam, khārīḥ, droṇaḥ, āḍhakam, ekaḥ, dvau, bahavaḥ, yuṅ, aupagavaḥ, citraguḥ. [Glosses:] high; low; Kṛṣṇa; glory; wisdom; a load; a large measure; a great measure; one; two; many; joining; descendant of Upagu; one whose cows are dappled. In such cases it merely expresses the meaning of the noun.

saṃbodhane ca, "Also in address." In the sense of address too, the first case endings occur: he rāma, he rāmau, he rāmāḥ. [Glosses:] O Rāma; O two Rāmas; O Rāmas.

Having thus explained the general rule for how the first of the seven groups of case endings applies, the way the second applies is as follows.

karturībsitatamaṃ karma, "What the agent most desires." Whatever deed is desired by the agent as the thing to be done is given the technical name "object" (karman).

karmaṇi dvitīyā, "In the object, the second." For the object, that is, in the sense of indicating the deed to be done, the second case endings apply: kaṭaṃ karoti, "he makes a grass mat"; odanam pacati, "he cooks food"; grāmaṃ gacchana, "he goes to the village."

The commentary also says, bhāvakarmate, that is, the first case applies in expressions of the bare action and of the object: sebyate sebitaḥ; lakṣmyā sadā hariḥ; śatena krītaḥ śatyaḥ.

tathāyuktaṃ cānīpsitam, "Also what is so connected but not desired." Not only is the deed desired by the agent called the object; even when something is not what the agent desires and not an object in the strict sense, the second case also occurs for whatever deed is done. [Glosses:] the worshipped, who is worshipped; the powerful one always accompanies; bought for a hundred, worth a hundred. For example, in biṣaṃ bhuṃkte, "he eats poison," though the poison is neither what the agent desires nor an object in the strict sense, the second case occurs in piṣam.

akathitaṃ ca, "Also what is not stated." The name "object" is also applied to such things as the recipient in giving, and to whatever is otherwise left unstated.

[Gloss:] eats poison.

With the roots duha, "to milk"; yāca, "to beg"; rudhi, "to obstruct"; praci, "to ask"; ci, "to gather"; brū, "to speak plainly"; śāsu, "to commend"; and ji, "to conquer"; and with nī, "to bring"; hṛ, "to carry off"; kṛṣa, "to dig"; mantha, "to churn"; vaha, "to convey"; daṇḍa, "to fine"; graha, "to take"; muṣa, "to steal"; and paca, "to cook": the object words must be supplied two by two, and only the second case applies to them. The examples given in verse in the commentary are these:

yau dudoharbharamanniyayācabasudhāṃ palaṃ, dudodhadaityānpātālaṃ papracchandraṃ cabāṃchitaṃ. dharmānbācinodvedamabrabhṣittānsvasevinaḥ, gārthibānanāśadbhakriṃ trilokīmajayadribbuna. dvārakāmanayadvanbhūn ruknīṇīmaharadpuraṃ, cakarṣakaṃsaṃ bibinaṃ mamanthakṣīradhiṃ sudhaṃ.

He who milked the earth for food,
Begged the earth from mighty Bali,
Shut the asuras in the underworld,
Asked Indra too what he desired,
Gathered all the dharmas from the Vedas,
Spoke them as well to his attendants,
Commended worship to the lords of the earth,
Won the three worlds from his enemies,
Brought his kinsmen to Dvārakā,
Carried off the maiden to his city,
Dragged the asura into the forest,
Churned the ocean for the nectar;

abahanmandaraṃ siṃdhumadaṇḍayadarīnasūna,
Carried Mandara to the ocean,
Fined his enemies their wealth;

jagrāhadyutaruṃ śakramamuṣṇāddi tijānsudhāṃ,
Took the wish-fulfilling tree from Indra,
Stole the nectar from the asuras;

bacatiprāṇināṃ karmayaḥ phalitihiraṃ bhaje,
He who cooks the deeds of living beings into their fruit,
Him, Hari, I worship.

Thus in each quarter of the verse there occurs one of the roots mentioned above, ending in a verbal ending, together with two companion words each ending in the second case.

gatibuddhipradyabasānārthaśabhakarmakarmāṇāmaṇikartāsaṇau, "The agent, in the form without ṇi, of verbs meaning going, understanding and eating, of those whose object is sound, and of intransitives, in the form with ṇi." When the words for going and the rest are used, the second case occurs for the agent of the plain form, that is, without ṇic, not accompanied by ṇic; and when accompanied by ṇic, the second occurs in the sense of the object. The example given in verse in the commentary is:

śatrūnagamayatsvargambedārthaṃ sthanabedayat, āśayaccāmṛtaṃ depānabdemaṅghyāpayadviṅghiṃ, āsayatsalilepṛthbīṃ yasmeśrīharirgatiḥ.

Thus in each quarter joined with the senses mentioned above, a second case ending appears. The verse runs:

He sent his enemies to heaven,
Made his own understand the meaning of the Vedas,
Made the gods too eat the nectar,
Made Brahmā in ancient times recite the Vedas,
Set the earth upon the waters:
He who does this, Hari, is my glory.

The commentary says that with nī and vaha the second does not occur for the agent; it is the third. Hence nāyati bhāraṃ bhṛtyena, bāhayati bhāraṃ bhṛtyena. [Glosses:] he has the load led by the servant; he has the load carried by the servant.

The commentary also explains that for the stem joined with ādi and khādi as well, the second does not occur, only the third. So ṭā is added to the stem devadatta joined with those two: ādayati devadattenānnaṃ, khādayati devadattenānni.

The commentary also cites: "Not for bhakṣa when it does not mean harming." When the word bhakṣa is used not in the sense of harming, the second does not occur for the agent: bhakṣayatyannaṃ baṭunā. [Glosses:] he makes the student eat food; he makes him eat food for the nourishment of the body. If it means harming, the second occurs: bhakṣayati phalīvardatasasyaṃ, glossed "he makes the oxen eat the crops."

The commentary also says that some earlier masters hold that when śru, graha and dṛśa are used, the second occurs for the agent. Hence śrāvayati gītaṃ devadattaṃ, grāhayati baṭuṃ dedaṃ, darśavati bhaktaṃ debaṃ. [Glosses:] he makes Devadatta listen to a song; he makes the student take up the Veda; he makes the god see the offering.

The commentary also says that when aya, kranda, śabdāpa and hveña are used, the second does not occur, only the third. Hence ayayayati sainikairarīna, krandayati sainikairarīna, śabhāyayati sainikairarīna, hvāyayati śūrairarīna. [Glosses:] he makes the troops go against the enemies; he has the troops make the enemies weep; he has the troops make the enemies cry out; he has the heroes challenge the enemies.

hṛkroranyatarasyāṃ, "Optionally for hṛ and kṛ." For the agent where the words hṛña and kṛña are used, the second optionally occurs: hārayati bhāraṃ bhṛtyaṃ, hārayati bhāraṃ bhṛtyena; kārayati kaṭāṃ devadattaṃ, kāralati kaṭaṃ devadattena.

The commentary also says that when abhivādi and dṛśa are used, the second optionally occurs for the agent, in the domain where taṅ and ān are used. Hence abhivādayate kurūn baṭu, abhivādayate gurūn baṭunā; darśayate rājā bhṛtyaṃ, darśayate rājā ghṛtyena. [Glosses:] he makes the servant fly along; he makes Devadatta play; he makes the student speak respectfully to the teacher; the king makes the servant look.

adhiśīṅsthāāpa, "Also of śīṅ, sthā and āpa with adhi." Where śīda, sthā and āpa preceded by the preverb adhi are used, the second occurs in the sense of the seventh: adhiśete bekuṇṭhaṃ hariḥ, adhitiṣṭhati baikuṇṭhaṃ hariḥ, adbhyāste baikuṇṭhaṃ hariḥ.

abhiniviśaśca, "Also of viśa with abhi and ni." Where viśa preceded by the preverbs abhi and ni is used, the second also occurs in the sense of the seventh: abhiviśate sammārgaṃ, niviśate sammārgaṃ. [Glosses:] Hari lies in heaven; Hari dwells in heaven. The commentary says that even when ni and abhi precede, in some cases the second does not occur but only the seventh. Hence pāpe abhiniviśaḥ, "firmly entering into evil."

ubānvadhyāṅbasaḥ, "For basa with upa, anu, adhi and āṅ." [Glosses:] he fully enters the good path; he firmly enters the good path. Where basa preceded by the preverbs upa, anu, adhi and āṅ is used, the second occurs in the sense of the seventh, as in the examples from upabasati baikuṇṭhaṃ hariḥ through ābasati baikuṇṭhaṃ hariḥ.

The commentary says that even when basa is joined with upa and the rest as the prior member, if the place where one stays is a place without food and drink, the second does not occur in the sense of the seventh; it is the seventh itself. Hence bane upabasati. [Gloss:] Hari dwells everywhere in heaven.

ubasarbatasoḥ kāryāṅdhigubaryādiṣu triṣu dvitīyāmreḍitānteṣu tato nyatrāpi dṛśyate: "For the action of 'both' and of 'all,' for dhik, for the three beginning with 'upari' when they end in a repetition, and elsewhere than these too, the second is seen." [Gloss:] dwells near Kṛṣṇa.

That is, for the action of words ending in ubhaya and sarvataḥ, meaning another noun connected with those two; for the use of dhik in the sense of reproach; and "for the three beginning with upari, ending in a repetition," meaning the three upari, adhi and adho when they end in a repeated form; and "elsewhere than these too," meaning that when abhitaḥ, paritaḥ, samayā, nikaṣā, hā, ṛte and prati are used, the second case also occurs. The examples, in order: upayataḥ gopā kṛṣṇaṃ, sarvataḥ kṛṣṇaṃ, dhik kṛṣṇabaktaṃ, uparyupari lokaṃ hariḥ, adhyadhi lokaṃ, adhodho lokaṃ, abitaḥ bṛṣ, paritaḥ kṛṣṇaṃ, samayā kṛṣṇaṃ, nikaṣā kṛṣṇaṃ, hā kṛṣṇaṃ, ṛto kṛṣṇaṃ, prati kṛṣṇaṃ. [Glosses:] the cowherds on both sides of Kṛṣṇa; everywhere around Kṛṣṇa; woe to him who is not Kṛṣṇa's; Hari above and above the world; over and over the world; below and below the world; around Kṛṣṇa; all about Kṛṣṇa; near Kṛṣṇa; close to Kṛṣṇa; alas, Kṛṣṇa; surely Kṛṣṇa; toward Kṛṣṇa.

antarāntareṇayukte, "When joined with antarā and antareṇa." When antara, "within," and antareṇa, "between," "boundary" or "apart," are used, the second case also occurs: antarā gārtapatyaṃ, glossed "within the householder's fire"; antareṇa darmaṃ sukhanna bhavati, "for one who cuts himself off from the Dharma there is no happiness."

anurlakṣaṇe, "anu in the sense of a characteristic mark." When anu is used in the sense of a characteristic mark, the second also occurs: jabamanu brabarṣata. [Gloss:] after the recitation it rained heavily.

hṛtīyārthe, "In the sense of the third." When anu is used, the second also occurs in the sense of the third case: nadīmanvabasitā senā. [Gloss:] the army stationed along the river.

hīne, "In inferiority." When anu is used in the sense of inferiority, the second case also occurs: anu hariṃ surāḥ. [Gloss:] the gods are below Hari.

uba, "Also in superiority." When upa is used in the sense of inferiority and of superiority, the second occurs: uba hari surāḥ. [Gloss:] the gods are near Hari.

lakṣaṇetthaṃbhūtākhyānabhāgabīpsāsu bratibarlanapaḥ, "In the senses of characteristic mark, being thus, share and repetition: from prati, pari and anu." When prati and the rest are used in those senses, characteristic mark and the rest, the second occurs. In the sense of characteristic mark: hari brāṃti, hari manu. In the sense of being thus: bhakto buṅdhaṃ prati, bhakho biṣṇuṃ pari, bhakhobuṅdha manu. In the sense of share: lakṣmīḥ harimbrati, lakṣmīḥ harimbrati, lakṣmīḥ hari manu. In the sense of repetition: bhūtaṃbhūtaṃ pari prabhuḥ, bhūtaṃbhūtaṃ pari prabhuḥ, bhūtaṃbhūtaṃ pari prabhuḥ. [Glosses:] toward Hari; around Hari; after Hari; a devotee toward the Buddha; a devotee around Viṣṇu; a devotee after the Buddha; Hari's fortune, toward; Hari's fortune, around; Hari's fortune, after; lord toward each and every being; lord around each and every being; lord after each and every being.

abhirbhāge, "abhi when it does not mean share." When abhi is used not in the sense of share, the second occurs: harimabhi bartato bhakhaṃ. [Gloss:] the devotee turns toward Hari.

atirtikramaṇe, "ati in the act of surpassing." When ati is used for an act of excelling, the second occurs: ate debān kṛṣṇaḥ, "Kṛṣṇa, surpassing the gods."

kālādhvanoratyaṃtasaṃyoge, "Time and road in unbroken connection." When used with regard to time, as in "he recites once each year," and in the sense of an unbroken stretch of road, the second occurs: māsaṃ kalyaṇī, māsamabhite, māsaṃ guḍadhānāḥ, krośaṃ kuṭalān hī, krośam giriḥ. Where it is otherwise, not an unbroken span, the second does not occur: māsasyadvirdhīte, krośasya kadeśaḥ parbata. [Glosses:] the second case with these; fair for a month; he reads for a month; he eats molasses and parched grain for a month; for a league the river is crooked; for a league, lightning; for a league, a mountain; he reads twice a month; a mountain in one part of a league.

Having explained the domain in which the second applies, I shall now explain the domain of the third.

svatantraḥ kartā, "The independent one is the agent." One who has independence, like a woodcutter, is given the technical name "agent."

sādhakatamaṃ karaṇaṃ, "What is most effective is the instrument." That by which any action can most readily be accomplished is given the technical name "instrument."

kartṛkaraṇayosnṛtīyā, "For agent and instrument, the third." In indicating the agent or the instrument of any action, the third case occurs, as in rāmeṇa pānahato bālīṇena ha bālī, where rāmeṇa is the agent and bāṇena the instrument. [Gloss:] Rāma killed the monkey with an arrow.

brakṛtyadibhyatīyā, "From prakṛti and the rest, the third." With prakṛti and the rest the third case also occurs: brakṛtyacāruḥ, brāyeṇasaḥ, gotīṇa gārgyaḥ, sameniti, biṣameniti, dvidroṇina dhānyāṃ krīṇāti, pañcakena paśūn hvati, sukhen duḥkhen yāti. [Glosses:] beautiful by nature; for the most part; a Gārgya by clan; goes evenly; goes unevenly; he has grain bought by two great measures; he has cattle sold by fives; from suffering he attains happiness.

debaḥkarma ca, "Of div, also the object." When the word div is used, the third optionally occurs also in the sense of the object: akṣeḥ dībyati, akṣān dībyati. [Gloss:] he has them play at dice.

ababargetpṛtīyā, "In attaining the result, the third." In the sense of complete knowledge, or of attaining the result of any action, when time and road are used in unbroken connection, the third occurs: ahnā bedondhḍitaḥ, "in a single day he read the Veda."

krośena bedoñabhītaḥ. [Gloss:] in a league's journey he reads it. If it is not in the sense of attaining the result, the third does not occur: māsamdhītonāyātāḥ. [Gloss:] though he read for a month, he did not understand.

sahayuktepradhāne, "When joined with 'together.'" In the sense where a word for "together" is used, the third occurs: putreṇasahāgataḥ. The commentary says that when sārdhaṃ, sākaṃ and samaṃ are used, the third occurs; hence putreṇa sarḍhamāgataḥ, putreṇa sakaṃ gataḥ, śiṣyiṇa samaṃ tiṣṇati. [Glosses:] he is with his son; he is with his son; he went with his son; he stays near his student.

yenāṃgabikāram, "That by which there is a deformity of the body." Where there is a deformity of some bodily part that can clearly indicate the rest, the third occurs in the sense of the first case: akṇākāṇaḥ, pādena khañjaḥ, karṇena badhiraḥ, śirasā khalbāṭaḥ. [Glosses:] one-eyed; lame in the foot; deaf in the ear; bald on the head.

itthaṃbhūtalakṣaṇe, "In a mark of being thus." In the sense of a mark that says "it is like this and this," the third occurs: kṣatreṇopādhyaṃyamadrākṣīta. [Gloss:] he looked on the student as like the preceptor.

saṃjñonyatarasyāṃ karmaṇe, "Optionally in the object of recognizing." In the sense of the object of recognizing, the third optionally occurs: pitrā sañjānīte, pitaraṃ sañjānīte. [Glosses:] he recognizes his father; he recognizes his father.

heto, "In the cause." For the cause that brings an action about, the third occurs: puṇyen dṛthṭo guruḥ. [Gloss:] through merit one sees the teacher. The commentary says that sometimes the third also occurs when the cause bringing the action about is repeated; hence śatena śatena batsān bāyayati payaḥ, śataṃ śata batsān bāyayati payaḥ. [Gloss:] he has the calves drink the milk a hundred at a time.

The commentary also says that when a word in the sense of slowness is used, the third occurs; hence alambe lambena. [Gloss:] slow through slowness.

The commentary also says that when a word in the sense of "true" is used, the third occurs; hence satāmarbo haribhakdbā. [Gloss:] Hari's devotee is true in meaning.

The commentary also says that when pūrva and avara are used, and in the sense of "worthless," that is, "bad," the third occurs; hence māsen bāurbaḥ abaraḥ, buṇnen hīnaḥ, śastreṇaṃ kalahaḥ. [Glosses:] earlier by a month; lacking in merit; fighting with weapons.

asṛṣṭasya byabahāre caturbhyarthe tṛhīyā, "In improper conduct, the third in the sense of the fourth." When the cause of an improper act is used, the third occurs in the sense of the fourth: dāsbā saṃyacchati kāmukaḥ. If it is not improper, the third does not occur: bhāryāyai saṃyacchati kāmukaḥ. [Glosses:] he gives his seed to the maidservant; he gives his seed to his own wife.

Having explained with these the domain in which the third applies, I shall now explain the domain in which the fourth applies.

karmaṇā yamabhibritis sabradānaṃ, "The one for whom there is full giving: the fourth." The one for whose sake one wishes to give and wishes him to receive, that is, through the act of giving, and the one for whose sake there is going and coming, are given the designation "recipient" (sampradāna).

caturnrīs pradāne, "In the recipient, the fourth." For one to whom the designation "recipient" has been given, the fourth case occurs: brāhmaṇebhyaḥ gāṃd dāti, debebhyaḥ puda dāti, upāṅghyāyāya sulbarṇaṃ dadāti. [Glosses:] he gives a cow to the brahmins; he gives flowers to the gods; he offers gold to the preceptor.

If it is not a recipient, then even though the sense is giving, the fourth does not occur: dānīyo pipraḥ. These are in the sense of the object of giving; in the sense of coming: pratye śete strī.

rucyarrthānāṃ priyamāṇaḥ, "Of words meaning 'to please,' the one pleased." For one who has the sense of craving, or who takes delight in craving, the fourth occurs: haraye rocate bhaktiḥ. [Glosses:] the pleasure that accords with my aim; do not give it to the brahmin; the woman lies down for her husband's sake.

śāghaṅghūsthāśabījñipsamānaḥ, "Of ślāgha, hnuṅ, sthā and śapa, the one to be informed." When the roots ślāgha, hnu, sthā and śapa are used, the fourth occurs for the one who is meant to know: gopī smarāta kṛṣṇāya ślāghate, kṛṣṇāyahnuti, kṛṣṇaya tiṣṭhate, kraṃṣṇāya śapate. [Glosses:] the cowherdess longs for Kṛṣṇa as a servant does; the cowherdess longs like a servant; she speaks ill to Kṛṣṇa; she stays for Kṛṣṇa; she swears to Kṛṣṇa.

bhāreruttamarṇaḥ, "Of dhāri, the creditor." When dhāri, "to hold," is used, the fourth occurs for the one who is the creditor: ahaṃ mokṣāya dhārapate budṅhaḥ. [Gloss:] the Buddha holds it for the sake of my liberation.

smṛheripsitaṃ, "For the one desired as a companion." When a word of longing is used, the fourth occurs for the one desired as a companion: harye sbṛhayati. [Gloss:] he longs for Hari.

kruṅhadruherṭhāsūyārthanāṃ yaṃ pratikopaḥ, "Of words meaning krudh, druh, īrṣya and asūya: the one toward whom there is anger." When krudh and the rest are used in the sense of anger, naming separately the one it is directed at rather than the act, the fourth occurs: haraye kruṅhyati, haraye drutyati, haraye īrṣyati, haraye śabūyati. [Glosses:] he is angry at Hari; he bears a grudge against Hari; he is jealous of Hari; he slanders Hari.

krudhadruhorupasṛṣṭayoḥ, "For krudh and druh when they are fitting." When krudh and druh are used not improperly but in a fitting sense, that is, when the sense is not anger, the fourth does not occur, and so the second itself occurs: brāhmaṇambhikrudhyati.

rādhīkṣoryasya bipraśnaḥ, "From rādha and īkṣa, for the one about whom the question is asked."

When rādha and īkṣa are used in the sense of asking, the fourth occurs: kṛṣṭhayarāṅhyate, kṛṣcāyekṣāte. [Glosses:] he is not angry at the brahmin; he bears no grudge against the brahmin; he asks Kṛṣṇa.

pratyātbhyaṃ śrubapūrbasya karta, "From prati and āṅ, the agent of the prior action of śru." When the stem prior to śru, which has the preverbs prati and āṅ, is used in the sense of the agent, the fourth occurs: piprāya ghāṃ pratiśriṇoti, biprāya gāmāśīṇoti. [Glosses:] he promises the brahmin a cow; he pledges the brahmin a cow.

anupratigṛṇaśca, "Also of gṛṇa with anu and prati." For that prior stem joined with gṛṇa preceded by anu and prati, the fourth also occurs in the sense of the agent: hotre anugṛṇāti, hotre pratigṛṇāti. [Glosses:] he answers the priest of the fire offering; he responds after the priest of the fire offering.

barikrayaṇe saṃpradānamanyatarasyāṃ, "In the act of purchase, optionally the recipient." When parikriya is used, the fourth optionally occurs for the agent that has the sense of recipient, or else it is the third: śatāla parikrītoñanubūti, śatena parikrīto nubūhi. [Gloss:] bought for a hundred, repeat after me.

tadrthecaturthībācya, "The fourth is to be stated in the sense of 'for the sake of that.'" "For the sake of that" refers to an excellent aim which, if pursued, will surely be quickly accomplished, but which is not yet manifest; for that aim the fourth occurs. The example given in verse in the commentary is:

saṃyamāya śrutaṃ dhantenaroṅharmāla saṃyamaṃ, dharmimokṣayamedhāyamedhābīṅhanaṃ dānāyabdukta ye.

One devoted to restraint holds learning for restraint's sake;
People hold restraint for the sake of the Dharma;
The wise hold the Dharma for the sake of liberation;
And wealth for giving and for food.

Here māya twice, kṣaya and nāya: the fourth is applied. Likewise, buṅdho bhabeyaṃ jagate hitāya mamārthāya manukampāya mebigho. [Gloss:] may I become a buddha for the benefit of beings.

The commentary also cites: hetuyogaca, "Also when a cause is joined." When a word in the sense of cause is used, the fourth occurs: brāhmaṇāya hetaṃ kṣīraṃ. [Gloss:] rice pudding for the brahmin's sake.

kriyārthobaparasyaca karmaṇisthaninaḥ, "Also in the object of a nearby word that has the sense of an action." For a nearby word that has the sense of an action, in the object, that is, in the sense of the second, the fourth optionally occurs: phalabhyo yāti. [Gloss:] he goes to obtain fruits.

tumarthācca bhābabacanāta, "Also from a word expressing a state in the sense of tum." When the suffix tum, and ghañ and the rest, are used in the sense of expressing a state, the fourth also occurs: yāgāya yāti. [Gloss:] he goes to the sacrifice.

namaḥsvastisvāhālabaṣaḍyogācca, "Also when joined with namas, svasti, svāhā, svadhā, alam and vaṣaṭ." When namas and the rest are used, the fourth occurs: namo buddhāya, namo dharmāya, namas saghāya, svasti prajābbyaḥ, svāhāpi tṛbhyaḥ, aṃl bhūtebbyaḥ, baṣaḍandrīya. [Glosses:] homage to the Buddha; homage to the Dharma; homage to the Saṅgha; well-being to all creatures; may the ancestors be well satisfied; satisfaction to the bhūtas; vaṣaṭ to Indra.

The commentary also cites: upapadabibhakteḥ kārkabibhaktarbalīyasī, "The case of the kāraka is stronger than the case of the nearby word." Although it was explained above that only the fourth case applies when namas is used, this scripture shows that it is not fixed one way. The fourth case explained above depends on the nearby word, but here the kāraka is the second, so when namas is used the second also sometimes applies. For example: oṃ namaḥ siddhaṃ, namaskaroti debāna. [Gloss:] homage to the siddhas.

manyakarmaṇyanādare bighāṣāprāṇiṣu, "In the object of manya, in contempt, optionally, for what is not a living being." In the object of manya, when there is contempt for what is not a living being, the fourth optionally applies, or else the second: natvāṃ tṛṇāya manye, natrāṃ tṛṇaṃ manye. If it is not contempt, the fourth does not occur: tvāṃ debaṃ manye. Again, even though it is not a living being, for "boat" the fourth does not occur: na tvāṃ nādaṃ manye. If it is a living being, then even though it is contempt, the fourth does not occur: na tvāṃ śukaṃ manye, na tvāṃ śrigalaṃ manye. [Glosses:] I do not count you even as a straw; I count you as a god; I do not count you even as a boat; I do not count you even as a parrot; I do not count you even as a jackal.

gatyacvakarmaṇi dvitīyācaturthoceṣṭāyāna ṅhvani, "In the object of a verb in the sense of going, the second and the fourth, when there is movement and it is not a road." For what is made the object of a root used in the sense of going, either the fourth or the second case occurs; that is, when there is movement, actually going, and the going is not along a road: prajaṃ brajati kṛṣṇā, brajāya braja ti kṛṣṇā. If there is no movement, the fourth does not occur: mansā banaṃ yāti. If it is a road, it is the second itself: mārgaṃ gacchañi. [Glosses:] he goes to the forest in his mind; he goes along the road.

The commentary also explains that even when it is a road, in the sense of going along a path preceded by ut, the fourth occurs: utpathena pathe gacchati. [Gloss:] he goes along a ruined way.

The commentary also says that when the sense is going, the fourth and the second may sometimes optionally occur without regard to whether there is movement or not; hence grāmāya gaṃtā, gramaṃ gaṃtā. [Glosses:] he goes to the village; the traveler goes along the road.

Having explained with these the domain of the fourth, I shall now explain the domain of the fifth.

ṅhrubamapāyepādānaṃ, "That which is fixed, from which there is separation, is the source." Whatever separates from what is fixed, or what was formerly gathered or joined and then falls or is split apart, is given the designation "source" (apādāna).

apādāne pañcamī, "In the source, the fifth." To what was given the designation "source" above, the fifth case applies: grāmādāyāti, ṅhṅabatoñaśvātpatati. [Glosses:] he came from the village; he fell from the running horse.
