The commentary also says that the fifth also occurs when words of aversion, of ceasing to delight, and of heedlessness are used; hence pāpājṅgupsate, pāpādriramati, dharmādpramādyati.

bhītvānpānāṃ phayahetuḥ, "Of words meaning fear and protection, the cause of fear."

When words meaning fear and words meaning protection are used, the fifth case also applies to the cause of fear. He feels jealousy toward evil. He ceases to delight in evil. He acts improperly toward the Dharma. corādvibheti. corāyvate.

paājersoḍhaḥ. "In being defeated, which is not conquering." When a word meaning being defeated, not conquering, is used, the fifth applies: pāpātparājayate.

bārṇānrānāmīpsitaḥ. "Of words meaning warding off, in what is desired." Where words meaning warding off are used, to keep it away: he is afraid of the thief; he guards against the thief. To what is desired, the fifth applies: yabibhyogāḥbāryati.

antarṅhoyinādarśanamichati. "By whom one wishes not to be seen." He is defeated by evil. "In concealment." When a word meaning concealment is used, the one by whom one wishes not to be seen takes the fifth: māturnilīyatekṛṣṇaḥ.

ākhyātopayoge. "In the reciter, and in formal instruction." He wards the oxen away from the barley. When the word for the reciter is used with the sense of formal instruction, the fifth also applies: upāṅhyāyādaṅhītebaṭuḥ. If the sense of formal instruction is not involved, the fifth does not apply: nagasyagī. Kṛṣṇa hides from his mother. tāṃśṝṇote. He hears the dancer's song.

janikartuḥprakṛti. "In the source of that which produces." The source, that is, the cause by which a result or a thing has been produced (the student recites from the preceptor), takes the fifth: brahmaṇaḥprajāḥbrajāyante.

bhubaḥprabhabaḥ. "From that out of which something comes into being." The place from which something comes into being takes the fifth: himabatogaṃgāprabhabati.

Since the commentary says, "When lyap is elided, the fifth stands in the sense of the second and the seventh," when the kṛt suffix lyap and the like (creatures are born from Brahmā) has been elided, the fifth applies in the sense of the second and seventh cases: prāsādātprekṣate. āsa (the Gaṅgā arises from the Snowy Mountains) nātprekṣata.

Again, the commentary quotes: praśnākhyānyośca. "In the stating of a question." When a statement asking something such as "from where?" is used, the fifth applies: kasmātatvamāgataḥ.

yataścaṅhvakālanirmāṇaṃtadrapañcamī. He looks from the palace. He looks from the seat. "That from which the measure of road or time is fixed also takes the fifth." When the measure of road or time is shown from some point, the fifth applies; and by the word "also," the first, second and seventh apply as well. Where have you come from? banāṅgrāmoyojanaṃ. kārtikyāḥāgrahāyaṇīmāse, and so on.

anyārāditarrtedikaśabdāñūttarapadājāhīyugte. "In connection with anya, ārāt, itara, ṛte, words of direction, añcu as a final member, and āc and āhi." When these words, anya and the rest, are used, and words (from the forest to the village is four krośas) whose final member is añc, or which end in the suffixes āc and āhi, the fifth applies: anyaḥkṛṣṇat. bhinnorāmāta. ārātarāmāta. itarorāmāt. ṛtebudṅhātkutomokṣat. pūcogrāta. ayamasmātbūrbaḥ. prākgrāmāta. dakṣiṇāgrāmāta. dakṣiṇāhigrāmāta.

Again, since the commentary explains that when a word meaning "before" is used the fifth sometimes applies: bhabādā. Other than Kṛṣṇa. Different from Rāma. Different from Rāma. Near Rāma. Other than Rāma. Without the Buddha, whence liberation? East of the village. This one is prior to us. East of the village. rabhyaḥ. Restrained from saṃsāra. South of the village.

Again, since the commentary explains that when a word meaning "outside" is used, as in "outside the village," the fifth applies: grāmādāhiḥ. Outside the village.

apaparībarjane. "Apa and pari, in the sense of exclusion." When apa and pari are used to express exclusion, they are given the designation "karmapravacanīya."

āṅamaryyadābacne. "Āṅ, in expressing a limit." When āṅ expresses the sense of a fixed boundary, such as a limit, it is given the designation "karmapravacanīya" by force of need.

pañcamyaāṅbaribhiḥa. "With apa, āṅ and pari, the fifth." When apa and the others, which were given the designation "karmapravacanīya" above, are used in those senses, the fifth applies in the sense of the second case: apharecasaṃsāreḥ. parihareḥsaṃsāraḥ. āmugtessaṃsāraḥ.

pratiḥ. pratiniphipratidānayoḥ. "Prati, in matching and in exchange." When prati is used and matching or exchange is meant, it is given the designation "karmapravacanīya."

pratiniṅhipratirānecayasmāt. "And also that from which" (Hari is apart from saṃsāra; Hari is wholly apart from saṃsāra; up to liberation from saṃsāra) "there is matching or exchange." When prati, which was given the designation "karmapravacanīya" above, is used, that from which matching or exchange is expressed takes the fifth in the sense of the second case: abhimanyurarjuntaḥprati. māṣānasmitilebhyaḥpratiyacchati.

akartaryreṇepañcamī. "Where it is not the agent, in a debt, the fifth." To the cause of a debt, where it is not the agent, the fifth applies: śatādvarṅāḥ.

bibhāṣāguṇeñastīyāṃ. "Optionally in a quality, when not feminine." Abhimanyu is a match for Arjuna. He exchanges these beans for sesame. To a quality that has become a subsidiary of the cause, when it is not of feminine gender, the fifth optionally applies: jāḍryādvadṅhaḥ. jāḍyenapaṅṅhaḥ. Bound because of a hundred. If it is a subsidiary of a quality, it does not apply: dhanenakulaṃ. If it is of feminine gender, it does not apply: budṅhyvamuktaḥ.

pṛthagbinānānābhistṛdīyānyatarasyāṃ. "Of pṛthak, vinā and nānā, the third optionally." When pṛthak and the others are used (bound because of dullness), the second and the fifth apply, and the third as well: Separately from Rāma. pṛthaka. A family by wealth. rāmeṇa. pṛthakarā. Freed by understanding. maṃ. Separately from Rāma. binā pāpina. Without evil. binā pāpāta. Without evil. pinā pāpaṃ. nānā prakāreṇa. nānāprakārāt. nānāprakāraṃ.

karaṇicasñokālpakṛcchvaktipayascāpatvabacanasya. "In the instrumental, of snyoka, alaṅ, kṛcchva and katipaya, when what is expressed is not a substance (asattva)."

...to that which is the instrument. When these words, stoka and the rest, express (without evil; with various garments, in various garments, of various garments) a sense that is not a substance, the third and the fifth apply: stekenamuktaḥ. stokānmuktaḥ. albenmuktaḥ. analpenamuktaḥ. kṛcchaṇamuktaḥ. kṛcchvanmuktaḥ. katipayenamuktaḥ. katipayenamuktaḥ.

If the sense is not one of non-substance, the fifth does not apply, only the third: stokenapiṣeṇahataḥ. When it is not the instrument of the action, the third does not apply either (freed by a little; freed from a little; freed by little; freed from little; freed with difficulty; freed from difficulty; freed by a few): stokaṃpacati.

dūrāntikārthebhyodvitīyāca. "From words meaning far and near (he died of a little poison), the second as well." When words meaning far and near in distance are used, the third and the fifth apply, and the second as well: grāmasyaṅūraṃ. grāmsyadūreṇa. grāmasyadārāta. grāmasyāntikaṃ. grāma (he cooks just a little) syāntikena. grāmscāntikṣat.

With these, the domain in which the fifth case applies has been explained. Now, although it does not belong among the kārakas, following the order of the cases, I shall explain the domain of the sixth. (At a distance from the village. By a distance from the village. From a distance from the village. Near the village. By nearness to the village. From nearness to the village.)

ṣaṣṣiśeṣe. "In the remainder, the sixth." When what remains apart from the first case and the others explained above and the seventh, which comes below, that is, apart from the six kārakas, is expressed, such as a relation, the sixth case applies: rājñaḥpuruṣaḥ. ācaryasyaśiṣyaḥ. rajñaḥkumār.

Again, since the commentary explains that occasionally the sixth may also be used in the sense of the object: bhajeśaṃbhoścaraṇayoḥ. One worships at the feet of Īśvara (Śiva).

ṣaṣṣīhetuprayige. "When cause is used, the sixth." When a word meaning cause is used, as in "the cause of this" (the king's man; the master's student; the king's son), the sixth applies: annasyahetoḥbsati.

sarbanāmnastṛtīyāca. "With a pronoun, the third as well." When pronoun stems expressing the sense of cause are used, the sixth applies, and the third as well: kasyahetoḥ. kenahetunā. Again, the commentary quotes (he dwells for the sake of food): "When the sense of cause is expressed in connection with sarva and the rest, all the cases as well." When the sense of cause is expressed in connection with pronoun stems, not only do the third and the sixth apply, but optionally all the cases (of what cause; by what cause): kāḥhetuḥ. kihituṃ. kenahenā, and so on.

ṣaṣṣyatasarthapratyayen. "In the sense of the suffixes at and tas, the sixth." When used in the sense of words joined with the suffixes at and tas, the sixth applies: dakṣiṇatogrāmasya. purastatagrvamasya.

enayādvitīyā. "With ena, the second as well." When ena is used, the sixth applies (what cause; for what cause; by what cause), and the second as well: dakṣiṇenagrāmaṃ. dakṣiṇenagrāmasya.

dūrūntikārtheḥṣaṣṣyanyatarasyaṃ. "Of words meaning far and near, optionally the sixth." When words for far and near in distance (south of the village; in front of the village) are used, the fifth applies, and the sixth as well: dūraṃthāmāta. dūraṃgrāmasya. nikaṭaṃgrāmāt. nikaṭaṃgrāmsya.

jñoñbidrthasyakaraṇi. South of the village. "Of jñā, when not in the sense of knowing, in the agent." When jñā is used, expressing not the sense of knowing but the sense of not knowing, the sixth applies to the agent, that is, in the sense of the third: sarbiṣojānīte. Far from the village. Far from the village. Near the village. Near the village. If it is not a case of non-knowing, it does not apply: svareṇaputraṃjānāti.

aṅhīgrthadayeśāṃkarmaṇi. "Of words meaning remembering, and of daya and iśa, in the object." When words expressing remembering, and the roots daya and iśa, are used, the sixth applies to the object, that is, in the sense of the second (he knows by fresh ghee): māturaṅhyeti. He remembers his mother. pituḥsmarti. He remembers his father. He knows his son by his voice. sarthiṣodyate. He partakes of ghee. jagatāmiṣṭe. He is lord of beings.

kṛñaḥpratiyanne. "Of kṛñ, in effort." When the root given as "ḍukṛñ, in doing" is used so as to convey effort, the sixth applies: eṅhodkasyopasaṃskurute.

rujārthānāṃbhābacanānāmajvareḥ. "Of words meaning illness that express a state, other than jvar." With words formed from roots having the sense of harm, such as illness and beating, other than jvar, that is, in a stem construed with a word of what is not understood (he takes great pains over the work of increasing the water), the sixth applies in the sense of the object: corasyarujati. corsyanihanti. When jvar is used, only the second: coraṃjaryati.

āśiṣināthaḥ. "Of nāth, in wishing." When the word nāth is used expressing a wish or a blessing, the sixth applies: sarbiṣonāthatedadāti.

jāsiniprahaṇanāṭakrāthapiṣāhiṅsarthanāṃ. "Of jāsiniprahaṇanā (he strikes the thief with illness; he kills the thief outright) ṭa, krāthapiṣa (he strikes the thief with fever), in their senses of harming." When these, jāsi and the rest, are used expressing harm (the lord bestows ghee), the sixth applies in the sense of the second: corsyojdāsyati. corsyaniprahanti. corsyonnaṭayati. corasyakrāthayati. corasyakrāthayati. corasyapinaṣṭi. If it is not in the sense of harm, it does not apply: ṅhānāḥpinaṣṭi.

byabahṛpaṇoḥsamarbayo. "Of hṛ with vi and ava, and of paṇ, in wagering." When hṛ prefixed with vi and ava, and paṇ, are used expressing the sense of wagering (he crushes the thief; he utterly slays the thief; he binds the thief; he beats the thief; he grinds the thief to powder; he grinds parched grain), the sixth applies in the sense of the second: śatasyabyabaharte. śatasyabyabaṇate. If wagering is not expressed, the sixth does not apply: brāhmaṇaṃpaṇāyati.

dibastadarthasya. "Of div, in that sense."

"Of div" as well: this is the sense of "and." When it is used in the sense of wagering, just as was explained, the sixth applies in the sense of the second: śatasyadībyati.

bibhāṣopasarge. (He wagers a full hundred.) "With a prefix, optionally." When div preceded by a prefix (he praises the brahmin) expresses the sense of wagering, the sixth optionally applies in the sense of the second: śataṃpradībyati. He stakes a full hundred. śatasyapradībyati. kṛtoñarthapra (he wagers a full hundred) yegikāloñadhikarṇe. "With a kṛt used in the sense of time, in the locus." When the kṛt suffixes and the rest are used expressing the sense of time, the sixth applies to the locus, that is, in the sense of the seventh case: pañcakṛtvañahhaḥbhuṃkte. dvirahnophuṃkte.

kartṛkrmaṇoḥkṛtiḥ. "In the agent and the object, with a kṛt." When a word both expresses the agent or the object and ends in a kṛt suffix or the like, the sixth applies. For the agent: tabagrvasaṃkā. tapagamikā. For the object: sarbasatvā (he eats food five times a day; he eats food twice a day) nāṃpuṣṭiṃkuru. namaḥsamantabuṅdhānāṃ.

ubhayaprāptokarmaṇi. "Where both are obtained, in the object." Where both the second and the sixth case would be obtained, the sixth applies to the object: citraṃgabāṃdohogoba (you eat) kena.

ktasyacabartamāne. "Of kta also" (bring increase to all sentient beings; homage to all the buddhas) "in the present." When the suffix kta is used expressing the present, the sixth applies: satāṃjvātaḥ. If it is not the present, it does not (the cowherd milks the dappled cows) apply: grāmaṃgataḥ.

nasuṃsakebhābe. "In the neuter, in the sense of the state." When the suffix kta expresses the state and is used with a neuter stem, the sixth optionally applies: satāṃgataḥ. saṅbhimtaḥ.

aṅhikaraṇabācinaśca. (Known by the good.) "Also when it expresses the locus." When a word ending in the suffix kta (he went to the village) is used, the sixth applies to the locus, that is, in the sense of the seventh: idmeṣāmāsetaṃ.

nalokābyayaniṣṣaṣalarthatṛṇaṃ. "Not with loka" (the good have gone) "the indeclinables, the niṣṭhā suffixes, ṣal and tṛṇ." When the word loka is used, when words of the class of indeclinables are used, and with words ending in the suffixes having the sense of niṣṭhā, the suffix ṣal, and the five suffixes tṛṇ and the rest (these sat here), the sixth does not apply. With the word loka: cakṛbānsṛṣtihaṃriḥ. Hari, maker of the world. With an indeclinable: alaṃkariṣṇuḥ. He made it full. With a word ending in a niṣṭhā suffix: haridebyānhatabān. Hari, slayer of the asuras. biṣṇunāhtāḥdetyāḥ. The asuras were slain by Viṣṇu. With a word ending in the suffix ṣal: iṣatkaraḥahāri. The five, tṛṇ and the rest, are these: tṛ, śānac, cān, śatṛ, and tṛṇ; these are the five. First, with a word ending in the suffix tṛ: lokānkartā. With śānac: somaṃpabamānaḥ. With cān: ātmānaṃmaṇḍayamānaḥ. Adorning himself. With śatṛ: bedamaṅhīyan. Reciting the Veda. With tṛṇ: lokānkartābrahma.

Again, since the commentary (by a little) explains that with dviṣ bearing the suffix śatṛ the sixth optionally applies in the sense of the second: murasyadviṣan. muraṃdviṣan.

akenorbhi (the maker of the world brings about ...) biṣyadārhamarṇyayoḥ. "Of aka and in, in the future and in indebtedness." When aka and in (Brahmā, maker of the world) are suffixes expressing future time, or are used with the sense of indebtedness, the sixth does not apply in the sense of the second: sataḥbāla. The enemy of the asura. ko'patarati. sukhamṛṇaṃdāyī.

kṛtyānāṃkartaribā. "Of the kṛt suffixes, in the agent, optionally." When words ending in kṛt suffixes and the rest are used, the sixth optionally applies in the sense of the agent: mayāsabyosvarasvastī. mamasebyosvarasvastī.

tulyarthairatulobamā (the debt will be repaid by the good person; he will repay the debt with ease) bhyāṃtṛtīyānyatarasyāṃ. "With words meaning equal, and with words of having no equal, optionally the third." When words meaning equal are used (Sarasvatī is worshipped by me; Sarasvatī is worshipped by me), and when "not comparing as equal," that is, words of having no equal, are used, the sixth and the third apply optionally: pitrātulyaḥputraḥ. bituḥtulyaḥputraḥ. pituḥsdṛśaḥputraḥ. pituḥsdṛśaḥputraḥ. pitrāsmakputraḥ. pitussamkputraḥ. buṅṅhasyatulyaḥnāsti. buṅṅhenatulyaḥnāsti. buṅṅhenatulyaḥnāsti.

caturthicāśiṣyayuṣyamdrabhadrakuśalsukhārthahitiḥ. "In a wish, with āyuṣya, madra, bhadra, kuśala, words meaning happiness, and hita" (a son like his father) "the fourth as well" (a son equal to his father). When a wish is conveyed (a son similar to his father) and āyuṣya and the rest, words meaning good (there is none equal to the Buddha), words meaning virtue, words meaning happiness and so on are used, the sixth and the fourth apply: āyuṣyaṃtababhūyāt. May you have long life. āyuṣyaṃtubhyaṃbhūyāt. madraṃtababhūyāt. May you be joyful. madraṃtubhāṃbhūyāt. bhadraṃtubhyaṃbhāyāt. bhadraṃtubhyaṃbhāyāt. kuśalaṃtabhūyāt. kuśalaṃtubhāṃbhūyāt. sukhaṃtababhūyāt. sukhaṃtubhyaṃbhūyāt. ciraṃjībitaṃmmabhūyāta. ciraṃjībehaṃmahyaṃbhūyāt. kalyāṇaṃtbabhūyāt. kalyāṇaṃtubhyaṃbhūyāta. hitaṃtababgūyāt. hitaṃtuphyaṃbvūyāt.

tṛptyarbrānāṃkaraṇeṣaṣṣibā. (May you be good. May you be virtuous. May you be virtuous.) "Of words meaning satisfaction" (may you be happy) "in the agent, the sixth" (may I live long) "optionally." When words meaning satisfaction (may you be virtuous; may it be of benefit to you) are used, the sixth optionally applies in the sense of the agent: paliḥtṛptaḥ. phalānāṃtṛphaḥ.

With these, the way the sixth applies has been explained. Now I shall explain the domain of the seventh.

āṅhāroñaṅhikaraṇaṃ. "The support, the place of abiding, is the locus." Whatever is the basis or the place where something abides is here given the technical designation "locus." (They are satisfied with fruits.)

saptamyaṅhikaraṇec. "In the locus, the seventh as well."

To that which was given the designation "locus" above, the seventh applies. Again, the commentary quotes: dūrāntikārthebhyaḥ, "From words meaning far and near." Since the word "also" in "in the locus also" above, together with this quotation, explains that even where it is not the locus, the seventh also applies in the sense of far and near in distance:

Now first, the sense of abiding in a place, that is, the locus, has four divisions: aupaśāṣikaḥ, sāmīpikaḥ, biṣyaḥ, abhabyāsyāḥ. In Tibetan these are the four: "closely joined," "having proximity," "pervasive," and "having a domain." The seventh applies to these four divisions of the sense of support, and the examples are in order. The first, "closely joined," is direct contact with what supports it, and an example of the seventh applying to it is: kaṭeāste. He sits on a grass mat. "Having proximity": nadyāmāste. He stays at the river, meaning that he stays near the river. "Pervasive": tileutelaṃ. The sesame oil in the sesame seeds. "Having a domain": hṛdibrahmāmṛhamparaṃ. In the heart is the supreme nectar of Brahmā.

Examples of near and far: bansyaṅūre. banasyāntike.

Since the commentary explains, "With a word bearing the suffix kta, the seventh optionally applies in the sense of the second": aṅhītībyākarṇe.

Again, the commentary quotes: sādvāsāṅhuprayogeca. "Also when 'good' and 'not good' are used." "Good" (far from the forest; near the forest) is a name for being free of evil. When it is used, the seventh applies (he studies grammar), and when "not free of evil" is used, the seventh also optionally applies: sāṅhuḥkraṃṣṇomātari. asāṅhuḥkṛṣṇomātule.

Again, the commentary explains that the seventh applies when it is used of an action that arises from a purpose, and the example given in verse is:

carmaṇidvipinaṃhantidantayorhantikuñjaraṃ
bāleucamārīhimñisimnipuṣkalkāhataḥ

and so on (Kṛṣṇa is good toward his mother; Kṛṣṇa is not good toward his maternal uncle). That is, in carmaṇi, dantayoḥ, bāleu and simni, the endings ṅi, os, sup and ṅi are what follow. For its skin one kills the tiger. For its tusks one kills the elephant. For its musk one kills the fragrant one.

yasya bhābenabhābalakṣaṇaṃ. "In that whose state is the mark of a state." To that whose action is the mark of the occurrence of another action, the seventh applies: goṣuduhyamāneṣagataḥ.

"Adhi, in lordship." When adhi is used expressing the sense of lordship, it is given the designation "karmapravacanīya."

yasmādaṅhikaṃyasyaceśvarbacnaṃtatrasaptasī. "That over which adhi is said, and whose lordship is expressed, takes the seventh." (He went while the cows were being milked.) When adhi, which was given the designation "karmapravacanīya," is used, and the sense of something's lordship is expressed, the seventh applies to that: aṅhibhubirāmaḥ.

ṣaṣṣicānādare. "In disrespect, optionally the sixth." When disrespect is expressed by the stem whose action marks the interval, the sixth and the seventh both apply: rudtiprājīt. He went off while they were weeping. rudataprābrājita.

svāmīśvarāṅhipatidāyādasākṣipratibhūprapasūteśca. "Of svāmī, īśvara" (Rāma, lord of the earth) "adhipati, dāyāda, sākṣi, pratibhū and prasūta also." To a stem used with these, svāmī and the rest, the sixth and the seventh apply optionally: ṅharmasvāmī. ṅharmasyasvāmī. ṅhanaīśvaraḥ. ṅhanasyaīśāraḥ. deśeaṅhipatiḥ. deśasyaaṅhipati. bhogedāyāṅa. bhogasyaṅāyāda. ṅhanesākī. danasyasākṣi. ṅhanepratibhū. ṅhanasyapratibhū. gabaṃprasūta. goṣuprasūta.

ayuktakuśalābhyāṃbāsebāyāṃ. (Lord of the Dharma. Lord of the Dharma.) "Of āyukta and kuśala" (lord of wealth) "in worship" (lord of the land) "optionally" (heir to wealth). When āyukta and kuśala (lord of wealth) are used expressing the sense of worship (guarantor for wealth; the calf of the cows), the sixth and the seventh apply optionally: āyuktaharipūjane. āyuktaḥhipūjanasya. kuśalaḥharipūjane. kuśalaḥharipūjansya.

yataścanirdhārṇaṃ. "Also of those from among which something is singled out." When something is singled out from others by way of class, quality, action and the like, that is, in the sense of specification, the sixth (he is wholly devoted to the worship of Hari) and the seventh (he is skilled in the worship of Hari) apply: nṛṇāṃdvijarnaśreṣṣa. nṛṣudvijaḥśreṣṣaḥ. gabāṃkṛṣṇāgoḥbhukṣīrā. goṣukṛṣṇāgoḥbhukṣīrū.

Again, the example given in verse in the commentary is:

puruṣāṇāṃkṣatīyaḥ śūraṇaśyāmānārīṇāṃdarṣaṇīyā
gacchatāṃṅhābanhābactaśīghāḥ ṅharmaśīdānāṃśradṅhāgrāḥ

These are with the ending ām of the sixth (of men, the twice-born is the best; among men, the twice-born is the best; of cows, the black cow gives the most milk; among cows, the black cow gives the most milk) or, alternatively, with the ending sup of the seventh applied (of men, the kṣatriya is bravest; of women, the dark one is fairest; of those who go, the runner is swiftest; of the white dharmas, faith is supreme):

rguruṣeṣukṣattīyaḥ śūrāḥśyāmānārīṣudarṣaṇīyā
Among women, the dark one is fairest.
gacchatsuṅhābantaśīghaḥ
Among those who go, the runner is swiftest.
ṅharmaśiteṣuśraṅdhāgraḥ
Among the white dharmas, faith is supreme.

Here the first line singles out by class, the second by quality, and the third (among men, the kṣatriya is bravest) and the fourth show it by action.

pañcamībibhakte. "In special reverence, the fifth." Special reverence, that is, when something is set apart from others by outstanding faith, takes the fifth case: udīcyādākṣiṇatyebhyaḥsuśrotriyāḥ.

sāṅhunibuṇārthābhyāmaḥyāṃsaptamyaprateḥ. "Of sādhu and nipuṇa, in the sense of worship, without prati, the seventh." When sādhu and nipuṇa, not preceded by the prefix prati, are used in the sense of worship, the seventh applies to the stem: nātarisāṅhuḥ. mātrinipuṇaḥ. (The southerners and the northerners are very devout.) When prati is added: sāṅhuḥmātvaraṃbrati. Again, since the commentary explains that even without prati the second optionally applies: sāṅhuḥanumātaraṃ.

prasitotsugābhyaṃhṛtīyāc. "Of prasita and utsuka, optionally the third."

(He is free of evil in honoring his mother. He is diligent in honoring his mother.) When prasita and utsuka are used (he is good toward his mother), the seventh applies, and the third as well: prasitohiṇā. prasitoharo. (He is good, following his mother.) utsukohariṇā. utsukoharo.

nakṣatecalupi. "Also with a constellation, when it is not seen." When a constellation is used in the sense of not being seen, the third and the seventh apply optionally: puṣyeṇagaccheta. puṣyegaccheta. If it is not in the sense of not being seen, the third does not apply: puṣyeśaneḥ.

Again, the commentary quotes: akarmaṅhātubhātubhiḥyogedeśakālāṅhvabhābebhābebhyaḥdvitīyābā. "When roots without an object are used, from place, time, road and state, optionally the second." (He went under Puṣya.) When roots without an object are used, the seventh applies to words of place and the rest (Puṣya and Saturn), and the second as well. Thus, for place: nadyāṃbasati. nīdaṃpasati. For time: rātṛṃśete. rātrośeta. For road: krośipasati. krośepasati. krośepasati. For state: yāgaṃtiṣṭhati. yāgetiṣṭhati.

itipāṇinibyākaraṇasyasūtrātkārakānisamāptāḥ. That is: the kārakas from the sūtra of the Pāṇinivyākaraṇa are complete.

(He dwells in the dust. He sleeps at night. He stays at a distance of a krośa. He stands at the sacrifice.)

With these, from The Chariot That Draws the Jewel of Excellent Explanation, notes setting out the sense, the words, the examples and so on of the root text and commentary of the great treatise on grammar, the Pāṇinivyākaraṇa, the coarser points of the kārakas, that is, of the way the cases apply, with their general rules and exceptions, drawn from the detailed presentation, are for the present complete.

Now I shall explain the system of compounds. samarthaḥpdabiṅhiḥ. "The rule for words is the combining of meaning." What teaches the rule for combining two or more words into a single meaning is the rule of compounding.

samāsścaturṅhā. "Compounds are of four kinds." Although the Kalāpa, the Cāndra, the Sarasvatī grammar and others hold that the number of compounds is six, this text includes the two, the dvigu and the karmadhāraya compounds, within the tatpuruṣa, and so holds that in general there are four compounds. What are the four? The avyayībhāva compound, the tatpuruṣa compound, the bahuvrīhi compound, and the dvandva compound: these are the four. Of the two words that are compounded, where the former word is the principal thing expressed, it is an avyayībhāva compound; where the latter word is principal, it is a tatpuruṣa compound; where something else, related to the two words explicitly stated, is expressed as principal, it is a bahuvrīhi compound; and where both words are principal, it is a dvandva compound.

abyayaṃpibhaktisamīpasamṛṅṅhipṛṅṅhyarthāphābātyayāḍhasaṃprati śabdaprādurbhābabścāṅyathānubūrgyayogapaṅyasādṛśyasaṃpathisāklhāṃtabacanneṣu. "The indeclinable, in the senses of case, nearness, accomplishment, increase, absence, passing away, untimeliness, the clear manifestation of a word, conformity, succession, simultaneity, similarity, excellence, entirety, and the word of ending." In these senses, the indeclinable and the rest, a word bearing sup and a word bearing sup become a compound of a single meaning, and these receive the name "avyayībhāva compound."

The commentary explains: "By joining many words into one word, many vowels into one vowel, and many words with case endings into one case ending, what was before wordy and awkward to say becomes brief and easy to say. This is the purpose of compounding."

Of these, I shall first explain the avyayībhāva compound. haroaṅhikritya: this is called the phrase or the sentence, and it is the basis on which a compound is made.

prathamānirṅdiṣṭaṃsamāsaupasajaṃnaṃ. "What is specified with the first in the compound rule is the upasarjana." Where a compound is formed in connection with the first case, the item that receives the first case is given the designation (concerning Hari) "upasarjana."

upasarjanaṃpūṃrbaṃ. "The upasarjana comes first." Here, in compounding, what was designated upasarjana above is placed first, wherever it stands in the phrase, at the end or in the middle. Thus aṅhiharokṛtya: as it stands, this is given the designation "prātipadika."

supoṅhātuprātipadikayoḥ. "Of sup, in a root and a prātipadika." In a root, and in compounding, the case endings present in the item to be compounded, which has been designated prātipadika, are elided. Not only that, but the elements that follow the word, such as the equivalents for base, particle and qualifier, are also elided: the ending di given to hari, and kṛtya, are removed: aṅhihari. When the case endings with their following elements have thus been removed, the case endings that make it a word again are applied to what has received the name of compound, and su, which stands for them, is given: aṅhiharisu.

abyayībhābaśca. "Also in what has become indeclinable." In what has become indeclinable, that is, an avyayībhāva compound formed with an indeclinable in front, all the case endings perish, and since it has no function, su is removed. After it, another word that shows the meaning must be added: aṅhihariprabṛttākathā. Likewise rāyamtikrānta: removing the case ending with its following elements gives atire. In this, the end of an avyayībhāva compound becomes neuter, and in the neuter the vowel becomes short, so: atiri. (The wealthy.) Likewise nābamatikrāntal. (Having surpassed the boat. Talk that has arisen concerning Hari. Endowed with the wealth of Dharma.) atinu. These are avyayībhāva compounds.

The commentary says that if the meaning is complete and it is easy to say, the operation of compounding applies as explained above, but if it does not show the meaning and is awkward to say, the rules of compounding do not apply. For example, to something like santiguṇāḥharo the operation of compounding does not apply. For nearness: kṛṣṇasyaupa gives upkṛṣṇasu.

nābyayībhābādtomastopañcamyāḥ. "Not from what has become indeclinable, except after a; it becomes am, where it is not the fifth." (Hari has good qualities.) Although it was explained that in general all case endings perish after an avyayībhāva compound (near Kṛṣṇa), as an exception, even from what has become indeclinable, when it ends in the letter a the case endings do not perish, and all case endings except the fifth become am: su becomes am, upakṛṣṇaṃ. For the fifth: upakṛṣṇāta, and so on.

tṛtīyāsptamyorbahulaṃ. "Optionally for the third and the seventh." Although it was explained above that, after what has become indeclinable and ends in the letter a, all the remaining case endings except the fifth become am, by this sūtra the third and the seventh case endings (near Kṛṣṇa; the two are lost) both become am, and since the general operation for a word ending in short a also applies, the form is to be made optional. For the third: upakṛṣṇen, upakraṃṣṇa. For the seventh: upakṛṣṇe, upakṛṣṇaṃ, and so on.

For prosperity: in madrāṇāṃsamṛṅhiḥ, the case endings are compounded as above, and su, the prefix for the meaning of samṛṅdhi, is put first: sumadraṃ. Further, the commentary explains: "Although they end in the letter a of what has become indeclinable (by near Kṛṣṇa), sumadra and unmattagaṅgal (at near Kṛṣṇa) in the seventh case (the prosperity of the virtuous) become am alone; they do not take the optional form." Therefore, for ṅi (good virtue): sumdraṃ, unmattagaṅgaṃ (at the mad Ganges).

For growth: in yamnānāṃbṛṅṅhiḥ, the growth of the barbarians, the case endings are compounded as above, and dur, the prefix for the meaning of pṛṅṅhi, is put first: duryyapanaṃ (the growth of the barbarians).

For the meaning of absence: in makṣikāṇāmabhābaḥ, the very absence of flies, the case endings are compounded as above, and nir, the prefix for the meaning of abhāba, is put first: nirmmakṣikāsu.

abyayībhābaśca. "And for what has become indeclinable." What has become indeclinable also takes the mark of the neuter gender: for the neuter, the vowel is shortened, and su becomes am: nīrmmakṣikaṃ.

For passing away: in himāniatitāni, the case endings are compounded, and nir, for the meaning of atitāni, is put first: nirtimaṃ.

For untimeliness: in nidrāyāḥakālaḥ, the case endings are compounded, and ati, the prefix for the meaning of akāla, is put first: atinidraṃ.

For the clear manifestation of a word: in hariḥiti (without a lamp), tihāri (without a needle).

For "after": in biṣṇoḥpścāt, the case endings are compounded (without a needle), and anu, for the meaning of pacya, is put first: anubaṣṇiu (not the time for sleep).

For "according to": in baṣṇuḥprati, the case endings are compounded: pratibiṣṇu (not the time for sleep).

For the later following the earlier: in jyeṣthaṃanukramya, anujyeṣṭhaṃ (this Hari; after Viṣṇu).

For simultaneity: in cakreṇyugpaṅṅhyehi (after Viṣṇu), the third case ending (toward each Viṣṇu) and what follows it are compounded, and saha, for the meaning of yugapaṅhyehi (toward each Viṣṇu), is put first: sahacakrasu. So it stands; and then:

abyayībhābecākāle (after). "Also for what has become indeclinable, where it is not time." Also in a compound that has become indeclinable (together with joining by the wheel), where the word joined is not a word of time, saha becomes sā: sacakraṃ.

For similarity: in hareḥsṝdraśyaṃ, the case endings are compounded as above, sā, for the meaning of sādṛśya, is put first, and sū perishes: sahari.

For excellence: in kṣatrāṃṇāṃsaṃpati, the case endings are compounded, and sā, for the meaning of samti, is put first: sakṣatraṃ.

For entirety: in tṛṇenaskalaṃatti (together with the wheel; Hari, by the lotus), the case endings are compounded as above, and āṅ, for the meaning of sakala, is put first (like Hari; he eats all the grass): ātriṇaṃatti (lord of the parasol).

For a word of limit: "He reads up to the end of the book on fire": in agnigranthaparyaṃtiaṅhīte (with the parasol), the case endings are compounded (he eats the grass entirely), and sā, for the meaning of granthabaryaṃta, is put first: sāgniaṅhite. Such are the examples.

yathāsādṛṅśye. "Of yathā, where it is not similarity." When the word yathā does not express the meaning of similarity, a nominal form and a nominal form become one in meaning: in śaktimanatikramyaggamyoti, the case ending together with what follows it is removed (he reads up to the end of the book on fire), and yathā, for the meaning of anati (unease), is put first: yathāśakhi. When it does express the meaning of similarity, the operation of compounding does not apply: yathāhariḥ, tathāharaḥ.

yābadabaṅhānaṇe (do it in whatever order is fitting). "Of yābata, for singling out." Where there is the meaning of singling out one from among many (according to one's ability), the joining of the word yābata also becomes an indeclinable compound: yābanhyamanhā (as Hari, so Hara). In ṇitabantobrāhmaṇānāṃāmantrayasva, the case endings and the words that follow are removed: yābadamnhramāmantrayasva (call here those brahmins, as many as there are vessels).

sūpapratināmatrārve. "Of sūpa, with prati in the sense of a mere amount." sūpa joined with prati used in the sense of "just so much" becomes an indeclinable compound: in sūpoalapoasminbhojane, the case ending together with what follows it is removed (call here as many as there are vessels), and prati is put first: pratisūpaṃ. Where it is not the sense of a mere amount, it does not become so, as in bṛkṣaṃprati, where the case endings are not compounded and it remains just as it is.

apaparibahirañcapaḥpañcamyāpā (this one eats only a little sauce). "apa, pari, bahira and añca: optionally with the fifth." When apa and the others are joined (only a little sauce), a nominal form in the fifth case and a nominal form optionally become one in meaning (toward each tree): apabiṣū, apapaṣṇoḥ; apabiṣū, piripiṣṇoḥ; bahirbanaṃ, banātabahiḥ; prābbani (east of the forest), banātabrāka.

āṅsaryāṅābhipiṅhyoḥ. "Of āṅ, for a boundary and for all." When āṅ is joined in the sense of a set limit, or of all, whole or entire, it too optionally becomes an indeclinable compound (apart from Viṣṇu; around Viṣṇu; outside the forest): āmukti, āmukteḥ; āblebhyaḥ, ābalaṃ.

lakṣaṇenābhipratīābhibukhye. "For abhi and prati of a characteristic, in the sense of being seen in front." Where abhi and prati, expressing a characteristic, have the meaning of being seen in front, the indeclinable compound optionally applies: abhyagyi, agnimabhiśalbhāḥptanti (bounded by liberation); badyagni, agnimpratiśalbhāḥpatinti (from all the children).

anuryatsamyā. "Of anu, for that to which it is near." Where the meaning of nearness is expressed, the word anu optionally takes the indeclinable compound: adreḥ samīpaṃ either remains in its own state (the moths fall toward the fire), or optionally (the moths fall into the fire one by one) the case endings are compounded, and anu, for the meaning of samīpa, is put first: anvadri. Likewise, banasyasamīpaṃ, or optionally anubanaṃ.

yasyacāyāmaḥ. "For the length of whatever it may be."

Anu, too, when it is joined in the meaning of extending along the length of whatever it may be (near the mountain), optionally takes the indeclinable compound: gaṅgāderghyaṇyatrakāśī either remains in its own state (near the mountain), or optionally (near the forest) the case endings and what follows them (and near the forest) are removed, and anu is put first for the meaning of derghya: anugaṃga.

tiṣutaguprabṛtīnica. "Also tiṣṭhatagu and the rest." tiṣṭhatagu and the rest (as long as the Gaṅgā, so long is kāśī) are to be made particles having the indeclinable compound. For example, tiṣṭhantigābaḥyasminkāle, compounded as a particle, gives teṣṭhaṅgu (that long Gaṅgā; likewise). batantigābaḥysminkāle gives bahadgu. āyantigābaḥysminkāle gives āyaṅgu. khaleyabaṃsminkālespakṭhaṃkṛyate gives khaleyapaṃ (the time when the cows stay). lūnyabaṃyasminkāle (the cows stay) gives (the time when the cows are obtained) lūnyabaṃ (the barley reaped). saṃhṛtaṃyapaṃ (the cows obtained; the time when the cows came forth; the time when the barley is carried off, yasmin, the cows came forth; the time when the barley is spread on the threshing ground) gāle gives saṃhṛtaṃyapaṃ (the barley on the threshing ground; the time when it is reaped; the barley carried off). These are formed as particles.

bārimdhyeṣaṣṣyabā. "bāre and maṅhye: optionally with the sixth." bār and maṅhye, in the meaning of the sixth case, optionally form an indeclinable compound as a particle: gaṅgāyāpāraṃ, or optionally bārgaṅkaṃ. Likewise gaṅgāyāmaṅhyaṃ, or optionally maṅhyegaṅgaṃ. Or optionally, by making a tatpuruṣa compound, gaṅgāyāpāraṃ gives gaṅgāparaṃ, and likewise gaṅgāyāmaṅhyaṃ gives gaṅgāmaṅhyaṃ, and so on.

saṃkhyāṃbaṃśyena. "For the number of a lineage." (To the far side of the Gaṅgā; to the far side of the Gaṅgā; the middle of the Gaṅgā; the middle of the Gaṅgā.) A word of number expressing the reality of a lineage also becomes an indeclinable compound (the far side of the Gaṅgā): dvoomunībaṃśyoo (the far side of the Gaṅgā; the middle of the Gaṅgā), or optionally dvimuni (the middle of the Gaṅgā). Likewise trimunibyākaraṇasyabidyā, or optionally trimunibyakaraṇaṃpidyā.

nadībhiśca. "Also with rivers." A word of number together with a word expressing a river also becomes an indeclinable compound: in saptānāṃgaṅgānāṃsamaharaḥ (the two lineages of sages; the two sages; the three sages who know grammar), the case endings and what follows them are compounded (the three sages who know grammar): sabtagaṅmā. Likewise dvayoḥymunyoḥsamharaṃ gives dviyamunaṃ.

anyapadārtheca (sleeping by the seventh Gaṅgā) saṃjñāyaṃ. "And in the meaning of another word, for a name." Where rivers stand in the meaning of another word, a nominal ending for a name becomes an indeclinable compound: in anmatñagaṅgāyasminde (like the Gaṅgā) śe (at the two Yamunās), the case endings and words (the two rivers Yamunā) together with what follows them are removed: unmattagaṅlaṃdeśe. If it is not a name, in śrīghraṃgaṅgārṅalaṃbegoyasya the indeclinable compound does not apply. Therefore, by making a bahuvrīhi compound (the land in which the Gaṅgā is wild): śīghragaṅgādeśaḥ.

abyayībhābeśratprabṛtibhyaḥ. "From śarat and the rest, in what has become indeclinable." (The wildness of the Gaṅgā of the land; the swift water of the Gaṅgā of any man.) At the end of a compound that has become indeclinable, the suffix ṭac is to be given to śarat and the rest (near autumn; the Gaṅgā land where it is not hot): in śaradaṃupa, the case ending is removed, upa is put first, and to ubaśarad the suffix ṭac is given; by cuṭu and so on, c and ṭ are removed, and d is kept; su becomes aṃ by the rule on the form of the preceding am: upajarsaṃ. Likewise, in pāśaṃprati, the case endings are compounded, prati is put first, and by giving the suffix ṭac: pratipāśaṃ. In the same way: bipāśaṃ, pracetasaṃ, sumanasaṃ, upānhaṃ, upānasaṃ, pratidiba, pratidiśaṃ, amadiśaṃ, apadiśaṃ, svanaḍuhaṃ, prabiśaṃ, (near autumn) upajarsaṃ. Since these (toward each noose) belong to the group beginning with śarat, the joining of words and (toward each noose; without a noose; supremely in mind) ṭac (a good mind; a goddess): upa and āṅ put first, ṭac; upa put first, from anas (goddess), ṭac; (toward each sun) ṭac; (the intermediate directions) su put first, anaḍuhana, ṭac (a good bull of the herd); (dwelling) ṭac; (near old age) ṭac. The procedure of compounding, the way the suffix ṭac is given, and so on, are as in the case of śarat.

pratiparssambhyokṣṇaḥ. "From prati, par, sam and anu, of akṣi." From akṣi joined with those prefixes, at the end of the indeclinable compound the suffix ṭac comes, and to it the technical designation "having the name bha" is given. taṅṅhitāḥ. "These are taddhitas." Although the suffix ṭac and certain others are not taddhita suffixes, they are given the name "taddhita suffix" because of what is required. In akṣiprati, prati is put first; to pratiakṣi the suffix ṭac is given; by cuṭu and so on, c and ṭ are removed; by the sūtra "also for the i of whatever," the i of the stem is removed. The designations just explained, "having the name bha" and "these are taddhitas," are given for the purposes of this text. pratukṣaṃ. Likewise, in akṣibyāṃbar, the case endings are compounded and par is put first: parakṣi. The commentary quotes: "From par, of akṣi, suṭ." Since it explains that when par is joined with akṣi the augment suṭ comes: suṭā. The ṭa marks its position and the u is for pronunciation. By sasajuṣa and so on, sa becomes ru (direct perception; beyond the eyes); the u is for pronunciation; by "from ata, of ru, before what is not prolonged, to what is not prolonged," rau; by "from a, guṇa," o; by "from eṅ at the end of a word, of ata," the a is removed: in paro'kṣi, by forming ṭac and so on as before: paro'kṣaṃ. Likewise samakṣaṃ. For both, the joining of words, the suffix ṭac and so on are as before.

anaśca. "Also from an." At the end of a compound that has become indeclinable and ends in an (hidden), the suffix ṭac is also to be given. nastaṅṅhite. "Of na, before a taddhita." (Hidden; good eyes; following the eye.) Before a taddhita suffix, the ti of a word ending in an is to be dropped: in rājāḥsmīpaṃ, the case endings are compounded, and upa, the prefix for the meaning of samīpa, is put first: uparājan. By "also from an," ṭac; by the sūtra just explained, the ti is removed: uparāj. Likewise, for ātmano'ṅhi too, by compounding as above and joining the suffix ṭac and so on (near the king): aṅhvātsaṃ.

nabuṃskādanyatarsvāṃ. "Optionally from the neuter."

From a word that is already of neuter gender before the compounding (near the king), not one that becomes neuter only after the indeclinable compound has been made, and that ends in an (the inner self), ṭac also optionally comes at the end of the indeclinable compound (the inner self): in carmanaḥ upa, the case endings are compounded and upa is put first; optionally, ṭac is given and the ṭi removed, and su becomes am. Or optionally su perishes and the n at the end of the noun is removed: ubacarmaṃ, upacarma.

nadīpoṇmāsvāgragāyaṇībhyaḥ. "From nadī, porṇamāsi and agrahāyaṇi." For these too, nadī and the rest, ṭac optionally comes at the end of what has become indeclinable: in naṅyaḥsamīpaṃ, the case endings are compounded and upa is put first for the meaning of samīpa; optionally, by joining ṭac (near the hide): upanadu, upanadi. Likewise, porṇamāsyāsmīpaṃ gives upaporṇapāsaṃ, or optionally (near the full moon, that is, the fifteenth) upaporṇamāsi. aglahāyaṇyāḥ (near the river) samīpo gives upāgrahāyaṇi, or optionally (without the planets) upāgrahāyaṇi.

jñayaḥ. "Of jñaya." (Near the river.) At the end of what has become indeclinable (near the full moon), whatever letter of the group jhaya there may be, ṭac optionally comes: in samiṅhaḥsamīpaṃ, the case endings are removed, upa is put first for the meaning of samīpa, and ṭac comes; or optionally, in the neuter, su becomes am or perishes, by the rule "optionally where there is no place": upasmiṅhaṃ, upasmita, upasmid.

gireścasenakasya. "From giri, of the one who makes offerings." In the meaning of one who makes offerings with the word geri, in a sense connected with "near the slope," ṭac optionally comes at the end of what has become indeclinable: in gereḥsamīpaṃ, the case endings are removed, upa is put first, and ṭac comes (near the slope); or, by optionally not making ṭac (near the slope): upagiraṃ, upagiri.

With these, the indeclinable compounds have been explained.

Now I shall explain the tatpuruṣa compound.

dvitīyāśritātītapatitagatātyasta (the letter ri) prābdābandiḥ. "Of the second, with resorted to, passed, fallen, gone, true (ṭac; near the mountain), obtained and become." When it is joined with those meanings, resorted to and the rest, the ending of the second case, a nominal form and a nominal form of one meaning, becomes a tatpuruṣa compound. For resorted to: in kṛṣṣaṃśritaḥ, the second case ending and what follows it are compounded: kṛṣṇaśitaḥ. Likewise, by compounding the case endings: for passed, odanbhuktaḥ; for fallen, phalapatitaḥ; for gone, grāmagtaḥ; for true, buṅṅhādyastaḥ; for obtained, arthaprāptaḥ; for become, (resorted to Kṛṣṇa) sukhabannaḥ. The commentary explains that when it is joined with the meaning of going, the second-case ending also becomes one in meaning; therefore (he ate food; ama; ama; the fruit fell; he went to the village; ema): grāmagrāmī.

svayaṃkten (the Buddha is true). "Of svayaṃ, with kta." (He gained the object.) A word with the suffix kta joined with svayaṃ (he became happy) also becomes one in meaning, a nominal ending with a nominal ending: ama spayaṃkṛtaṃ (done by myself).

banhākṣebe. "Of khaśā, for what is bad." (In the meaning of bad: he wanders off to the village; he wanders off to the village; ema.) khaṭā joined with a word that has the suffix kta and expresses this also takes the tatpuruṣa compound, a nominal form and a nominal form of one meaning (he sat on the bed): in khaṭvāṃārūḍhaḥ, the follower of the second case is removed: kharūṭhaḥ.

sāsī. "Of sāmi." sāmi joined with what ends in the suffix kta also becomes a tatpuruṣa compound: sāmikṛtaṃ.

kālāḥ. "Times." A second-case ending that expresses time also, before a word with the suffix kta, takes the tatpuruṣa compound, a nominal form and a nominal form of one meaning: in mā (he sat on the bed) saṃpramitaḥcandraḥ, the follower of am is removed: māspramitaḥcandraḥ.

tritīyātdkṛ (ama; half done) tārthenguṇabacnina. "The third, in expressing a quality whose meaning is made by it." In expressing a quality whose meaning is made by it, the third-case ending, a nominal form and a nominal form of one meaning (the moon measured by the month), becomes a tatpuruṣa compound: in śaṃkula (the moon measured by the month) yākhatḍaḥ, the follower of the third is compounded: śaṃkulākhaṇḍaḥ. Likewise ṅhānhārjā. If it does not express a quality, the tatpuruṣa compound does not apply: in a case like akraṇākāṇaḥ, the follower of the third is not dropped.

pūrbasadṛśasmonārthakalahanipuṇamiśra (chopping with an axe) ślakṣṇeḥ. "Of pūrbasadṛśa, sa, meaning, deficient (chopping with an axe), ba, kalaha, ni, thā in the sense of a quarrel, puṇa, miśra and ślakṣḍa." (Blind in one eye.) When joined with pūrba and the rest, the third-case ending becomes one in meaning: in māsenpūrbaḥ, the case endings are compounded: māspūrbaḥ. Likewise kṛṣṇasdṛśaḥ, ṭārāmsamaḥ, ṭābūṇyahinaḥkhāśāstākalahaḥ, ṭābūṇyuhinaḥkhaśastrakalahaḥ, ṭāśāstranipuṇaḥ, dugdamiṭāśraḥ, nayanślākṣṇaḥ. The commentary explains that what is joined with abara also becomes one in meaning with the third-case ending; therefore: māsābaraḥ. (Earlier by a month; kṛrtakaraṇe; ṭā; Kṛṣṇa, the lesser; like Rāma; lacking in merit; fighting with weapons; skilled in treatises.)

kṛtā (mixed with milk) ṭāe (good eyes) bahulaṃ. "Variously, with kṛt, for the instrument and the agent." When the third-case ending in the sense of instrument or agent (ṭā; other than by a month) is joined with a word that has a kṛt suffix or the like, since "variously" applies in three senses, many outcomes arise: becoming a tatpuruṣa compound of one meaning, not becoming one, becoming one optionally, and so on. For example, where the operation of compounding applies: in hariṇātrātaḥ, the follower of the third is removed: haritrātaḥ. Likewise nakheḥbanniḥ gives nakhabtināḥ. Where the procedure of compounding does not apply: in a case like bhikṣabhiḥuditaḥ, the case endings are not dropped. Likewise dātreṇalūnabān, khaḍgeḥchenvabān, and so on.

kṛta (protected by Hari) tyairṅhikārthabacani. "With the kṛtyas (protected by Hari; scratched by nails), in expressing the meaning of excess (scratched by nails)."

(Hungry from begging.) A third-case ending of a word with a kṛt or similar suffix (reaped with a sickle; cut with a knife) that expresses a meaning of excess, a nominal form and a nominal form of one meaning, takes the tatpuruṣa compound: in kāgeḥpeyānadī, the case endings are compounded: kākapeyānadī. Likewise, in bāṣencheṅthani, too, the case endings are compounded, and by joining the helper word tṛṇa, which makes the meaning clear: bāṣpacheṅyaṃtṛṇni.

annenabyañjanaṃ. "For seasoning with food." When seasoning with food is expressed (crows drink the water; crow-drunk water), the third-case ending becomes one in meaning: in kṣi (sprinkled by mouth) reṇsiktaodanaḥ, the case ending and what follows it are removed: kṣirodnaḥ.

bhakṣe (the gods eat by mouth) ṇamiśrīkarṇaṃ. "For the act of mixing with food." When the act of mixing food is joined, the third-case ending becomes one in meaning: guḍenmiśrāḥṅhānāḥ gives (milk mixed with barley flour) guḍaṅhānaḥ.

caturthītādarthārthabalihitasukharakṣiteḥ (for that purpose, milk and barley flour). "The fourth, of 'for that purpose', bali, and hitasukharkṣeta." When "for that purpose" is expressed in a good sense, and when bali and the rest are joined, the fourth-case ending too, a nominal form and a nominal form of one meaning (mixed with molasses and parched grain; molasses and parched grain), becomes a tatpuruṣa compound: in yūpāyaṅāru (wood for a sacrificial post), the case endings are compounded: yūpṅāru (wood for a sacrificial post). The commentary explains that sometimes, although it is "for that purpose," the case endings are not compounded; therefore in a case like raṃṅhanāyasthīl (a vessel for the trader), the case endings are not dropped.

When joined with bali: in bdūtāyabaliḥ, the case endings are compounded: btūtabliḥ. Likewise denarasukhaḥ and degohitaṃ.

pañcamībhayen. "The fifth, with fear." When joined with an expression of the cause of fear, the fifth-case ending becomes one in meaning: in corātbhayaṃ (a torma for the bhūtas; a torma for the bhūtas), the follower of the fifth case ending is compounded (no ease for men; ease for men; protection for the ...; benefit for cattle): corbhayaṃ. Likewise ṅisbṛkabhitiḥ gives basibṛkabhiḥ.

apetāpodhamuktapatitāpatrasteerlpa (afraid of thieves) śaḥ. "Of abeta, apoḍha, mukta, batita, abo and trasta, for what is slight." When joined with abeta and the rest expressing a slight matter (afraid of robbers; afraid of the wolf; afraid of the wolf), the fifth-case ending becomes one in meaning: in sukhādapetaḥ, the follower of the fifth is compounded: sukhāpetaḥ. Likewise ṅasikalpāpoḍhaḥ, ṅasicakramuktaḥ, ṅasisragpatihaḥ, taraṃgāptrasta.

stokāntikaṅūrārbakṛchrāṇikten. "Of stoka, antika, words meaning far, and kṛchra, with kta." When joined with words having the suffix kta, with stoka, antiga, words meaning far (joined from happiness), and kṛchra (joined with happiness), having the suffix kta (equal in strength; freed from the wheel; fallen from a good destiny; frightened of the waves), the fifth-case ending is not dropped but stays in its place; even so, these are called compounds without dropping. sñokānmustaḥ (slightly freed), alcānmuktaḥ, antikānluktaḥ, dūrānmuktaḥ, kṛchrānmuktaḥ: in these the follower of the fifth is not removed.

ṣaṣṣī. "The sixth." The ending of the sixth case too, a nominal ending and a nominal ending, becomes one in meaning: in rājñaḥpuruṣaḥ, the case endings are removed, giving rājan (freed from a little; freed from what is near; freed from hope; freed from what is far; freed from suffering; log); by "the n at the end of a noun is to be dropped," the n is removed: rājapuruṣaḥ, the king's man. The commentary explains: "When it is joined with a word ending in a kṛt or similar suffix (the king's man, that is, the king's envoy) and a characteristic is expressed, the sixth-case ending becomes one in meaning." Therefore, in byāssyakṛtiḥ, the follower of the sixth is compounded: byāskṛtiḥ. Likewise bhāratbrabaṇaṃ.

ṅas yājkādibhiśca. "Also with yājaka and the rest." When joined with yājaka and the rest, the sixth-case ending too, a nominal form and a nominal form, becomes one in meaning: in dvijasyayājkaḥ (made extensive), the case endings are removed: dvijayājkaḥ. Likewise ṅas dvijayājkaḥ (bhārtasas, opening what is heard), dvijāṅhyapakaḥ, ṅas dvijadvarttakaḥ, ṅas dvijahotṛkaḥ. The commentary quotes: "graha, ratha and batti (the twice-born's sacrificer), joined with gaṇaka, also become one in meaning (the twice-born's sacrificer)." Therefore (the worshipper of the twice-born; the twice-born bathes; the twice-born recites; the twice-born anoints; the twice-born performs the fire offering): rathagaṇkaḥ, pattigaṇakaḥ, pattigaṇakaḥ.

nanirṅnārṇe. "Not where there is specification." Where there is the meaning of specification, the sixth-case ending does not become one in meaning: in a case like nṛṇāṃdvejaḥśreṣthaḥ, the case endings are not dropped.

pūrṇaguṇasuhitārtha (the count of planets; the count of chariots; the count of downfalls) sadbyayatabyasmānāṅhikarṇena. "Of full, quality, the meaning of well satisfied, true, indeclinable, tavya, and making one superior among equals." (Among men the twice-born is supreme.) When those meanings, full and the rest, are joined, and the indeclinable, and a word with the suffix tavya, and the meaning of making one superior among equals, the sixth-case ending does not become one in meaning. For full: satāṃṣaṣṣaḥ. For quality: guṇasyapatraṃ, guṇasyapatraṃ. Further, the commentary explains that in the meaning of a quality that is constantly attached, the sixth-case ending does become one in meaning; therefore in a case like candanaganṅhaḥ, the scent of sandalwood, it becomes one in meaning. For well satisfied: (the satisfaction of the well satisfied) suhi (the true ones, the sixth) tānāṃtṛptiḥ; phalā (the praise of quality, that is, the learned) nāṃtraṃptiḥ (satisfied by fruits). For true: dvijasyakurbaṇaḥ, satāṃkurbaṇaḥ. For the indeclinable: satāṃkṛtvā. For tavya: satāṃkartabyaṃ. Further, the commentary explains that even when joined with a word having the suffix tavya, it sometimes also becomes one in meaning; therefore: ṅas dvijakartabyaṃ. For the meaning of making one superior among equals: rājño (to listen; done by the twice-born; done by the true ones; having been done by the true ones; the doing of the true ones) syaṃ.

ktencapūjāyāṃ. "And of kta, for honoring."

When a word with the suffix kta is joined with the meaning of honoring, the sixth-case ending does not become one in meaning (done by the twice-born): rājī (the king has no laziness) matobuṅṅhaḥpūjitaḥ.

karmaṇica. "Also for the object." When joined with something in which there are two meanings of object, the sixth-case ending does not become one in meaning: cāryatigbāṃdohogopena.

tṛjakābhyāṃkartaraṃ. "From tṛc and aka, for the agent." From a stem joined with tṛc and aka, the suffixes for the meaning of the agent (the custom of kings is to honor the Buddha; drica), the sixth-case ending does not become one in meaning: bhabataḥśīmān, pacakascacaturaḥ. Further (the herdsman milks the cows and makes his living), the commentary explains that when the word for lord is joined, although it ends in tṛc, the operation of compounding applies; therefore: trica bhubaḥbhartaḥ.

nityakrīḍājībikayoḥ. "Always, for play and livelihood." (Your glorious one; the master of cooking.) When joined with a word that expresses the meaning of play or of livelihood, the sixth-case ending always becomes one in meaning. For play: uṅṅā la ṅas kapuṣpabhaṃjaṃkaḥ. For the meaning of livelihood (lord of the earth): ṅas citralekhakaḥ.

būrbāparāṅtarottaramekdeśinekāṅhikaraṇe. "Of pūrba, apara, aṅhara and uttara, where one part is set apart within a single body." When pūrba and the rest are joined with the setting apart of one part within a single body (he wears a garland of flowers; he draws pictures), the sixth-case ending becomes one in meaning: in pūrbaṃkāyasya (the heart of the body), the follower of the sixth is compounded: pūrbakāyaḥ (the upper body). Likewise aparkāyaḥ (the right side of the body), aṅharakāyaḥ (the lower body), and uttarakāyaḥ. The commentary explains that sarbā, saya and maṅhya joined with ahā also become one in meaning with the sixth-case ending; therefore: ṅas sarbāhnaḥ, ṅas maṅhrāhdāḥ, sāyātnaḥ.

arṅhaṃnapusakaṃ. "arṅha in the neuter." The word arṅha having the neuter gender takes the tatpuruṣa compound: arṅhaṃpippalyaḥ gives arṅhapippali.

dvitīyatṛtīyatṛtīyacaturthatūryāṇhyanyatarastāṃ. "Optionally for dvitīya, caturtha and turya." When dvitīya and the rest (the whole day; midday; evening) are joined, the sixth-case ending becomes one in meaning, and the two stems in the joining of words may optionally exchange their order (the making of pippali): in dvitīyaṃbikṣāyāḥ, the case endings are compounded, and by optionally exchanging the order or not: dvitīyabhikṣā, bhikṣādvitīyaṃ. Likewise tṛtīyaṃbhikṣāyāḥ gives tritīyabhikṣā, bhikṣātṛtīyaṃ. In the same way: caturthabhikṣaaṃ, bhikṣācaturthaṃ; turyabhikṣa, bhikṣāturyaṃ (the second alms). The commentary quotes: "Optionally when pāda and hasta are joined with tala and agra." It explains that when pūda (the second alms) is joined with tala and hasta with agra, the sixth-case ending (the third alms; the third alms) becomes one in meaning (the fourth alms), and exchanging the order (the fourth alms) is also optional; therefore: in pādsyatalaṃ, the case endings are removed, and by optionally exchanging the order or not: pādtalaṃ, talapādaṃ. Likewise hastasyaagraṃ gives hastāgraṃ, agrahastaṃ.

brāptāpannecdvitīyayā. "Also of the second, for prāpta and āpanna." "Of the second, for prāpta and āpanna." When joined with the two, prāpta and āpanna (the sole of the foot), the second-case ending becomes one in meaning, and exchanging the order of the stems (the sole of the foot) is optional: in prāptojībikā (the tip of the hand; the tip of the hand), the case endings are compounded, and by optionally exchanging the order of the stems or not: prāptajīpikā (who has obtained a livelihood), jībikāprāptaḥ (who has obtained a livelihood). Likewise, ābannojībikāṃ (who has entered upon a livelihood) gives āpannajībikā (who has entered upon a livelihood), jīpikāābannaḥ.

kālāḥprimāṇinā. "Of times, for a measure." When a measure of time is expressed, the sixth-case ending becomes one in meaning: in māsojātasya, the case endings are compounded: māsajāḥ.

sabtamīśoṇḍaḥ. "The seventh, of śauṇa and the rest."

When joined with śauṇḍa and the rest, the seventh-case ending, a sup together with a sup, becomes one in meaning: it becomes a tatpuruṣa compound. In akṣeṣu śauṇḍaḥ (one skilled at dice, a dice expert), we get akṣeṣuśauṇḍaḥ. (A month passed.) Likewise, byavahāradhūrtaḥ (one keen in trade, diligent in trade, a trader). Likewise, by compounding after the seventh case ending: ṅi svarasaṃbītaḥ (one skilled in melody); ṅi pākapravīṇaḥ; ṅi biṅyapaṇḍitaḥ (one learned in knowledge); sāstrakuśalaḥ (one skilled in treatises); and netracabalaḥ (one with restless eyes).

siṅgāśuṣkapakvapanṅaiśca. "And with siddha (accomplished), śuṣka (dried), pakva (cooked) and bandha (bound) also." When joined with siddha and the others too, the seventh-case ending becomes one in meaning: in kāmpilye siṅghaḥ, we get kāmpilyasiṅghaḥ (one who attained accomplishment in the land of Kāmpilya). Likewise, ātapaśuṣkaḥ (dried by heat), ghṛtapakvaḥ (cooked in butter), nigaḍabanāhaḥ (bound with iron chains).

kugatiprādayaśca. "And ku, gati, pra and the rest, sups, also." The word ku joined with another stem, those named gati, and pra and the rest joined with words having a verbal sense: a sup together with a sup becomes one in meaning, a tatpuruṣa compound. And by the word "also," in the sense of inferior or little, the word ku also becomes kat, kava and kā. In kutsitaḥ puruṣaḥ (a bad man), the case endings are compounded and ku shows the meaning of kutsita: kupuruṣaḥ (a bad man). Likewise, kupipraḥ (a bad brahmin); kulavaṇaṃ, kālavaṇaṃ, kadlavaṇaṃ, kavalavaṇaṃ (bad salt, or a little salt, or impure salt); kaduṣṇaṃ, koṣṇaṃ, kavoṣṇa, kapoṣṇaṃ (slightly warm, lukewarm); kvannaṃ, kādannaṃ, kānnaṃ, kapānnaṃ (bad food, or a little food or poor food).

ūryyādicviḍācaśca. "And ūrī and the rest, and cvi and ḍāc, also." To ūrī and the rest, and to those ending in the two suffixes cvi and ḍāc, one gives the technical designation "named gati"; this naming is made for the sense of the earlier rule, "and ku, gati, pra and the rest also." For example: am ūrīkṛtya (having considered); su am urrīkṛtya; su am alaṃkṛtya (having adorned); su yam antaḥkṛtaṃ su (made into an interval); ṅa tham naskṛtaṃ; ṅi buriskṛtaṃ (placed in front); tiraskṛtaṃ (made invisible). These are the ones named gati. And for the ending cvi: ṅas śuklīkṛtya (having made white). For ḍāc: sukhākṛtaṃ (made happy). For sukha with ḍāc, the c is dropped by the rule beginning cu, ṭu; since ḍ applies, the ṭi is dropped; for that purpose the ḍ is dropped; and the s of this is dropped.

Cited in the commentary: acchagatyarthabadeṣu. "Accha, with words meaning going, and with vad (speak)." The word accha, when joined with words meaning going and speaking, also becomes one in meaning: di acchagatya; di acchavadati. Again, since the commentary explains that urasi and manasi also, when joined with words meaning going, become one in meaning: su urasigatya; su manasigatya.

tiraso'nyatarasyāṃ. "Of tiras, optionally." The s of the word tiras, when the ka class or the pa class follows, optionally becomes visarga (gone far; or, said at length), or else it brings in s itself: tiraskṛtā, tiraḥkṛtvā; tiraspati, tiraḥpati (the lord of the invisible). In the commentary it says: haste kṛdya (crawling on the belly; having put in the hand); bedaṃjībikā (captivating; one who lives by the Vedas); pāṇokṛtya (having put in the hand). "Even though the seventh case ending is not elided after it, it is still called a compound of the analysis."

Examples of pra and the rest: su prakṛtya (nature); saṃbhavati; suhṛtaṃ (a friend, or one devoted at heart); abhiṣeka (bestowing empowerment); prācāryaḥ (an eminent teacher); pratipakṣaṃ (on each side); tināthaḥ (protector of each); ṅuḥ naraḥ (a bad man); duḥkṛtaṃ (a misdeed).

Again, cited in the commentary: svatī pūjāyāṃ. "Su and ati, in the sense of honoring." Su and ati, when expressing the sense of honoring, also become one in meaning: in suṣṭeṇaśrī, deleting the anubandha and the case ending, we get suśrī (beautiful form, or glory, or excellence). Likewise, in yatiśayena rājā, we get atirājā (an outstanding king). In suṣṭasya uktaḥ, we get sūktā (well spoken). In atiśayena jñā, we get atijña (outstanding in knowledge).

Again, since the commentary explains that āṅ becomes one in meaning in the sense of a little and in the sense of pervading thoroughly: for the meaning of iṣatabaṅhaṃ, we get ābaṅhaṃ (slightly bound). Likewise, for the meaning of abhibyāptiḥ nagaraḥ, we get ānagaraḥ (a town thoroughly pervaded).

Again, cited in the commentary: atyādayaḥkrantādayaḥkrāntādyarthetvitīyāla. "Ati and the rest, in the sense of pervading and so on, with the second." Ati and the rest, when expressing the sense of pervading and so on, the second-case ending becomes one in meaning: in atikrānto mālāṃ, deleting the case ending together with its anubandha, we get atimālā su (a garland that thoroughly pervades).

ekapibhakhicāpūrbanipāte. "And of a single case in the analysis, when it is not placed first." In the procedure of compounding the words of the analysis into a single case, where two words are set down in the construction, the later word, the one not placed first, is given the name upasarjana.

gostriyorupasarjasya. "Of go and of the feminine, when upasarjana."

The word go at the end of a compound whose case endings have been combined, and a word ending in a feminine suffix, when it bears the name upasarja, becomes short. The technical designation "named upasarja" given above was also for the sake of this purpose. Therefore the ā of mālā becomes short: atimālaḥ (a pervading garland). Likewise, in atikrānta gaṅgāṃ, we get atigaṃga (thoroughly pervading the Gaṅgā; pervading the Gaṅgā). Likewise, in urgataḥ belā also, deleting the case ending and the anubandha, the end of the stem becomes short: udvelaḥ (the time of going pervasively; the time of pervading). Likewise, in abhimukhaṃ prasannaḥ, we get abhimukhaḥ (facing toward). In prati akśaṃ, deleting the second-case ending: pratyakṣaḥ (each die separately).

If it is not a feminine suffix ending, it does not become short: atitantrī (one surpassing the strings); atilakṣmī (one exceedingly glorious, or exceedingly prosperous); atiśrīḥ.

Since the commentary explains that ava and the rest, when joined with kuṣṭa and the rest, the third-case ending becomes one in meaning: in avakuṣṭaḥ kokilayā (the cuckoo sings sweetly), deleting the case ending together with its anubandha, we get avakokilaḥ.

Again, since the commentary explains that pari and the rest, when expressing the sense of glāna and the like, the fourth-case ending becomes one in meaning: in the phrase parigklānaḥ aṅyayanāya (unwilling to recite fully; unwilling to study), deleting the case ending together with its anubandha, we get paryaṅyayanaḥ. Likewise, in alaṃ subaraḥ kumāryai, deleting the case ending together with its anubandha, we get alaṃkumāriḥ (a well-adorned youth for a maiden; a maiden of fine adornment).

Since it is said that nir and the rest, when joined in the sense of pervading and so on, the fifth-case ending becomes one in meaning: in nithkrāntaḥ kauśāmbhyaḥ, we get au nilgośāmviḥ.

Again, since the commentary explains that when joined with iba the case endings are not elided, and that is called a compound without elision: in such as tau ibaḥ (like those two) and bāsasī iba (like two garments), the case endings are not elided and the junction is made: tābiba, bāsasāpa.

pūrbakālaikasarbajartpurāṇanacakebalāḥ samānāṅhikaraṇena (certainly; endowed with a treasury). "Earlier time, eka, sarba, jarat and purāṇa, even when not single, with a co-referent." When joined with earlier time, that is, past time, and also when joined with eka and the rest, where it is not a single word but co-referential, a sub together with a sup becomes one in meaning: in snātena anuliptaḥ, compounding after the third case, we get snātānuliptaḥ (anointed after bathing). Likewise, in ekena snataḥ (the bathing of one), we get ekasnataḥ (one bath). Similarly, in sarbeṇa snataḥ (the bathing of all), we get sarbasnataḥ. Similarly to these, in jartābayaḥ (being old), we get jaradvayaḥ. Likewise, in burāṇena uktaḥ, we get burāṇoktaḥ.

If it is a single word, there is no convention of compounding: for something like būrbaḥ there is no compounding procedure. Where it is not co-referential, that is, where the meanings conflict, then even though there are two or three words they do not become one in meaning: for something like bahni purāṇa (reading the Purāṇa) or secanaṃ jala (pouring water on a fire with cupped hands), the operation of compounding does not apply.

tatūruṣaḥ samānāṅhikaraṇaḥ karmaṅhārayaḥ. "A co-referential tatpuruṣa is a karmadhāraya." Among tatpuruṣa compounds, the co-referential one, that is, one in which the two words, earlier and later, have meanings that apply equally to a single thing, is called a karmadhāraya compound: in ekā cās sāṭī ca, deleting the case ending together with its anubandha, it stands as ekāsāṭī.

busbatkarmadhātīyaḥdeśīyeṣu. "Like the masculine, in karmadhāraya, jātīya and deśīya." In the context of the karmadhāraya compound, where it is joined with a co-referential meaning (it is one, and it is also the garment), and where the word jāti or the word deśa follows (sāṭī is the name of a garment worn by Indian women), at the end of the former of the two words strung together, whatever feminine suffix ending there is other than ū becomes short, like a masculine stem; so kā became short: ekasāṭī.

Likewise, in pācokā cāso sī ca (she is a cook, and she is a woman), we get pācakasti (a woman cook). Similarly, in patsamā cāsau bhāryyā ca (she is a wife, and she is the fifth), we get bāñcamabnāryyā (the fifth wife). Similarly to these, in dattā cāso bhāryyā ca (she is Dattā, and she is a wife), we get dattabḍāryyā (the wife Dattā). Likewise, in sukeśā cāsa bhāryyā ca (she has beautiful hair, and she is a wife), we get sukeśabhāryyā (the wife with beautiful hair). Likewise, in brāhmaṇā cāso btāryyā ca (she is a brahmin woman, and she is a wife), we get brāhmaṇabhāryyā (the brahmin wife). Likewise, in pācakaścāso jātīyaśca (he is a cook, and he is of a kind), we get pācakajātīyaḥ (of the cook kind). Likewise, in pācakaśca deśīyaśca (he is a cook, and he is of this region), we get bācakadeśīyaḥ (the cook of the region). Likewise, in sarbe ca debaśca (all, and also god), we get sargadebaḥ (all the gods). Likewise, in jaraśca soobtiśca (he is old, and he is lord), we get jaratścati (an old lord).

upamānāni sāmānyabacaneeḥ. "Standards of comparison, with words expressing what is common." Comparisons such as "this is like that," when they express a shared meaning, also become one in meaning: in ghanaśca ipaśtāmaḥ (it is dark blue like a cloud), compounding the case ending and the word for "like," we get ghanaśyāmaḥ (cloud-blue).

upamitaṃ byāghrātibhiḥ. "The compared, with byāghra and the rest." When byāghra and the rest express the sense of comparison, they also become one in meaning: in puruṣobyāghraibaśrūraḥ (a man brave like a tiger), deleting the case ending together with its anubandha, we get puruṣabyāghraśrūraḥ.

biśeṣaṇaṃ biśeṣyeṇa bahulaṃ. "The qualifier with the qualified, variously." The sup ending that qualifies by a single meaning, and the qualified …

… become one in meaning as the basis of a compound (a man like a tiger): in raktā cāsoo latā ca (it is red, and it is a creeper), deleting the case ending together with its anubandha, we get raktalatā (a red creeper). Likewise, in kṛṣṇaśca so sarbaśca (it is black, and it is a snake), we get kṛṣṇasarbaḥ (a black snake). Likewise, in lohitā cāsoo ahiśca (it is red, and it is a snake), we get lotitāhaṃḥ (a red snake). Likewise, in nīlaṃ ta dutpalaṃ ca (it is blue, and it is an utpala lotus), we get nīlotpalaṃ (a blue lotus).

Again, cited in the commentary: śākapārthibādīnām uttarapadalopaśca. "Of śākapārthiba and the rest, also elision of the later member." In this context of the karmadhāraya compound, for śākapārthiba and the rest, the latter of the earlier words, that is, the middle one of the three words strung together, is elided: in śākaḥ priyaḥ pārthibaḥ (a lord of the earth who delights in leaves; "lord of the earth" is a name for a king), deleting the latter of the earlier words and the case endings, we get śvakabārthibaḥ. Similarly, in debaḥ pūjako brāhmaṇaḥ (a brahmin who worships the gods), deleting pūjaka, the latter of the earlier words, and the case ending, we get debabrāhmaṇaḥ.

nañ. "Of nañ." Placing the negative nañ in front is also a tatpuruṣa compound.

nalopo nañaḥ. "Elision of the n of nañ." In the context of compounding, the n of nañ is elided when a later word follows: in ṅharmaṃ pirunghaḥ (contrary to Dharma; a brahmin of outward views), deleting the case ending, nañ is placed first in the sense of virūḍha, and by this sūtra the n is deleted: aṅharmaḥ. Likewise, in pāpābhabaḥ, we get apāpaḥ (sinless). Similarly, in na brāhmaṇaḥ, we get abrāhmaṇaḥ (not a brahmin).

tasmānnuḍaci. "After that, nuṭ before ac." When the n of the negative nañ has been deleted and, after it, a following word beginning with ac occurs, nuṭ is added as an augment. This has the same purpose as the Kalāpa's statement, "before a vowel, the letters are reversed." In śvāt anyaḥ (other than a horse), the case ending is compounded; nañ is placed first in the sense of anya; by "elision of the n of nañ" the n is deleted; by this sūtra nuṭ is added, the ṭ serving to mark its position and the u for the sake of pronunciation: anaśvaḥ.

Cited in the commentary: nañonalopaḥ tiṅi kṣeye. "Elision of the n of nañ before tiṅ, in the sense of absence." The n of nañ placed before a word ending in tiṅ is also elided if it expresses the sense of absence: in na pacasi (you do not cook), deleting the n, we get apacasi.

nabhrāṇnapānnabedanāsatyanmucinakulanakhanpuṃsakankṣatranagnankranākeṣu prakṛtyaḥ. "In nabhrāṭ, nabāt, nabed, nāsatya, namuci, nakula, nakha, napuṃsaka, nakṣatra, nagna, nakra and nāka also, by nature." The letter n of bhrāṭ and the rest, although it stands at the beginning of the other word, is not elided but remains in its natural state: nabhrāṭ (mab lab); nabāt (protecting the name); nabed (not knowing); nāsatya (not true); namuci (not releasing); nakula (without family, that is, a mongoose); nakha (a nail); napuṃsaka (a neuter); nakṣatra (a star); nagna (naked); nakra (not fleeing); nāka (heaven).

sanmahatparamottamotkriṣṭaḥpūjyamaniḥ. "Sat, mahat, parama, uttama and utkṛṣṭa, with what is honored." When sat and the rest are joined to express the sense of honoring and of thinking well of something, they also become one in meaning, a karmadhāraya compound within the tatpuruṣa: in satcaso dharmaśca (it is holy, and it is Dharma), deleting the case ending together with its anubandha, we get saṅdharmaḥ (the holy Dharma). Likewise, in mahāṃścāsa debaśca (he is a god, and he is great), deleting the case ending together with its anubandha, we get mahaddebaḥ (the Great God (Śiva)).

ānmahataḥ samānāṅhikaraṇajātīyayoḥ. "Ā for mahat, with a co-referent and with jātīya." The end of mahat becomes āt before a co-referential word, that is, a word sharing the same substrate, and before jātīya. This is the same as the Kalāpa's statement, "for mahat, before a co-referential word, the letter ā is made." Its ṭi becomes āt: mahādebaḥ (the Great God). Likewise, in paramaśca so debaśca (he is supreme, and he is a god), we get paramadebaḥ (the supreme god). In uttamaśca soo guruśca (he is supreme, and he is a guru), we get uttamaguruḥ (the supreme guru). In utkṛṣṭaścāsoo debaśca (he is splendid, and he is a god), we get udkṛṣṭadebaḥ (the splendid god).

Cited in the commentary: ghāsakarabiśiṣṭeṣvapiśācyi. Since it is explained that ā is also to be spoken when ghāsa, kara and biśiṣṭa follow, so that mahatī followed by ghāsa and the rest also becomes mahā: mahatī with ṭa, bhās with su; in mahatyāghāsaḥ, compounding the case ending, mahatī is changed: mahāghāsaḥ (much grass). Likewise, in nā mahatyākaraḥ, we get mahākaraḥ (done by the great; a great work). Likewise, in nāmahatyābiśiṣṭaḥ, we get mahābiśiṣṭaḥ (excellent through greatness; great and excellent).

taṅhitārthottarapadasamāhāre ca. "Also in the sense of a taddhita, with a following word, and in an aggregate (many)." When the later word has the sense of a taddhita, or when there is a following word, or an aggregate, it becomes one in meaning, a tatpuruṣa compound: in būrbasyāṃ śālāyāṃ bhaba (in the eastern guesthouse), compounding the case endings, we get pūrbaśālabhaba. Then there is the rule dikpūrbapadād asaṃjñāyāṃ ñā: "From a former word of direction, when not a name, ña." Since this says that when there is a former word of direction and it is not a name, the taddhita suffix ña comes in the sense of the thing, the later word bhaba, which has the taddhita sense, is deleted, and the suffix ña of that sense is added; ña goes, and there is vṛddhi: paurbaśālaḥ (of the eastern guesthouse).

diksaṃkhye saṃjāyāṃ. "Direction and number, as a name." The words for direction and numbers, when they express a name, become one in meaning: in dakṣiṇā cāsoo agniśca (it is the south, and it is fire), we get dakṣaṇāgninaḥ (the southern fire). Likewise, in sapha ca te grāmāśca (they are villages, and they are seven), we get sabtagvāmāḥ (the seven villages). Likewise, in sapta ca ṛṣayaśca (they are sages, and they are seven), we get saptarṣayan (the seven sages).

saṃkhyāpūrbo dviguḥ. "One with a number first is dvigu." Where a thing is connected with a number word and the number word is placed first, that is given the technical designation "dvigu compound," a division within the tatpuruṣa compound.

In banca su kapāleṣu saṃskṛtaḥ (prepared in five kapālas), compounding the case endings and the anubandhas, we get pañcakapāla (five kapālas gathered).

saṃskṛtaṃ bakṣaḥ. "In what is prepared, for food." Since it is said that the taddhita suffix aṇ comes in the sense of food, in the sense of what has been prepared, aṇ would apply. However: dvigoḥ lug napatye. "For dvigu, elision, when not in the sense of offspring." In this context of the dvigu compound, the taddhita suffixes that are not offspring suffixes are elided. So even if aṇ is given to pañcakapāla, that is acceptable; even if it is given, by this sūtra it is elided and the form is the same. If it is an offspring suffix, it is not elided: in dvayoḥ mitrayoḥ putraḥ (the son of two friends), compounding the case endings, the offspring suffix ñi is added, ñ goes, and there is vṛddhi: dveemitriḥ. In such a case it is not elided.

Again, in pañcaphiḥ gobhiḥ krīta (bought with five cows), compounding the case endings, we get pañcaguḥ. There is the rule tena krētak, "By that, in exchanging goods." Although it follows from this that the taddhita suffix ka comes in the sense of exchanging goods by means of that, that is, of trade, there is also the rule athyarbbapūrbāṅdvigorlug asaṃjāyāṃ (of the dvigu). "From a dvigu with a former word meaning 'more,' elision, when not a name." From one whose former word has the sense of "more," in this context of the dvigu compound, when it is not a name, the taddhita suffixes are elided; whether ka is given or not, there is no difference in form.
