Again, in pañca gābo ṅgana yasya (one whose wealth is five cows), deleting the case ending together with its anubandha, we get pañcagoṅhanaṃ. goratangitaluki. "From go, the taddhita is not elided." Since it says that at the end of a word ending in go and at the end of a tatpuruṣa compound the taddhita suffix ac comes and is not elided, the suffix ac is added: pañcagapaḥ (wealth of five cows).

dvigurekapacanaṃ. "The dvigu takes the singular." At the end of what has been made a dvigu compound, for the most part only the singular of the case endings applies.

sa napuṃsakaṃ. "That is neuter." Those dvigu compounds that take the singular at the end become neuter in gender. In the neuter, su becomes am: pañcagapaṃ ṅhanaṃ (five cows).

akārāntottarabado dviguḥ. "A dvigu whose later word ends in the letter a." In the context of the dvigu compound, after a later word ending in the letter a, the suffix ḍīp, which expresses the feminine, comes: in trayāṇāṃ lokānāṃ (of the three worlds), compounding the case ending and adding the feminine suffix ḍīp, we get trilokī (the three worlds).

ābaṃto bā. "Optionally, for one ending in āp." In the context of the dvigu compound, if the end of the later word ends in āp, optionally ḍīp comes, or optionally it becomes neuter in gender: in trayānāṃ khaṭvānāṃ (of the three beds), we get trikhaṭvī (the three beds, feminine), or tribaṭvaṃ (three beds).

Cited in the commentary: anorlopaśca stīyābā. "Elision of an, and optionally the feminine." The ending an of a dvigu is elided, and optionally it becomes feminine in gender: in pañcānāṃ karmāṇāṃ (of the five actions), deleting the case ending, we get pañcakarman. By the sūtra "from go, the taddhita is not elided," ac is added and an is deleted; and since ḍīp is optionally added, we get pañcakarmī (the five actions, feminine) or pañcakarmaṃ (the five actions).

Again, cited: battādoo na dīṅ. "For pātra and the rest, ḍīp does not come." At the end of what has been made a dvigu compound, for pātra and the rest, the suffix ḍīp, which expresses the feminine, does not come: in pañcanāṃ pātāṇāṃ (of the five vessels), deleting the case ending, ḍīp does not come: pañcapātraṃ (five vessels). Likewise, caturyugaṃ (four forms); tribhubanaṃ (three levels).

tadpuruṣasyāṃguleḥ saṃkhyābyeyādeḥ. "From aṃguli, in a tatpuruṣa, with a number, an indeclinable and the rest first." In the context of the tatpuruṣa compound, to the stem aṃguli preceded by a number or an indeclinable, the suffix ac is added: in dvoo aṃgulī pramāṇamasya (whose measure is two fingers of a creature), deleting the case ending together with its anubandha and adding the suffix ac, we get dvyaṃgulaṃ (two fingers). Likewise, niraṃgulaṃ (fingerless).

agassarbeekadeśasaṃbyātapuṇyācca rātēḥ. "From ahan, sarba, saṃkhyāta and puṇya, and from rātri also." After ahan and the rest in the fifth case, the word rātri takes the suffix ac, and by the word "also" it does so after an indeclinable and a number placed first as well: in ahaśca rātriśca (day and night), compounding the case endings and adding the suffix ac, we get ahorātraṃ (day and night).

rātrāhnāhāḥ puṃsi. "Rātra, ahna and aha are masculine." Those, rātri and the rest, optionally become masculine in gender: in sarbaśca soorātriśca (it is the night, and it is all), compounding the case endings, the suffix ac is given by the sūtra on ahan and the rest and it becomes neuter in gender, or else by this sūtra it becomes masculine: sarbarātraṃ, sarbarātriḥ (the whole night). Likewise, in pūrbadātriḥ, we get būrbarātraṃ or pūrbarātriḥ (the earlier part of the night). Likewise, am saṃkhyātarātraṃ or am saṃkhyātarātriḥ (the counted nights); am puṇyarātraṃ or puṇyarātriḥ (the merit of the night); śca dvirātraṃ or dvirātriḥ (two nights); atirātraṃ or atirātīḥ (deep night).

rājāhaḥsakhibhyaṣṭac. "From rājan, ahan and sakhi, ṭac." In this context of the tatpuruṣa compound, the suffix ṭac is added to the end of those three stems, rājan and the rest: in mahāṃścāsoo rājā ca (he is great, and he is king), deleting the case ending together with its anubandha, it reverts to mahat rājan; by this rule ṭac is added; by the rule beginning cu, ṭu, the c is deleted; by "the an is elided," the an is deleted: mahārājaḥ (a great king). Likewise, in atiśayena rāja, we get atirājā; in that, atirāja or atirājī (an outstanding king). Likewise, in rāmasya sakhā (the friend of Rāma), we get rāmasakhaḥ. In mahāṃścāsoo sakhā ca, with ṭa, which is deleted because it is the marker of ṭit, ḍh and the rest, we get mahāsakhaḥ; by the rule on co-referents and the rest, mahat becomes mahā.

ahnaṣakhoreba. "Of ahan, ṭa and kha, exclusively." After those, ṭa and kha …

(The friend of Rāma; Rāma's friend. He is great, and he is a friend; a great friend.) From the end of go and of ahan, the suffixes ṭa and kha come, and when those suffixes follow, the ṭi of ahan is necessarily elided: in utdamaścāsoo ataśca (it is the best, and it is a day), deleting the case ending, giving the suffix ṭa and deleting the ṭi, we get uthamāhaḥ (the best day). Likewise, in dve ahanī (two days), compounding the case ending, giving the suffix kha, kha becoming īna and the ṭi being deleted, we get ṅhyahīnaḥ (two days).

Again, the commentary explains that even though it ends in rājan, in such a case as madrāṇāṃ rājī (the king of the Madras), apart from the elision of the case ending, the suffix ṭac does not apply: madrarājñā (a virtuous queen).

Again, cited in the commentary: since it is explained that at the end of ahan, in the sense of a group that is spoken of as a sacrifice, the suffix kha comes: ahīnaḥ kratuḥ (a group that performs sacrifice).

ahṣoñahna etebhyaḥ. "Ahan becomes ahna after these." "These" means: from the end of ahan that has sarba and the rest before it, the suffix ṭac comes, and ahan also becomes ahna: in sarbaścāsoo ahaśca (it is all, and it is the day), deleting the case ending and the rest and adding the suffix ṭac, by this sūtra it becomes ahna: sarbāhna (the whole day).

ahnoñadantāta. "From ahna ending in at." When ahan comes to end in at, if in its former word there is the letter r, which causes n to become ṇ, the n of ahna also becomes ṇ: sarbāhḍaḥ. Likewise, in pūrba ahaḥ, we get pūrbāhṇaḥ (the morning). In pari ahaḥ, we get parādṇa (the afternoon).

na saṃkhyādeḥ samāhare. "Not in an aggregate beginning with a number and the rest." In an aggregate beginning with a number and the like, the end of ahan does not become ahna: in dve ahinā, compounding the case ending and giving the suffix ṭac, since the end does not become ahna, we get dvyahaḥ (two days). Likewise, tryahaḥ (three days).

uttameekābhyāṃ ca. "And from uttama and eka." The end of ahan following uttama and eka also does not become ahna; and since uttama and puṇya have the same meaning, in puṇyaścāsooagaśca (it is merit, and it is a day), compounding the case ending and giving the suffix ṭac, we get puṇyāha su.

Cited in the commentary: puṇyasutinābhyāṃ napusakaṃ. "After puṇya and sudina, neuter." The word ahan following puṇya and sudina becomes neuter in gender: buṇyāhaṃ (a day of merit). Likewise, in ekaścāsoo ahaśca (it is one, and it is a day), we get ekāhaḥ (one day).

agrākhyāyām urasaḥ. "From uras, in the sense of the tip." From uras at the end of a tatpuruṣa compound, in the sense of the tip, the suffix ac comes: in aśvasya urasaḥ agre akhyā (the tip of a horse's chest), deleting the case ending and joining ac in the sense of agra and ākhyā, we get aśvarasaṃ (the crest of a horse's chest).

anoñaśmāyassarasāṃ jātisaṃjātisaṃjñayoḥ. "Of anas, aśma, ayas and saras, in the sense of class and of name." For these, anas and the rest, at the end of a tatpuruṣa compound, in the sense of a class or a name, the suffix ac comes: in su upa anasaṃ (near the kitchen), deleting the second-case ending and giving ac, we get su am upānasaṃ (near the kitchen). Likewise, in amṛtaṃ aśmaḥ, with ṭac and su, we get amṛdāśmaḥ (the pill of immortality, or a nectar pill). Likewise, in kālaṃ ayasaṃ, we get kālāyasaṃ (black iron). Likewise, in māṇyūkānāṃ sarasāṃ, we get māṇḍūkasarasaṃ (the frogs of the lake).

grāmakooṭābhyāṃ ca takṣṭaḥ. "And from takṣi after grāma and kooṭa." From takṣi preceded by grāma and kooṭa, too, at the end of a tatpuruṣa compound, the suffix ṭac comes: in grāme takṣi (a carpenter of the village), deleting the case ending and giving the suffix ṭa, we get grāmatakṣaḥ. Likewise, in kooṭaścāsoo takṣi ca, we get kooṭatakṣaḥ (a crafty carpenter).

ataḥ śunaḥ. "From śvan after ati." From śvan preceded by ati, too, at the end of a tatpuruṣa compound, the suffix ṭac is added: in ahiśayena śvā, deleting the case ending together with its anubandha and giving ṭac, we get atiśvaḥ (a wild boar), and, with ḍīp by the rule on ṭit, ḍit and the rest, atiśvī (a wild sow).

upamānādaprāṇiṣu. "From a standard of comparison, for what are not living beings." For the word śvan, in a comparison, when it is not a living being, ṭac comes at the end of a tatpuruṣa compound: in ākarṣa śvā iba (a hook like a dog), we get ākarṣaśvaḥ. If it is a living being, ṭac does not come: in bānaraḥ śvā iba (a monkey like a dog), compounding the case ending and the rest, ṭac does not come: bānaraṅśvā.

uttaramraṃgapūrbācca sakthanaḥ. "And from sakthi preceded by uttara, mṛga and pūrba." From sakthi preceded by uttara, mṛga and pūrba, ṭac comes, and by the word "also" it comes in a comparison too: in uttarasyasakthi iba (like a northern spear), we get uttarasakthaṃ. Likewise, in būrbasya sakthi iba (like an eastern spear), we get pūrbasakthaṃ. In mṛgasya śraṃṅga iba sakthi (a spear like a deer's horn), we get mraṃgasakthaṃ. In phalakasya iba sakthi (a spear like a ploughshare; a spear like Tibetan iron), we get palakasaktha.

nābo dvigoḥ. "From nau, from a dvigu." From the word nau, at the end of a dvigu compound, ṭac is added: in dve nāpoo (two boats), with ṭac and su am, we get dināvaṃ (two boats). Likewise, tīnāvaṃ (three boats) and pañcanāvaṃ (five boats).

aṭhācca. "And from ardha." From nau following ardha, too, the suffix ṭac is added: in adhaṃnābaḥ, compounding the case ending and giving ṭac, we get ardhanābaṃ.

khāryāḥ brācī. "From khārī, according to the easterners." The paṇḍitas of the east hold that ṭac is optionally added to khārī preceded by a number or by ardha: in dve khāryo, deleting the case ending and making ṭac optional, we get dvekhāre or dvekhārī (singer). Likewise, in arṅhaṃ khārī, we get arṅhakhāraṃ.

dītribdhāmañjalaḥ. "From añjali after dvi and tri."

When dvi or tri comes before it, añjali optionally takes ṭac. In dve añjalī (gloss: two loads, a pair), deleting the case ending and making ṭac optional, we get dvyañjalaṃ or dvyañjali, two loads. Likewise, in tisraḥ añjalayaḥ (gloss: making loads), we get tryañjalaṃ or tryañjali.

brahmaṇo jānapadākhyāyāṃ. "From brahman, when it names a country." Brahman connected with a country (gloss: country; handfuls, a pair) takes ṭac. In svarāṭhā brahma, deleting the case ending (gloss: a pair of handfuls) and giving ṭac (gloss: handfuls, three), we get svarāṣṭrabrahma. (Gloss: vṛ, beautiful. For the feminine, tri and catur are made into tisṛ and catasṛ.)

kumahadbhyām anyatarasyāṃ. "From ku and mahat, optionally." Brahman preceded by ku or mahat optionally takes ṭac: kubrahmaḥ or kubrahmā (gloss: the lesser Brahmā). Likewise mahābrahmaḥ or mahābrahmā (gloss: the Great Brahmā).

tatropapadaṃ saptamīsthaṃ. "There, what stands in the seventh is an upapada." (Gloss: the fourth section on compounds.) Of two words joined together, the former, which stands in the seventh case, is given the name upapada, a word in proximity.

upapadam atiṅ. "An upapada with what is not tiṅ." After a word that has been named an upapada above, whatever word follows that does not end in tiṅ, the tatpuruṣa compound of the same meaning necessarily applies. In kumbhaṃ kāraḥ, compounding the case ending, we get kumbhakāraḥ, a maker of pots, that is, a potter.

tumuṇṇvulau kriyāyāṃ kriyārthāyām iti saptamyā nirdeśād idantasyopapadatvaṃ. "With tumun and ṇvul, and with an action: an upapada not ending in tiṅ, in the domain of the seventh." An upapada not ending in tiṅ that is connected with words ending in the suffixes tumun and ṇvul, and with action suffixes such as the kṛt suffixes, even if it is in the domain of the seventh case, also takes the tatpuruṣa compound of the same meaning. In svādukāra bhukte: amaivāvyayena. "With an indeclinable, only am." If the indeclinable connected with the compound just mentioned is present, the augment am appears. By this, am; before am, the prior form; m becomes the nasal: svāduṃkāraṃ bhukte. With tumun: in kāle bhaktuṃ, we get kālabhuktuṃ.

tṛtīyāprabhṛtīny anyatarasyāṃ. "Those beginning with the third, optionally." When upadaṃśa follows, the ending of mūlaka, the third case and the rest, optionally forms a compound of the same meaning. In mūlakena upadaṃśaḥ bhukte (gloss: he eats with relish), either keeping it in its own place or compounding the case ending (gloss: having eaten at the right time), we get mūlakopadaṃśaṃ bhukte.

ktvā ca. "And with ktvā." In connection with a word ending in the suffix ktvā, the ending of the third case also forms a compound of the same meaning: uccaiḥ kṛtvā. (Gloss: upajña; having a root; well chewed with the teeth.)

upajñopakramaṃ tadādyācikhyāsāyāṃ. "Upajñā and upakrama, when one wishes to tell of the first of something." Words connected with upajñā, upakrama and the like, when they carry the sense of that wish, form a tatpuruṣa compound of the same meaning, and they also take the neuter gender (gloss: with ṭa deleted; having been made high). In pāṇineḥ upajñā, compounding the case ending, we get pāṇinyupajñaṃ (gloss: what Pāṇini first discovered). Likewise, in nandasya upakramaḥ, we get nandopakramaḥ (gloss: the first undertaking of joy; the first undertaking of joy).

chāyā bāhulye. "Chāyā, when there are many." In this context of the tatpuruṣa compound, the word chāyā, when connected with an expression of many, also takes the neuter gender. In śalabhānāṃ chāyā, we get śalabhachāyaṃ, the shadow of the moths.

sabhā rājāmanuṣyapūrvā. "Sabhā preceded by rājan or by a non-human." The word sabhā preceded by the words for king or for a non-human takes the neuter gender. In inasya sabhā (gloss: the shadow of the moths; of this one), we get inasabhaṃ. Likewise, in īśvarasya sabhā, we get īśvarasabhaṃ. In rājñaḥ sabhā, we get rājasabhaṃ. Likewise, in piśācasya sabhā, we get piśācasabhaṃ.

aśālā ca. "And when it is not a hall." Although "non-human" came above, by this sūtra a sabhā in the sense of a gathering that is not like an assembly in a guesthouse (gloss: the path; the assembly of Īśvara; the assembly of Īśvara; the king's assembly; the king's assembly) takes the neuter gender. In strīṇāṃ sabhā (gloss: the assembly of piśācas; the assembly of piśācas; the assembly of women), we get strīsabhaṃ.

vibhāṣā senāsurāchāyāśālāniśānāṃ. "Optionally for senā, surā, chāyā, śālā and niśā." The final member of these compounds with senā and the rest optionally takes the neuter gender. In dvijānāṃ senā, we get dvijasenaṃ or dvijasenā, the host of the twice-born, that is, of the brahmins. Likewise, in yavānāṃ surā, we get yavasuraṃ or yavasurā, beer of barley. In vṛkṣasya chāyā, we get vṛkṣachāyaṃ or vṛkṣachāyā, the shade of a tree. In gavāṃ śālā, we get gośālaṃ or gośālā, a cattle shed. In suniśā, we get suniśaṃ or suniśā, a good night.

Among the subdivisions of the tatpuruṣa compound, the karmadhāraya and the compound preceded by nañ do not take the neuter gender. In a case such as dṛḍhā senā, deleting the case ending, it does not become neuter (gloss: go, the feminine and the like are shortened), and we get dṛḍhasenaḥ. Likewise, in na senā, we get asenaḥ.

paravalliṅgaṃ dvandvatatpuruṣayoḥ. "In dvandva and tatpuruṣa, the gender is like that of the latter member." (Gloss: this host, too; a pleasing host.) In some cases of the tatpuruṣa compound and the dvandva compound, of the two stems joined together, the former moves to the latter position and the latter moves to the former, and in that case the operations of joining stem and case ending are carried out in accordance with whichever of the three genders belongs to the stem that has moved to the latter position. In kukkuṭaś ca mayūrī ca, a cock and a peahen, compounding the case endings, optionally exchanging the order of the stems, and following the procedure for joining with case endings according to whichever comes last, we get mayūrīkukkuṭau, or else kukkuṭamayūryau. Likewise, in ardhasya pippalī (gloss: of long pepper), we get pippalyardhaṃ, or else ardhapippalī.

pūrvavad aśvavaḍavau. "Aśva and vaḍava, as with the former." Aśva and vaḍava take the case endings as the former member does. In aśvaś ca vaḍavā ca, we get aśvavaḍavau.

vārdharcaḥ. ardharcaḥ. "Ardharca, optionally." Ṛc connected with ardha optionally takes the neuter gender, and otherwise it is simply masculine.

In ṛcaḥ ardhaṃ, deleting the case ending, exchanging the order of the members and giving ṭac, we get ardharcaṃ or ardharcaḥ. (Gloss: a horse and a mare.)

dvyaṣṭanaḥ saṃkhyāyām abahuvrīhyaśītyoḥ (gloss: a horse and a mare). "Of dvi and aṣṭan, before a number, when it is not a bahuvrīhi and not aśīti." The final of dvi and aṣṭan, before a word expressing a number, when the compound is not a bahuvrīhi and the number is not aśīti, eighty, becomes ā (gloss: half of the etymology). In dvyadhikā daśa, deleting the case ending together with the anubandha, dvi becomes dvā, and we get dvādaśaḥ, twelve.

A quotation: paṅkti viṃśati triṃśac catvāriṃśat pañcāśat ṣaṣṭi saptati aśīti navati śatam ete saṃkhyāśabdā nipātāḥ. "Paṅkti, viṃśati, triṃśat, catvāriṃśat, pañcāśat, ṣaṣṭi, saptati, aśīti, navati and śataṃ: these number words are particles." That is: paṅkti, a full ten; viṃśati, a full twenty; triṃśat, thirty; catvāriṃśat, forty; pañcāśat, fifty; ṣaṣṭi, sixty; saptati, seventy; aśīti, eighty; navati, ninety; śataṃ, a full hundred. Since it says, "these number words are particles," those number words are treated as particles when they are expressed: they are nipātas.

In dvyadhikā viṃśati, accomplishing it as above, we get dvāviṃśatiḥ, twenty-two, two more than twenty. Likewise, in dvyadhikā triṃśat, we get dvātriṃśat, thirty-two, two more than thirty. In aṣṭādhikā daśa, we get aṣṭādaśa, eighteen, eight more than ten. In aṣṭādhikā viṃśati, we get aṣṭāviṃśati, twenty-eight, eight more than twenty. In aṣṭādhikā triṃśat, we get aṣṭātriṃśat, thirty-eight, eight more than thirty. With aśīti, eighty, it does not change: in dvyadhikā aśīti, compounding the case ending, we get dvyaśīti, eighty-two, two more than eighty. Likewise, in aṣṭādhikā aśīti, we get aṣṭāśīti, eighty-eight, eight more than eighty.

Quoted in the commentary: prāk śatād aprayoge. "Not when joined with more than a hundred." "More than a hundred" means that when it is joined with two hundred, eight hundred, two thousand, eight thousand and so on, the final of dvi and aṣṭan does not become āt, as in dviśataṃ, two hundred, and aṣṭaśataṃ, eight hundred.

Again quoted in the commentary: "Also of aṣṭan, when kapāla or go follows." When kapāla or go comes after it, the final of aṣṭan becomes āt: aṣṭākapālaḥ, eight skull-cups, and aṣṭāgavaḥ, eight cattle.

tres trayaḥ. "Of tri, trayas." Tri, when a word expressing a number follows, becomes trayas. In tryadhikā daśa, deleting the case ending together with the anubandha, tri becomes trayas, and we get trayodaśa, thirteen, three more than ten. Likewise, in tryadhikā triṃśat, we get trayastriṃśat, thirty-three. When it is joined with more than a hundred it does not change: triśataṃ, three hundred; trisahasraṃ, three thousand.

vibhāṣā catvāriṃśatprabhṛtau sarveṣāṃ. "For all of them, optionally, from catvāriṃśat onward." From forty onward, when not joined with a hundred, a thousand and so on, the change of the final of dvi and aṣṭan to āt, the change of tri to trayas, and the rest are made optional: dvācatvāriṃśat or else dvicatvāriṃśat, forty-two. Likewise, aṣṭācatvāriṃśat or else aṣṭacatvāriṃśat, forty-eight; trayaścatvāriṃśat or else tricatvāriṃśat, forty-three. The same reasoning applies to all such cases.

Quoted in the commentary: "The final of eka becomes āt, or optionally uk." The final of eka joined with a number becomes āt, or optionally takes the augment uk. In ekādhikā daśa, one more than ten, we get ekādaśa, eleven, or ekodaśa. Likewise, ekānnaviṃśati, or else ekonaviṃśati, twenty lacking one, that is, nineteen, and so on.

Again quoted in the commentary: "For ṣa, u, and also ḍa." When ṣaṣ meets daśan, the letter ṣ becomes u and d also becomes ḍ. In ṣaḍadhikā daśa, deleting the case ending, we have ṣaṣ daśan; by this sūtra the latter ṣ becomes u; a with u takes guṇa and becomes o; d becomes ḍ; and we get ṣoḍaśa, sixteen.

With these, the tatpuruṣa compound has been explained. Now I shall explain the bahuvrīhi compound.

anekam anyapadārthe. "Several, in the sense of another word." Several words ending in sup enter into the meaning of another word ending in sup: two words, or many, may be compounded. Where it is not their explicitly stated meaning, a compound that joins several sup-endings into a single meaning, making the principal thing to be expressed some other meaning, connected with the meaning of those words but not explicitly stated, is called the bahuvrīhi compound.

saptamīviśeṣaṇe bahuvrīhau. "The seventh and the qualifier, in the bahuvrīhi." In this context of the bahuvrīhi compound, the seventh case receives special treatment. When two or more words are joined, if the former has the sense of the seventh case, it simply stays in front; and if, in the construction, the latter word has the sense of the seventh case, it is placed in front. This is a distinctive feature of the bahuvrīhi compound.

In prāptam udakaṃ yasya saḥ, deleting the case endings together with the anubandhas, we get prāptodako grāmaḥ (gloss: this one, to which the river has come; a village that has gained a river). Likewise, in ūḍho ratho yasya saḥ (gloss: the one whose chariot is drawn), we get ūḍharatho 'naḍvān (gloss: a draft ox that draws a chariot). In uddhṛtam odanaṃ yasya saḥ (gloss: the one whose food is set aside), we get uddhṛtaudanā (gloss: food set aside). In pītam ambaraṃ yasya saḥ (gloss: the one whose garment is yellow), we get pītāmbaro hariḥ (gloss: Hari of the yellow garment). In vīrāḥ puruṣakāḥ yasmin (gloss: the one in which are heroes and men), we get vīrapuruṣako grāmaḥ (gloss: a village of heroic men). Nīlojjvalavapuḥ. In uccaiḥ mukhaṃ yasya, we get uccairmukhaḥ (gloss: high-nosed; whose nose is high; whose face is pale; pale-faced). In kharasya mukham iva mukhaṃ yasya saḥ (gloss: this one whose face is like the face of a donkey), we get kharamukhaḥ (gloss: donkey-faced).

Quoted in the commentary: saptamyupamānapūrvapadasyottarapadalopaś ca. "And the deletion of the latter word when the former word is in the seventh case." In the construction, the latter word, which has a word in the seventh case near it and before it, is also to be deleted. In kare sthitaṃ dhanaṃ yasya saḥ (gloss: this one whose wealth rests in his hand), deleting sthitaṃ, the latter word near kare after the seventh case, and deleting the case ending together with its anubandha as well, we get karadhanaḥ (gloss: wealth in hand). The commentary also says that this deletion applies to words of collection and of making in the sixth case. In keśānāṃ saṅghātaḥ cūḍā yasya (gloss: whose topknot is a mass of hair), we get keśacūḍaḥ (gloss: a topknot of gathered hair; a topknot of equal hair). In suvarṇasya vikāro 'laṃkāro yasya saḥ (gloss: this one whose ornament is made of gold), we get suvarṇālaṃkāraḥ (gloss: a golden ornament).

striyāḥ puṃvad bhāṣitapuṃskād anūṅ samānādhikaraṇe striyām apūraṇīpriyādiṣu. "A feminine which has been stated as masculine, and which does not have ūṅ, is like the masculine when in apposition with a feminine, except before an ordinal, priyā and the like." A word ending in a suffix that forms the feminine gender, but which was earlier stated as having the masculine gender, where the suffix is not ūṅ, when it is in apposition, that is, in a word with a common substrate, and when no word ending in an ordinal suffix, or priyā and the like, follows it, has its vowels made short like the masculine. In citrā gāvaḥ yasya (gloss: whose cows are dappled), deleting the case endings together with the particles, by this sūtra the ā-final citrā becomes short, and we get citraguḥ (gloss: dappled). In rūpavatī bhāryā yasya (gloss: whose wife is beautiful), deleting the case endings together with the particles, we get rūpavadbhāryaḥ (gloss: a beautiful wife). If it was not earlier stated as having the masculine gender, it does not become short. In gaṅgā bhāryā yasya (gloss: whose wife is Gaṅgā), it does not become short, and we get gaṅgābhāryaḥ. With the suffix ūṅ: in brahmabandhūr bhāryā yasya (gloss: whose wife is a brahmin's daughter), it does not become short, and we get brahmabandhūbhāryaḥ (gloss: a beautiful wife; a wife who is a brahmin's daughter).

apūraṇīpramāṇyoḥ. "From pūraṇī and pramāṇī." From words ending in the ordinal suffix and from pramāṇa, which, as explained above, do not become short, the suffix ap is added at the end of the compound of words ending in the ordinal suffix and of the word pramāṇa. In kalyāṇī pañcamī yāsāṃ rātrīṇāṃ, compounding the case endings and so on, kalyāṇīpañcamī remains; giving the suffix ap, we get kalyāṇīpañcamā rātrayaḥ (gloss: those nights whose fifth is auspicious; nights whose fifth is auspicious). For pramāṇa: in strī pramāṇī yasya saḥ (gloss: this one whose authority is a woman), we get strīpramāṇaḥ (gloss: a woman as authority).

nadyṛtaś ca. "And from nadī and ṛt." After a final that bears the name nadī, and when a ṛt-final word follows, the suffix kap is also added at the end of the bahuvrīhi compound, and then the former becomes short, like a masculine. In kalyāṇī pañcamī yasya saḥ (gloss: this one whose fifth is auspicious), compounding the case endings and so on, kalyāṇīpañcamī remains; the suffix kap is given after the final ī that bears the name nadī, by its force the former becomes short, and we get kalyāṇipañcamīkaḥ. Likewise, from a ṛt-final: in bahavaḥ kartāro yasya (gloss: who has many makers; one with many makers), we get bahukartṛkaḥ. With priyā and the like: in kalyāṇī priyā yasya (gloss: whose beloved is auspicious; the beloved of an auspicious woman), it does not become short, and we get kalyāṇīpriyaḥ. Doing the construction, the manner of compounding and so on in the same way, we get: bhāryā manojñā, bhāryā kalyāṇī, bhāryā subhagā, bhāryā durbhagā, bhāryā samā, bhāryā capalā, bhāryā svā, kalyāṇī sacivā, bhāryā kāntā, bhāryā bhakṣī, kalyāṇī duhitā. (Gloss: a lovely wife; a virtuous wife; a fortunate wife; an unfortunate wife; an equal wife; a wife who has gained the root; a wealthy wife; a virtuous queen; a beautiful wife; a charming wife; a virtuous daughter.)

tasilādiṣv ā kṛtvasucaḥ. "Before tasil and the rest, up to kṛtvasuc." That is, those from tasil up to kṛtvasuc. Words joined with those ending in the taddhita suffixes from tasil up to kṛtvasuc also become like the masculine. In rūpavatī tasmāt, from that beautiful woman, deleting the fifth case ending, giving for that meaning the taddhita suffix tasil, the l and the i being named it, by this sūtra it becomes like the masculine, and we get rūpavattaḥ. Likewise, with the suffix kṛtvasuc: in rūpavatīṃ pañca kṛtvaḥ, we get rūpavatpañcakṛtvaḥ. Likewise, before the suffix caraṭ it also becomes like the masculine: in āḍhyā carī, we get āḍhyacarā.

Again quoted in the commentary: jātīyakalpadeśyadeśīyarūpyapāśādiṣu (gloss: from that beautiful woman). "Before jātīya, kalpa, deśya, deśīya, rūpya, pāśa and the like."

When these taddhita suffixes, jātīya and the rest, follow (gloss: five beautiful women), it also becomes like the masculine (gloss: a woman who behaves like a rich man; a woman who behaves like a rich man). In paṭvī jātīya, we get paṭujātīya. Likewise, in paṭvī kalpa, we get paṭukalpa. In paṭvī deśya, we get paṭudeśya. In paṭvī deśīya, we get paṭudeśīya. In paṭvī rūpya, we get paṭurūpya. In paṭvī pāśa, we get paṭupāśa.

The commentary also says, "It also becomes like the masculine before the suffixes tva and tal" (gloss: the class of learned women; the state of a learned woman; the state of a learned woman). So in paṭvī tva, we get paṭutvaṃ; likewise, in paṭvī tā, we get paṭutā. The commentary also says, "It also becomes like the masculine when the suffix śa follows." So in paṭvī śa, we get paṭuśaḥ.

Again quoted in the commentary: kukkuṭyādīnām aṇḍādiṣu. "Of kukkuṭī and the rest, before aṇḍa and the rest" (gloss: learnedness itself; the state of a learned woman). When aṇḍa and the rest follow, kukkuṭī and the rest become like the masculine. In kukkuṭyā aṇḍaṃ yasya (gloss: whose egg is a hen's), we get kukkuṭāṇḍaṃ (gloss: a hen's egg). Likewise, in mṛgyāḥ padaṃ yasya (gloss: whose foot is a doe's), we get mṛgapadaṃ (gloss: a doe's foot). In mṛgyāḥ kṣīraṃ yasya (gloss: whose milk is a doe's), we get mṛgakṣīraṃ (gloss: a doe's milk). In kākyāḥ śāvaḥ yasya (gloss: whose young is a female crow's), we get kākaśāvaḥ (gloss: a female crow's young).

kyaṅmāninoś ca. "And before kyaṅ and mānin." When kyaṅ, one of the suffixes that form nominal roots, follows, and when the word mānin follows, it also becomes like the masculine. In eṇī iva ācarati, she fancies herself like a doe (gloss: a woman who fancies herself like a doe), we get eṇāyate. In darśanīyāṃ mānaṃ yasya, we get darśanīyamāninī (gloss: whose thought is that she is fair to see; thinking herself fair to see).

na kopadhāyāḥ. "Not of one with k as its penultimate." A word that has the taddhita k as its penultimate does not become like the masculine. In pācikā bhāryā yasya, we get pācikābhāryaḥ. Likewise, in rasikā bhāryā yasya, we get rasikābhāryaḥ. In madrikā bhāryā yasya, we get madrikābhāryaḥ. Even when it is the taddhita suffix k, if it is aka, it becomes like the masculine: in pākā bhāryā yasya (gloss: whose wife is a cook; a wife who cooks), we get pākabhāryaḥ (gloss: whose wife is accomplished; a famed wife; whose wife is good; a good wife).

saṃjñāpūraṇyoś ca. "And of a name and an ordinal." A word with a suffix having the sense of a woman's name or of an ordinal does not become like the masculine. In dattā bhāryā yasya (gloss: whose wife is a cook; a cooking wife), we get dattābhāryaḥ. Likewise, in pañcamī bhāryā yasya, we get pañcamībhāryaḥ (gloss: whose wife is Dattā; the wife Dattā; whose wife is the fifth; the fifth wife).

vṛddhinimittasya ca taddhitasyāraktavikāre. "And of a taddhita that is a cause of vṛddhi, when it does not mean dyeing red." Before a taddhita suffix, such as one with the anubandha ñ or ṇ, which is a cause of vṛddhi arising in the preceding stem and which does not have the sense of coloring red, it also does not become like the masculine. In a case such as sraughnī bhāryā yasya (gloss: the taddhita aṇ; whose wife is a woman of the land of Srughna; a wife from the land of Srughna), it does not become short, and we get sraughnībhāryaḥ. Likewise, in māthurī bhāryā yasya (gloss: whose wife is from the land of Mathurā; the taddhita yan, pan; a wife from the land of Mathurā), we get māthurībhāryaḥ.

svāṅgāc ceto 'mānini. "And from a part of one's own body, of what ends in īt, when mānin does not follow." Words of the feminine gender ending in īt that express a part of one's own body also do not become like the masculine when mānin does not follow. In sukeśī bhāryā yasya (gloss: whose wife has beautiful hair), we get sukeśībhāryaḥ (gloss: a wife with beautiful hair). When mānin follows, even though it is a part of one's own body, it becomes like the masculine: in sukeśī māninī yasya (gloss: who thinks herself beautiful-haired; thinking herself beautiful-haired), we get sukeśamāninī.

jāteś ca. "And of a class." A word of the feminine gender ending in ṅīṣ that expresses a class also does not become like the masculine. In brāhmaṇī bhāryā yasya (gloss: whose wife is a brahmin woman; a brahmin wife), it does not become short, and we get brāhmaṇībhāryaḥ.

saṃkhyayāvyayāsannādūrādhikasaṃkhyāḥ saṃkhyeye. "With a number: indeclinables, āsanna, adūra, adhika and numbers, in the sense of what is counted." When a number is joined with an indeclinable, with āsanna, adūra or adhika, or when numbers are joined with numbers, these too form a bahuvrīhi compound of a single meaning.

bahuvrīhau saṃkhyeye ḍac abahugaṇāt. "In the bahuvrīhi, ḍac for a number, except after bahu and gaṇa." At the end of a bahuvrīhi compound, the suffix ḍac is added to a number word that is not bahu or gaṇa. In upagatāḥ daśa yeṣāṃ te (gloss: those to whom ten have come near), by the earlier sūtra just explained, deleting the case endings together with the particles, we have upadaśan. By this sūtra, ḍac; the c is deleted as one of cu, ṭu and the rest; by the elision of ṭi, an is deleted; ḍ is deleted because it serves that purpose; with jas, we get upadaśāḥ (gloss: the near tens).

ti viṃśater ḍiti. "The ti of viṃśati, before what has ḍ as it." When a suffix that has ḍ as its it follows, not only is the ṭi of viṃśati elided, but ti too is elided. In āsannaḥ viṃśatiḥ yasya, by the sūtra on numbers with indeclinables, āsanna and the rest, the case endings are deleted together with the particles; by "in the bahuvrīhi," ḍac; by this sūtra, ti is deleted; because ḍ is it, ṭi is deleted; and we get āsannaviṃśāḥ. Likewise, in adūraḥ viṃśatiḥ yasya (gloss: whose seat is twenty; the near twenty), we get adūraviṃśāḥ (gloss: whose not-far is twenty). In adhikaḥ viṃśatiḥ yasya, we get adhikaviṃśāḥ (gloss: whose surplus is twenty; twenty more). For a number joined with a number: in dvau trayo vā mānaṃ yeṣāṃ te (gloss: those whose measure is two or three), deleting the case endings, particles and so on, with ḍac, we get dvitrāḥ. After bahu and gaṇa, ḍac does not apply: in upa bahu yasya (gloss: who has many near), we get upabahavaḥ (gloss: the many near). Likewise, in upagaṇo yasya (gloss: whose group is near, two or three), we get upagaṇāḥ.

Quoted in the commentary: saṃkhyāyās tatpuruṣasya ḍac. "Ḍac for a tatpuruṣa with a number."

Not only in the bahuvrīhi: the suffix ḍac also comes at the end of a tatpuruṣa compound with a number. In nirgatāni triṃśataḥ aṅgulibhyaḥ, deleting the case endings together with the particles, we have nistriṃśat (gloss: a group near); with ḍac, and the ṭi deleted, we get nistriṃśaḥ (gloss: bad, thirty fingers).

diṅnāmāny antarāle. "Names of directions, for an intermediate quarter." When it expresses the name of an intermediate quarter, such as "south-east," a bahuvrīhi compound is also formed. In dakṣiṇasyāḥ pūrvasyāḥ antarālaṃ, deleting the case endings together with the particles, we get dakṣiṇapūrvaḥ (gloss: bad, thirty; the quarter between south and east; south-east).

tatra tenedam iti sarūpe. "'There,' 'by that,' 'this,' when of the same form." In the domain of battle, words ending in sup that express "seized there" and "this, struck by that," when they are of the same form, form a bahuvrīhi compound of a single meaning.

anyeṣām api dṛśyate. "It is seen in others as well." Not only are the meanings just explained complete and of a single meaning; in addition, the final of the former stem in the compound, whatever vowel it is, when what follows does not begin with a vowel, also becomes a final long ā.

ic karmavyatihāre. "Ic, for an action of battle." The suffix ic is added at the end of a bahuvrīhi compound in the sense of battle. In keśeṣu keśeṣu gṛhītvā idaṃ yuddhaṃ pravṛttam (gloss: the way this fierce fight went, seizing by the hair and by the hair), by the sūtra "there, by that, this" and so on, the case endings are deleted together with the particles, giving keśa keśa; by the sūtra "it is seen in others as well," the short a of the former stem becomes āt; by this sūtra, ic; and we get keśākeśi (gloss: a hair-fight). Likewise, in daṇḍaiś ca daṇḍaiś ca idaṃ yuddhaṃ pravṛttam (gloss: the way this fierce fight went, seizing staffs and staffs), we get daṇḍādaṇḍi (gloss: a staff-fight). In muṣṭibhiḥ muṣṭibhiḥ idaṃ yuddhaṃ pravṛttam (gloss: the way this fierce fight went, with fists and fists), we get muṣṭāmuṣṭi (gloss: a fist-fight).

or guṇaḥ. "Guṇa of u." When a taddhita suffix comes after a stem that ends in the letter u, that u becomes guṇa. In bāhubhiḥ bāhubhiḥ idaṃ yuddhaṃ pravṛttam (gloss: the way this fierce fight went, with arms and arms), deleting the case endings, particles and so on as above, the former stem takes āt, then ic, by this sūtra guṇa, and we get bāhābāhavi (gloss: an arm-fight). In asibhiḥ asibhiḥ idaṃ yuddhaṃ pravṛttam (gloss: the way this fierce fight went, with knives and knives), compounding the case endings and so on, since what follows the final of this former stem is a vowel, it does not become ā; with ic, we get asyasi (gloss: a knife-fight). If they are not of the same form, the compound does not apply: for example, in a case like halena muśalena idaṃ yuddhaṃ pravṛttam (gloss: the way this fierce fight went, with a plough and with a pestle), the compound does not apply.

tena saheti tulyayoge. "'With that,' saha, in an equal connection." When saha, in an equal connection, is joined with a word ending in the third case, "with that," it forms a bahuvrīhi compound of a single meaning.

vopasarjanasya. "Optionally, of the subordinate." In this context of the bahuvrīhi compound, saha also optionally becomes sa, and what becomes sa is given the name upasarjana, the subordinate. The purpose of this is to place sa before whatever the stem is. In putreṇa sahaḥ, by the earlier sūtra "with that, saha," the case endings are compounded, and by this sūtra it is made optional, so we get saputraḥ or putrasahaḥ (gloss: with a son). Likewise, in karmakeṇa sahaḥ, we get karmakasahaḥ or sakarmakaḥ (gloss: with action; with action; with action). In lomakena sahaḥ, we get salomakaḥ or lomakasahaḥ (gloss: with thu; with hair; with a deceiver).

bahuvrīhau sakthyakṣṇoḥ svāṅgāt ṣac. "In the bahuvrīhi, from sakthi and akṣi, when expressing beauty of form, ṣac." At the end of a bahuvrīhi compound, after sakthi and akṣi expressing the sense of beauty of form, the suffix ṣac is added. In dīrghasakthiḥ yasya (gloss: whose spear is long), compounding the particles and so on, giving ṣac, deleting the c by the rule on cu, ṭu and the rest, and deleting the ṣ because it bears the name it, we get dīrghasakthaḥ (gloss: a long spear). Likewise, in puṇḍarīkam iva akṣiṇī yasya saḥ (gloss: whose eyes are like a white lotus), we get puṇḍarīkākṣaḥ. In jalam iva akṣiṇī yasya saḥ (gloss: whose eyes are like water), we get jalākṣaḥ (gloss: a water-eye). If it does not have the sense of beauty of form, ṣac does not apply: in sthūle akṣiṇī yasya (gloss: whose eyes are coarse), compounding the case endings, particles and so on, ṣac does not apply, and we get sthūlākṣi (gloss: coarse-eyed).

aṅguler dāruṇi. "Of aṅguli, for wood." At the end of a bahuvrīhi compound, the suffix ṣac is added to the word aṅgula when it expresses the sense of wood. In pañca aṅgulayaḥ yasya (gloss: which has five limbs), compounding the case endings and so on, with ṣac, we get pañcāṅgulaṃ dāru (gloss: wood with five limbs).

dvitribhyāṃ mūrdhnaḥ. "From dvi and tri, of mūrdhan." At the end of a bahuvrīhi compound, the suffix ṣac is added to mūrdhan following dvi and tri. In dvau mūrdhānau yasya (gloss: whose heads are two), deleting the case endings and so on, giving ṣac and deleting the ṭi, we get dvimūrdhaḥ (gloss: two-headed). Likewise, in trayo mūrdhānaḥ yasya (gloss: whose heads are three), we get trimūrdhaḥ (gloss: three-headed).

antarbahirbhyāṃ ca lomnaḥ. "And from antar and bahis, of loman." At the end of a bahuvrīhi compound, the suffix ap is added to loman following antar and bahis. In antar lomāni yasya saḥ (gloss: whose hair is inside), compounding the case endings, particles and so on, giving ap, the p bearing the name it, and deleting the ṭi, we get antarlomaḥ (gloss: inner hair). Likewise, in bahir lomāni yasya saḥ (gloss: whose hair is outside), we get bahirlomaḥ (gloss: outer hair).

ac nāsikāyāḥ saṃjñāyāṃ nasaṃ cāsthūlāt. "Ac for nāsikā, in a name, and nasa, when it is not after sthūla." When nāsikā, not preceded by the word sthūla, expresses a name, the suffix ac is added at the end of the bahuvrīhi compound, and then nāsikā itself becomes nasa.

pūrvapadāt saṃjñāyām agaḥ. "From a former word, in a name, when it is not g."

In this context of the bahuvrīhi compound, if the former word contains a letter that is a cause for n becoming ṇ, then even though it is not a single word, and even if letters other than g stand between, n becomes ṇ. In durnāsikā yasya, the case endings and so on are deleted; by the previous sūtra ac is added and nāsikā becomes nasa; by this sūtra n becomes ṇ, giving durṇasaḥ. Likewise, in khare iva nāsikā yasya, we get kharaṇasaḥ (gloss: barṇāḥ). When sthūla stands before it, it does not become nasa: in sthūlā nāsikā yasya (gloss: whose nose is like a bu gang na pa), it does not become nasa; ac is added, giving sthūlanāsikaḥ. The commentary cites (gloss: or an unlovely nose; whose nose is like a donkey's):

khurakharābhyāṃ vā. "Or from khura and khara." (gloss: a hoof, a donkey nose.) When khura and khara are the former words, nāsikā becomes nasa, and ac is optional. In khure iva nāsikā yasya (gloss: whose nose is thick), the case endings and so on are compounded; nāsikā becomes nasa; ac is made optional, giving khurṇāḥ and khurṇasaḥ (gloss: a thick nose).

upasargāc ca. "And from a preverb." After a preverb, nāsikā too becomes nasa, and ac is optional. (gloss: whose nose is like a hoof.)

upasargād bahulam. "From a preverb, variously." In this context of the bahuvrīhi compound, if the preverb contains a letter that is a cause for n becoming ṇ, then the n in some cases becomes ṇ and in some cases does not, and so on; it occurs variously (gloss: a nose like a hoof). In prakarṣeṇa nāsikā yasya, the case endings and so on are compounded; by the previous sūtra nāsikā becomes nasa and ac is added; by this sūtra n becomes ṇ, giving praṇasaḥ. Likewise, in uccaiḥ nāsikā yasya, we get unnasaḥ. The commentary cites:

veḥ graḥ. "Gra after vi." When the preverb vi comes first, nāsikā becomes gra: in vigatā nāsikā yasya (gloss: whose nose is very beautiful), we get vigraḥ (gloss: noseless; an excellent nose).

nañduḥsubhyo halisakthyor anyatarasyām (gloss: whose nose is high; a high nose). "From nañ, dur and su, optionally for hali and sakthi." When nañ, dur and su precede hali and sakthi, ac is optionally added at the end of the bahuvrīhi compound (gloss: whose nose has gone awry). In na haliḥ yasya, the particles and so on are deleted, and ac is made optional, giving ahalam and ahaliḥ. Likewise, in na sakthi yasya, we get asakthaḥ and asakthiḥ; and suhalaḥ, suhaliḥ, susakthiḥ, duḥhalaḥ, duḥhaliḥ, duḥsakthaḥ, duḥsakthiḥ. (glosses: whose has no plough; without a plough; whose has no spear; without a spear; a good or fine plough; a good or lovely spear; a bad plough; a bad plough; a bad spear.)

nityam asic prajāmedhayoḥ. "Always asic for prajā and medhā." When nañ, dur and su come before prajā and medhā, the suffix asic is always added at the end of the bahuvrīhi compound. In na prajā yasya, the case endings, anubandhas and so on are deleted; of asic, c is the anubandha and i is for pronunciation, giving aprajāḥ (jas). Likewise, in duḥprajā yasya we get duḥprajāḥ (jas); in suprajā yasya, suprajāḥ (jas); in na medhā yasya, amedhāḥ (jas); in duḥmedhā yasya (gloss: whose has no offspring), durmedhāḥ (jas); and in sumedhā yasya, sumedhāḥ. (glosses: without offspring: asic, su; whose people are bad: asic, su, bad people; whose people are good: asic, su, good people; whose has no intelligence: asic, su, without intelligence; whose intelligence is poor: asic, su, poor intelligence; whose intelligence is good: good intelligence.)

dharmād anic kevalāt. "Anic from dharma, after one alone." In this context of the bahuvrīhi compound, the suffix anic is added to dharma when one word, any word at all, stands before it, not two or three. In kalyāṇo dharmo yasya, the case endings, particles and so on are compounded; anic is added; c is the anubandha and i is for pronunciation, giving kalyāṇadharmā. An example in which anic is not added when two words or more are present: in supradharmo yasya (gloss: whose Dharma is excellent), the case endings, particles and so on are deleted, giving supradharmaḥ (gloss: su, whose Dharma is through virtue; pra, an excellent Dharma).

dakṣiṇermā lubdhayoge. "Dakṣiṇermā, in connection with a striker." (gloss: Dharma, virtuous. With su after dharman, the upadhā is lengthened and the n at the end of the name is deleted.) Dakṣiṇermā is a bahuvrīhi compound given as a set form, said of a deer wounded on the flank, as if struck by an arrow.

prasambhyāṃ jānunor jñuḥ. "After pra and sam, jñu for jānu." In this context of the bahuvrīhi compound, when the preverbs pra and sam come first, the word jānu becomes jñu (gloss: a deer whose right flank is struck). In pragate jānunī yasya, the case endings, particles and so on are compounded and jānu becomes jñu, giving prajñuḥ. Likewise, in saṃjānunī yasya, we get saṃjñuḥ. The commentary cites:

ūrdhvād vibhāṣā. "Optionally after ūrdhva." After ūrdhva as the former word, jānu likewise becomes jñu or does not (glosses: a swift knee; one with reeds; knees excellent; whose knees are good). In ūrdhve jānunī yasya, we get ūrdhvajānuḥ, or else ūrdhvajñuḥ (gloss: good knees).

dhanuṣaś ca. "And of dhanus." In this context of the bahuvrīhi compound, the end of the word dhanus becomes anaṅ. In śārṅgaṃ dhanur yasya, the case endings, particles and so on are compounded (gloss: whose knees are thick); the end becomes anaṅ; ṅ is the anubandha and the vowel a of na is for pronunciation (gloss: thick knees), giving śārṅgadhanvā.

jāyāyā niṅ. "Niṅ for jāyā." The end of the word jāyā, when a bahuvrīhi compound has been made, becomes niṅ. In yuvatir jāyā yasya (gloss: of a thin bow), the case endings, particles and so on are deleted; the ā is removed from yā and becomes niṅ, with ṅ as the anubandha, giving yuvajāniḥ, with su. (gloss: dhanus is changed to anaṅ; with su, the upadhā of n is lengthened; su is deleted by the rule on hal and so on; the n at the end of the name is deleted; yaṇ replaces ik before ac. A thin bow.)

lopo vyor vali. "Deletion of v and y before val." (gloss: whose wife is young.)

Of a root or a non-root, a vowelless y and a vowelless v are deleted when any letter of the group val follows, giving yuvajāniḥ. Likewise, in lakṣmīr jāyā yasya, we get lakṣmījāniḥ.

gandhasyed utpūtisusurabhibhyaḥ. "I for gandha after ut, pūti, su and surabhi." When ut and the others come first, the a at the end of the word gandha becomes it in this context of the bahuvrīhi compound (glosses: of one whose wife is youthful; whose daughter is this fortunate and glorious one, or this excellent one; a fortunate, heroic daughter). In udgandho yasya, the case endings and so on are deleted, and a becomes it, giving udgandhiḥ. Likewise, in pūtir gandho yasya, we get pūtigandhiḥ; in sugandho yasya, sugandhiḥ; and in surabhir gandho yasya, surabhigandhiḥ.

alpākhyāyām. "When smallness is expressed." The end of gandha, when connected with the sense of expressing smallness, also becomes it in this context of the bahuvrīhi compound (glosses: whose scent pervades; a pervading scent; whose scent is pure; a pure scent; whose scent is good; a good scent; whose scent is of the yak; yak scent). In ghṛtasya gandho yasya, we get ghṛtagandhiḥ.

upamānāc ca. "And for a comparison." The end of gandha, when it expresses the sense of a comparison, also becomes it: in padmasyeva gandho yasya, we get padmagandhiḥ.

pādasya lopo 'hastyādibhyaḥ. "Deletion of pāda, except after hastin and the rest." (glosses: whose scent is of butter; butter scent.) In this context of the bahuvrīhi compound, except after hastin and the others, the end of pāda is deleted. In vyāghrasya pādāv iva pādau yasya (gloss: whose scent is like a lotus's), the case endings, particles and so on and the end of pāda are deleted, giving vyāghrapād. For hastin and the rest: in hastinaḥ pādāv iva pādau yasya, the case endings, particles and so on are deleted, but the end of pāda is not, giving hastipādaḥ (gloss: whose feet are like a tiger's feet). Likewise, in kusūlapādo yasya, we get kusūlapādaḥ.

kumbhapadīṣu ca. "And in kumbhapadī and the rest." (gloss: tiger feet.) At the end of a bahuvrīhi compound, for kumbhapāda and the others, when a woman is spoken of, pāda becomes pad and, with ṅīp added, kumbhapadī and the rest are to be taken as set forms (glosses: whose feet are like an elephant's feet; an elephant's feet; whose feet are crooked; crooked feet). In kumbhasya pādāv iva pādau yasya, the case endings and so on are compounded, giving kumbhapādaḥ; when a woman is spoken of, by this rule we get kumbhapadī (gloss: a pot-footed woman). Likewise, in śataṃ pādā yasya (gloss: whose feet are a hundred), we get śatapādaḥ (hundred-footed) and śatapadī (a hundred-footed female).

saṃkhyāsupūrvasya. "Of one preceded by a number or su." (glosses: whose feet are like a pot's feet; pot-footed.) The end of pāda preceded by number words or by the preverb su is also deleted in this context of the bahuvrīhi compound: in dvau pādau yasya, we get dvipāt and dvipād. Likewise, in sahasraṃ pādā yasya, we get sahasrapāt; and in supādo yasya, we get supāt and supād.

vayasi dantasya datṛ. "Datṛ for danta, for age." In this context of the bahuvrīhi compound, danta connected with the sense of expressing age becomes datṛ when su or a number comes before it (glosses: whose feet are two; two feet; whose feet are a thousand; a thousand feet; a thousand feet; a thousand feet; whose feet are beautiful; beautiful feet). In dvau dantau yasya, the case endings and so on are deleted, and danta becomes datṛ; the anubandhas ṛ and uk serve the purpose of num, giving dvidan. Likewise, in catvāro dantā yasya, we get caturdan; likewise, in ṣaḍ dantā yasya, ṣoḍan; and in sudantā yasya, sudan. (glosses: whose teeth are two; with su after datṛ, since num is the purpose of the anubandhas ṛ and uk, they are deleted; su is deleted by the rule on hal and so on; the r is deleted, being due for deletion as the end of a conjunct; two teeth; whose teeth are four; four-toothed; whose teeth are six; six-toothed, that is, a horse or a donkey; whose teeth are beautiful; with beautiful teeth, that is, in the prime of youth.) When it does not have the sense of age, it does not become datṛ: in dvau dantau yasya, we get dvidantakarī (gloss: two-tusked, that is, an elephant).

agrāntaśuddhaśubhravṛṣavarāhebhyaś ca. "Also from agra, anta, śuddha, śubhra, vṛṣa and varāha." When agra and these others come first, danta optionally becomes datṛ in this context of the bahuvrīhi compound. In kuḍmalāgradanto yasya, the case endings and so on are deleted, and since danta optionally becomes datṛ, we get kuḍmalāgradantaḥ and kuḍmalāgradan. Likewise, in śuddho danto yasya, we get śuddhadantaḥ and śuddhadan; in śubhro danto yasya, śubhradantaḥ and śubhradan (gloss: white teeth); in vṛṣasya danto yasya, vṛṣadantaḥ and vṛṣadan (glosses: whose teeth have curved tips; whose teeth are a bull's; bull's teeth; curved tooth tips); and in varāhasya danto yasya, varāhadantaḥ and varāhadan (glosses: whose teeth are a boar's; whose are pure; pure teeth; whose teeth are white; boar's teeth). In the commentary, by the word "also" it is explained that this happens optionally after mūṣaka and ahi as well: in mūṣakasya danto yasya, we get mūṣakadantaḥ and mūṣakadan; likewise, in aher danto yasya, ahidantaḥ and ahidan. (glosses: hand teeth; whose teeth are a mouse's; mouse teeth; mouse teeth; mouse teeth; whose teeth are a snake's; snake teeth; snake teeth.)

kakudasyāvasthāyāṃ lopaḥ. "Deletion for kakuda, for a stage of life." In this context of the bahuvrīhi compound, the end of the word kakuda connected with the sense of a stage of life is deleted. In ajātaṃ kakudaṃ yasya, the case endings and so on are deleted and the end of kakuda is deleted too, giving ajātakakud and ajātakakut. Likewise, in pūrṇaṃ kakudaṃ yasya, we get pūrṇakakud and pūrṇakakut.

udvibhyāṃ kakudasya. "Of kakuda after ut and vi." (gloss: whose hump is full.) In this context of the bahuvrīhi compound, when the preverbs ut and vi come first, the end of the word kakuda is also deleted (glosses: a hump not full, that is, a small child; whose hump is full; a full hump, that is, in the prime of youth). In utkakudaṃ yasya, we get utkakud and utkakut. Likewise, in vikakudaṃ yasya, we get vikakut and vikakud.

suhṛddurhṛdau mitrāmitrayoḥ. "Suhṛd and durhṛd, for friend and enemy."

When a friend or an enemy is spoken of, in this context of the bahuvrīhi compound, hṛdaya preceded by the preverbs su and dur becomes hṛt (glosses: whose hump is clear; a clear hump; a prominent hump; whose hump is excessive; an excessive hump). In suhṛdayaṃ mitraṃ yasya, we get suhṛd and suhṛt. Likewise, in durhṛdayaḥ śatrur yasya, we get durhṛt and durhṛd.

uraḥprabhṛtibhyaḥ kap. "Kap from uras and the rest." At the end of a bahuvrīhi compound with uras and the others, the suffix kap is added (glosses: whose heart-friend is good; a dear one, a heart-friend, or a confidant; whose enemy is ill-minded; whose chest is broad; vyūḍhaḥ; an enemy, or ill-minded). In vyūḍham uro yasya, the case endings and so on are deleted and kap is added, with p as the anubandha. Since it was stated above that the s of what is not a taddhita is deleted, and this is a taddhita k, it is not deleted, giving vyūḍhoraskaḥ. Likewise, in priyaṃ sarpir yasya, we get priyasarpiṣkaḥ.

inaḥ striyām. "From in, in the feminine." From a word ending in in at the end of a bahuvrīhi compound, when the feminine is spoken of, kap is added as suffix. In bahavo daṇḍino yasmin deśe, the case endings, anubandhas and so on are deleted (glosses: broad; whose joy is fresh butter; joy, fresh butter); kap is given, with p as the anubandha; the n at the end of the name, being due for deletion, is deleted; ṭāp is given, giving bahudaṇḍikā.

na kapi. This is the rule on kap. In general, by the rule "short before k, of aṇ," the long vowels of the group aṇ become short before the suffix k; but, as an exception, they do not become short before the suffix kap. In bahvyo lakṣmyo yasmin deśe (glosses: a region with many staff-bearers; many female staff-bearers), the case endings and so on are compounded; by "and for those ending in nadī and ṛ," kap is added; by this sūtra the vowel does not become short, giving bahulakṣmīkā.

śeṣād vibhāṣā. "Optionally from the remainder." Except for what has already been explained for the feminine, the remainder: from this sūtra on, for both the feminine and the non-feminine, kap is optionally given or not given (gloss: a region of many excellences; many glorious women). In bahavo daṇḍino yasmin deśe, the case endings and so on are compounded, and since kap is made optional, we get bahudaṇḍikaḥ, or else bahudaṇḍī.

āpo 'nyatarasyām. "Optionally of āp." Although it was generally explained that aṇ does not become short before the suffix kap, as an exception to that, what ends in āp optionally becomes short before the suffix kap (glosses: a region of many staff-bearers; many staff-bearers; many staff-bearers; with su after daṇḍin, the n is lengthened by the rule on in, han and so on, and the n at the end of the name and su are deleted by the rule on na and so on). In bahvyo mālā yasya (gloss: whose garlands are many), the case endings and so on are deleted; by "optionally from the remainder," kap is made optional; and on the side where it is given, since by this sūtra the vowel is optionally shortened or not, we get bahumālakaḥ, bahumālākaḥ and bahumālaḥ (gloss: many garlands). Further, the commentary explains that even what does not end in āp, if it ends in ā, is optionally shortened before kap. So in susomapā yasya, the deletion of the case endings and so on being accomplished as above, we get susomapakaḥ, susomapākaḥ and susomapāḥ (gloss: many garlands).

na saṃjñāyām. "Not in a name." This is the rule on names. When the name of any thing is expressed, kap is not added at the end of the bahuvrīhi compound (gloss: whose is this one who drinks the good and the peaceful). In viśve devā asya, the anubandhas and so on are deleted and kap does not apply (glosses: one who drinks the good and the peaceful; one who drinks well the peaceful; drinks well the peaceful), giving viśvadevaḥ.

īyasaś ca. "And of īyas." With a word formed with the suffix īyas, kap is likewise not added at the end of a bahuvrīhi compound (gloss: these gods of every kind). In bahavaḥ śreyāṃso 'sya, the case endings and so on are deleted and kap does not apply, giving bahuśreyān (gloss: gods of every kind).

vandite bhrātuḥ. "Of bhrātṛ, when praised." From bhrātṛ expressing the sense of praise, kap is not added at the end of the bahuvrīhi compound (gloss: these many virtuous ones). In subhrātā yasya, the case endings and so on are deleted, and kap does not apply (gloss: with su after bhrātṛ, by "for those with the anubandha uk" and so on, num is added, whose purpose is the u; the upadhā is lengthened; the end of the conjunct, being due for deletion, the s is deleted; su is deleted by the rule on hal and so on; many glorious ones), giving subhrātā. When it does not have the sense of praise, kap is added: in mūrkho bhrātā yasya (gloss: whose brother is good), the case endings and so on are deleted and kap is given, giving mūrkhabhrātṛkaḥ.

sarvanāmasaṃkhyayoḥ. "Of pronouns and numbers." In a bahuvrīhi compound, sarva and the other pronouns and the number words, whichever of two or three words is present (glosses: a good brother; whose brother is foolish), are placed before those words (gloss: a foolish brother). In sarvaḥ śveto 'pi vidyate yasya saḥ, we get sarvaśvetaḥ (all white). Likewise, in dvau śuklau vidyete yasya (gloss: whose two are white), we get dviśuklaḥ (two white).

nendvādibhyaḥ. "Not from indu and the rest." In general, in this context of the bahuvrīhi compound, if a word that has taken the seventh case is later in the word order of the phrase, then once the compound is finished it must be placed first; but, as an exception, indu and the rest are not moved to the latter position (gloss: whose this is all white). In indur mūle yasya, the case endings and so on are deleted, and although the seventh case was given to mūle, indu is not moved after it, giving indumūliḥ. Likewise, in indur śekhare yasya, we get induśekharaḥ; in śaṅkhaḥ pāṇau yasya, śaṅkhapāṇiḥ; in cakraṃ pāṇau yasya (gloss: whose root has the moon), cakrapāṇiḥ; in vajraṃ pāṇau vidyate yasya saḥ, vajrapāṇiḥ; in padmaṃ pāṇau vidyate yasya saḥ (glosses: the moon at the root; whose forehead has the moon), padmapāṇiḥ; and in padmaṃ nābhau vidyate yasya (glosses: the moon at the forehead; whose hand holds a conch; conch in hand; whose hand holds a wheel; wheel in hand; who has a vajra in hand), padmanābhiḥ (glosses: Vajrapāṇi, vajra in hand; who has a lotus in hand).

niṣṭhā. "Niṣṭhā."

What has a suffix with the name niṣṭhā, expressing the sense of past from the root, that is, the suffixes kta and ktavatu, is likewise not placed later in this context of the bahuvrīhi compound (glosses: lotus in hand; whose navel has a lotus; a lotus at the navel). In kṛtaḥ kaṭo yasya, the case endings, anubandhas and so on are deleted, giving kṛtakaṭaḥ.

vāhitāgnyādiṣu. "Optionally in āhita, agni and the rest." Although it is generally explained that what has a suffix with the name niṣṭhā is placed as the former word, as an exception, what ends in a niṣṭhā suffix and is joined with āhita, agni and the rest is optionally placed later (glosses: whose was made by a god; made by a god). In agnir āhito yasya, the case endings and so on are compounded, and since the word ending in the suffix kta is optionally moved to the front or not, we get agnyāhitaḥ and āhitāgniḥ. Likewise, in putro jāto yasya, we get putrajātaḥ (gloss: a son is born) and jātaputraḥ.

The commentary says: "The bahuvrīhi compound has two divisions: that whose qualities are not its own, and that whose qualities are its own." (glosses: by whom a fire offering was made in the fire; a fire offering made in the fire; a fire offering made in the fire; to whom a son is born.) An example of that whose qualities are not its own: in bahu dhanaṃ yasmin, the case endings and so on are compounded, giving bahudhanaḥ; in asti dhanaṃ yasya, astidhanaḥ. An example of that whose qualities are its own: in lambau karṇau yasya, lambakarṇaḥ; likewise, in mahāprajñā yasya, mahāprajñaḥ.

iti bahuvrīhisamāsaḥ samāptaḥ. With these, the bahuvrīhi compound has been explained. (glosses: in whom there is much wealth; much wealth; whose wealth exists; wealth exists; whose two ears are long; long ears; whose wisdom is great; great wisdom.)

Now the dvandva compound will be explained.

cārthe dvandvaḥ. "Dvandva in the sense of 'and'." The compounding of many words ending in case endings in the sense of "and" is called the dvandva compound. It has four divisions: the sense of gathering while remaining separate (samuccaya), the sense of an accompaniment while remaining separate (anvācaya), the sense of mutual connection (itaretarayoga), and the sense of collective aggregation (samāhāra). Of these four, mutual connection and collective aggregation take the dvandva compound, because they are capable of any action; but the senses connected with the two, gathering while remaining separate and accompaniment while remaining separate, do not take the dvandva compound, because they are isolated from the action.

dvandve ghi. "Ghi in the dvandva." In this context of the dvandva compound, the words that were given the name ghi above, by "the rest, not sakhi, is ghi," are placed first. In hariś ca haraś ca, the word named ghi is placed first in this way; then the case endings, particles and so on are compounded, and with au we get hariharau. Likewise, in paṭuś ca guptaś ca, we get paṭuguptau. The commentary explains that if the compounding of case endings is between one word named ghi and one not named ghi, the one named ghi is placed first; but where many words are arranged, it is not fixed to one order (glosses: Hari and Hara too; Hari and Hara; the skilled and the hidden too; the skilled and the hidden). For example, in hariś ca haraś ca guruś ca, "Hari and Hara and the teacher," with jas we get hariharaguravaḥ (gloss: Hari, Hara and the teachers): here, although guru is named ghi, it comes after hara.

ajādyadantam. "What begins with ac and ends in at." In this context of the dvandva compound, a word that has an ac, that is, any vowel, at its beginning and at at its end is placed first. In īśaś ca kṛṣṇaś ca, we get īśakṛṣṇau. Here too, as was explained above for the words named ghi, where many names are arranged it is not fixed to one order. For example, in aśvaś ca rathaś ca indraś ca, we get aśvarathendrāḥ, with indra coming after ratha. The commentary cites (glosses: Īśvara and Kṛṣṇa; Īśvara and Kṛṣṇa):

"After a word that begins with ac and ends in at, the word named ghi follows." When a word beginning with ac and ending in at and a word named ghi come together, the one named ghi is placed after (glosses: horse, chariot and Indra; horse, chariot, Indra). In indraś ca agniś ca, with au we get indrāgnī, with agni, the word named ghi, coming after. Likewise, in indraś ca vāyuś ca, with au we get indravāyū. If a word begins with ac but does not end in at, there is no rule fixing it first: in vṛkṣaś ca aśvaś ca (glosses: Indra and fire; Indra and fire), we get vṛkṣāśvau.

alpāctaram. "What has fewer ac." (glosses: Indra and wind; Indra and wind.) In this context of the dvandva compound, of two words with fewer and with more vowels, the one with fewer is placed first (gloss: tree and mare). In śivaś ca keśavaś ca (gloss: tree and mare), we get śivakeśavau. Where many words are arranged, it is not fixed: in śaṅkhaś ca dundubhiś ca vīṇā ca, we get śaṅkhadundubhivīṇāḥ. The commentary cites:

laghvakṣaraṃ pūrvam. "A light syllable first." (glosses: Śiva and the slayer of the asuras; Śiva and the slayer of the asuras.) In this context of the dvandva compound, of a long and a short vowel, the short is placed first (glosses: conch, drum and sweet-sounding lute; conch, drum, lute). In kuśaś ca kāśaś ca, the grasses kuśa and kāśa, the case endings and so on are deleted, giving kuśakāśam. The commentary further cites:

abhyarhitaṃ ca. "And what is honored." Since it is explained that the word for one who is honored, that is, an object of respect, is placed first, in tapasaś ca parvataś ca we get tapasaparvatau, with the object of respect, the ascetic, coming first (glosses: the ascetic and the mountain; the ascetic and the mountain). Likewise, in brāhmaṇaś ca kṣatriyaś ca viṭ ca śūdraś ca, the case endings and so on are compounded, giving brāhmaṇakṣatriyaviṭśūdrāḥ (glosses: the brahmin, the kṣatriya, the vaiśya and the śūdra; brahmins, kṣatriyas, vaiśyas and śūdras). The commentary further cites:

bhrātur jyāyasaḥ. "Of the elder brother." In this context of the dvandva compound, of brothers, elder and younger and so on, the word for the elder is placed first. In yudhiṣṭhiraś ca arjunaś ca, we get yudhiṣṭhirārjunau. It further cites:

saṃkhyāyā alpīyasaḥ. "Of numbers, the smaller first."

Of a number and what is joined with a number, the smaller is to be set first. In dvau ca daśa ca, we get dvādaśa.

dvandvaś ca prāṇitūryasenāṅgānām. "And the dvandva, for the limbs of living beings, of musical instruments and of armies." (glosses: firm in battle and the accomplisher of existence; firm in battle, the accomplisher of existence; that is, Yudhiṣṭhira and Arjuna.) In compounding the words of a dvandva for the limbs of living beings, the limbs of musical instruments (glosses: two and ten; twelve) and the limbs of an army, the case endings at the end of the compound for the most part take the singular only. In dantaś ca oṣṭhaś ca, the case endings, particles and so on are deleted, and by this sūtra su in the singular is added, giving dantauṣṭham. Likewise, in mārdaṅgikaś ca pāṇavikaś ca, we get mārdaṅgikapāṇavikam; and in rathikaś ca aśvahastī ca, rathikāśvahasti.

jātir aprāṇinām. "Of classes that are not living beings." (gloss: tooth and lip.) The common words for classes that are not living beings, when they denote a collective aggregation, become singular in meaning (glosses: round drum and staff drum; round drum and staff drum; chariot and elephant; chariot, horse and elephant). In dhānāś ca śaṣkulyaś ca (gloss: roasted grain and cakes), the case endings and so on are deleted, giving dhānāśaṣkuli (gloss: roasted grain and cakes).

viśiṣṭaliṅgo nadīdeśo 'grāmāḥ. "Regions that are not towns, and rivers, of different gender." Words for regions that do not denote towns, and words for rivers, when they denote a collective aggregation, become singular in meaning. In gaṅgā ca śoṇaś ca, we get gaṅgāśoṇam. Likewise, in kuravaś ca kṣetraṃ ca, we get kurukṣetram. If they are not of different gender, there is no collective aggregation, but the dvandva compound of mutual connection applies: in gaṅgā ca yamunā ca, the case endings and so on are deleted, and since here it is not a collective aggregation, the singular does not apply (glosses: Gaṅgā and the red river; the Kurus and the field), giving gaṅgāyamune (gloss: the Kurus, the field). If it denotes a town, there is no collective aggregation, but only mutual connection: in jāmbavaś ca śālūkinī ca (gloss: the river Gaṅgā and the river Yamunā), we get jāmbavaśālūkinyau.

kṣudrajantavaḥ. "Small creatures." Small creatures (gloss: the river Gaṅgā and the river Yamunā), when they denote a collective aggregation, become singular in meaning. In yūkā ca likṣā ca (glosses: the town of Jāmbu and the town of Sālū; the town of Jāmbu and the town of Sālū), we get yūkālikṣam.

yeṣāṃ ca virodhaḥ śāśvatikaḥ. "And of those whose enmity is perpetual." Living beings who are each other's perpetual enemies, always hostile, when they denote a collective aggregation, become singular in meaning (glosses: louse and nit; nit and louse). In ahiś ca nakulaś ca, we get ahinakulam. Likewise, in aśvaś ca mahiṣaś ca, we get aśvamahiṣam; and in kākaś ca ulūkaś ca, kākolūkam. Since the commentary explains that the gods and the asuras, although perpetual enemies, do not form a collective aggregation but only mutual connection (glosses: snake and mongoose; snake and mongoose), in devaś ca daityaś ca (glosses: horse and buffalo; horse and buffalo) we get devadaityau (glosses: crow and owl; crow and owl).

śūdrāṇām aniravasitānām. "Of śūdras who are not excluded." Where the occupation belonging to a śūdra class is not excluded, that is, is one of those who dwell within, it forms a collective aggregation and becomes singular in meaning (glosses: gods and asuras; gods and asuras). In rajakaś ca tantuvāyaś ca (gloss: the washerman and the rope maker), we get rajakatantuvāyam. If it is excluded, there is no collective aggregation: in caṇḍālaś ca mṛtapaś ca, we get caṇḍālamṛtapau.

gavāśvaprabhṛtīni ca. "And gavāśva and the rest." For the group of cow and the rest, too, the collective aggregation becomes singular in meaning (gloss: the washerman and the rope maker). In gauś ca aśvaś ca, we get gavāśvam (glosses: the fierce one and the corpse; the fierce one and the corpse). Likewise, in dāsī ca dāsaś ca, we get dāsīdāsam; in gauś ca eḍakā ca, gaveḍakam; in kubjaś ca vāmanaś ca, kubjavāmanam; in putraś ca pautraś ca, putrapautram; in śvā ca caṇḍālaś ca (gloss: cow and horse), śvacaṇḍālam; in strī ca kumāraś ca (glosses: servant and maid; servant and maid), strīkumāram; in uṣṭraś ca kharaś ca (glosses: cow and ewe; cow and ewe; hunchback and dwarf; hunchback and dwarf), uṣṭrakharam (glosses: son and grandson; son and grandson; dog and the fierce one); in bhagavatī ca bhagavāṃś ca (glosses: dog and the fierce one; woman and youth), bhagavatībhagavatam; in mūtraṃ ca purīṣaṃ ca (glosses: woman and youth; camel and donkey), mūtrapurīṣam; in māṃsaṃ ca śoṇitaṃ ca, māṃsaśoṇitam; in darbhaś ca śaraś ca (glosses: camel and donkey; the Fortunate One and the Fortunate Lady), darbhaśaram; and in arjunaś ca puruṣaś ca (glosses: the Fortunate One and the Fortunate Lady; urine and excrement), arjunapuruṣam.

vibhāṣā vṛkṣamṛgatṛṇadhānyavyañjanapaśuśakunyaśvavaḍavapūrvāparādharottarāṇām (glosses: urine; flesh and blood; flesh and blood; kuśa grass and reed; kuśa grass and reed; the accomplisher of existence and the person; the accomplisher of existence and the person). "Optionally of trees, wild animals, grasses, grains, condiments, livestock, birds, horse and mare, east, other, lip and north." These words too optionally become singular in meaning when they denote a collective aggregation; it is optional.

Take cūtaśca aśokaśca, "the cūta tree and the juniper." Here the case endings and so on are dropped, and since it is optionally made either a mutual conjunction or a collective, we get sya cūtāśokaṃ, "cūta and juniper" taken together, and jas cūtāśokāḥ, "the cūta trees and junipers," in the plural.

Likewise, the cry-maker: ruruśca pṛṣtaśca, here su rurupṛṣataṃ, and dāḥ with jas. kuśaśca kāśaśca, here su kuśakāśaṃ, and śāḥ with jas. yabśca māṣaśca, here su yabamāṣaṃ, and ṣāḥ jas. ṅaṅhi ca ghṛtaṃ ca, here su daṅhighṛtaṃ, and au śīte. gauśca mahiṣaśca, here su gomahiṣaṃ, and ṣau au śu. The ruru deer and the spotted deer; ruru deer and deer, together; in the plural. The grasses kuśa and kāśa. kaśna haṅsaśca: kuśa and kāśa, in the plural. Barley and beans: here su kuśahaṃ; barley and beans, in the plural. Curd and milk: saṃ sāḥ jas; curd and milk, in the plural. The cow and the buffalo: aśvaśca baḍabaśca; cow and buffalo, together; here su aśvabaḍabaṃ, and with jas bāḥ. pūrbaśca aparaśca, here: the parrot and the goose; pūrbāpari, and with jos rāḥ. aṅharśca uttaraśca, here: parrot and goose together; su aṅharodharaṃ, and with jas rāḥ, in the plural.

bi pratiṣitthaṃcānṅhikaraṇabāci: "Also when they express things that are mutually opposed and are not substances." The horse and the mare; horse and mare, in the plural. East and other: of those that are opposed and are not substances; east and other, in the plural. Lip and north, or lower and upper. When these are expressed, too, the collective, lip and north, in the plural, optionally becomes singular in meaning. Take śitaśca uśnaṃc: here phu śitośnaṃ o śne. Likewise kāmśca kroṅhaśca: here kāmkroṅhaṃ, au ṅhau. sukhaṃ ca duḥkhaṃ ca: here su sukhaduḥkhaṃ, au khe.

niṅṅhipayādīni: "Not daṅhipayas and the like." Dadhipayas and the like do not become a collective that is singular in meaning. Cold and hot; cold and hot, the pair. Desire and anger. daṅhi. Desire and anger, the pair. Pleasure and suffering, the pair. For cayaśca, pleasure and suffering, the pair: here the case endings and so on are dropped, giving daṅhipayasī. Likewise iṅṅmāśca barhiśca: here iṅhmabartiṣī. bākcamanaśca: here vāṅmanaso. maṅhu ca sarbiśca: here maṅhusarbiṣī. Honey and fresh butter, the pair. The woman of faith and the woman of intelligence; curd and milk. śrāṅṅhāc meṅhāca: here śrāṅṅhāmeṅhe, śrāṅṅhāmeṅhe. The woman of faith and the woman of intelligence, the pair. Curd and milk, the pair. The bright half and the dark half. śuklaśce. The bright and the eye of the peacock's feather; the bright and the peacock's feather, the pair. Speech and mind; speech and mind, the pair. Honey and fresh butter. kraṃśṇaśca: here śuklakraṃṣṇo. ādyaśca abasānaṃ ca: here ādyābasāne. yajac anubākyaṃ ca: here yajānupākye. ulūkhalaṃ ca muśalaṃ ca: here ṅas ulūkhalamuśale. hariśca basalbāśca: here o haribāsalbo. brahma ca prajāpatiśca: here, the bright half and the dark half, the pair. Beginning and end; beginning and end, the pair. The sacrifice and the accompanying recitation, the pair. Mortar and pestle; mortar and pestle, the pair. Hari and Śakra (Indra). brahmaprajāpatrī. śibaśca baiśraba: Hari and Śakra, the pair; Brahmā and Prajāpati, the Lord of Creatures; ṇaśca: here śibabaiśrabaṇau. somśca rudraśca: here somarudro. narādaśca parbataśca: here naradparpato. sūryaścacndramaśca: here sūrya, Brahmā and Prajāpati, Śiva and Vaiśravaṇa, candramaso. rāmśca lakṣmaṇaśca: here rāmlakṣmaṇo. bhī Śiva and Vaiśravaṇa, the pair. The moon (Soma) and Rudra; the moon and Rudra, the pair. The sage Nārada and Parvata. maśca arjunśca: Nārada and Parvata, the pair. The sun (Sūrya) and the moon; sun and moon, the pair. Here bhimārjuno. kampalaśca aśvataraśca: here kampalāśva Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa; Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, the pair; tarau. These are included among dadhi and the like.

ānaṅṛtāṃdraṃdve: "In a dvandva, those ending in raṃta take ānaṅ." Bhīma and Arjuna. In this context of the dvandva compound, Bhīma and Arjuna, the pair. A woollen blanket and a horse; blanket and horse, the pair. If the end of the prior word is one ending in ṛt, ending in raṃt, it becomes ānaṅ. Take hotā ca potā ca: here the case endings and so on are dropped, and the end of what is called hotraṃ becomes ānaṅ; the n is replaced and it is joined: hotāpotaro. Likewise mātā ca pitā ca: here mātāpitaro. Likewise pitā ca putraśca, father and son: here pitālutro, father and son, the pair.

debatādvaṃdveca: "Also with deities, in a dvandva." The fire-offering priest and the grandson. In this context of the dvandva compound, when a word for a deity follows as well, the end of the prior stem becomes ānaṅ: the fire-offering priest and the grandson, the pair. Mother and father. Mitra and Varuṇa. mitraśca, father and mother, the pair, baruṇaśca: here mitrabaruṇo.

īdgniḥsombaruṇayoḥ: "Before sombaruṇa, agni takes īta." In this context of the dvandva compound, when soma and baruṇa follow, the end of agna becomes īt.

agneḥsūtstomasomāḥ: "After agni, stut, stoma and soma." In this context of the dvandva compound, Mitra and Varuṇa, the pair, when stut, stoma and soma occur after agni, the s of those stems becomes the letter ṣ. Take agniścastomaśca: here the case endings and so on are dropped; by this sūtra sa ṣa; by ṣaṭul ṣaḍu, as fitting, taṭ, giving agniṣḍut. Likewise agniśca stomaśca: here agniṣṭomo. Likewise agniścasomaśca: here the case endings and so on are dropped, and by the previous sūtra the end of agni becomes īt, giving agniṣomo. Fire and praise. Since the commentary explains that optionally it becomes neither ṣ nor ī, there is also agnisomo. Fire and praise, together. Likewise agniśca baru: fire and sacrifice; fire and sacrifice, together; fire and the moon; ṇaśca: here agrnībarunau, iṅgṛṅṅhau. Although it was explained above that when baruṇa follows, the end of agne becomes īt, fire and the moon, the pair, when baruna has undergone strengthening and follows, it does not become īr, nor does it become ānaṅ; fire and Varuṇa; it remains simply ir. Take agniścabarunaśca, fire and Varuṇa, the pair: here agnibāruṇo. Cited as authority in the commentary: diboṅyābā, "for dib it is ṅhyābā."

In this context of the dvandva compound, the stem called diṅ becomes dyābā. Take dyābācabhūmiśca: here, with au, dyābābhūmī. Heaven and earth; heaven and earth, the pair.

dvaṃdvāccudṛṣahūṇtātsamāhāre: "After a dvandva ending in cu dṛ ṣa ha, in the collective." Agni and the son of Varuṇa; Agni and Varuṇa's son, the pair. After a dvandva compound, in the collective, from those ending in cu, that is, in the c-class, from the stem draṃṣat, from those ending in the letter ṣ and from those ending in the letter h, the suffix ac comes. Heaven and earth; heaven and earth, the pair. Take lbākca tvaka ca: here the particles and so on are combined, ac is given, ca is the indicatory letter, giving lbāktvacaṃ, speech and skin. Likewise śrīśca sraṭ ca, glory and garland: here śrisraja, glory and garland. śamī ca draṃṣacca, the śamī tree and stone: here, with aca, śamīdṛṣataṃ, śamī tree and stone. bāk ca, speech and skin, tviṭ ca: here bāktviṣaṃ. chatraṃ ca upānaccha: here chatropānahaṃ.

pumānshrilā: "With the masculine, of the feminine." In this context of the dvandva compound, when there are both a masculine and a feminine, that feminine stem is elided. Take brāhmaṇaśca batcaṇī ca: here the case endings, the pure and the clear, the pure and clear together, dust and shoes, dust and shoes together, the particles and so on, and brāhma ṇī as well, are dropped, giving brāhmaṇa.

ṅhrātraṃputrosvasvaṃduhidraṃbhyaṃ: "With brother and son, of sister and daughter." In a dvandva compound, if it is elder brother and sister, the brahmin and the brahmin woman, the sister's stem is elided; with son and daughter, the daughter's name is elided. Take svasācabhrātāc: here the case endings, the particles and so on, the brahmin man and woman, the pair, and svasraṃ as well, are dropped, giving bhrātaro. Likewise putraśca buhitāc: here, since the case endings and so on and duhehraṃ as well are dropped, butrau.

napuṃsakamanpuṃskenekabaccastānyatarasyāṃ: "The neuter, with what is not neuter, and also singular in form, optionally for this." Sister and elder brother; brother and sister, the pair; son and daughter; son and daughter together. In a dvandva compound, when a neuter stem and a stem that is not neuter are joined, the stem that is not neuter is optionally elided, and by the word "also" the collective too optionally occurs.
