Take śuklaṃcakmpalśca: here the case endings and so on and the masculine stem kamrala are dropped, giving śyakkhaṃ, or else śuklau; or, by not dropping it, śaklakamālo. White and a blanket.

pitāmātrā: "With father, of mother." In a dvandva compound of father and mother, the mother alone is optionally elided. Take mātācapitāc: here the case endings, white and blanket, and so on are dropped, and since mātṛ is optionally elided or not elided, pitarau, white blanket, white blankets, the pair, or mātāpitaro.

śva, white blankets, the pair, śuraḥśvaśbra: "With father-in-law, of mother-in-law." In a dvandva compound of father-in-law and mother-in-law, mother and father, the mother-in-law alone is optionally elided. Take śvaśruśca śbaśurśca, father-in-law and mother-in-law: here the case endings and so on are dropped, and since śvāśrū is optionally elided or not elided, father and mother, the pair, father-in-law and mother-in-law, the pair, śvuśrūśvaśuro.

tyaṅādīnisarbernaṃtyaṃ: "With dyat and the like, of all, always." In this context of the dvandva, with tyad and the like, all other stems are always elided. Take sa ca debadadtaśca: here the case endings together with the particles are dropped, giving tau. Since the commentary explains that when two of dyad and the like come together, the former is elided, take sacāyaśca: here the case endings, the particles and so on, and the prior noun are dropped, giving yau.

grāmyapaśusaṃgheṣvastī: "In gatherings of village livestock, of the feminine, when they are not young." He and Devadatta; Devadatta and he, the pair. In this context of the dvandva compound, when a gathering of livestock that live in a village is expressed, that are not young or small, that is, grown, that and which, that and which together, the feminine stems remain and the other stems are optionally elided. Take gābaśca imāśca: here the case endings and so on are dropped, and since go is optionally elided or not elided, imāḥ, or else gabimāḥ. ga Likewise ajāśca imāśca: here imāḥ, or else aj imāḥ. If they do not live in a village, there is no elision: rurabaśca imāśca, these wool-bearers and these; imā is idaṃ formed in the feminine: here ruru imāḥ. If they are not livestock, there is no elision even though a gathering is meant: these cows, these cows, these goats and these, brāhmaṇāśca imāśca, these goats: here brāhmaṇa imāḥ. If they are young, the ruru deer and these, there is no elision: batsāśca imāśca: here batsa imāḥ, these ruru deer. With these, the dvandva or pairwise compounds have been explained.

Now, from the explanation of the procedures common to all four kinds of compound: the brahmins and these, these brahmins. ṛgpūrbṅrāḥpathāmanakṣe: "From ṛca, pur, ṅhur, the calves and these, these calves, and pathin, when not with akṣa, apa." From those stems, with ṅhur when it is not joined with akṣa, the suffix apa comes at the end of a compound. Take arṅhasyarak: here the case endings are combined, apa is given with its indicatory letter, giving arṅhacaḥ, half a verse of the Veda. Likewise biṣṇoḥpūḥ, the city of Viṣṇu: here baṃṣṇupuraṃ, Viṣṇu's city. rājñaḥṅhūḥṅhūḥ, the king's yoke: here rājalhuraṃ. sakhyuḥpanthāḥ: here saakhipathaḥ. ramyāścāso panbāśca: here ramyapathāḥ. mahāṃścapandbāśbāso: here mahābathaḥdakṣiṇāyāḥpanthāḥ, dakṣiṇābathaḥ. From ṅhur joined with akṣa, apa does not come: take akṣaśca ṅbūśca: here akṣaṅhūḥ. The king of those. The path of a friend; friend's path. With pathin, ab is given, and the ṭi portion is elided. That too is this delightful path; the delightful path. Great, and also this path; the great path. The path of the south: it is a tatpuruṣa compound; the southern path. The wheels of a chariot and this iron that joins the two of them.

dvyantarupaschenbhyoñapait: "After dī, antaṅ and the prefixes, the a of apa becomes īta." In the context of compounds, if dvī, antar or a prefix comes first, the letter a of the stem called apa becomes īta. Take dvirgatāpoyasmin: here the case endings, the particles and so on are dropped, a becomes īt, and since a meets a like vowel it is lengthened, giving dvīpo. Likewise antaḥapaḥbyāstiyasya: here antarāṃpaṃ. samapoadūreyasya: here samīpaṃ.

ūdanordeśe: "After anu, in the sense of a region, adut."

When the stem called apa follows anu, its a becomes ūt where a region is meant. That into which one goes, with water on two sides; water on two sides. The water that pervades the space between; water in between. Nearby, that which is not far; near. Take anuaposamān tuṃyogyaṃ: here the case endings and so on are dropped and a becomes ū, giving anūpaḥ.

acabratyanrapapūrbātlamalamnaḥ: "From sām and loman preceded by pratianuaba, aca." When prati and the others come first, from sāma and loman, the suffix aca is to be given at the end of the compound. Having given it, the object it is applied to. Take ācāryaṃpratiaṅhītesāmabedaṃ: here, given and offered, the case endings, the indicatory letters and so on are dropped, aca is given, and ca is the indicatory letter, giving pratisāmaṃ. Likewise anuaṅhītesāmobedaṃ: here anusāmaṃ, the following verses. abarakṣārthaṃmatraṃsṅamabedaṃ: mantras, verses and Veda for the sake of protection. Here absā, the Veda of verses that the master recites to each separately, maṃ, protective verses. The hair, applied separately. lomanaṃpratiyuktaṃ: here, separate verses; the Veda of verses that is recited after; the hair separately; pratilomaṃ. anulomanoyasya: here anulomaṃ. abaursilomāniyasa: here the case endings and so on are dropped and aca is given, giving abalomaḥ. These are bahuvrīhi compounds.

The commentary explains that from ṅhūmi preceded by kṛṣṇa, pāṇḍa, udaka or a numeral, aca comes. Hence kṛṣṇaścā, the hair that follows the current, the hair that follows, that whose chest is smeared all over, saubhūmiśca: here the case endings and so on are dropped, smeared all over, and since aca is given, kraṣṇṛbhūmaḥ. Likewise pāṇḍuścāsobhūmiśca: here pāṇḍubhūmaḥ. udakścāsobhūmiśca: here udakbhūmaḥ. dvobhūmiḥ: here dvibhūmaṃ. trayobhūmiḥ: here jibhū, it is black and it is earth, maṃ. Of these, the three beginning with kṛṣṇa are karmadhāraya compounds, a subdivision of the tatpuruṣa, black earth, it is pale and it is earth, pale earth, it is earth and it is damp, and the two beginning with dvi are numeral compounds: two earths; two earths, the pair; two earths; the three earths; three earths.

akṣṇoñadrśanāt: "From akṣi, when it is not seeing." From what has the sense of akṣi but not of seeing, aca comes at the end of a compound. Take gabāṃakṣiiba: here, with aca, the case endings and so on are dropped, giving galbākṣaḥ. If the sense is seeing, it does not come: in a case such as bibrasyaakṣi, aca does not come; the case endings and so on are dropped, giving boprākṣiḥ.

acaturbicaturasucaturstrāṃbuṃsṅhenvanaḍuhaṛksāmabādmansākṣibhrubadāragaborbaṣṭhiba, like the eye of a cow, that is, a window, naktaṃdibarātrindibāhardibasarja, a window that looks like a cow's eye, sanaṃśreyaspuruṣāyuṣarbyāyuṣa, a brahmin's eye, ṛgyajuṣajātokṣamahokṣabraṃṅṅhokṣopaśungoṣthaśvāḥ, a brahmin's eye. That is: aca acatura acabicatura acatura aca sucatur acastrāṃpusa acastrāṃpuṃsa acaṅhenvanḍuh acarokasāma aclbādmanasa a akṣibhupa acadā ragaba. aca ūrbaṣṭhiba acapadaṣṭhiba nakta diba acarātriṃdiba acaachirdiba acasarjas aca niśreyas acapuruṣāyuṣāyuṣa acadbyāyuṣa acatyāyuṣa acaraṃgyajuṣa acajatokṣa acabraṃṅṅhokṣa acaupaśun acagoṣthaśva. With these twenty-five, acatura and the rest, aca is given as a particle at the end of the compound.

Take apagtānicatvāriasya: here a comes first in the sense of apagata, the case endings and so on are dropped, aca is given, and ca is the indicatory letter, giving acaturaḥ. Likewise migtānicatvāriasya: here bicaturaḥ. suṣṭucatvārilasya: here sucaturaḥ. These three are bahuvrīhi compounds, and aca is given at their end. This one whose four have gone. Likewise strīcapuṃmānśca: here strīpuṃso. ṅhenuśca anaḍvāṃca: four absent or gone; here ṅhenvanaḍuho. ṛkcvasāmaśca: here, without four; one whose four are excellent; four good ones; ṛksāme. lbākacamanaśca: here lbādmanse. akṣiṇīcabhruboca: here akṣibhrubaṃ. dā Woman and man as well; woman and man, the pair. The wish-granting cow and the bull as well. raśca gośca: here dāraga, cow and bull, the pair, verse and verse-foot as well, baṃ. ūrcabaṣṭhībānca: here ūrbaṣṭhībaṃ. Verse and verse-foot. Speech and mind as well. padaścaṣṭhībānca: speech and mind, the pair; the two eyes and the two eyebrows; eyes and eyebrows; cow and bull. Here padaṣṭhībaṃ. naktaṃcadibca: here naktaṃdibaṃ. rātriṃcadibaca: here rātriṃdibaṃ. ahaśca dibca: cow and bull; thigh and hip joint; thigh and hip joint; here ahardibaṃ. Foot and knee. These are dvandva compounds. sarajsā: here sarjasaṃ. That is an avyayībhāva compound. Foot and knee. Night and day as well; day and night. Day and night as well; day and night. Day and night as well. niścitaṃśreyaḥ: here niśreyaṃ. puruṣasya, day after day, āyuḥ: here buruṣāyuṣaṃ. dvayoḥāyuḥ: the dust is pleasant; that dust; here dvyayuṣaṃ. trayāṇāṃ āyuḥ: here tryāyuṣaṃ. These are tatpuruṣa compounds. ṛkcayajuśca: here ṛgyajuṣaṃ. That is a dvandva compound. Definitely good; definitely good; the life of a man; the life of a man; the life of the two. jataśca ukṣaśca so: here jatokṣaṃ. The victorious bull. The life of two; the life of three. mahāṃścaukṣaścāso, it is a bull and it is great: here mahokṣaṃ, the great bull. braṃṅṅhaśca ukṣaścāso, it is old and it is a bull: here braṃṅthokṣaṃ, the old bull. These are karmadhāraya compounds, a subdivision of the tatpuruṣa. It is a bull and it is a victor.

śunaḥsmīpaṃ: here upaśunaṃ. That is an avyayībhāva compound. goṣṭheśvāḥ: here goṣṭhāśvāḥ.

brahmahastibhyaṃparccasaḥ: "From barcas after braṅmahasti." From barccas preceded by brahma or hasti, the suffix aca enters at the end of the compound. Take brahmacabarcaścāso: here the case endings, near the dog, near the dog, and so on are dropped and aca is given, giving brahmabarcasaṃ. Likewise, the dogs in the pen; the pen dogs. hastiśca barcamścāsau: here hastibarcasaṃ. That is a karmadhāraya compound, a subdivision of the tatpuruṣa, with aca given at its end.

It is of Brahmā and it is splendor.

Cited as authority in the commentary: alparājabṅyāṃca, "From albarāja as well." Brahmā's splendor. From barcas preceded by alpa or rājan, too, at the end of a compound, it is an elephant and it is splendor, elephant splendor, aca comes. Take aldaṃbarcoyasya: here alṅabarcasaṃ. That is a bahuvrīhi. rājācbarcaścāso: here rājbarcasaṃ. That is a karmadhāraya.

abasamanṅhebhyaḥtmasaḥ: "From abasaṃanṅha, with tamas." From tamas preceded by aba, saṃ or anṅha, aca comes at the end of a compound. One whose splendor is small; small splendor. It is a king and it is splendor; royal splendor. Take abatamoyasya: here abatamasaṃ. Likewise saṃtamoyasya: here saṃtamasaṃ. anṅhajñānaṃtamoyasya: here anṅhatamasaṃ. These are bahuvrīhi compounds.

Cited as authority in the commentary: svasibaśīyaḥśreyasaḥ, "From baśiyas and śreyas after sras." From baśīyas preceded by svas, one who smells everywhere, and from śreyas as well, always angry, one who is always angry, aca, one who is always angry, one who is deluded, without knowledge and angry, deluded and angry, comes. Take svaḥbśīyaḥ: here sābaśīyasaṃ. Likewise svaḥ śreyaḥ: here svośreyasāṃ, the good of heaven.

anvabataptādrahasaḥ: "From rahas after anuapa and taṅta." From rahas preceded by anu, aba or tapta, aca comes. Take batiṣṭharahasi, he dwells after, in solitude: here, the abode of heaven, heaven's abode, anuraha, the joy of heaven, saṃ. abatiṣṭharahasi: here abarahasaṃ. These two are avyayībhāva compounds. taptataparhasitiṣṭhayasyasaḥ: here taptarhasaṃ. That is a bahuvrīhi.

braterursaḥ: "From uras after prati." From uras preceded by prati, aca comes. Take ursipraticihnaṃ, after, in solitude; he dwells always in solitude; always in solitude; bartate: here pratyurasaṃ. That is an avyayībhāva compound. One whose austerity is solitude in austerity; austerity in solitude.

anugabamāyāme: "After anu, with go, in the sense of length." From go preceded by anu, when the sense of length is expressed, aca comes. Each has its own characteristic. Take anāyāmaṃyānyuktaṃgabāṃ: here anugabaṃ. Each chest separately. It becomes an avyayībhāva. The oxen that draw a cart stretched out behind; following oxen.

Cited as authority in the commentary: upasargādabhvanaḥ, "After a prefix, with aṅhvan." With aṅhvan preceded by a prefix, aca comes and an is also elided. Take pragataḥaṅhrānaṃ: here prāṅhāḥ.

napūjanāt: "Not after praise." From what has the sense of praise, no suffix at all comes at the end of the compound. Take suṣṭurājā: here surājā. Likewise atiśayenārā, the path that goes forth, jā: here, the path forth, atirājā. These are avyayībhāva compounds.

kimaḥkṣepe: "Of kim, in disparagement." When the word kim has the sense of disparagement, no suffix at all comes at the end of the compound. Take kim, a good king, not excellent; an outstanding king; rājā.

nañastatpuruṣāt: "From the naña tatpuruṣa." The outstanding king. From the end of a naña tatpuruṣa compound no suffix at all comes. Take narājā: here arājā. Likewise nasakhā: here asakhā.

pathobibhāṣā: "Of pathin, optionally." What king? With the word pathin, at the end of a naña tatpuruṣa compound, aca is given or not given; it is optional. Take napanthāḥ, not a path: here, since aca is made optional, apanthāḥ or apthaṃ. Not a king; not a friend; not a friend.

The commentary explains that in this context of compounds the m of abaśyam and the like is held to be elided. As it is said: lumpedbaśyamaḥkṛtyetuṃkāmamanasorpi samorāgitatatayorgāṃsasyapaciyuṭghañoḥ. In Tibetan this is: Before a kṛta, the m of abaśyam is elided; before kāma and manas, that of dum as well; before hita and tata, that of saṃ optionally; and the a of māsa, before yuṭ and ghaña. That is what is said. If after what is called abaśyam there comes something ending in a kṛt suffix, such as one added to a root, the m of abaśyam is elided. Take abaśyaṃbhābyaḥ: here, since something with a suffix such as kraṃta follows, it is dropped, giving abaśyabhābyaṃ. Likewise, if after something with the suffix tuma added to a root either kāma or manas follows, the m of tum is elided. Take gantuṃgāmaḥ: here the m is dropped, giving gantukāmaḥ. Likewise gantumanāḥ: here gantumanāḥ. That is indeed right. Likewise, if after the prefix saṃ either hita or tata follows, the m of saṃ is optionally elided. Take saṃhitaḥ: here, since the m of saṃ in its own position is optionally dropped, sahitaḥ or saṃhitaḥ. Likewise saṃtataḥ, one who wishes to go, or satataḥ. If after māṃsa there comes something formed from the root paca with the suffix ghaña, one who makes the mind go, or with the suffix yuṭa, the a of the sa of māṃsa is elided or else optionally not elided. Take māṃsasyapacanaṃ: here māṃspacan, or else māṃsapacanaṃ. Likewise māṃssyapākaḥ, a good friend: here māṃspāka, good, good, or else māṃsapākaḥ. Such are the examples.

Again, since the commentary says that before kabā and manas too the m of sam is optionally elided, take saṃkāmoyasya: here sakāmaḥ, or else, cooked meat, sakāmaḥ. Likewise, cooked meat, gsamnoyasya: here samanaḥ, or else saṃmanaḥ.

uṅkasyodssajñā, cooked meat, yāṃ: "In a name, the ud of udka." udaka connected with the sense of a name becomes what is called uṅ. Take udakaścaso, one who truly desires, truly desiring, meghaścā: here udameghaḥ. One who truly desires; one whose mind is joyful; a clear mind; a clear mind. Likewise lohitścāsouṅkaśca, it is red and it is water: here lohitodaḥ, red water. kṣīraścāsouṅkaśca, it is milk and it is water: here kṣīrodaḥ, milk water. peṣabāsabāhana, it is water and it is a cloud; water cloud, ṅhiṣuc: "Also with peṣabāsbāhanaṅhi." udaka joined with these, peṣa and the rest, also optionally becomes what is called uda. Take udakenapeṣaṃ: here uṅpeṣaṃ, or else udakabaiṣa. Likewise udkebṅasaḥ: here udbāsaḥ, or else udakbāsaḥ. udkasyabāhanaḥ: here udabāhanaḥ, or else udakbāhanaḥ. udakaṃṅhiyasmin: here udṅhiḥ, made into flour with water, or else udkaṅhiḥ.

ekahalādopūryitabyeñanyatarsyāṃ: "With a single initial hal, before what is to be filled, optionally." One who abides in the water; the abode of water; the abode of water; one who has obtained water; that in which is a treasury of water; the treasury of water; the treasury of water. When the word that accompanies udaka, connected with the sense of filling, has as its first letter a single hal, that is, when it is not two or three letters stacked, udaka itself optionally becomes uda. Take udkasyapūrṇaṃkumbhaṃ: here udkumbhaṃ, or else udakkumbhaṃ. Likewise udkasyapūraṇaṃpātraṃ: here udbātraṃ, or else udkabātraṃ. If the first letter is stacked, it does not change: take udkasyabūraṇaṃsthālī: here udakasthālī.

A vase filled with water. gamanṭhau danasaktubaintubajrabhārahārbī, a water vase, baṅhagāheṣuca: "Also with mantha, a water vase, a vessel filled with water, odna saktu bantu bajra bhār hārabī pa, a water vessel, a water vessel, ṅha gāha." When these, mantha and the rest, follow as well, a vessel filled with water, a water vessel, udka optionally becomes what is called ud. Take udkamanthaḥ: here udmanthaḥ, or else udkamanthaḥ. Likewise udakaśca odanaṃca: here udodanaṃ or udakodnaṃ. udakenmiśritosaktuḥ: here udsaktu or udakasaktu. udkasyabintuḥ: here udabaṃnduḥ or udakbinduḥ. udaka, water, syabajraḥ: here u, the water churn, the churn, dakbajraḥ, hail, udakabajraḥ. Hail. u, rice porridge and water as well, dakasyahār, water and rice porridge, that is, roasted barley flour mixed with water, which is food, ryaḥ, a load of water: here, a drop of water, udahāra. A load of water; a load of water. udaka, a drop of water, a drop of water, bhāraḥ. Hail. udakasyahārpī: here udahārabī or udakhārabī. udakebaṅhaḥ: here udabaṅhaḥ. udakaścasogāhaśca: here udagahaḥ or udekagahaḥ.

Cited as authority in the commentary: ikohrasvo'ṅyogālabasya, "The ika that is not dība is short, according to Gālava." A water wheel; a water wheel; a water wheel. Water thrown out; sour water. It is water and it is deep; deep water. Since it is explained that in this context of compounds the long vowels of ik that do not end in dība optionally become short in each compound, as the ancient sage Gālava holds, take grāmaṇyaḥputraḥ: here grāmaṇiputraḥ, or else grāmaṇībutraḥ.

ekātṅṅīteca: "Of eka, before a taddhita as well." The end of what is called ekā becomes short before a taddhita suffix. Take ekāsabhaba: the taddhita suffix ta is added in the sense of the state, the case endings are dropped, and ā becomes short, giving nābaekatā. dyā, the son of the village slanderer, poḥsaṃjñāchandasorbahulaṃ, the son of the village slanderer: "Of dīpa and āpa, in a name or in metre, frequently." The state of being one. The end of dīb and the end of āpa frequently become short in names, in metre and the like. Take rebatyaḥmidraḥ: here the case endings are dropped, and rebati, the one state, becomes short, giving rebatimitraḥ. Likewise śalāyāḥbhaḥ: here śelbahaṃ.

iṣṭakeṣīkāmālānāṃcitatūlabhāriṣu: "Of iṣṭakā, īṣīkā and mālva, before cita, tūla and bhāra." When after iṣṭakā and the others there come, in order, cita and the others, the kinsman of the stars, the end of iṣṭakā and the others becomes short. One who has obtained stone. Take siṣṭakāyācita: here iṣṭakāyāḥtūlaṃ: here īṣīkatūlaṃ. Likewise īṣīkāyāḥtūlaṃ: here īṣīkatūlaṃ. mālācāsaubharīca: here mālbhārī.

jyotirjanpadarātinābhināmagotrarūpastānbarṇabyobacana banṅśuṣu: "With jyotiṣa, janapada, rātrinābhināmgotra, rūpa, svān, barṇa, bayas, ba," a wall of bricks, a wall of bricks, bricks that are equal, or similar, or alike, "can and bantu."

jyotiṣ: a garland, this one is also heavy; a heavy garland. When these, jyotiṣ and the others, follow, the word samāna becomes sa. Take samānaṃ jyotir yasya saḥ, "he whose light is equal": the case endings, particles and so on are dropped, samāna becomes sa, and we get sajyotiḥ. Likewise, samānaṃ janapado yasya saḥ gives sajanapadaḥ; samānā rātrir yasya saḥ gives sarātriḥ; samānā nābhir yasya saḥ gives sanābhiḥ; samānaṃ nāma yasya saḥ gives sanāma. Here the glosses read: he whose light is equal, this one; one of equal light. Samānaṃ gotraṃ yasya saḥ gives sagotraḥ; he whose birthplace is equal, this one; one of equal birthplace. He whose night is equal, this one; one of equal night. He whose navel is equal, this one; one of equal navel. He whose name is equal, this one; one of equal name. Samānaṃ rūpaṃ yasya saḥ gives sarūpaḥ. He whose lineage is equal, this one; one of equal lineage. Samānaṃ sthānaṃ yasya saḥ gives sasthānam. He whose form is equal, this one; one of equal form. Samāno varṇo yasya saḥ gives savarṇaḥ. Samānaṃ vayo yasya saḥ gives savayaḥ. Samānaṃ vacanaṃ yasya saḥ gives savacanaḥ. He whose abode is equal, this one; one of equal abode. Samāno bandhur yasya saḥ gives sabandhuḥ. He whose color is equal, this one; one of equal color. He whose age is equal, this one; one of equal age. He whose speech is equal, this one; one of equal speech. He whose kinsmen and friends are equal, this one; one of equal kin.

Quoted in the commentary: "With piṇḍa, gandha, lohita, kukṣi, veṇī, patnī and pakṣa." When these, piṇḍa and the others, follow, samāna also becomes sa. Samānaḥ piṇḍo yasya saḥ gives sapiṇḍaḥ. Likewise, samāno gandho yasya saḥ gives sagandhaḥ; samānaṃ lohitaṃ yasya saḥ gives salohitaḥ; samānaḥ kukṣir yasya saḥ gives sakukṣiḥ; samānā veṇī yasya saḥ gives saveṇī; samānā patnī yasya saḥ gives sapatnī. Here the glosses read: he whose lump is equal, this one; one of equal lump. He whose smell is equal, this one; one of equal smell. He whose red blood is equal, this one; one of equal blood. He whose belly is equal, this one; one of equal belly. He whose braid is equal, this one; one of equal braid. He whose wife is equal, this one; one of equal wife. Samānaḥ pakṣo yasya saḥ gives sapakṣaḥ; he whose side is equal, this one; one of equal side.

"Caraṇe brahmacāriṇi": with brahmacārin in the sense of a course of conduct. When brahmacārin, connected with the meaning of a course of conduct, follows, samāna also becomes sa. Samāno brahmacārī yasya saḥ gives sabrahmacārī; he whose pure conduct, the conduct of Brahmā, is equal, this one.

"Tīrthe ye": with tīrtha when the suffix ya follows. When tīrtha with the suffix ya follows, samāna also becomes sa. Samānaṃ tīrthyaṃ yasya saḥ gives satīrthyaḥ; he whose sacred abode is equal, this one; one of equal sacred abode.

"Vibhāṣodare": with udara it is optional. When udara with the suffix ya follows, samāna optionally becomes sa or does not. Take samānam udaryaṃ yasya saḥ: the case endings, particles and so on are dropped, and since the change of samāna to sa is optional, we get sodaryaḥ, or else samānodaryaḥ. He whose belly is equal, this one; one of equal belly.

"Dṛgdṛśavatuṣu": with dṛk, dṛśa and vatu. When dṛk and dṛśa follow, and words with the suffix vatu, samāna also becomes sa. Samānaṃ dṛg yasya saḥ gives sadṛk. Likewise, samānaṃ dṛśo yasya saḥ gives sadṛśaḥ. With the suffix vatu: samānaṃ ghaṭavad yasya saḥ gives saghaṭavān. He whose seeing is equal, this one; seeing as equal. He whose seeing is equal, this one; seeing as equal. He whose belly, with its pot, is equal, this one; equal in having a pot.

"Idaṃkimor īśkī": of idam and kim, īś and kī. When dṛk, dṛśa and the suffix vatu follow, idam becomes īś and kim becomes kī. Take iyaṃ dṛg asya: the case endings and so on are dropped, idam becomes īś, and by the rule that ś before a following a is not single, ś is dropped, giving īdṛk. Likewise, iyaṃ dṛśo yasya gives īdṛśaḥ. Kaḥ dṛg asya gives kīdṛk; ko dṛśo yasya gives kīdṛśaḥ. He whose seeing is this, this one. Examples of how, with the suffix vatu, it becomes ī and so on will be explained below.

"Ā sarvanāmnaḥ": ā of a pronoun. Seeing this; he whose seeing is this, this one; seeing this; seeing this. He whose seeing is what; seeing what; he whose seeing is what; seeing what. When dṛk and dṛśa follow, and the suffix vatu, the final of sarva and the others becomes ā. Take sa dṛg asya, "he whose seeing is that": the case endings, particles and so on are dropped, the final of tad, which is one of sarva and the others, becomes ā, and we get tādṛk. Likewise, sa dṛśo yasya gives tādṛśaḥ; yaḥ dṛg asya gives yādṛk; yaḥ dṛśo yasya gives yādṛśaḥ; and with vatu, tāvān and yāvān, "as much as that" and "as much as which."

Again, take asau dṛg asya: the case endings, particles and so on are dropped, and by this sūtra adas becomes adū; the final of the d of adas becomes u and m. He sees that; he whose seeing is that; whatever he whose seeing is that; whatever is seen; whatever he whose seeing is that; one possessing that. This gives amūdṛk. Likewise, asau dṛśo yasya gives amūdṛśaḥ; he whose seeing is that.

Again, take viṣvañcam añcatīti: the case endings and so on are dropped, and by the rule above, "viṣvagdevayoś ca," the ṭi of viṣvak becomes adri; by joining them we get viṣvadryaṅ. Likewise, devam añcatīti gives devadryaṅ. Seeing this. Yam añcatīti gives yadryaṅ; he whose seeing is this, this one; seeing this. This one who worships the doorkeeper.

"Aṣaṣṭhyatṛtīyāsthasyānyasya dug āśīrāśāsthāsthitotsukotikārakarāgaccheṣu": of anya, when it does not stand in the sixth or the third case, there is the augment duk, when āśīṣ, āśā, āsthā, āsthita, utsuka, ūti, kāraka, rāga and cha follow. Worshipping the doorkeeper; this one who worships a god; worshipping a god; this one who worships whatever; worshipping whatever.

When āśīṣ and these others, or a word with the suffix cha, come after anya, where anya is not compounded in the third or the sixth case, anya receives the augment duk. Take anya āśīḥ: the case endings are compounded and the augment duk is given; the k is for the sake of position and the u for the sake of pronunciation, giving anyadāśīḥ. Likewise, anya āśā gives anyadāśā; anya āsthā gives anyadāsthā; anya āsthita gives anyadāsthitaḥ. Anya utsukaḥ, glossed "wishing for another" and "another's well-being," gives anyadutsukaḥ, another's well-being. Another parrot. Anya ūtiḥ, where the word ūti is glossed "wishing for another," gives anyadūtiḥ: a parrot toward another. Those who think of others: thinking of another. Dwelling continually on another; dwelling continually on another. Anya kārakaḥ: one who acts for another. On ūti, dwelling continually on another, it is said that there are six great calamities: excessive rain, no rain, rats, locusts, parrots, the army of one's own king, and the army of a foreign king. This gives anyatkārakaḥ. Anya rāgaḥ gives anyadrāgaḥ. If the compound is in the sixth or the third case, the augment duk does not occur: anyasya āśīḥ gives anyāśīḥ, and anyena āśīḥ gives anyāśīḥ. With the suffix cha: after anya, the cha of the taddhita suffix becomes īya, the augment duk is added, and we get anyadīyam. One who acts for another. Attached to another; attached to another.

Quoted in the commentary: "Arthe vibhāṣā," with artha it is optional. When the word artha follows, glossed "another's aim" and "another's wish," anya optionally receives the augment duk or does not. Anyasya artham gives anyadartham, or else anyārtham. Another's aim.

"Koḥ kat tatpuruṣe 'ci," ku becomes kat in a tatpuruṣa before a vowel. As the examples above also explained, in a tatpuruṣa compound, when a stem beginning with a vowel follows, the stem ku becomes kat. Ku annam, "bad food," gives kadannam.

Quoted in the commentary: "Trau ca," and also with tri. When the stem tri follows, ku also becomes kat: ku trayaḥ gives kattrayaḥ, three bad ones. "Rathavadayoś ca," and also with ratha and vada. When ratha and vada follow, ku also becomes kat: ku rathaḥ gives kadrathaḥ, and likewise ku vadaḥ gives kadvadaḥ, a bad speaker. "Tṛṇe ca jātau," and with tṛṇa when it denotes a kind. When tṛṇa expressing a kind follows, ku also becomes kat: kutṛṇasya jātiḥ gives kattṛṇam, a bad kind of grass; bad grass.

"Kā pathyakṣayoḥ," kā with pathin and akṣa. When pathin and akṣa follow, ku becomes kā: ku panthāḥ gives kāpathaḥ, a bad path; likewise ku akṣaḥ gives kākṣaḥ, a bad chariot axle. "Īṣadarthe ca," and also in the sense of "slight." When ku expresses the sense of "slight," it also becomes kā: īṣaj jalam, meaning "a little flowing water," gives kājalam, a little water.

"Vibhāṣā puruṣe," with puruṣa it is optional. When the word puruṣa follows, ku optionally becomes kā or does not: kutsitaḥ puruṣaḥ, "a contemptible man," gives kupuruṣaḥ, or else kāpuruṣaḥ. A bad man, a contemptible man.

"Kavaṃ coṣṇe," and kava with uṣṇa. When uṣṇa follows, the word ku becomes kava, and by the word "and" it also becomes kat and kā: ku uṣṇam gives kavoṣṇam, kaduṣṇam and koṣṇam, lukewarm. Since the commentary explains that before agni too it becomes kava and the rest, ku agniḥ gives kavāgniḥ, kadagniḥ and kāgniḥ, a feeble fire, a poor fire.

"Pṛṣodarādīni yathopadiṣṭam," pṛṣodara and the others are as taught, that is, in whatever forms are correct. In the forms pṛṣodara and the rest, an augment is given, a letter is changed, a letter is elided, letters are transposed, and so on; even though this is not covered by the rules, they take whatever forms are easy to pronounce and correct. Take pṛṣad udaraṃ yasya saḥ, "whose belly is speckled": the case endings, particles and so on are dropped, leaving pṛṣat udara; by this sūtra the t is dropped, a takes guṇa, and we get pṛṣodaram. Gavāṃ indraḥ: the case endings are dropped, leaving go indra; by this sūtra the augment a is given, and we get gavendraḥ, lord of cattle. Hinastīti, "it harms": ti is dropped, leaving hiṃs, and by this sūtra the letters change their order; the two vowels stay in place while h and s are transposed, giving siṃhaḥ, the lion, the one that excels in harming. A wild animal with a belly like a dog's. Gūḍha ātmā yasya, "whose self is hidden": the case endings and so on are dropped, and by this sūtra ā becomes u, giving gūḍhotmā, one whose nature is secret, or whose nature is concealed. Mahyāṃ rautīti, "it cries out on the ground": the case endings and so on are dropped, rauti becomes ra, leaving mahīra, and by this sūtra hī is turned into yū, giving mayūraḥ: this one that cries out, crying on the ground, the peacock. In this way, everything not covered by the sūtras is established by this sūtra.

"Nahivṛtivṛṣivyadhirucisahitaniṣu kvau," with nahi, vṛti, vṛṣi, vyadhi, ruci, sahi and tani, when kvi follows. When nahi and the others, ending in the suffix kvi, follow, the final of the preceding noun becomes long. Upanahyate, "it is bound close to the foot": for this meaning, nah preceded by upa takes kvi; kvi is entirely lost, and by this sūtra pa becomes long, giving upānat, a shoe. For the meaning nitarāṃ vartate, "where things take place," a country, we get nīvṛt. For the meaning prakarṣeṇa varṣati, "it rains heavily," we get prāvṛṭ, the rainy season. For the meaning viśeṣeṇa vidhyati, "it pierces thoroughly," we get vīvyadh. For the meaning prakarṣeṇa rocate, "it shines brightly," we get prāruk, the very bright. For the meaning turaṃ sahate we get turāṣāṭ. For the meaning paritanoti we get parītat. A bad country; heavy rain, heavy rain; it pierces thoroughly, piercing thoroughly; it shines brightly, shining brightly.

"Vanagiryoḥ saṃjñāyāṃ koṭarakiṃśulukādīnām," of koṭara, kiṃśuluka and the others, before vana and giri, when it is a name.

when it is a name. Quick to endure. Fully flourishing, victorious. When koṭara and the others come before vana, and kiṃśuluka and the others come before giri, koṭara and the rest become long. Take kiṃśulukasya giriḥ: the case endings are compounded, and by this sūtra ka becomes long, giving kiṃśulukāgiriḥ. Koṭarāṇāṃ vanam gives koṭarāvaṇam.

"Vanaṃ puragāmiśrakāsidhrakāsārikākoṭarāgrebhyaḥ": vana, after puragā, miśrakā, sidhrakā, sārikā, koṭara and agra. Lac mountain; lac mountain. When puragā and these others come before vana, the letter na of vana becomes ṇa. The fortress forest, that is, a forest with many birds' nests; the fortress forest. Puragāṇāṃ vanam gives puragāvaṇam. Likewise, miśrakāṇāṃ vanam gives miśrakāvaṇam; sidhrakāṇāṃ vanam gives sidhrakāvaṇam; sārikāṇāṃ vanam gives sārikāvaṇam; agrasya vanam gives agravaṇam. A forest of guggulu trees. A mixed forest; a mixed forest. A pine forest; a pine forest. A thorny forest; a thorny forest. An aguru forest; an aguru forest.

Quoted in the commentary: "Śuno dantadaṃṣṭrākarṇakundavarāhapucchapadeṣu dīrghaḥ," a long vowel is stated for śvan before danta, daṃṣṭrā, karṇa, kunda, varāha, puccha and pada. When danta and these others come after śvan, the final of śvan becomes long. Take śunaḥ dantaḥ, a dog's tooth: the case ending is dropped, n is dropped by the rule eliding the final of a noun, and by this sūtra it becomes long, giving śvādantaḥ, a dog's tooth. Likewise, śunaḥ daṃṣṭrā, a dog's fang, gives śvādaṃṣṭrā, a dog's fang. Śunaḥ karṇaḥ, a dog's ear, gives śvākarṇaḥ, a dog's ear. Kundaḥ, a dog's curved fang, gives śvākundaḥ. Śvā ca varāhaś ca gives śvāvarāhaḥ. Śunaḥ pucchaḥ gives śvāpucchaḥ. Śunaḥ padam gives śvāpadam. A dog's curved fang; a dog and a boar, dog-boar; a dog's tail, dog-tail; a dog's foot, dog-foot.

"Prenirantaḥśarekṣuplakṣāmrakārṣyakhadirapīyūkṣābhyo 'saṃjñāyām api": after pra, nir, antar, śara, ikṣu, plakṣa, āmra, kārṣya, khadira, pīlu and ūkṣā, even when it is not a name. When it comes after pra and these others, the na of vana becomes ṇa even when it is not a name. Take prakarṣeṇa vanam: the case endings and so on are dropped, and since the change of na to ṇa is optional, we get pravaṇam or pravanam. Likewise, nirgataṃ vanam gives nirvaṇam or nirvanam. Antar vane gives antarvaṇam or antarvanam. Śarāṇāṃ vanam gives śaravaṇam or śaravanam. A forest made excellent. Ikṣūṇāṃ vanam gives ikṣuvaṇam or ikṣuvanam. Plakṣāṇāṃ vanam gives plakṣavaṇam or plakṣavanam. An excellent forest. A forest gone bad; a bad forest. An intervening forest; an intervening forest. A forest of reeds. Āmrāṇāṃ vanam, a forest of reeds, gives āmravanam or āmravaṇam. A forest of sugarcane; a forest of sugarcane. A forest of plakṣa trees. Kārṣyāṇāṃ vanam gives kārṣyavanam or kārṣyavaṇam. A forest of plakṣa; a forest of plakṣa. Khadirāṇāṃ vanam gives khadiravaṇam or khadiravanam. Pīlūnāṃ vanam gives pīluvanam or pīluvaṇam. A mango forest; a mango forest. A forest of kārṣya trees. Ūkṣāṇāṃ vanam gives ūkṣāvaṇam or ūkṣāvanam. A forest of kārṣya trees; a forest of kārṣya trees. A forest of khadira; a forest of khadira; a forest of khadira. A forest of pīlu trees; a forest of pīlu trees. A forest of ūkṣā.

"Upasargasya ghañy amanuṣye bahulam": of a prefix, frequently, before ghañ when it does not denote a human being. When a word with the suffix ghañ, not denoting a human being, follows, the final of a prefix frequently, that is, optionally, becomes long. Take prakarṣeṇa karaḥ: the case endings and so on are dropped, and since lengthening the pra is optional, we get prākāraḥ, a rampart, or else prakāraḥ. Parivūrṇasya hāsaḥ, "the laugh of one who is full," gives parīhāsaḥ, or else parihāsaḥ.

"Vibhāṣauṣadhivanaspatibhyaḥ": optionally, after words for medicinal plants and trees. When a word for a medicinal plant comes first, the na of vana optionally becomes ṇa or does not. Take mūrvāṇāṃ vanam: the case endings and so on are dropped, giving mūrvavaṇam or mūrvavanam. Likewise, śirīṣāṇāṃ vanam gives śirīṣavaṇam or śirīṣavanam. Dūrvāṇāṃ vanam gives dūrvavanam or dūrvavaṇam. "Irikādibhyo na": not after irikā and the others. Even though they are words for medicinal plants, after irikā and the others the na of vana does not become ṇa: irikāṇāṃ vanam gives irikāvanam. A forest of śirīṣa trees. A forest of dūrvā; a forest of dūrvā grass. A forest of kakkola.

"Pānaṃ deśe": pāna, in the sense of a region. When the preceding word contains a letter that is the cause of the change of na to ṇa, and the meaning expresses a region, the na of pāna becomes ṇa. Kṣīraṃ pānaṃ yeṣāṃ te, "those whose drink is milk," gives kṣīrapāṇam. Likewise, surāpānaṃ yeṣāṃ te, "those whose drink is liquor," gives surāpāṇam. Those for whom drinking milk is pleasant; drinking milk. Those for whom drinking liquor is pleasant; drinking liquor.

"Vā bhāvakaraṇayoḥ": optionally, in the senses of state and instrument. When the preceding word contains a letter that is the cause of the change of na to ṇa, and the sense is that of a state or an instrument, the na of pāna optionally becomes ṇa. Kṣīreṇa pānam gives kṣīrapāṇam or kṣīrapānam. Likewise, kṣīrapānaṃ karoti pātram gives kṣīrapāṇaṃ pātram or kṣīrapānaṃ pātram.

"Girinadyādīnāṃ vā": optionally, of giri, nadī and the others.

When the cause is present, the na of nadī after giri and the others optionally becomes ṇa. Girer nadī gives girinadī or giriṇadī. A drinker of milk. Likewise, cakrakāraṃ nadī yasya: a vessel that makes one drink milk; this gives cakraṇadī or cakranadī, a milk-drinking vessel. A river on a mountain; water on a mountain. Water whose course is circular; water-wheel.

"Prātipadikāntanumvibhaktiṣu ca": and also with the final of a stem, with num, and with case endings. When the preceding word contains a letter that is the cause of the change of na to ṇa, the na at the end of the following stem, the n of the augment num, and the n of a case ending, as when ṭā becomes ina, optionally become ṇa. For a stem: māṣaś cāsau vāpī ca, "these lentils and also a sowing," gives māṣavāpiṇau. Lentil seed. For num: vrīhivāpaṃ yasya, "whose seed is rice," with jas and śi and the augment num, gives vrīhivāpāṇi, rice seeds. For a case ending: māṣavāpaṃ yasya, with ṭā becoming ina, gives māṣavāpeṇa. "Yuvādīnāṃ na": not of yuvan and the others. Even when all the conditions of the preceding sūtra are present, yuvan and the others do not have na become ṇa: ramyaś cāsau yuvā ca, with ṭā, gives ramyayūnā. Likewise, ramyasyāhaḥ gives ramyāhnā. He whose seed is lentil seed; lentil seed.

"Kumati ca": and also with what contains ku. When the preceding word contains a letter that is the cause of the change of na to ṇa, and the first letter of the following word contains ku, that is, a letter of the ka class, na also optionally becomes ṇa. This one also, the heart-stealer, has come of age; the heart-stealer who has come of age. The playing sun; the sun at play. Hareḥ kāminī, "the beloved of Hari," gives harikāmiṇī. Likewise, śuṣkaś cāsau gomayaṃ ca gives śuṣkagomayeṇa. The desire of Hari. This one is dry, and the cow dung too; dry dung.

"Padavyavāye 'pi": also when a word intervenes. Even when the conditions of the preceding sūtras are all present, if a word intervenes, na does not become ṇa. Māṣaś ca kumbhaś ca vāpaś ca, "lentils, a pot and seed," gives māṣakumbhavāpena. Likewise, catuś cāṅgaś ca yogaś ca, "four, limbs and joining," gives caturaṅgayogena. With lentils, a pot and seed; with the joining of the four limbs.

"Pāraskaraprabhṛtīni ca saṃjñāyām": pāraskara and the others also, when it is a name. Pāraskara and the others, when they express a name, take the forms as they are, that is, the inserted particle. Pāraṃ karoti gives pāraskaraḥ. Likewise, kiṃ kiṃ dhā yasya gives kiṣkindhā. Vanasya patiḥ gives vanaspatiḥ. One who goes to the far shore; one who goes to the far shore. Whose what is what. The lord of the forest; forest-lord.

"Adhaḥśirasī pade": adhas and śiras before pada. The visarga of adhas and śiras becomes s when pada follows. Adhaḥ padam gives adhaspadam, the lower foot; the lower foot. Likewise, śiraḥ padam gives śiraspadam, a foot on the head.

"Pañcamyāḥ stokādibhyaḥ": of the fifth case, after stoka and the others. After stoka and the others, the fifth case ending is not elided before the following word: stokān muktaḥ, dūrān muktaḥ, alpān muktaḥ, kṛcchrān muktaḥ, katipayān muktaḥ. Freed from a little; freed from afar; freed from a few; freed from hardship; freed from somewhat.

"Ojaḥsahombhastamasas tṛtīyāyāḥ": of the third case, after ojas, sahas, ambhas and tamas. After ojas and these others, the third case ending is not elided before the following word: ojasākṛtam, sahasākṛtam, ambhasākṛtam, tamasākṛtam. Done with splendor; done together; done with water; done in anger.

"Manasaḥ saṃjñāyām": after manas, when it is a name. After manas, the third case ending is not elided before the following word when a name is expressed: manasāguptaḥ, manasādevī. Hidden by the mind; goddess through the mind.

"Ājñāyini ca": and also with ājñāyin. After manas, the third case is not elided even when ājñāyin is the following word: manasājñāyī. Commanded by the mind.

"Ātmanaś ca pūraṇe": and after ātman with an ordinal. After ātman too, the third case ending is not elided before a following word with a suffix forming an ordinal: with ṭā, ātmanāpañcamaḥ and ātmanāṣaṣṭhaḥ. Fifth with oneself; sixth with oneself.

"Prakṛtyādibhyaś ca": and after prakṛti and the others. After prakṛti and the others too, the third case is not elided before the following word: prakṛtyācāruḥ, prakṛtyācāruḥ. Form by intrinsic nature; beautiful by intrinsic nature.

"Vaiyākaraṇākhyāyāṃ caturthyāḥ": of the fourth case, in a grammatical name. After ātman, in the sense of a grammatical term, the fourth case is not elided before the following word: ātmanepadam, ātmanebhāṣā. "Parasya ca": and of para. As in the meaning above, not only after ātman but also after para, the fourth case is not elided before the following word: parasmaipadam, a word for the sake of another; parasmaibhāṣā, speech for the sake of another. A word for the sake of oneself; speech for the sake of oneself.

"Haladantāt saptamyāḥ saṃjñāyām": of the seventh case, after what ends in a consonant or in a, when it is a name. After a word ending in a consonant or ending in a, the seventh case is not elided before the following word when it is a name.

"Gaviyudhibhyāṃ sthiraḥ": sthira after gavi and yudhi. The s of sthira after gavi and yudhi becomes ṣ. Take gavi sthiraḥ: by the preceding sūtra the seventh case is not elided, by this sūtra s becomes ṣ, and since s has become ṣ, tha also becomes ṭha, giving gaviṣṭhiraḥ. Likewise, yudhi sthiraḥ gives yudhiṣṭhiraḥ. Yet it is not fixed that the ending is never elided: araṇye sthiraḥ gives araṇyasthiraḥ. Varṣe jaḥ gives varṣajaḥ. Abiding among cattle; abiding among cattle; Yudhiṣṭhira. Abiding in the wilderness; dwelling in the wilderness. Born in the rains.

"Hṛddyubhyāṃ ca": and after hṛd and div. After hṛd and div too, the seventh case is not elided before the following word: hṛdispṛk, divispṛk. Touching the heart; touching the heavens.

"Madhyād gurau": after madhya, with guru. After madhya, the seventh case is not elided when guru is the following word: madhyeguruḥ. "Antāc ca": and after anta. After anta, the seventh case is not elided when guru is the following word: anteguruḥ. Heavy in the middle; heavy at the end.

"Amūrdhamastakāt svāṅgād akāme": after a part of one's own body other than mūrdhan and mastaka, when kāma does not follow. After a part of one's own body, the seventh case is not elided before the following word, but it is elided before mūrdhan, mastaka and kāma.

Kaṇṭhekālaḥ, urasilomā, udaremaṇiḥ. Black-throated. Hair on the chest. A jewel on the belly. Heavy at the end. Take mūrdhani śikhā: this gives mūrdhaśikhā. Mastake śikhā gives mastakaśikhā. Mukhe kāmo yasya gives mukhakāmaḥ. A crest on the crown; crown-crest. A crest on the skull. One whose desire is in the face; desire in the face.

"Bandhe ca vibhāṣā": with bandha it is optional. The seventh case at the end of the preceding word is optionally elided or not elided when bandha follows: haste bandhaḥ, bound on the hand, gives hastabandhaḥ, bound on the hand, or else it stays as it is. Likewise, cakre bandhaḥ, bound to a wheel, gives cakrabandhaḥ.

"Tatpuruṣe kṛti bahulam": in a tatpuruṣa, frequently, before a kṛt. In a tatpuruṣa compound, a word ending in the seventh case is frequently not elided before a following word with a kṛt suffix and so on: stamberamaḥ, one that delights in clumps of grass, and karṇejapaḥ, one who whispers in the ear.

"Prāvṛṭśaratkāladivāṃ je": of prāvṛṣ, śarad, kāla and div, before ja. After prāvṛṣ and these others, the seventh case is not elided when ja is the following word: prāvṛṣijaḥ, śaradijaḥ, kālejaḥ, divijaḥ. Born in the rains; born in autumn; born in due time; born in heaven.

"Vibhāṣā varṣakṣaraśaravarāt": optionally after varṣa, kṣara, śara and vara. After varṣa and these others, the seventh case is optionally elided or not when ja is the following word: varṣejaḥ or varṣajaḥ; kṣarejaḥ or kṣarajaḥ; śarejaḥ or śarajaḥ; varejaḥ or varajaḥ. Born in the year; born in change; born of an arrow; born in dominion; born of the best.

"Śayavāsavāsiṣv akālāt": with śaya, vāsa and vāsin, not after a word of time. The seventh case of the preceding word, when it does not merely mean time, is optionally elided or not when śaya and the others follow: sveśayaḥ or svaśayaḥ; grāmevāsaḥ or grāmavāsaḥ; grāmevāsī or grāmavāsī. Lying in one's own. Stayed in the village; stayed in the village.

Quoted in the commentary: "Apo yonijamatiṣu": after ap, with yoni, ja and mati. The seventh case after ap is not elided when yoni and these others are the following word: apsuyoniḥ, apsujaḥ, apsumatiḥ.

"Ṣaṣṭhyā ākrośe": the sixth case, in abuse. When it conveys abuse, the sixth case ending is not elided before the following word: caurasya kulam, a family of thieves; dāsasya kulam, a family of slaves.

"Vāgdikpaśyadbhyo yuktidaṇḍahareṣu": after vāc, diś and paśyat, with yukti, daṇḍa and hara. After vāc, diś and paśyat, the sixth case is not elided when yukti, daṇḍa and hara, in that order, are the following word: vāco yuktiḥ, the application of speech; diśo daṇḍaḥ, the staff of the directions; paśyato haraḥ, one who steals while being watched.

"Śunaḥ śepapucchalāṅgūleṣu": after śvan, with śepa, puccha and lāṅgūla. After śvan, the sixth case is not elided when śepa and these others are the following word: śunaḥśepaḥ, śunaḥpucchaḥ, śunolāṅgūlaḥ. A dog's member; a dog's tail; a dog's tail.

"Putre 'nyatarasyām": optionally with putra. When putra is the following word and it conveys abuse, the sixth case is optionally not elided: dāsyāḥputraḥ or dāsīputraḥ; vṛṣalyāḥputraḥ or vṛṣalīputraḥ. When it is not abuse, the ending is always elided: brāhmaṇyāḥ putraḥ gives brāhmaṇīputraḥ. Son of a slave woman; son of a slave woman. Son of a low-caste woman. Son of a brahmin woman; son of a brahmin woman.

"Ṛto vidyāyonisaṃbandhebhyaḥ": after words ending in ṛ that are related through learning or birth. After a word ending in ṛ that is connected by a relation of learning or of birth, the sixth case is not elided before a following word that has a relation of learning or birth: hotuḥputraḥ, the son of the fire-offering priest; hoturantevāsī, the pupil of the fire-offering priest.

"Vibhāṣā svasṛpatyoḥ": optionally with svasṛ and pati. When svasṛ and pati are the following word, the sixth case after the preceding word ending in ṛ is optionally elided or not: nanānduḥpatiḥ or nanāndṛpatiḥ; duhituḥpatiḥ or duhitṛpatiḥ; mātuḥsvasā or mātṛṣvasā. The husband of the husband's sister. The husband of the daughter, that is, the son-in-law.

"Mātṛpitṛbhyāṃ svasā": svasṛ after mātṛ and pitṛ. When svasṛ comes after mātṛ and pitṛ, the s becomes ṣ: mātuḥsvasā or mātṛṣvasā; pituḥsvasā or pitṛṣvasā. The mother's sister, that is, the maternal aunt.

"Mātuḥpitṛbhyām anyatarasyām": optionally after mātṛ and pitṛ. When svasṛ is the following word after mātṛ and pitṛ, it optionally does not become ṣ: mātṛṣvasā or mātṛsvasā, the mother's sister, the maternal aunt; pitṛṣvasā or pitṛsvasā, the father's sister, the paternal aunt. When the case ending is not elided, it does not become ṣ, and the examples of this have already been shown above.

ti pāṇinivyākaraṇasya sūtrāt samāssamābhāḥ Thus the compounds from the sūtras of the Pāṇinivyākaraṇa are complete.

From The Chariot That Draws the Jewel of Excellent Explanation, notes setting out the sense of the root text and commentary of the great treatise on grammar, the Pāṇinivyākaraṇa, together with its examples, procedures and so on, the main points of the procedures of compounds, general rules together with exceptions, are for the present complete.

Now, as it is said, "Forming another noun from a noun, by way of its own relation, is the taddhita," I shall explain the domains in which the taddhita suffixes apply.

"Prāg dīvyato 'ṇ": aṇ, before "dīvyati." Before the sūtra that comes below, "by that he plays, he conquers, he wins, he digs," in the domains of the taddhita explained up to that point, aṇ optionally applies; this is the general rule.

"Tasyāpatyam": in the sense of his offspring. For any stem whatever, from a word ending in the sixth case, aṇ and the others apply in the sense of "his offspring."

"Samarthānāṃ prathamād vā": optionally from the first of those that are semantically connected.

"Semantically connected" means a word that agrees in sense, not one that is incongruous or at odds in meaning, which supplies the suffix of offspring; even when it stands before the base to which the offspring suffix and the rest are given, aṇ and the others optionally apply. In the phrase upagorapatyaṃ the case ending is deleted, and in the sense of apatyā the suffix aṇ is given.

tatdhiteṣacāmādeḥ: in taddhitas, of the first of the vowels. When taddhita suffixes have ñ or ṇ as their indicatory letter, the first of the vowels of the noun to which the suffix is given is strengthened. Son of Upagu: aupagu an; since the ṇ serves that purpose, it is deleted. The u takes guṇa, u becoming o, and by the sūtra "ec becomes ay and the rest" we get aubagabaḥ. When the feminine is expressed, by "ṭi, ta, ḍha and the rest" comes dīpa, giving aupagabī.

apatyaṃpautraprabhṛtigotraṃ: offspring, in the case of the grandson and so on, is lineage. For the grandson and the rest, who are spoken of as offspring, aṇ and the others also apply in making the lineage understood. Son of Upagu. ekogotre: in the lineage there is one. The suffixes of offspring (daughter of Upagu) also apply in making the lineage understood; that is what "a single suffix" means. aupagapaḥ: of the lineage of Upagu.

taḥiña: after a, iñ. From a stem ending in a, iñ applies in the sense of offspring. In the phrase dakṣasyāpatyaṃ the case ending together with apatya is deleted. By this sūtra, iñ in the sense of apatya; by the sūtra "in taddhitas" and the rest, strengthening; the ñ, having served that purpose, is deleted; by "of ya, also before i," the final a of the stem is deleted, and so we get dākṣiḥ.

yañiñośca: from yañ and iñ (son of Dakṣa). When the grandson and so on are expressed, phak applies after stems ending in yañ and iñ. kitica: also when k is the indicatory letter. With a taddhita suffix that has k as its indicatory letter, too, the first vowel of the noun is strengthened. dākṣeḥ, son of Dakṣa: in the phrase abatyaṃ the case ending together with apatya is deleted. To dakṣa bearing the suffix iñ this sūtra gives phak. The k is for strengthening. Pha becomes āyaṇa: dākṣayaṇaḥ.

gargādibhyoyañ: from garga and the rest, yañ. From garga and the rest, in the sense of offspring (grandson of Dakṣa), yañ applies. In gargasyāpatyaṃ the case ending and the rest are deleted. This sūtra gives yañ; by "in taddhitas," strengthening; the ñ serves that purpose; by "of ya, also before i" (grandson of Dakṣa), the a is deleted: gārgyaḥ. In the same way, in the sense of patsasyāpatyaṃ we get bātsyaḥ.

yaññośca: of yañ and añ also (son of Garga). The suffixes yañ and añ are elided before the plural case endings: to gārgya and bātsya is added jas; although yañ is elided, the meaning remains: gargāḥ, batsāḥ.

Again, in gargasyāpatyaṃ (son of Garga), the case ending and the rest (son of the very one who has died; son of one whose kinsman has died) are deleted. By "from yañ and iñ," phak; the k is for strengthening; pha becomes āyaṇa; by "of ya, also before i," the a is deleted. When it stands as gārgya āyaṇa: āpatyasyacarddhitenāti (son of the ancient one; son of one whose kinsman has died; grandson of Garga): also of the offspring suffix, before a taddhita, when it is not ā. If the y of the offspring suffix stands at the end after a stacked consonant without vowel, it must be elided before another taddhita suffix whose first letter is not ā; but here, since it is ā, the y is not elided, and applying this we get gārgyāyaṇāḥ. In the same way, in the sense of bātsyasyāpatyaṃ we get pātsyāyaṇaḥ.

bahādibhyaśca: also from bahu and the rest. From bahu and the rest, iñ applies for offspring: in the sense of bahurapatyaṃ we get bāhabiḥ. In the same way, in the sense of upabindorpatyaṃ (grandson of Garga) we get pabindapiḥ (grandson of one whose kinsman has died; grandson of one whose kinsman has died). For uḍulomnaḥapatyaṃ we get auḍulomiḥ. Since the commentary explains that uḍuloman takes a in the sense of many offspring (sons of many), for the sense of uḍyalomnaḥbahu (son of the red one; son of Upabindu; son of the spotted one) apatyāni (son of the spotted one; son of Upabindu) we get uḍulomāḥ (son of Uḍuloman; son of Uḍuloman). For uḍuyoman, iñ and strengthening; by "of n, in taddhitas," the ṭi is deleted. In the sense of agniśarmnaḥapatyaṃ we get āgdiśarmiḥ. For sukṛṣṇasyāpatyaṃ we get kārṣṇiḥ. For arjunasyāpatyaṃ (the many sons of Uḍuloman) we get ārdunuḥ.

suthātukaṅca (the many sons of Uḍuloman): and akaṅ for sudhātṛ. For sudhātṛ, when offspring is expressed, iñ applies and the final becomes akaṅ. In sudhātuḥāpatyaṃ (son of Agniśarman; son of Kṛṣṇa) the case ending, apatyaṃ (son of Kṛṣṇa; son of Bingnup) and the rest are deleted; iñ; the final becomes aka (son of Arjuna), together with its indicatory letter: saubhādakiḥ.

The commentary cites: byāsabarūḍhaniṣādacanḍalapiṃbānāṃceṣṭiḥ: it is held for byāsa and barūḍhaniṣādacaṇḍalabiṃba (son of Sudhātṛ) as well. Since for vyāsa and these others iñ is held to apply for offspring and their final to become akaṅ, in byāsasyapatyaṃ the case ending (son of Sudhātṛ) and the rest are deleted; iñ, and the final becomes aka: byāska plus iñ.

nayvābhyāṃpadānhābhāṃpūrbaututābhyamaica: not of y and v at the beginning of a word, and to them aic. Before a taddhita suffix that is a cause of strengthening, if the word to which the suffix is given has a y or a v (son of Vyāsa) that is initial or next to the initial, it is not strengthened, and to them the augment aic is given. That is, since aic is a combined term applied respectively, ai is given where there is a y and au where there is a v. In the Kalāpa, this is the same as what is found there: "not of y and v at the beginning of a word, and strengthening as an augment." Here, since it is y, ai is given: baiyāsakiḥ. Doing the derivation as before, we get bārūḍhakiḥ, naiṣādakiḥ, cācḍalakiḥ and paimbakiḥ.

gotrekudibhyaśclañ: from kuñja and the rest, also in the sense of lineage, cphañ.

For kuñja and the rest, cphañ applies in the sense of offspring and also when the lineage is expressed. In the sense of kuñjasyāpatyaṃ (son of the expanded one) or kuñjasyagotraḥ (son of the gentle one; son of the forest man; son of Gatumapo; son of one colored like the dimī, that is, son of the very red one), cpañ is given. The ñ is for strengthening, and the c is for the sake of the accent. As for pha, since the commentary says, "sometimes it becomes ayaṇa, sometimes āyana" (son of the elephant), it becomes āyana (lineage of the elephant): kauñjāyanaḥ.

prātacphañorstriyāṃ: from vrāta, and of cphañ, when it is not feminine. For vrāta and the rest, when it is not feminine, after cphañ the suffix ñya applies in its own sense. Giving cphañ to vrāta and deriving it as above, in the sense of brātāyanasyasvāthraṃ we get brātāyānyaḥ. In the same way, kauñjāyanyaḥ (lineage of the son of the elephant).

ñyadayastadrājāḥ: ñya and the rest are tadrāja. The suffixes ñya and the rest are given the designation tadrāja, "its king."

tadrajasyabahuṣutenibāstiyvaṃ: of the tadrāja, in the plural, when it is not feminine (the son of Vrāta in its own sense; the son of Vrāta in its own sense), it is elided by that (the son of the elephant in its own sense). Those designated tadrāja above are elided before the plural case endings that do not express the feminine. To brātāyanya and kauñjāyanya, already derived above with ñya, jas is added; by this sūtra the ñya is deleted: brātāyanāḥ, kauñjāyanāḥ.

naḍādibhyaḥphak: from naḍa and the rest, phak. For naḍa and the rest, phak applies in the sense of offspring and of lineage. In the sense of naḍasyapatyaṃ or naḍasyagotraṃ we get nāṭāyaṇa, the son or the lineage of the sage Naḍa. In the same way, cārāyaṇaḥ, the son or the lineage of the sage Cara (the son of the elephant in its own sense, and so on); āmuṣyāyaṇaḥ, the son of the sage So-and-so.

śibādibhyoñan: for śiva and the rest, aṇ. For śiva and the rest, aṇ applies for offspring: in the sense of śibasyāpatyaṃ we get śibaḥ.

ṛṣyāṃkurubhyaśca: also from the sages, Andhaka, Vṛṣṇi and the Kurus. For the offspring of the lineage of the sages, the lineage of Andhaka, the lineage of Vṛṣṇi and the lineage of the Kurus, aṇ applies. For the offspring suffixes, the phrase is formed only with the case ending (son of Śiva), the sixth case, and apatya (son of the one so called); work out the lineages by analogy with the earlier ones. For the lineage of the sages, with aṇ, bāśiṣṭhaḥ; with aṇ, briṃśrāmitraḥ. For the lineage of Andhaka, with aṇ, śvāphalkaḥ; with aṇ, rānyāsaḥ. For the lineage of Vṛṣṇi, bāsudebaḥ and sāhadebyaḥ. For the lineage of the Kurus, nākulaḥ.

māturutsaṃkhyāsibhadrapūcāyāḥ: from mātṛ preceded by a numeral, sam or bhadra, ut. From mātṛ preceded by a numeral, by sam or by bhadra (son of Vasiṣṭha; son of Viśvāmitra), aṇ applies for offspring (son of Śvaphalka; son of Randhyāma), and the ṛ of tṛ becomes ut (son of Vasudeva; son of Sahadeva): (son of Nakula) ṇaimāturaḥ, khāṇmāturaḥ, sāmāturaḥ, bhādramāturaḥ, bhādramāturaḥ.

kanyāyākaninaca: and kanīna for kanyā. For kanyā, aṇ applies for offspring, and it becomes kanīna: kānānaḥ.

struḍhaka: from feminines, ḍhak. For drimnatṛ: aṇ, and the first vowel is strengthened; the ṛ of tṛ becomes ut; and by the rule on the r of aṇ and the rest, the augment r. Son of two mothers; son of six mothers; son of the all-mother; son of the good mother. For words ending in a feminine suffix, ḍhak applies for offspring. In the Cāndra this is the same as what is said there: "from dīpaāpatiūṅ." (Son of the daughter.) In pinatāyāḥapatyṛ, ḍhak; the k is for strengthening; ḍha becomes eya: baiṇateyaḥ. In the same way, māteyaḥ and yaubateyaḥ; to yuthañi, ḍhak.

śubhādebhyaśca: also from śubhra and the rest. From śubhra and the rest, too, ḍhak applies for offspring: śaubhreyaḥ, son of the white one; gadgeyaḥ, son of Gaṅgā.

ḍhalopokadrāḥ: before ḍha, elision, except for kadrū. (Son of the woman who composes; to mahe, ḍhak; sapebu, that is, red-eyed; son of the young woman.) Before the taddhita suffix ḍha, the final u of words other than kadhū is elided: kāmaṇḍaleya. To maṇḍala, by "śubhra and the rest," ḍhak; by this sūtra the u is deleted; ḍha, and so yaḥ. For kadhū it is not elided: kṣadrabeyaḥ (son of Kadrū). The commentary cites baṇḍoścana: not of paṇḍu either. Before the suffix ḍha, the u of paṇḍu is not elided either: pāṇḍabeyaḥ, son of the pale one, or of the pale white one.

itaścāniñaḥ: also from i, when it is not iñ.

That is, an i such as the one in "after a, iñ" (the u of kamaṇḍalu; to kadrū, by "śubhra and the rest," ḍhak; strengthening; ḍha becomes e; the u takes guṇa). From a word ending in i that is not the i of the taddhita suffix iñ that has been given, ḍhak also applies for offspring (to paṇḍu, by "śubhra and the rest," ḍhak; ḍha becomes iya; the u takes guṇa): ātreyaḥ, son of the one who knows ornaments; naidheyaḥ, son of the one who holds certainty.

kalyāṇyādīnāminaṅ: and inaṅ of kalyāṇī and the rest. For the offspring of kalyāṇī and the rest, ḍhak applies, and the final of kalyāṇī and the rest also becomes inaṅ: kālyāṇineyaḥ, son of the virtuous woman; jaubṛṇineyaḥ, son of the aged woman. (To atri and nidhi, ḍhak; by this sūtra, strengthening; ḍha becomes eya; by "of ya, also before i," the i is deleted.) jyiṣṭhaneyaḥ.

hṛdbhagasindhvanhepūrbapadasyaca: when hṛd, bhaga and sindhu are at the end, also of the prior word. Before a taddhita suffix that is a cause of strengthening, when hṛd (to kalyāṇī and jubriṇī, by the sūtra, ḍhak, and the final becomes inaṅ; the a of the n with its indicatory letter is for pronunciation) and the rest are the latter word and another word (son of the eldest woman; to jyiṣṭha, ḍhak and inaṅ) stands before it, the first vowel of both the prior and the latter word is strengthened: sauhārdaḥ, son of the dear-hearted one; saubhāgineyaḥ, son of the good sister; sausaindhabaḥ, son of the good Sindhu.

The commentary cites anuśatikādīnāṃca: and of anuśatika and the rest. (To suhṛd, by "his offspring" and so on, aṇ; both prior and latter strengthened. To subhaginī, by "from feminines, ḍhak," ḍhak; by this sūtra both prior and latter strengthened. To susindhu, by "his offspring," an; by this sūtra both prior and latter strengthened.) For anuśatika and the rest, too, before a taddhita suffix that is a cause of strengthening, the first vowel of both the prior and the latter word is strengthened (to anuśarika, by "his offspring," aṇ; by this sūtra both prior and latter strengthened): āṇuśātikaṃ. (To parastrī, by "kalyāṇī and the rest," inaṅ: ḍha and the final inaṅ; by this sūtra both prior and latter strengthened; ḍha becomes iya.) pārastraineyaḥ.

kulaṭāyābā: optionally of kulaṭā. For kulaṭā, ḍhak applies for offspring, and the final of kulaṭā optionally becomes inaṅ: kaulaṭineyaḥ, kaulaṭeyaḥ.

caṭakāyāḥairaka: from caṭakā, airak. From both caṭaka and caṭakā, airak applies for offspring (son of another man's wife). In caṭakāyāḥapatyaṃ we get cāṭākairaḥ. In the same way, in caṭakasyābatyaṃ we get cāṭakairaḥ. Again, in the commentary (son of the wanton woman; son of the wanton woman): the airak given to caṭakā, which bears a feminine suffix, is elided before a plural case ending: caṭakā; jas is added and the airak is deleted.

godhāyāḥḍhāka: from godhā (son of the sparrow; son of the sparrow; to caṭaka, airak, the k being for strengthening; son of the female sparrow), ḍhrak. From godhā (son of the female sparrow), ḍhrak applies for offspring: gaudheraḥ, son of the lizard or of the spring woman. The commentary cites āragudīcī (sons of the female sparrow): for the easterners, ārak. Since the paṇḍitas of the east hold that ārak is given after godhā for offspring, we get gaudhāraḥ, son of the lizard or of the spring woman.

kṣudrābhyobā: optionally from low women. (To godhā, ḍhrak; strengthening; ḍha becomes e; by the rule on the elision of y and v, the y is deleted.) From low women, ḍhrak optionally applies for offspring; alternatively ḍhak applies: kolaṭeraḥ, son of the wanton woman; kaulaṭeyaḥ (ḍhak, ḍha becoming eya). With ḍhrak, dāseyaḥ (to godhā, ārak, for strengthening); with ḍhak, ṣvaseyaḥ. With ḍhrak, kāṇeraḥ; with ḍhak, kāṇeyaḥ.

pitṛṣvapuśchaṇa: from pitṛṣvasṛ, chaṇ. From svasṛ preceded by pitṛ, chaṇ applies for offspring (to kulaṭa, ḍhrak; strengthening; ḍha becomes e; by the rule on the elision of y and v, the y is deleted): paihṛṣvasrīnayaḥ (son of the wanton woman).

ḍhakilopaḥ: before ḍhak, elision. From svasṛ preceded by pitṛ (son of the leaking woman; son of the slave woman), ḍhak applies for offspring, and before ḍhak the ṛ of svasṛ is elided: paitṝṣvaseyaḥ, son of the father's sister, that is, of the aunt. (To pitṛṣvasṛ, chaṇ; the ṇ is for strengthening; cha becomes īya; by "ik before a vowel becomes yaṇ"; su. Son of the father's sister, that is, of the aunt.)

tṛṣvasuśca: also from mātṛṣvasṛ. From svasṛ preceded by mātṛ, too, chaṇ and ḍhak apply for offspring, and before ḍhak the ṛ is also elided (to pitṛṣvasṛ, ḍhak; by this sūtra the ṛ is deleted; ḍha becomes eya; strengthening; su): mātṛṣvasrīyaḥ, son of the mother's younger sister or of the maternal aunt; mātṛṣvaseyaḥ, son of the mother's younger sister or of the maternal aunt.

rājarśvasurādyata: from rājan and śvaśura, yat. From rājan and śvaśura, yat applies for offspring: rājanyaḥ, śvasurlaḥ.

rājñojātauyata: from rājan, for the caste, yat. (To mātṛṣvasṛ, chaṇ; ṇ for strengthening; cha becomes īya; by "ik before a vowel becomes yaṇ"; su. To mātṛṣvasṛ, ḍhak; by "kiti ca," strengthening; ḍha becomes eya; by this sūtra the ṛ is deleted.) From rājan, yat applies also when a caste is expressed. In the sense of drasyarājñaḥjātṛ (to rājan and śvasur, yat; the t is deleted; yat; su) we get rājanraḥ.

kṣatrādlhaḥ: for kṣatra, gha. For kṣatra, gha applies for lineage and for offspring: kṣatriyaḥ. The commentary cites kṣatrājdrāhauiñ: from kṣatra, iñ applies also when the caste (the royal caste) is expressed: kṣatriḥ.

kulātbaḥ: from kula, kha. From the word kula alone (the royal caste), and also from kula when it has become the latter member after another word, kha applies for offspring (from kṣatra, gha becomes iya; a royal companion, son of the king): kulīnaḥ, āḍhyakulīnaḥ.

apūrbapadādanyatarasyāṃyataḍhakañau: from it when no prior word stands before it (the royal caste), yat and ḍhakañ optionally. From kula with no other word before it, yat and ḍhakañ optionally apply for offspring: kulyaḥ, kauleyakaḥ, and (to kha, son of the royal caste; to kula, kha becomes īna; son of the wealthy companion) ṣkulīnaḥ.

mahākulādañakhañau: from mahākula, añ and khañ. From mahākula, añ and khañ optionally apply for offspring: māhākulaḥ, son of the great family; mahākulīnaḥ (to kula, yat, son of the family; to kula, ḍhakañ, the ñ being for strengthening, ḍha becoming eya).

duḥkulātaḍhaka: from duṣkula, ḍhak (son of the family). From duṣkula, ḍhak optionally applies for offspring: dauṣkuleyaḥ, duṣkulīnaḥ.

svasuścha: from svasṛ, cha.

From svasṛ (the ñ being for strengthening; son of the great family; the ñ being for strengthening, kha becomes īna), cha applies for offspring: sāsrīyaḥ, son of the sister. (To svasṛ, cha; cha becomes īya; the sounds are joined.)

bhrāturbyacū: from bhrātṛ, also vyat. From bhrātṛ, vyat applies for offspring (ḍhak, the k serving to exclude; ḍha becomes eya; son of a bad family; kha becomes īna), and by the word "also," cha applies too: bhrātribyaḥ, son of the brother; bhatrīyaḥ (to bhrātṛ, cha; cha becomes īya).

byansaphatne: vyan, for a rival. From bhrātṛ, when the offspring of a rival is expressed, vyan applies: bhātṛbyaḥ.

rebatyādibhyaṣṭhaka: from revatī and the rest, ṭhak. From revatī and the rest, ṭhak applies for offspring. ṭhasyekaḥ (to bhrātṛ, vyat; the t serves the rule on accent): ṭha becomes ika. The ṭha of the suffix becomes ika: raibatikaḥ, son of Revatī; śvapālikaḥ (to bhrātṛ, vyan, the n being for the accent; su; son of the rival's elder brother), son of the horse keeper.

anṛṣyānaṃtaryebidādibhyoña: from vida and the rest, when they are not sages, for an unbroken line, añ. From vida and the rest, when they are not sages, añ applies for offspring and also for the unbroken (to revatī, ṭhak; the k is for strengthening; ṭha becomes ika) line, that is, for the grandson and so on (to aśvapāla, ṭhak; the k is for strengthening; ṭha becomes ika): baidaḥ, grandson of the Veda; aurbaḥ.

yaskadibhyogotre: from yaska and the rest, for lineage. From yaska and the rest, añ applies when lineage is expressed, and it is elided before the plural case endings: yāskaḥ, of the lineage of the staff; with jas, yaskāḥ, the lineages of the staff. (To this and to urba, añ; the ñ is for strengthening. Son of the wave.) In the same way, lāhyaḥ; with jas, lahyāḥ.

atṛbhṛgukutsabasiṣṭhagotamādgirobhyaśca: also from atri, bhṛgu, kutsa, vasiṣṭha, gotama and aṅgiras. From atri (to yaska, añ, the ñ being for strengthening; to yaska, jas; before the plural the añ is deleted; by "when there is no cause," a pair) and the rest, too, the offspring suffixes are elided before the plural case endings (lineage of the obtained; lineages of the hearth): with jas, atrayaḥ; with jas and ṇya, bhṛgapaḥ; with jas and ṇya, kutsāḥ; baśiṣṭhāḥ; with śas and ṇya, gotamāḥ; with śas and ṇya, adgirasaḥ.

janapadaśaptākṣatriyādaña: from a word for a country, from a kṣatriya, añ. From a word expressing a kṣatriya connected with a word for a country, añ applies for offspring. (Sons of Atri, formed with ḍhak; sons of Danpong; sons of Kutsa; sons of Vasiṣṭha; sons of Gotama; sons of Aṅgiras, or of the sun.) Son of the king of the Pañcālas: pāñcālaḥ (to pañcāla, añ; the ñ is for strengthening). kālidgaḥ, son of the king of Kaliṅga.

hrasvaṃlaghu: a short one is light. A syllable in which a short vowel stands is light. saṃyogeguru. saṃyogeguru: before a conjunct, heavy. When a conjunct, that is, a stacked consonant, follows, the vowel before it, even though it is short, is not light but heavy. dīrghaṃca: a long one too. Any syllable in which a long vowel stands, or a long vowel by itself, is also heavy.

aniñoranārṣayorgurūpottamayoṇyaṅgotre: from what is not a sage and has a heavy syllable next to the end, for lineage, aṇ and iñ become ṣyaṅ. From a word expressing what is not a sage, which has a heavy syllable next to the end, the ending of aṇ and iñ in the sense of lineage is to be changed to ṣyaṅ in the feminine. Here the ṅ serves the rule on ya and cāp, and the ṣ, making it ṣit, serves ṅīṣ: kaumudagandhyā, bārāhā.

aśvapatyadibhyaśca: also from aśvapati and the rest. From aśvapati and the rest, too, aṇ applies for offspring: with aṇ, aśvapataḥ; with aṇ, gaupataṃ; with aṇ, gānapataṃ.

dityadityadipatyuttarapadātaṇyaḥ (the fragrance of the kumuda; the wild sow): from diti, aditi and āditya, and from pati as the latter word, ṇya. From diti, aditi and āditya, and from words in which pati has become the latter member, ṇya also applies for offspring (son of the lord of horses; son of the lord of cattle; son of Gaṇapati): daityaḥ, son of Diti; with ṇya, adṛtyaḥ, son of Aditi; ādaitāḥ, son of the all-giving woman; with ṇya, prājāpatyaṃ; with ṇya, saināpatyi.

The commentary cites yamācca: also from yama. From yama, too, ṇya applies for offspring: yāmyaṃ. The commentary also cites debasyayaññau (ṇya, the ṇ being for strengthening; to āditya, ṇya, the ṇ being for strengthening; by the rule on the elision of y after a consonant, the earlier y is deleted; son of the lord of creatures; son of the lord of the army): of deva, yañ and añ. From deva, yañ and añ apply for offspring (son of Yama): with yañ, daibyaṃ, son of the god; with yañ, daibaḥ.

The commentary also cites baheṣaḥṭilopoyaṇ: from baheṣa, yaṇ, and the ṭi is elided. From baheṣa, yaṇ applies for offspring and the ṭi is elided too: bāhyaḥ. The commentary also cites īkaka: īkak. From bahiṣa, īkak applies for offspring and the ṭi is elided as well: bāhīkaḥ, son of the outside.

utsādibhyoñña: from utsa and the rest, añ. From utsa and the rest, añ applies for offspring (son of the outside; or here "outside" applies to itself): with añ, autsaḥ; with añ, audapānaḥ.

stvapuṃsābhyaṃnañsnañaubhabanāta: from strī and puṃs, for the abstract state, nañ and snañ. (To bāheṣa, īkak; the k is for strengthening; the ṭi is deleted.) From strī and puṃs, when the abstract state is expressed, nañ and snañ apply respectively: with nañ, streṇaḥ (woman); pauṃsnaḥ. These are the offspring suffixes (son of Varuṇa; son of the drinking water).

tenaraktaṃrāgāta: from a dye, "dyed with that." From a word ending in the third case that expresses a dye with which something is dyed, such as ochre or saffron, aṇ applies. In the sense of kaṣāyenaraktaḥ (male; to puṃs, snañ; strengthening; by the rule on eliding the end of a conjunct, the first s is deleted) we get kāṣāyaḥ. In the same way, in the sense of kudkumenaraktaḥ, with aṇ, kaudūnaḥ.

lākṣārocanāśakalakarddaḥṭhka: from lac, rocana, śakala and kardama, ṭhak.

From lac and these others (dyed with ochre), ṭhak applies in the sense of "dyed with that." In the sense of lṅakṣā (dyed with ochre; aṇ, the ṇ being for strengthening; dyed with saffron) gayāraktaḥ we get lākṣikaḥ (dyed with saffron). Doing the derivation in the same way, with ṭhak, raucanikaḥ; with ṭhak, śākalikaṃ. Since the commentary explains that from śakala and kardama aṇ optionally applies in the sense of "dyed with that," with aṇ we get karddamaṃ, and with aṇ śākalaṃ (dyed with lac; to lākṣā, ṭhak, the k being for strengthening, ṭha becoming ika).

The commentary cites nilātadana (dyed with indigo; dyed with bark; dyed with mud): from nīla, an. From nīla, an applies in the sense of "dyed with that" (an, the n being for the accent): nilaṃ, dyed with indigo. The commentary also (dyed with mud) cites pitātkaca: from pīta, kac (dyed with wood). From pīta, kac applies in the sense of "dyed with that": pitakaṃ, dyed yellow; in kac, the c is for the accent. The commentary also cites haridrayaḥañ: from haridrā, añ. From haridrā, añ applies in the sense of "dyed with that": hāridraṃ.

nakṣatreṇayuktaḥkālaḥ: for a time of conjunction with a lunar mansion. When a time of conjunction, in which the moon is joined with a lunar mansion, is indicated, aṇ applies. In the sense of puṣyiṇayuktaḥ the case ending together with yukta is deleted; with aṇ, pauṣaḥ. To that, by "ṭi, ḍha and the rest" (dyed with turmeric; añ, the ñ being for strengthening), ṅīp is given: pauṣī. Doing the derivation in the same way (joined with Puṣya, that is, the month of Puṣya), apart from the mere change of form when each stem meets its case ending, we get māghaḥ and māghī (full moon in Maghā); phālguṇaḥ and phālguṇṣi (the month of Puṣya); citraḥ and caitrī; baiśākhaḥ and biśākhī; jaiṣṭhaḥ (full moon in Jyeṣṭhā, that is, the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight) and jaiṣbī; āṣāḍhaḥ (to aṣāḍha, aṇ and ṅīp) and āṣāḍśī; śrābaṇaḥ (to śravaṇa, aṇ and ṅīp) and śrābaṇrī (to maghā, aṇ and ṅīp; to phalguṇa, aṇ; to citra, aṇ; the month whose full moon is in Citrā; to viśākha, aṇ; full moon in Viśākhā; the month of Jyeṣṭhā); bhādrapadī (full moon in Pūrvabhādrapadā; the month of Śravaṇa; full moon in Śravaṇa); āśaṭhenaḥ (to aśvinī, aṇ) and āśinī (full moon in Aśvinī); kārtikaḥ (to kṛttikā, aṇ and ṅīp) and kārtikī (the month of Mṛgaśiras); mārgaśiraḥ and mārgaśirī.

dṛṣṭaṃsāma: for "seen as a sāman" (the month of Pūrvabhādrapadā; to bhadrapada, aṇ). In the sense of "seen as a sāman" (full moon in Pūrvabhādrapadā; to bhadrapada, aṇ and ṅīp), añ applies to a word ending in the third case (the month of Aśvinī; to aśvinī, aṇ and ṅīp; the month of Kṛttikā; full moon in Kṛttikā; to mṛgaśiras, aṇ and ṅīp; full moon in Mṛgaśiras). In the sense of baśiṣṭhanadṛṣṭaṃ we get bāśiṣṭhaḥ.

paribṛtorthaḥ: a chariot covered all round. In the sense of "a chariot covered all round," añ applies to vastra and to carma. In the sense of pastreṇaparidraṃtorathaḥ (a chariot covered all round with cloth; seen by Vasiṣṭha) we get bāstaḥ (covered with cloth; añ, the ñ being for strengthening; añ, the ñ being for strengthening; seen by Vasiṣṭha). In the same way, cārmaṇaḥ, covered with leather.

tatrotdhṛtripātrebhyaḥ: from vessels, for "poured into that." From words for vessels, in the sense of "poured into that vessel," añ applies to a word ending in the seventh case. In the sense of sarabeuddhṛtaṃ we get sārabaḥ.

saṃskṛtaṃbhakṣāḥ: foods that are well prepared. When foods well prepared are expressed, añ applies to a word ending in the seventh case: bhrāṣḍāḥ.

sāsminpaurṇasātisaṃjhāyi: "that is in this," when it is the name of a full moon (poured into an earthen bowl). When a month complete from beginning to end (poured into an earthen bowl; añ, the ñ being for strengthening) is expressed, añ applies to words ending in the first and seventh cases. In the sense of pauṣīpaurṇamāsīasmin (añ and strengthening; cooked) we get bauṣomāsaḥ.

sāsyasebatā: "that is its deity." When it is said that that is its deity, añ and the rest apply to words ending in the first and sixth cases. In the sense of buddodebatāyasya, with añ, bauddhaḥ (full moon in Puṣya: in this is the full moon). Doing the derivation in the same way, with aṇ, śaibaḥ (añ and strengthening; the month of Puṣya); with aṇ, aindraḥ; and bārtasātyaṃ.

kasyeta: of ka, it. To the word ka, which applies to many meanings, when it expresses a deity, aṇ applies and the final of ka becomes it (whose deity is the Buddha): gāyaṃhabiḥ (belonging to the Buddha).

śukrudghana: from śukra, ghan. From śukra, when it is said that this is its deity, ghan applies (of Indra; of Jupiter; to bṛhaspati, yañ and strengthening): śukriyaḥ (purified).

somādyana: from soma, yaṇ. From soma, when it is said that this is its deity, yaṇ applies (Prajāpati; to ka, aṇ; ka becomes ki; the ṇ is for strengthening; by "ec becomes ay" and the rest): saumyaḥ (to soma, yaṇ, the ṇ being for strengthening).

pāyvṛtubitruṣasoyata: from vāyu, ṛtu, pitṛ and uṣas, yat (to śukra, ghan, the n being for the accent; gha becomes iya). From vāyu and these others, when it is said that this is its deity, yat applies: bāyabyaṃ; yoalbaṛtabyaṃ, of the seasons; uṣasyaṃ (of the burning one; cool, and also the moon; to pitṛ, yat).

rīṅritaḥ: of ṛt, rīṅ. Before suffixes that are not kṛt and the like, before suffixes for all roots, and before cvi, ṛt becomes rīṅ; the ṅ is for the accent: yartapitaḍyaṃ (of the ancestors; wind; to vāyu and ṛtu, yat, the t being for the accent; the u takes guṇa, and before what follows it ends in av).

agneḥḍhaka: from agni, ḍhak. From agni, when it is said that this is its deity, ḍhak applies: āgneya (by Agni).

debatādāṃdeca: for deities, also in a dvandva. When it is said that this is its deity, añ applies to the end of a dvandva compound, and by the word "also" the vowels of both the prior and the latter word are strengthened. In agniścamarutaśca the case endings and the rest are deleted; this sūtra gives añ; (to agni, ḍhak, the k being for strengthening, ḍha becoming e; by "of ya, also before i") the i is deleted; both prior and latter are strengthened: āgnimārutaṃ.

nendrasyaparasya: not of indra when it follows.

Even when it stands at the end of a dvandva compound, if the word indra is the latter member (as also with the Agni-deity and the Vāyu-deity), strengthening is not applied to that word: saumendraṃ. By the exclusion implied in the word "latter," when the word indra is the prior member, both are strengthened: aindagnaṃ.

dīrgdāccavaruṇasya: also of varuṇa after a long vowel. Even when it stands at the end of a dvandva compound, if the final vowel (ac) of the prior word is long, no strengthening takes place on the varuṇa that follows it (the moon and Indra: soma, indra, añ): endrabaruṇaṃ.

tasyasamūhaḥ: its collection (by Indra, pi, la). When its collection is to be expressed, aṇ and the rest apply after a word ending in the sixth case. In the sense of kākānīsamūhaḥ, aṇ: kvakaṃ. Forming the words in the same way: bānaspatyaṃ. strīṇi, a collection of women: bausnaṃ (bhañ, aṇ). Indra and cause, view.

bhikṣādibbyoñ(ṇā): aṇ after bhikṣa and the rest. From bhikṣa and the rest, when its collection is to be expressed, aṇ applies after the sixth-case ending (a gathering of crows): in the sense of bhikṣāṇāṃsamuhaḥ (a flock of crows), yat, aṇ (a collection of trees), neñ, aṇ (a collection of men), aḍā: bhaikṣāṃ. aṇ: kṣetraṃ. yaubayaṃ: yaba, til, aṇ.

gotrokṣoṣḍrorabhrarājarājarājaṇyarājaputrabatsamanuṣḍyajādbuñ: buñ after gotra, yukṣana, uṣṭa, urabhra, rāja, rājaṇya, rājaputra, batsa, manuṣḍya and aja (a collection of blodmo). From these, gotra and the rest, when a collection is to be expressed, buñ applies after the sixth-case ending (a collection of students, a collection of fields, a collection of khadmoma).
