nivāpacatiśarīropasamādhāneṣādeścakaḥ. "For dwelling, for fire, for the body, and for a heap of heavy things, the initial c too becomes k" (gloss: obtained good; obtained bad). To ciñ, accumulating, ghañ comes, and when dwelling, fire, the body or a heap of heavy things is expressed, the c becomes k: kāyaḥ.

ghañicaghāṣakaraṇayoḥ. "Before ghañ too, for the state and for the instrument." Before a ghañ used in the sense of the state or of the instrument, the n of rañja is also elided: rāgaḥ.

spadoḥjave. "Spadaḥ, for swiftness." By adding ghañ to spanpi, moving, spadaḥ is a set form (nipātana) for going swiftly (gloss: the body, entire).

ḍvitaḥktṛḥ. "For those marked with ḍu, ktri." After roots marked with ḍu, ktri comes in the sense of the action.

ktreḥmamanityaṃ. "From ktri, mam, always" (gloss: attachment). At the end of the affix ktri, mam always comes. To ḍukṛñ and ḍupacaṣ, by the previous sūtra (gloss: going swiftly), ktri is added, and by this sūtra mam is also added at the end of the affix: kraṃtvimi, paktrimaṃ, and so on.

ṭvitoñathuca. "From those marked with ṭu, athuc." After roots marked with ṭu, athuc comes in the sense of the action and so on. By adding athuc to ṭuvepṛ and to ṭuośvi: vepadruḥ (gloss: trembling), śrayathuḥ (gloss: increasing), and so on.

yajayācayatavicharakṣonaṅ (gloss: made; artificial). "From yaja, yāca, yat, vicha and rakṣa, naṅ." After yaja and these others, naṅ comes in the sense of the action and so on: pajñaḥ, yācñā, yatnaḥ, viśnaḥ, rakṣṇaḥ.

upasargegtoḥkiḥ. "After a preverb, from ghu, ki." After a preverb, from ghu, ki.

After roots called ghu following a preverb, ki comes: ādiḥ, niṅhiḥ, viṅhiḥ, viṅhiḥ, praṇiṅhiḥ, upaṅhiḥ, pariṅhiḥ.

svaponana. "From svap, nan." After svap, in the sense of the action (gloss: giving age; begging; going; protecting), nan comes: svapnaḥ.

striyāṃktin. "In the feminine, ktin." For the feminine gender too, ktin (gloss: first, or beginning; treasure; permitted; medicine, or; body, or remainder; circumference) comes for the state and for the agent: kṛtiḥ, buṅhiḥ, smṛtiḥ, and so on. Since the commentary says that ni comes after glā, hā, jyā and tvara (gloss: dream): glāniḥ, hāniḥ, jyāniḥ, turṇiḥ. Again, since the commentary explains that ni also comes after what ends in ṝ: kīrṇīḥ, gārṇiḥ, and so on.

ūtiyūtajūti (gloss: skilled; intelligence; mindfulness) sātihetikīrtayaḥ. "Ūti, yūti, jūti, sūhi, heti and kīrti." To av, yu and ju (gloss: exhaustion of joy; empty; aged; swift), by the rule beginning jvaratvara, and to sā, hi and khṝ, kti being added, ūti and these others (gloss: harming; clear) are also set forms (nipātana).

prajayajabhyāṃkyapa. "From vraja and yaja (gloss: protecting; mixed; going; bringing to an end; going; fame), kyap." After vraj and yaj, kyap comes in the sense of the action and so on: vrajyā, ijya (gloss: worship of the gods).

saṃjñāyāṃsamajaniṣadanipatamanavidaṣuñaśiṅbhṛñiṇaḥ. "For a name, from samaja, niṣada, nipata, man, vid, ṣuñ, śīṅ, bhṛñ and iṇ." After samaja and these others, kyap comes for a name and for the state: samajyā, niṣadyā (gloss: going); by pacasvapi and the rest, samprasāraṇa; nipatya, mantā, vadyā, sutyā (gloss: pure), śayyā (gloss: lying down), bhṛtyā (gloss: klarna), ityā (gloss: going).

kṛñośaca. "From kṛñ, śa." After kṛñ, for the state, śa comes. The c serves accent and the ś serves the purpose of śit; for the reason that the ś is marked, yak (gloss: lump; eats for certain); by śayak and the rest it is lengthened (gloss: certainly fallen; pride; knowledge); the augment tuk (gloss: whatever goes); and by the rules giving a and īya: kriyaḥ. Alternatively, kyap being added: krvāṝtyā.

paricaryāparisaryā. "Paricaryā and parisaryā." By adding ya to cara and sṛ preceded by pari, paricarya and parisaryū are set forms.

aḥpratyayāt. "After an affix, a." After roots ending in an affix such as san, a comes (gloss: making): jāgarā, cikīrlā (gloss: making), and so on.

guroścahalaḥ. "And after a heavy syllable, from what ends in a consonant." After a root ending in a consonant that follows the root's heavy first syllable (gloss: serving fully; going fully), a comes for the state: īhā, īkṣā.

ṣiddhvidādibhyo'ṅ. "From those marked with ṣ (gloss: new sleep; wishing to do) and from bhid and the rest, aṅ." After roots marked with ṣ and after bhid and the rest, aṅ comes for the feminine. For those marked with ṣ: mṛjā, jarā, vacā, and so on. For bhid and the rest (gloss: making; looking): bhidā, chidā, vidā, kṣipā, guhā, medhā, and so on.

cintipūjikathikumpicarcaśca. "And from cinti, pūji, kathi, kumbi and carca." After cint and these others, too, aṅ comes for the state (gloss: pure; old woman; cooking woman): cintvā, pūjā, kathā, kumba, carcā (gloss: split; cut; knowledge; desire; secret, or hidden; wise mind).

taścopasarge. "And after āt, with a preverb." After roots ending in ā preceded by a preverb, aṅ also comes: sanṭhṇā, saṃsthā, bradā, and so on.

ṇyasaśranthoyuca (gloss: like the mind; worship; talk; tent; worship). "From ṇi, ās and śrantha, yuc." After roots ending in ṇic, and after ās and śrantha, yuc comes: kāraṇā, āsanā, śrantānā.

pareḥpā. "Optionally after pari" (gloss: holding all; abiding properly; giving thoroughly). After iṣu preceded by pari, yuc optionally comes: paryeṣaṇaḥ. Alternatively, kti being added: parīṣṭiḥ.

ṇvulabahulaṃ. "Ṇvul, variously." For the feminine gender, in the state, the agent and others (gloss: wishing to do; seat; relaxed), ṇvul variously comes: āsikā (gloss: sitting), śāyikā (gloss: lying down), and so on. Since the commentary explains that kāra (gloss: searching fully) comes after letters in their own sense (gloss: in the sense of "fully"; the letter a): ākāraḥ, ikāraḥ, for the vowels, and kakāraḥ, khakāraḥ, gakāraḥ, and so on. Again, since the commentary says that for the letter r, ipha optionally comes: rephaḥ, rakāraḥ.

ajādibhyaḥiñ. "From those beginning with a vowel, iñ." After roots beginning with a vowel, iñ comes for the state and so on (gloss: the letter i): ājiḥ, ādiḥ (gloss: the letter ka, the letter kha, the letter ga), and so on.

vapādibhyaḥiṇ. "From vapa and the rest, iṇ." After vapa and the rest (gloss: the letter r), iṇ comes for the state and so on: vāpi, vāsiḥ, and so on.

kṛṣādibhyaḥik. "From kṛṣ and the rest (gloss: increasing; eating), ik." After kṛṣ and the rest, ik comes for the state: kṛṣiḥ, giriḥ, kariḥ.

vibhāṣākhyānāparipraśnayoriñ. "For narration and for questioning (gloss: sowing seed; dwelling), iñ, optionally." When narration or questioning is to be understood, iñ optionally comes for the feminine state: kātvaṃkāriḥkāmakārṣī. Alternatively, ṇvul being added (gloss: dug; mountain; harming): kātvāṃkāirikākīmakārṣī.

ākrośenañyaniḥ. "For abuse, after nañ, ani." When abuse is to be understood, ani comes after a root preceded by the negative nañ: ajanani, and so on.

lyuṭca. "And lyuṭ as well" (gloss: what work did you do, making the words into chapters?). After a root, in the sense of the action, lyuṭ (gloss: what work did you do, making the words into chapters?) commonly comes, and it is of the neuter gender: jñānaṃ, mānaṃ, pramāṇaṃ, gamanaṃ, bhojanaṃ, and so on.

vāyau. "Optionally, before yu." Before yu, that is, lyuṭ (gloss: unknowing, or unborn), aja optionally becomes vi: vayanaṃ, ajanaṃ.

Cited in the commentary: ṣṭhivuṣivorlyunyupadhādīrghovā. "Of ṣṭhivu and ṣivu, before lyuṭ, the penultimate (gloss: wisdom; respect; great respect; going; food) is optionally lengthened." Before lyuṭ, the penultimate of ṣṭhīvu and ṣivu is optionally lengthened: ṣṭhṭivanaṃ (gloss: casting away), sīvanaṃ (gloss: teaching; increasing). Alternatively, guṇa being applied by the rule on a penultimate light vowel before puk and the rest: ṣṭhevanaṃ (gloss: casting away), sevanaṃ (gloss: teaching).

puṃsisaṃjñāyāṃghaḥ. "In the masculine, for a name, gha."

In the masculine, gha also comes for an action and for a name: pakaḥ, gocaraḥ, sañcaraḥ.

chādeḥghe'dbyupasargasya. "Of chādi before gha, when it does not have two preverbs." Chādi, when no pair of preverbs or the like precedes it, becomes short before gha: bracharaḥ. When there are two preverbs it does not change: samubrachadaḥ.

vahavrajavyajāvaṇanigamāśca. (gloss: tserpa; domain of activity; conduct.) "Vaha, vraja, vyaja, avaṇa and nigama as well." Vaha, to obtain; vraja, to go; vyaja, debt; apa, to pervade; ni with the gamḷ above: gha being applied to these, (gloss: covering) vahaḥ, vrajaḥ, vyajaḥ, apaṇaḥ, (gloss: having grasped, it closely covers) nigamaḥ: these are set forms (nipātana).

khanoghaca. "From khana, gha as well." From khan, in the sense of an action, gha comes, and ghañ also comes: ākhanaḥ, ākhānaḥ.

īṣaduḥsuṣukhala. "When īṣat, dur and su precede, khal." (gloss: obtaining; going; debt; pervading.) To a root following ṣat, dur and su, in the sense of an action, khal comes: īkhatkaraḥ, duḥkaraḥ, sukaraḥ, and so on.

kartṛkarmaṇoścabhūkṛñoḥ. (gloss: digging all around.) "Also from agent and object, for bhū and kṛñ." When īṣat, dur and su come before the agent and object words, khal also comes from bhū and kṛñ following them: īṣadāḍyaṃbhavaṃ, durāḍhyaṃbhavaṃ, (gloss: makes slightly; makes with difficulty; makes easily) svāḍhyaṃbhavaṃ, īṣadāḍhyaṃkaraḥ, durāḍhyaṃkaraḥ, svāḍhyaṃkaraḥ.

ātoyuca. "From ā, yuc." To a root ending in ā, following īṣat, dur and su, in the sense of an action, yuc comes, and mum is not given by the rule on kha and the rest (gloss: becomes slightly rich; becomes rich with joy; becomes rich easily; makes slightly rich; makes rich easily). Khal does not come: īṣatvānaḥ, duḥbānaḥ, supānaḥ.

śāsiyudhidṛśidhṛṣimṛṣibhyaśca. "From śāsi, yudhvi, dṛśi, dhṛṣi and mṛṣi as well." From these, śāsi and the rest, following īṣat, dur and su, yuc also comes: suśāsanaḥ (gloss: well taught), suyodhanaḥ (gloss: fights well; drinks a little; hard to drink; easy to drink), sudarśanaḥ (gloss: sees well), sudharṣaṇaḥ (gloss: drinks well), sumarṣarṣaḥ.

alikhalāoḥpratiṣedhegdā. "From alaṃ and khalu, in prohibition, ktvā." When alaṃ and khalu are used in the sense of prohibition, khvā comes: alaṃkṛtvā, khalukṛtvā.

samānakartṛkayopūrvyākyāle. "For those with the same agent, at the earlier time." (gloss: endured well, or endured greatly.) Of the actions of the same agent, when the earlier time is expressed, ghā comes: ghukhābrājati, pitvābrajati.

kṣīskandasyandoḥ. "Of skanda and syanda, before ktvā." (gloss: makes ornament; makes certain.) The letter n of skanda and syanda is not elided before ktvā. By "car before khar," and by the rule on jhar before something like jhar, the upper t being dropped: skantvā, syantvā. To syandū, iṭ being optionally given by the rule on roots whose ū goes and the rest: (gloss: goes having eaten; goes having drunk) syanditvā.

mriḍamṛdhagudhakuṣabadavasaḥktvā. "From mṛḍa, mṛdha, guṅha, kuṣa, kliśa, vada and vas, ktvā." The gtvā with iṭ following these, mṛḍ and the rest, also bears the name of one whose k goes (gloss: having dried; having scattered): mṛḍitvā, mṛthitvā, kudhitvā, kuṣṛtvā, kliśaktvā (gloss: sorrow), kliṣḍā (gloss: having scattered). Vad and vas being changed by samprasāraṇa through the rule on vaci, svapi and the rest: uditvā, uṣitvā.

nopadhātvāphāntādvā. "From na as penultimate, from a final tha or pha, optionally." From roots such as śrantha and gunpha, which have the letter n as penultimate (gloss: having gathered; rich; snow frog; having pierced; iṭ being optional by the rule on roots whose u goes and the rest) and have a tha or pha at the end, the ktvā that follows, with iṭ, (gloss: having spoken; having sat) is optionally made to bear the name of one whose k goes: śrathitvā (gloss: from the sūtra, tsepa), śanthitvā, guphitvā, gunpitvā, and so on.

bañciluñcaṛtaśca. "From vañci, luñci and ṛt as well." From vañci, luñci and ṛt as well, the ktvā that follows, with iṭ, optionally bears the name of one whose k goes: bacitvā (gloss: having gone), bañcitvā, lucitvā (gloss: nyepa), luñcitvā, ṛtitvā. With the t dropped by the rule on jhar-like sounds and the rest: ṛtvā (gloss: the Lord; assembly).

tṛṣimṛṣikṛśeḥkāśyapasya. "From tṛṣi, mṛṣi and kṛśi, in the view of Kāśyapa." That the khyā with iṭ following these, tṛṣi and the rest, optionally bears the name of one whose k goes is held by the ancient sage Kāśyapa (gloss: he is said to be the name of the father of the sun (Sūrya); the Lord): traṣitvā, trārṣitvā, mṛṣitvā, marṣitvā, kṛśitvā, karśitvā.

jṝpraścoḥktvī. "From jṝ and vraśca, before ktvā." To the ktvā following jṝ and vraśc, iṭ always comes: jaritvā, vraścitvā.

uditobā. "After one whose ut goes, optionally." To the ktvā following a root whose ut goes, iṭ (gloss: thirst) optionally comes (gloss: patience). For śamu and (gloss: subtle) damu, the iṭ of ktvā being made optional, in the alternative without iṭ, by the rule that turns a nasal-bearing root to ā and the rest, (gloss: having grown old): śamitvā, śātvā (gloss: cutting), damitvā, dātvā.

kramaścaktī. "Of krama also, before ktvā." The penultimate of kram is optionally lengthened before ktvā without iṭ: krāntā, krantā. When there is iṭ it is not lengthened: kramitvā.

pūdaśca. "From pūṅ as well." To the ktvā following pūṅ, iṭ optionally comes: pavitvā (gloss: Śiva), būtvā (gloss: tulga).

jāntanaṃśāṃvibhāṣā. "Of j-finals and naśa, optionally." The letter n of roots ending in j and of niśa is optionally elided before ktā (gloss: legs stretched out): for bhañja, (gloss: legs stretched out) bhaktvā, bhaṃktvā, naṣṭvā, naṃṣṭrā, and so on.

jahāteścahiktvi. "Of jahāti, (gloss: having been cleansed; pure) hi before ktvā." Jahāti, that is, the root called ohāṅ, "to go," becomes hi before ktvā: hitvā.

samāse'nañapūrvektvolyapa. "In a compound not preceded by nañ, lyap for ktvā." (gloss: having entangled; not seen.) Where no compound with nañ precedes, at the end of a compound ktvā becomes lyap; the pa has the special purpose of bringing the augment tuk: prakṛtya. When there is nañ: akṛtvā (gloss: having gone), and so on.

pālyapi. "Optionally before lyap." The elisions of the nasal explained above are made optional before the lyap that replaces ktvā: āgatya, āgamya, praṇatya, and so on.

nalyapi. (gloss: natural form; not made.) "Not before lyap." Before the lyap that replaces ktvā, ghu, mā, sthā and the rest do not change to ī: vidhāya (gloss: holding apart), bradāya (gloss: giving forth), prasthāya (gloss: setting out), and so on. (gloss: entirely.) To mīṅ, (gloss: bowing down) ktvā having become lyap, and the root having changed to ā by the rule on mīnāti and the rest: nīmāya, and so on.

lyapilaghupūrvāt. "Before lyap, after a preceding light syllable." The final of ṇic, when a light syllable precedes it, becomes ay before lyap: ṇica, bigaṇayyaḥ.

bibhāṣāyyaḥ. "Ay optionally." Āpḷ ending in ṇic (gloss: certainly harms) optionally becomes ay before lyap: prābayya, prāpya, the ṇi being dropped where there is no iṭ. Since the commentary explains that kṣi is optionally lengthened before lyap (gloss: wishing to gather fully; wishing to bow down): prakṣiya, prakṣitya.

mayateridanyatarasyāṃ. "Of mayati, it optionally." The ā of mayati, that is, mēṅ, "to harm," (gloss: rabtu jabpa) becomes it before lyap: abamitya, abamāya.

lyapica. "Before lyap as well." Before lyap, peñ does not change to samprasāraṇa (gloss: wholly exhausted): prabāya.

bibhāṣāpare. "After pari, optionally." Before lyap, vyeñ following pari changes to samprasāraṇa (gloss: harms all around): parivīya, parivyāya.

ābhīkṣtyeṇamulca. "In repetition, ṇamul as well." When the earlier action of a single agent takes the qualification of repetition (gloss: continuing on), ktvā comes and ṇamul also comes: bhuktvābhuktvāprajati, bhojaṃbhojaṃprajati, and so on.

karmaṇyaktośekṛñaḥkhamuña. (gloss: rolled up completely.) "When kṛñ is joined with an object, khamuñ." To kṛñ following an object word, when it conveys abuse, khamun comes; the kha is for the sake of mum, and the ña for the sake of vṛddhi: cauraṃkāri. If it is not abuse (gloss: goes having eaten and eaten), ktvā is applied: sādhukṛtvāstauti.

svādumiṇamul. "With 'sweet,' ṇamul." Kṛñ following a word meaning "sweet" takes ṇamul: svādukāraṃbhukte, "having made it sweet, he eats." Or, with ktvā applied, (gloss: does the act of a thief) svādukṛtvāphukte, "having made it sweet, he eats."

anyathibaṃkathamitthaṃbhyaśca. (gloss: having said "Well done!", he praises.) "From anyathā, evaṃ, kathaṃ and itthaṃ as well." Kṛñ following anyathā, kathaṃ, itthaṃ and many others takes ṇamul: anyathākāraṃbhukte, evaṃkāraṃbhukte, kathaṃkāraṃbhukte, itthaṃbhukte, and so on.

jībādvideḥ. "From jīva, from pidi." When vidi is heard following jīva, ṇamul comes: jībavedaḥbhukte.

nimūlasalayoḥkaṣa. "With nimūla and sala, from kaṣa." (gloss: he eats having done it otherwise; he eats having done it thus; he eats having done it how; he eats having done it like this.) From kaṣa following nimūla and sal, ṇamul comes: nimūlalakāṣaṃ, salakāṣaṃ.

śuṣkacūrṇa (gloss: he eats having obtained a living) rukṣeṣupiṣaḥ. "With śuṣka, curṇa and rākṣa, from piṣa." To piṣa following śaṣka, curṇa and rūkṣa, ṇamul comes: śuṣkapeṣaṃ, cūrṇapeṣaṃ, rūkṣabeṣaṃ.

samūlākṛtajīveṣuhanakṛñ (gloss: certainly harms from the root) grahaḥ. "With samula, ākṛta and jīva, from han, kṛñ and graha." From han, kṛñ and graha, following samūla, ākṛta and jīva respectively, (gloss: grinds dry; grinds fine; grinds coarse) ṇamul comes: samūlabhātaṃ, ākṛtakāraṃ, jībagrāhaṃ.

hastakarayoḥbartigrahābhyāṃ. "With hasta and kara, from varti and graha." From varti and graha following hasta and kara, ṇamul comes: hastagrāhaṃ, karagrāhaṃ, hastabartaṃ, karabartaṃ.

svepuṣaḥ. "With sra, (gloss: destroys it from the root; made by acting all around; makes one hold on to life) from buṣa." From puṣa following sva, ṇamul comes: svapoṣaṃ.

upamānekarmaṇica. "In comparison, with an object." In comparison, (gloss: seized with the hand; seized the hand; seized the hand) ṇamul also comes from an agent word and from an object word: ratvānidhāyaṃ.

upadaṃśastṛtīyāṃ. "With the third, from ubadaṃśa." From upadaṃśa following a nearby word that ends in the third case (gloss: self-victor), ṇamul comes: mūlakenobadaṃśabhūṃkte, "he eats, biting along with the root vegetable."

apādāneparīpsāyāṃ. "In the source, in utmost haste." (gloss: from āt, yuk; holds firmly like a jewel.) With a nearby word ending in the source, that is, the fifth case, in the sense of an action that conveys great haste, ṇamul comes: śayāyāḥ (gloss: rose from lying down) utthāyaṃ.

dvitīyāṃca. "With the second as well." From a nearby word ending in the second case as well, when conveying haste, in the sense of an action, ṇamul comes: yaṣṭiṃgrahaṃyudhyanta.

abyayeyathābhibriyākhyānekṛñaḥktrāṇamulau. (gloss: to the tthā preceded by ut, ḍamul, with the augment suk; in ut, dropped by the rule on tthā, mhū and the rest.) "With an indeclinable, in expressing delight, ktvā and ṇamul from kṛñ." From a nearby word that is an indeclinable, (gloss: having seized the staff, they make them fall) for an action that conveys the sense of expressing delight, ktvā and ḍamul come: urcaicakṛtyapriyāṃbrute, uccaikṛtvāpriyāṃprūte, uccaikāraṃpriyīprūte, and so on.

iti pāṇinivyākaraṇasya sūtrātkṛtādayasāmābhūḥ, that is: here ends kṛt and the rest, from the sūtra of the Pāṇinivyākaraṇa.

With these, from The Chariot That Draws the Jewel of Excellent Explanation, which sets down as notes the meaning of the root text and its commentary, the procedures, the illustrative examples and so on, for the great treatise on grammar, the Pāṇinivyākaraṇa (gloss: expressing delight, he raised it high; expressing delight, he raised it high), the main procedures for deriving nouns from roots, kṛt and the rest, with general rules and exceptions, are for the time being complete.

At the end of the commentary there come a colophon and verses of auspicious wishes:

prakṛākaumātīseyi rāmacandraprakāśitā, asatvacastamovartūtācca korabriyāciri.

In Tibetan:

This treatise, the Very Clear,
Was made fully clear by Rāmacandra.
It binds the last of untrue speech,
And ever gladdens the discerning and the noble.

So it is said.

Second, the expression of auspiciousness:

ācārya bātu bhagabāna śiṣyaṃ pātu bināyakaḥ, nirbighīsyācca sarvatra bāṇinīya prasādataḥ.

In Tibetan:

May the Blessed One protect the teacher;
May the Guide protect the disciple.
Through the kindness of the sage Pāṇini,
May there be no obstacle anywhere.

maṅgalaṃ lekhakānāṃ ca bāthakānāṃ ca maṅgalaṃ, maṅgalaṃ sarvabhūgānaṃ bhūmibhūpati maṅgalaṃ.

May the writers be fortunate,
May the readers be fortunate,
May all living creatures be fortunate,
May the land and the lord of the land be fortunate.

So it is said.

Thus, among the eight great treatises on grammar, the one that excels in meaning, procedure and the rest, and is, in short, like the mother of all the sciences of language, is the Pāṇinivyākaraṇa. It was bestowed in person by the noble Lokeśvara upon the great brahmin Pāṇini, whom our Teacher, the peerless King of the Śākyas, prophesied in the Root Tantra of Mañjuśrī and elsewhere. This work, called The Chariot That Draws the Jewel of Excellent Explanation, sets down as notes the meaning, procedures, illustrative examples and so on of its root text and commentary. It came about in this way.

Our peerless refuge and sublime ally, for all of us who dwell among the snow mountains, is the noble Padmapāṇi himself, who has arisen in the form of a vajra-holder endowed with the three vows. For a purpose I mention him by name: the Victorious Lord, the great Omniscient One, Ngawang Lobsang Gyatso Jigme Gocha Thubten Langtsö De Tsangse Shepai Dorje. He cared for the paṇḍita brothers with the rays of his peerless compassion, and without effort granted them every requisite they could wish for, including many hundreds of zho of gold and silver. To me, his subject, he also gave this command: "Translate the root text into Tibetan, and set down as notes the meaning and the illustrative examples of the commentary." Through the immeasurable kindness of that holy one, I trained a little in the tradition of grammar.

I am the least of his subjects, born of the Se clan in the region of Dar in Upper Tsang, Ngawang Phuntsok Lhundrub, also named Tsewang Rabten Dorje, a dull and idle Tibetan. In the presence of the brothers, the mahāpaṇḍita Balabhadra, born of a pure brahmin family in Kurukṣetra in the Noble Land and learned in the five fields of knowledge, and the paṇḍita Gokulanātha Miśra, I listened carefully to the derivation of the words of the root text, its meaning, its illustrative examples and so on, and translated the root text into Tibetan.

I took as my basis the commentary composed by the great master Rāmacandra called the Prakriyā, that is, "The Procedure." The procedures that are hard to understand, such as those of the Complete Explanation, I adorned in the margins with the oral tradition of learned masters and expanded somewhat, and those that are easy to understand I kept brief.

I began it on an auspicious day of the waxing moon in the Chutö month, in the male dog year called Nachang, which is reckoned by fire, sky and ocean, and by ten cycles of sixty years with thirty-two mixed in, when I had reached the age of twenty-five. (note: detailed annotations on the derivations of the root text have been added.) I completed it in the iron rat year called Kündén, on the third victory day of the waxing half of the month of Caitra, at the auspicious time of the conjunction of Bashé, in my own quarters, Gyüteng Jilpo, at the great Dharma college of glorious Drepung. May this work, too, benefit the teaching and all sentient beings.

Since my own understanding is still very young, there may be impure translation in this work, or contradictions and errors in the illustrative examples, the meanings and so on. If any appear, I pray that the supreme lamas and the assembly of the learned bear with them patiently and correct them properly.

By this virtue, may the glorious Lord of Speech,
Who holds as his ground the precious gold where all the secrets of dense splendor gather,
The sole friend of the boundless beings to be trained throughout the three realms,
Whose sun and moon of excellent intelligence circle and pervade the vast sky of the knowable,
Who possesses the splendor of knowledge deeper than the ocean, remain firm for as long as there is time.

And may the white parasol of the twofold law, wrought by the good deeds of countless beings,
Adorned with the finial of a wish-fulfilling jewel that grants the splendor of every wish, excellent and vast,
Raised high in the sky, never to be stopped, filled with the cool shade of benefit and happiness,
Dispelling the torment of adversity for the teaching and for beings, become supremely and surpassingly beautiful.

If, in this work, the dust of wrong ideas has clouded
The lovely face of the meaning of the text, so that it is not clear,
I do not hide it before the eyes of the supreme and holy learned;
I pray that you polish it with the three pure examinations.

From the sole father of the Ganges, his way of knowledge,
May the clear, slow-flowing river of excellences that issues forth
Wash away all the stains of ignorance of thinking beings,
And enter the precious ocean of omniscience.

Translator's notes

The opening verses are ornate praise in which the names of the author's teachers seem to be woven (for example Ngawang, Kelzang, Gelek, Rinchen Jungné, Padkar), the second and third verse in particular being obscure; they are translated by their surface sense. "Balabhadra" renders སྟོབས་བཟང, taken as the Sanskrit name of the Indian paṇḍita who taught the author; this identification is uncertain. In the Mañjuśrī tantra quotation, དཔང་ཕྱུག is read as དབང་ཕྱུག (Lokeśvara). The master of the Siddhāntakaumudī is spelled བྷ་ཊོ་ཛཾ་བྷ་དྲ in the Tibetan; he is Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita. The Kāśikā is attributed here to "Kāśikara," as the text has it. In the commentary on the it rule, the name "possessing intent" (དགོང་པ་དང་བཅས་པ) is translated literally; the Tibetan otherwise renders the term it as "going" (འགྲོ་བ). རྐྱེད is read as རྐྱེན "affix". Several evident copyists' slips are read: བསཱུ་བ as བསྡུ་བ "collection"; ལྷ་བུ as ལྟ་བུ "like"; དགའ in the vṛddhi rule as དག "both"; ངུར as དུར "dur"; བྲད as བྲང "chest"; ཡྕེ as ལྕེ "tongue". The Tibetan spellings of the Sanskrit sūtras and collection names are kept letter for letter, even where they differ from the standard forms of Pāṇini's text. The gloss list of the twenty prefixes is loosely arranged in the Tibetan; the glosses are assigned to the nearest prefix. The string of glosses at the start (also, exceedingly past, good, and so on) appears to continue the glosses of the twenty prefixes from the previous piece. Evident copyists' slips read: མེ་ཟད as མི་ཟད "indeclinable"; ཀྱེ as ཀྱི; ཉར as ཧར in the hari example. The line "pen tip here; mchang this; ma this" and the phrase ཞེ་ལོང་ཞིག look like scribal jottings that entered the text; they are rendered literally. The worked examples (dadhi ānaya, madhu atra and so on) are kept exactly as the Tibetan spells them, though several stages are garbled. This is a Tibetan commentary on Pāṇinian grammar; the sūtras are 6.1.78 to 6.1.91 and related rules and vārttikas. The Sanskrit forms are given in their intended standard spelling; the Tibetan transcriptions are often defective (b for v, dropped or extra letters, e.g. "edhrati," "kṛrṇekatvam," "braśnauhaḥ"). The piece is interspersed with interlinear glosses (meanings of the examples, such as "they said," "the cow here," "the wealth of Kṛṣṇa," "debt of a debt") that have been copied into the running text, often displaced from the example they explain; they are translated where they stand. The verse defining the akṣauhiṇī is likewise displaced into the svaira discussion. Its first word, སུས་འགྱུར, is unclear; it is read as སུམ་འགྱུར, "threefold." In "oneness with Kṛṣṇa," གཉིད is read as ཉིད. The example for ūṭh is read as prasthauhaḥ; the Tibetan transcription is garbled. ཚིག་ཕྲད is taken in the Pāṇinian sense of nipātana, a form set down as given. This piece continues a Tibetan commentary on Pāṇinian sandhi rules (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.92 to 6.1.123 with vārttikas). The Sanskrit rules and examples are given in their intended standard form; the Tibetan transcriptions are often defective (b for v, dropped letters, as in "ubārābhīyati," "hayīṣā," "gavaśaḥ"). As in the preceding piece, interlinear glosses giving the meanings of examples (for instance "a fat cat" for sthūlotu, "homage to the Buddha" for buddhāyoṃ namaḥ, "the enemy of the asuras" for daityāri, "the best of lands" for go'gram) have been copied into the running text, often displaced; they are translated where they stand. Some glosses are obscure: the opening phrase about "ṛt," "non-attainment; grasping" under eve cāniyoge, and "from where, destroyed?" under paṭiti are rendered literally. In "acts toward it like a sage," the glossator appears to read ṛṣabha as ṛṣi. This piece continues the Tibetan commentary on Pāṇinian sandhi. Sanskrit rules and examples are given in their intended standard form; the Tibetan transcriptions are often defective. Interlinear glosses giving the meanings of examples ("the lord of cows" for gavendra, "a window" for gavākṣa, "O Devadatta, here," "Rāma lies down," "the Blessed One explains," "you six," and so on) are copied into the running text, often displaced; they are translated where they stand. In "the m into which adas has been changed," དམར is read as མར. Under nipāta ekāj anāṅ, the text's ན་ཡིན is read as མ་ཡིན ("do not make sandhi"), which the rule requires. Under śāt, the Tibetan says the ta class does not become the ṭa class; Pāṇini's rule concerns the ca class, but the text is translated as it stands. The final gloss དྲཻ་བ is obscure and is left untranslated as a stray syllable group. This piece continues the Tibetan commentary on Pāṇinian consonant sandhi (Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.4.45 to 8.3.31 with vārttikas), with comparisons from the Kalāpa grammar. Sanskrit rules and examples are given in their intended standard form; the Tibetan transcriptions are often garbled (for instance "urbpānaṃ" for utthānam, "kibhālayati" for kivhvalayati). As before, interlinear glosses giving the meanings of examples ("the lord of speech," "the son of six mothers," "six plows," "fames," "the driver of an elephant," "a year," "whatever world") are copied into the running text, often displaced, and are translated where they stand. Some glosses are obscure and are rendered literally (for example "easy giving," "he went yesterday," "six good verses"); "hṇo" is a stray fragment. The inserted Kalāpa quotation under jhayo ho'nyatarasyām is partly duplicated in the Tibetan and is translated once. This piece continues the Tibetan commentary on Pāṇinian sandhi (Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.3.31 to 8.3.36, 6.1.73 to 6.1.76, with vārttikas), with a comparison from the Kalāpa. Sanskrit rules and examples are given in their intended standard form; the Tibetan transcriptions are often garbled (for instance "sacchvaddhā," "pradyaddādmā"). Interlinear glosses giving the meanings of examples ("the giving of faith, or the giving for the departed" for śraddhā, "a cuckoo," "you, cut!", "O wielder of the wheel, protect!", "protect men!", "a barbarian," "shame," "the shadow of glory") are copied into the running text, often displaced from their examples; they are translated where they stand. Several glosses are obscure and are rendered literally ("not the mother of those six," "fresh butter, coiled," "the drawing of a field," "the purifier of the buddhas," "what is young?"). ཐྐ and ལྤ are taken as the jihvāmūlīya and upadhmānīya. This piece of a Sanskrit grammar (on visarga sandhi, following Pāṇinian sūtras) carries short Tibetan interlinear glosses of the Sanskrit examples, which the copy has scattered into the running text, often away from the words they gloss ("Hari sleeps" for hariḥ śete, "Homage to Ākāśagarbha" for namaḥ khagarbhāya, "Worship Śiva" for śivo 'rcyaḥ, "Homage to the Buddha" for namo buddhāya, "Day and night" for ahorātra, and so on). As in the preceding piece, they are translated where they stand. "Surabu" after bṛhaspatiḥ is an unidentified gloss and is left as written; one gloss after "lord of the day" is written smu ba, evidently a slip for smra ba, "speech". The Sanskrit sūtras and examples are given in normalized romanization where the Tibetan spelling is plainly garbled (for instance the jihvāmūlīya and upadhmānīya forms, which the Tibetan writes as stacked letters, and the forms with pati in the final examples of ro 'supi). As in the preceding pieces, short Tibetan glosses of the Sanskrit examples have been copied into the running text, often out of place ("Rāma and", "Rāmas", "O Rāma", "O two Rāmas, O Rāmas", "To Rāma", "Rāma, Rāma"); they are translated where they stand. In the first listing of the su set the Tibetan gives only six groups, lacking ṅe bhyām bhyas and reading bhyas for bhis; it is given as written, while the full seven groups appear in the next paragraph. Sanskrit sūtras and endings are given in normalized romanization where the Tibetan spelling is evidently garbled. The work named in the colophon, "The Chariot That Draws the Jewel of Excellent Explanation", is a Tibetan title and is translated. "Called it" renders the Tibetan "bearing the name 'going'", a calque on the Pāṇinian technical term it (indicatory letter). As in the preceding pieces, short Tibetan glosses of the Sanskrit forms ("To the Rāmas", "By the two Rāmas", "For Rāma", "Of the two Rāmas", "In that Hari" and so on) have been copied into the running text, often out of place; they are translated where they stand. In the list of sarva and the rest, the Tibetan gives glosses after some words and then a separate run of glosses for the later words ("east, or seven, or before ... you, I, being"), which has been inserted into the following sentence; both are kept where they stand. The gloss "par" after pūrva is left as written, and "yad" renders a syllable the Tibetan spells as "also". Sanskrit sūtras and forms are given in normalized romanization where the Tibetan spelling is evidently garbled (for example dāmebhyaḥ for rāmebhyaḥ, sarvāma for sarvān). "Hari statra" is reproduced as written. As before, short Tibetan glosses of Sanskrit words ("heaven", "Exceedingly all", "For the sake of all joy", "Of east, beyond, and other", "Earlier by an equal", "The firsts", "The seconds") have been copied into the running text and are translated where they stand. The run of glosses after prathame, prathamāḥ corresponds to prathama, alpa, ardha, katipaya and nema; its first item is partly garbled in the Tibetan ("first, or at the start"; "few"). The compound term bahuvrīhi, which the Tibetan calques, is given in Sanskrit. Sanskrit sūtras and forms are given in normalized romanization where the Tibetan spelling is evidently garbled. As in the preceding pieces, short Tibetan glosses of the Sanskrit words ("Old", "Not old", "Two days", "Drinker of all" and so on) are scattered through the text and are translated where they stand. The run of glosses after the list of substitutes (from "Foot" to "Padaḥ is formed") is badly garbled in the Tibetan: some items match the stems (foot, water, nose, heart, night), others cannot be matched with confidence; they are rendered literally. The Tibetan reads pūṣa and pūṣan where Pāṇini has yūṣa and yūṣan; this text's reading is kept. "Without the sun" renders a stray two-syllable gloss after "masculine stems" whose reference is unclear. The piece ends in mid-sentence; the rule is completed in the next piece. Sanskrit sūtras and forms are given in normalized romanization where the Tibetan spelling is evidently garbled. This is a Sanskrit grammar; the declined forms and sūtras written in Tibetan letters are given in standard romanization, and where the Tibetan spelling contains an evident scribal slip in a form (for example "hari" for harim, "haribhe" for haribhyaḥ, "heviśvapāḥ" spelled oddly, "haryauḥ" for haryoḥ) the evident form is given. The paradigms are rendered exactly as the text lists them, even where forms are missing (the sixth and seventh cases of viśvapā give only two forms each, and the seventh lists viśvapoḥ). The Tibetan glosses after hari ("the Remover, the Śiva-drinker, the dyer, the gandharva") are rendered literally and their exact intent is uncertain. The glosses "the lord of glory, fire, the sun, poetry" belong to śrīpati, agni, ravi and kavi in the preceding sentence but stand displaced in the Tibetan within the sakhi rule; they are translated where they stand. This is a Sanskrit grammar; declined forms and sūtras written in Tibetan letters are given in standard romanization, and evident scribal slips in the Tibetan spelling of forms (for example the word for kati written lati, sakhīnā for sakhīnām, katīnī for katīnām, tabhiḥ for tribhiḥ, triṇu for triṣu) are silently read as the evident forms. Several Tibetan glosses stand displaced in the text and are translated where they stand, in parentheses: "lord" (a gloss of pati) inside the sentence on kati, and "lord of beings" (a gloss of prajāpati) inside the sūtra on saṃkhyā. "Those that bring in the many" renders the Tibetan for the first members of the sūtra bahugaṇa. No form is given for kati in the seventh case. The paradigms are otherwise given exactly as the text lists them. This is a Sanskrit grammar; declined forms and sūtras written in Tibetan letters are given in standard romanization, with evident scribal slips in the spelling of forms silently read as the evident forms (for example pradhau for pradhyau, sradhī for pradhī, sakhūḥ for sakhyuḥ). As in earlier pieces, many short Tibetan glosses of Sanskrit stems stand displaced in the text; they are translated in parentheses where they stand. They gloss words named nearby: "one who worships the gods" and "one supremely excellent" (devayajī and atilakṣmī from the previous piece), "a good mind" (sudhī), "beautiful form, or glory..." and "a barley merchant" (suśrī and yavakrī), "supreme mind" (pradhī), "holder" (probably didhī), "leader" (nī), "the village informer" (apparently grāmaṇī, rendered literally), "one who reaps a field" (probably lūnī), "Viṣṇu; wind; sun" (viṣṇu, vāyu, bhānu), and "jackal" (kroṣṭu). The Great God is the gloss of śambhu. The forms grāmaṇiyām and lūnī are given as the Tibetan spells them. This is a Sanskrit grammar; forms and sūtras written in Tibetan letters are given in standard romanization, with evident scribal slips in the spelling of forms read as the evident forms (for example kroṣṭā for kroṣṭrā, bhātṛ for bhartṛ). The hūhū paradigm is given as the text lists it, although the second-case forms look disturbed. As in earlier pieces, short Tibetan glosses of Sanskrit stems stand displaced in the text and are translated in parentheses where they stand: "very moving" (perhaps aticamū), "a good cutter" (sulū), "self-existent" (svayambhū), "arising in the rainy season" (varṣābhū), "the masculine maker arising; arising again" (kārābhū and punarbhū), and "holder" (bhartṛ). The word read as kaṭasū is uncertain, since the Tibetan gloss interrupts it. This is a Sanskrit grammar; forms and sūtras written in Tibetan letters are given in standard romanization, with evident scribal slips read as the evident forms (for example "bhartriṭsa" for bhartṛṣu, ramāye for ramāyai, "explained not complete" read as "explained"). The colophon in Sanskrit is given letter for letter as the Tibetan spells it, followed by the text's own Tibetan rendering of it. The glaui paradigm is given as the text lists it, though the second-case forms appear disturbed. Short Tibetan glosses stand displaced in the text and are translated in parentheses where they stand: "grandson; fire offering; fire offering" (naptṛ, hotṛ, potṛ), "male" (nṛ), "son-in-law; brother" (jāmātṛ, bhrātṛ), "gold, or wealth" (rai), "she who is hard to approach; the goddess of Nagarakoṭa" (Durgā and Ambikā). Two glosses are unclear: one read as "the sun" (the Tibetan has a word that looks like a slip for the word for sun, perhaps glossing sudyo), and the gloss on ramā, read as "the playful one" on the assumption of a slip. The text is a Sanskrit grammar; the Sanskrit forms written in Tibetan letters are given in normalized romanization. Several short Tibetan words scattered among the paradigms ("the variegated one," "old woman," "Vasudhārā; the goddess who pierces," "she who drinks the variegated; the cowherdess," "intelligence") appear to be interlinear glosses that have entered the main text; some seem misplaced (the last pair evidently glosses viśvapā and gopā, the first perhaps viśvā). They are kept in parentheses, as in the preceding piece; "the goddess who pierces" is a literal rendering of an unclear gloss. Evident slips read: the second sarvābhyām for bhyas as sarvābhyaḥ; "lāṭ" in the ramā option as yāṭ; the doubled "dvitīyāyai" and "tṛtīyasyai" as the two alternants of each; "pṛbhyīḥ" as pṛdbhiḥ; "mingma bra'a" in the vraśc rule as "word-final." The third plural of uttarapūrvā is not given in the Tibetan, and the final form for niś with su is left incomplete as written ("ni ta"). The Sanskrit grammatical forms written in Tibetan letters are given in normalized romanization; obvious misspellings in the Tibetan (for example "na tisṛcatasṛ ... lam yin" for "la min," "vaṭ" for āṭ, "he stē" for he stri) are read in their evident sense. As in the preceding pieces, short Tibetan words scattered among the paradigms ("mind," "three dear ones," "four dear ones," "the white one," "flowing; a river," "the glorious lady," "Tārā," "woman," "hearing," "memory") appear to be interlinear glosses that have entered the text, several out of place; they are kept in parentheses. Sanskrit grammatical forms written in Tibetan letters are given in normalized romanization, with evident misspellings read in their intended sense (for example "long ā" in the heading of the vadhū section, which the closing line confirms as long ū). As in earlier pieces, many short Tibetan words among the paradigms appear to be interlinear glosses that have entered the text, some out of place (for example "the milch cow" for dhenu, "the vixen" for kroṣṭrī, "the bride" for vadhū, "she who comes into being again" for punarbhū, "she who appears in the rainy season" for varṣābhū, and the kinship terms for the svasṛ group); they are kept in parentheses. "The slender one" and "the one in between" are literal renderings of unclear glosses. In the punarbhū rule the clause rendered "whether absent or, as in the example, present" is obscure in the Tibetan and its sense is uncertain. Sanskrit grammatical forms written in Tibetan letters are given in normalized romanization, with evident misspellings read in their intended sense; for example, the Tibetan says jas and śas "become" with the replacement śi dropped, which the sūtra quoted supplies. As in earlier pieces, short Tibetan words among the forms ("wealth; forest; fruit," "the heart," "water," "seat," "head") appear to be interlinear glosses that have entered the text, some out of place; they are kept in parentheses. Sanskrit grammatical forms written in Tibetan letters are given in normalized romanization, with evident misspellings read in their intended sense. As in earlier pieces, short Tibetan words among the forms ("the one who enjoys glory," "water," "bone," "good intellect," and the list "curd; strength; eye" with the sentences glossing the commentary's examples) appear to be interlinear glosses that have entered the text; they are kept in parentheses. In these glosses "strength" stands where the Sanskrit example has sakthi, "thigh"; the Tibetan word may be a slip, but it is rendered as written. Many of the Sanskrit paradigm forms are miswritten in the Tibetan transmission (for example madhubhiḥ written with bh for dh, the ṅi ending labelled ṅe, sulubhiḥ written as sulubhyāṃḥ, several priyakroṣṭṛ forms written without r, lihi written lihe, and pradyo/pradyu written in a garbled way); they are given here as the rules stated in the text require. The form "pradyanoḥ" among the os forms is as written and appears to be a corrupt duplicate. Short Tibetan glosses inserted in the source (honey, one who cuts well, excellent wealth, a good boat, one who tastes) are interlinear explanations of the stem meanings and are rendered as such; the gloss "a good boat" stands misplaced in the source beside prarai and has been placed with sunau, to which it belongs. The isolated word "set" after the vocatives of lih is rendered "So they are set out." Many of the Sanskrit forms are miswritten in the Tibetan transmission (for example dh and d interchanged in the duh and druh paradigms, bi and bu for vi in viśvauh-, ukthaśās written uklaśās and avayāj written alayāj); they are given as the rules stated in the text require. In the druh paradigm the source repeats dhrugbhyām and has a meaningless syllable string before dhruḍbhyaḥ, and gives dhruṭsu twice for sup; these are rendered as the full sets of optional forms the text describes. Brief Tibetan glosses inserted in the source (to be bewildered, an ox, white) are interlinear explanations of stem meanings and are rendered as such. The stem written bhūvaha is given as written. Many Sanskrit forms are miswritten in the Tibetan transmission (for example tvarā for turā, sudyam for sudyām, sudivaḥ for sudivā, a corrupt form for caturṇṇām, a stray śvetavāha before śas, and duplicated ukthaśāsoḥ and turāṣāṭ); they are given here as the rules stated in the text require. The heading "ending in the letter p" before sudiv is read as "ending in v", since div ends in v. In the remark on the commentary to "of what ends in atu or as," the Tibetan reads "before su that is saṃbuddhi"; this is read as "not saṃbuddhi," in line with the rule as given in the preceding passage and with the argument for optionality that follows. The vocatives of priyacatur are written in the source without priya. Brief Tibetan glosses in the source (a fine day, the horse of Śakra, four, four joys) are interlinear explanations of stem meanings and are rendered as such. Several Sanskrit forms are miswritten in the Tibetan transmission (for example vṛtraghnaḥ written as a garbled bṛtrahaghan); they are given here as the rules stated in the text require. In the explanation of "elision before hal," the Tibetan has yid ("mind"), evidently a slip for id, the syllable being elided, and is translated so. The short Tibetan glosses inserted in the source (a king or one who shines, shining severally, one who worships the gods, Brahmā, one who destroys growth) are interlinear explanations of stem meanings; "Brahmā" appears to belong with brahman in the line above. In the closing remark, the Tibetan says the n "does not become n"; given the rule it blocks, this is read as ṇ. Several Sanskrit forms are miswritten in the Tibetan transmission (for example vṛtrahan written with p, maghavan forms spelled in varying ways, pathā written pathū, pathibhiḥ written pibhiḥ); they are given here as the rules stated in the text require. The sixth-case set of vṛtrahan gives only two forms. In explaining "guṇa with a" the Tibetan writes au, but the result maghonaḥ shows o is meant. The brief Tibetan glosses in the source (the kṛṣṇasāra deer, abundant, the sun, Śakra, a dog, youth or the prime of life, a path) are interlinear explanations of stem meanings; the first group is placed after maghavan in the source and its exact reference is unclear. This piece is part of a Sanskrit grammar following Pāṇinian sūtras; the sūtras and paradigm forms, written in Tibetan letters, are given in romanized Sanskrit, normalized where the Tibetan spelling has evident scribal slips (for example ṛbhukṣin for the written ṛbhukṣan, bhudbhiḥ for bhudhīḥ, budhām for bubhām). Śakra at the instrumental of ṛbhukṣin is a gloss on the word's meaning (Indra). The words "seven, nine, ten" after the stem aṣṭan are terse; they are taken as contrasting aṣṭan with the other n-final numerals, which do not take ā. A Pāṇinian grammatical paradigm; sūtras and forms written in Tibetan letters are given in romanized Sanskrit, normalized where the Tibetan has evident slips (for example rāḍbhyām for the written rānbhyām, ūrgbhyām for ūbhyām, viśvārāṭ for viśvārīta). The word མདོས here is the abbreviation for sūtra, not a thread-cross. The gloss after tvāhau sau reads "བོད། ངའམ་བདག", most likely a slip for "you; I or self." A Pāṇinian paradigm of the pronouns yuṣmad and asmad; sūtras and forms written in Tibetan letters are given in romanized Sanskrit, normalized where the Tibetan has evident slips (for example vaya for the written paya, yuṣmābhiḥ for yuṣṣābhiḥ, at for the written aha in the gloss on pañcamyā at). A Pāṇinian paradigm; sūtras and forms written in Tibetan letters are given in romanized Sanskrit, normalized where the Tibetan has evident slips (for example atitvām for the written atitī, ativayam for atipayam, atitava for atiṭava and atirava, atyaham for atiatvam). "Compound with an indeclinable" renders the Tibetan term literally; the forms are compounds of ati with the pronoun. A Pāṇinian grammar; sūtras, forms and Sanskrit examples written in Tibetan letters are given in romanized Sanskrit, normalized where the Tibetan spelling is plainly faulty. Where the Tibetan spelling of an example is too garbled to restore with confidence (the examples for vaḥ and naḥ in the second case), only its meaning is given. In the source, the glosses "son of you two, son of us two" have slipped into the sūtra na cavāhāhaivayukte; they are placed here with the example they translate. The rule on words of seeing is translated as this text states it. This piece consists of Sanskrit grammatical paradigms and Pāṇinian rules transcribed into Tibetan letters, and many forms are miswritten in the transcription (for example "su pa ṅaḥ" for supadaḥ, "su pā dā" for supātsu, "agni ma trū" for agnimatsu, "prākṣa" for prākṣu, "amumu ya kṣāṃ" for amumuyagbhyām, "amumu ta ñcaḥ" for amumuyañcaḥ); the evident correct forms are given. The phrase rendered "or ṅ" (Tibetan sngon nam shar) in the explanation of kṅiti is obscure and is taken as glossing the marker ṅ. The word mdos ("thread-cross") in "by the sūtra viṣvagdevayoś..." is taken as a slip for mdo, "sūtra." A few syllables in the discussion of the earlier masters' views (ing dai mi zad pa'o) appear to be an intrusive gloss and are not rendered. In the udac paradigm the sixth case gives only two forms; the genitive singular is missing in the Tibetan. As in the preceding pieces, many Sanskrit forms are miswritten in the Tibetan transcription (for example "prādbhyām, prāddhiḥ" for prāṅbhyām, prāṅbhiḥ; "mahate" for mahataḥ; "suvṛdbhyām" for suvṛḍbhyām; "he bhavoḥ, he aghola" for he bhagoḥ, he aghoḥ); the evident forms are given. The instrumental singular of mahat is missing in the Tibetan, and the stray words "byin" after ṅasi in the prāñc paradigm is not rendered. "Ja śa su ta" is read as yaśasvat, "abhavat" as aghavat, and "ṅhimra" as dhīmat. The words "animal fat" (dud 'gro rgyags po) after tiras appear to be a gloss on tiryañc, "animal"; only "animal" is rendered. As in the preceding pieces, many Sanskrit forms are miswritten in the Tibetan transcription (for example "dharmagurām" for dharmagupam, "baḍbhyā" for viṭtsu, "nadbū, naḍyu" for naṭsu, naṭtsu, and "ṣaḍbhyāṃ, ṣadbhaṃ" for the genitive plural of ṣaṣ, here given as ṣaṇṇām, ṣaḍṇām); the evident forms are given. Some forms are missing in the Tibetan (the instrumental plural and the ablative singular of tyādṛś), and the first of the commentary's "krin" is read as kvin. A stray gloss in the viś paradigm, "seeing equally, or seeing alike," evidently belongs to sadṛś just above and is not repeated there; a few isolated syllables in the dadhṛṣ paradigm (rtsem, rtses) make no sense and are not rendered. As in the preceding pieces, the Sanskrit forms are often miswritten in the Tibetan transcription (for example "cikīnaḥ" for cikīḥ, "pipatārṣe" for pipaṭhīrṣu); the evident forms are given. The latter half of the dos paradigm is disordered in the Tibetan (case labels and forms are displaced, and a form "śoṣi" appears), and it has been set out in the evident order. The stems read here as supis and sunus are uncertain from the transcription. Two short glosses, "babar skyong" after pipakṣ and an extra "wishing to do" inside a rule citation for cikīrṣ, are obscure; the second has been rendered as the gloss on cikīrṣ, the first is not rendered. As before, mdos ("thread-cross") in "by the sūtra" is read as mdo, "sūtra." As in the preceding pieces, many Sanskrit forms are miswritten in the Tibetan transcription (for example "vidvadū" for vidvatsu, "suhidsau" for suhiṃsau, "uśamla" for Uśanā); the evident forms are given. The stem written "su hi nsa," with the gloss "living very well," is read as suhiṃs; the gloss does not fit that stem well, and the reading is uncertain. The final stem "su bas" is uncertain and is given as written, suvas. The gloss bsang pa on Uśanas is rendered "the pure one." The Tibetan says the marker of asuṅ is d; it is evidently ṅ. This is a grammatical manual on Pāṇinian declension; the Sanskrit forms and sūtras, written in Tibetan letters, are given in standard romanization. Several syllables appear to be copyists' slips and are translated by their evident reading: the d of adas is said to become "n" where the sūtra and the forms require m; "from the many" in the colophon is read as "from the sūtras"; "thread-cross" (mdos) in the gir section and the stray words "clear light" (in the div section) and smrag (in the gir section) make no sense in this grammatical context and are treated as intrusions; "rba" is read as sarvā; dur is read as dhur. The Tibetan gloss on upānah ("bound on closely") is rendered as "a sandal bound on the foot"; the syllables following it are unclear. Where the Tibetan writes two garbled bhis-type forms for upānah and two bhis-type forms for catur under "the two bhyas," the expected bhyām and bhis/bhyas forms are given. The stem in the div-section (dyūrṇut) is reconstructed from the Tibetan spelling and the described sandhi. A grammatical manual on Pāṇinian declension; Sanskrit forms and sūtra names are given in standard romanization, and several evident scribal slips in the Tibetan transcription of the forms are silently read as the expected forms (for example syā for the Tibetan "stā", ṅas asyāḥ, and the alternative enām, ene, enāḥ, which the Tibetan writes as enā, ena, enaḥ). The stray syllables phog ga in the diś section and sa dag bam in the sajuṣ section have no sense in context and are treated as intrusions. The phrase after vāgbhiḥ, "speech or utterance," is taken as a gloss on the meaning of vāc. A grammatical manual on Pāṇinian declension; Sanskrit forms and sūtra names are given in standard romanization, reading evident slips in the Tibetan transcription as the expected forms (for example svanaḍuhī for au, brahmāṇi and ahāni for jas, sudaṇḍine for ṅe). The opening "ending in" letter is garbled in the Tibetan and is read as h from the stem svanaḍuh; ahan is introduced as "ending in m," read as n. Short Tibetan words inserted among the forms are taken as meaning glosses: "good ox" for svanaḍuh (the added "garuḍa" in that gloss makes no sense and is left aside), "Brahmā" at brahman, "day" at ahan, and "a fine staff" at sudaṇḍin. The seventh-case list for brahman omits the singular, and the sixth-case list for bahvaryaman ends with what is in fact the seventh plural; both are given as the Tibetan has them. A grammatical manual on Pāṇinian declension; Sanskrit forms and sūtra names are given in standard romanization, reading evident slips in the Tibetan transcription as the expected forms. Several stray syllables in the Tibetan (repeated "condition," "together with," and "au ṣa") have no sense among the forms and are treated as intrusions; "bow" is taken as a gloss on dhanus. The tyad section is headed "ending in ṅ," read as d; under dhanus the Tibetan says "bhyām and bhyas" where bhyām and bhis are meant. The stem written go a ca is given as goac, and ja kā ta, bha ta and pa yas are read as jakṣat, bhāt and payas. This piece lists Sanskrit indeclinables, partly written in Tibetan letters and partly given only by Tibetan glosses of their meanings; Sanskrit items are romanized in standard form, and the Tibetan glosses are translated as they stand, in the order given. Many glosses are terse or obscure (for example "fainted," "the sense of the mother," "settled on its base," "a knock," "ash," "beggar," "savadi"), and several of them, such as "wisdom," "suchness," "mantra," "patience," "multicolored," "mind," "joy," and "the day after," may be copyists' insertions or loosely attached glosses rather than meanings of a specific neighboring item; they are translated literally without attempting to match them to Sanskrit words. The stray word "swiftly" inside the taddhitaś cāsarvavibhaktiḥ explanation is omitted there as an evident intrusion. The garbled suffix list after kṛtvasuc is rendered as "kṛtvasuc, śas, tasi, and cvi and the rest." This piece is a set of notes on Pāṇini's grammar in which short Tibetan interlinear glosses on the Sanskrit example words have been run into the main text, often displaced from the word they gloss (for instance the glosses on the feminine forms ajā, eḍakā and so on, and on karttrī, daṇḍinī and so on, appear several words later in the Tibetan). I have placed each gloss beside the word it evidently explains. A few intrusive fragments yield no sense and are not rendered: "having made" and "on" inside the Sanskrit verse, a stray "ma" after udeto, "de phan mi" among the flower compounds, and "dang babs" after the glosses on jyeṣṭhā and so on. Several glosses do not obviously match their words (e.g. "having remembered" for kṛtvā, "drinking" with tosun, "ill" for tudantī); I give them as written. The Tibetan spells the feminine suffix ṅīp as "dīpa" and once writes "ṭūpa" for ṭāp; I use ṅīp and ṭāp. "Mi zad pa," literally "unexhausted," renders avyaya, "indeclinable"; the text plays on both senses. The final words of the passage on rājayudhān read "is not destroyed" (mi 'jig), evidently a slip for "does not apply" (mi 'jug), which I translate. The Tibetan rendering of the avyaya verse has "together alike" and adds the gloss "rnam par mgyogs pa," rendered by sense. As in the preceding piece, short Tibetan glosses on the Sanskrit example words are run into the text, often displaced; I place each beside the word it evidently explains. A few intrusive fragments yield no sense and are left out: "a hired woman" after bahuyajvana, "a word-maker" among the tyak examples, "or" and "two" in the passage on nirbhastrakā, and "yes and not" near jībakā. In the passage on parṇakā the Tibetan says that a becomes i both in the sense of thread and in other senses; one of the two clauses has presumably lost a negative (the Sanskrit tradition exempts this word in the sense of woollen cloth), but I translate it as written. "Changes into e" for nirbhastrakā reads ཨེར, evidently for ཨིར "into i", which I follow. In the sūtra on the northerners, the Tibetan writes "byung pa rnams" where "byang pa rnams," "the northerners," is plainly meant, and I translate accordingly. As in the neighbouring pieces, Tibetan glosses on the Sanskrit example words are run into the text and are often displaced; I place each beside the word it evidently explains. Several at the opening belong to examples in the preceding piece: "she who has exhaustion," "she who takes five" (pañcatāyī), "she who has eyes" (ākṣikī) and "she who is salty" (lāvaṇikī). Some intrusive fragments yield no clear sense and are not rendered in the body: "day-maker," "many who use bad speech" (apparently on the īkak examples), "a woman who makes offerings," "a woman with a conch," "slender-bodied," "sgang yo sam," "sda ma," "two rivers," and "a tree with two thorns." In the sūtra on sapatnī and the rest, the Tibetan has the word "child" (byis pa) in the middle of the Sanskrit, which I leave out. The text writes ṅīp as "dīpa" and ṅīṣ as "dīṣa"; I use the standard names. Here མཆོད་སྦྱིན means "sacrifice" (yajña), not the personal name Yajñadatta. As in the neighbouring pieces, Tibetan glosses on the example words are run into the text, often displaced; I place each beside the word it evidently explains. The two glosses at the opening, "she who has a lord along with another" and "she who has one lord," belong to sapatnī and ekapatnī in the preceding piece. A few fragments yield no clear sense and are left out of the body: "bha'i ta," "sna ba mo," "dra las"/"dral" (perhaps glossing paddhati), "pale grey," "clear," "gsab ba," and "intelligence." In the sūtra on manu the Tibetan says the final becomes au "or else au"; the second au is evidently meant to be ai (giving manāyī), but I translate as written. The text writes "gung drangs" for "lung drangs," "quotes," and "lus drangs" likewise. In the sūtra on varṇa the Tibetan renders varṇa as "vowel" (dbyangs), which I follow. As in the neighbouring pieces, Tibetan glosses on the example words are run into the text, often displaced; I place each beside the word it evidently explains. One gloss at the start, "the wife of the sun," belongs to sūryā in the preceding piece. Fragments that yield no clear sense are left out of the body: "gos to ma," "brang yo na," "the daughter-in-law's...," "ha mo," and "beautiful hooves," "beautiful thighs" (perhaps glossing lost examples). The Tibetan rendering of the sūtra vāhaḥ reads "from bu ta," which seems corrupt; I give the sense of the Sanskrit. The text writes ṅīṣ as "dīṣa" and occasionally "dīma" or "dviṣa"; I use ṅīṣ throughout. This piece of Pāṇinian notes is interlaced with interlinear Tibetan glosses that in the print have been displaced from the Sanskrit forms they explain; they are marked here as glosses and kept in their printed position. Several are obscure or slightly miswritten: "su nga" (for alābū, gourd) is left as written; གྲེ་མོ་ཆེ is read as བྲེ་མོ་ཆེ "a large measure"; རྒྱུད་མོ as སྒྱུག་མོ "mother-in-law"; བྱང་པོའི་བརླ as གླང་པོའི "elephant's"; བྱེ / ཕྱེ before དགའ་བྱེད as ཀྱེ "O"; and ཉེ་བར for the misprinted ཧེ་བར. The glosses "she of pure earth and sky," "the full-grown one," "destroyer of desire" and "the ptarmigan hen" are literal and uncertain in their reference. Sanskrit examples are romanized as the Tibetan spells them. The final rule (akathita) is rendered loosely: ངེས་བར་ཀུན་སྦྱིན་པ is taken as verbs of giving. The Sanskrit rules and examples are romanized as the Tibetan spells them, often irregularly. The Tibetan verse renderings of the two commentary verses are heavily miswritten; I have read them by their evident sense and the Sanskrit they render: ཟ as "milked," སྙ་མིན and བྷ་མིན as ལྷ་མིན "asuras," དཔང་པོ and ད་རང as "Indra," འགྲིབ as འདྲི "asked," གཤུམ as གསུམ, བ་གཏན as "kinsmen," སྒོ་ལྔ་ན་གནས as Dvārakā, དཔག་བས་མང་ཤིང as the wish-fulfilling tree, བས་ཚོད་པ as ལས་འཚེད་པ, and འདྲོ་ག་བྱེད as འཕྲོག་བྱེད "Hari." Line 11 (dragging Kaṃsa in the Sanskrit) is obscure in the Tibetan. Among the displaced glosses, "fly along" (ཕུར་འགྲོག) and "play" (read རྩེད for ར་ལྡེ) are uncertain, and "Hari lies in heaven" reads མཐོ་རིས for མཐར་ས. སྔོན་བགྱི is read as སྔོན་གྱི "earlier," གཏོང as མཐོང "see," and ཨ་རུ as anu. As in the preceding pieces, displaced interlinear Tibetan glosses are marked as glosses; several are miswritten and are read by their evident sense: ཆང་རབ་ཏུ་ལབ as ཆར་རབ་ཏུ་ཕབ "it rained heavily," ཁྱག་འཇུག as ཁྱབ་འཇུག "Viṣṇu," འཕྲོག་ཁྱེད as འཕྲོག་བྱེད "Hari," འབྲུ་དྲི་ཐེ་པོ་ཆེ་གཉིས་ཆོང as grain bought by two great measures, ཕུགས་ལྔ་སྤྲོང as cattle sold by fives, ཤོ་ཙལ as ཤོ་རྩེད "dice play," and གློག་གོ as ཀློག་གོ "reads." The glosses "fair for a month" (ཟླ་བ་ལ་པིཥྗི), "for a league, lightning," and "goes evenly / goes unevenly" (སོང་ཆ, ཨོང་ཞེས) are obscure as written. "dhik in the sense of reproach" renders the unclear འཛིན་པ་སྟེང་ན་པའི་དོན. In the rule on time and road, བར་མཆད་པ is taken as "unbroken," as the sūtra (atyantasaṃyoga) and the counter-examples require. Sanskrit forms are romanized as the Tibetan spells them. Displaced interlinear glosses are marked as glosses and read by their evident sense where miswritten (ལབ་ལང as བ་ལང "cow," ཆེ་ཏོག as མེ་ཏོག "flowers," ལེའུ as བེའུ "calves," བྲམ་བྱེད as དམ་བྱེད "swears"). ཐིག་ལེ in the glosses on the rule of improper conduct is taken as "seed," in keeping with the sense of the example; this is an interpretation. The glosses "do not give it to the brahmin" (ཤོག་མ་སྤྲོད), "the cowherdess longs like a servant" (འབྲོག་ཁྱེད་འབྲན་སྲེད་བ་བྱེད) and "the pleasure that accords with my aim" are obscure as written. The Tibetan renders spṛha's "desired" as "desired as a companion" (གྲོགས་འདོད) and upasṛṣṭa ("with a preverb") as "fitting" (ཉེ་བར་འོས་པ); I translate the Tibetan as it stands. Sanskrit forms are romanized as the Tibetan spells them.
