A grammatical commentary on Sanskrit compounds, with interlinear Tibetan glosses mixed into the running text; they are marked "gloss" and placed where they occur, which is often displaced from the word they explain. Sanskrit examples are given in standard romanized form. The four senses of "and" are identified with the standard samuccaya, anvācaya, itaretarayoga and samāhāra. The gloss "slayer of the asuras" (ལྷ་མིན་འཇོམས) renders Keśava; "tree and mare" glosses vṛkṣāśvau. A grammatical commentary on the dvandva compound, with interlinear Tibetan glosses mixed into the running text; they are marked "gloss" and placed where they occur, often displaced from the word they explain. Sanskrit examples are given in standard romanized form; "rathikāśvahasti" follows the garbled form as best it can be read. "Firm in battle" and "the accomplisher of existence" are the Tibetan renderings of Yudhiṣṭhira and Arjuna; "the fierce one" glosses caṇḍāla. In the gloss "cow and ewe," མ་མོ is taken as eḍakā, a ewe, not the goddess class. The last sūtra's list ends with pūrva, apara, adhara and uttara; the Tibetan renders these as "east, other, lip and north," and that is kept. This piece of a Sanskrit grammar (examples of dvandva compounds) has interlinear Tibetan glosses copied into the running text, so the Sanskrit examples, their derived forms and the Tibetan glosses are interleaved and often displaced from the example they gloss; the translation follows the order of the source. Evident copyist slips read as follows: ས་ཡང as བ་ལང "cow"; ལས་དང་ཁྲོ་བ as འདོད་དང་ཁྲོ་བ "desire and anger" (glossing kāma and krodha); སྒང་མར་གསར as སྦྲང་མར་གསར "honey and fresh butter"; ཡིན in "the s of those stems" as ས་ཡིག. The gloss ཚ་བོ "grandson" for the potṛ priest is as the Tibetan has it. The stray syllables སྒྲ་སྒྲོགས ("cry-maker"), ངག and དབུ are fragments of glosses; the first is translated literally, the other two are omitted as meaningless in place. The gloss གསལ་བ་དང་སྒྲོ་མདོངས is translated literally ("the bright and the eye of the peacock's feather"); its intended Sanskrit is uncertain. As in the preceding pieces, interlinear Tibetan glosses have been copied into the running text, so many glosses stand away from the example they explain; the translation keeps the source order. Evident copyist slips read as follows: དཔལ་དང་འཕྲད་པ and དཔལ་འཕྲང as དཔལ་དང་འཕྲེང་བ "glory and garland" (śrī and sraj); ཕགས་པ as པགས་པ "skin"; ལམ་ནིང and ཕ་ལམ as ལ་མ་ནིང and ཕ་ལ་མ ("with the neuter", "with father, of mother"); ཨ་པ་ལྦིན as ཨ་པ་བྱིན "apa is given"; ཨ་ཀ་འདྲ་བ་ལ་རེད་པོ as རིང་པོ "lengthened". The glosses "the pure and the clear" and "dust and shoes" are translated literally; the second probably glosses chatra and upānah (parasol and sandals). "Wool-bearers" renders the Tibetan gloss བལ for the ruru example. The stray syllable ག after gabimāḥ is kept as written. Here གྲོགས glosses Sanskrit sakhi and is rendered "friend", not the god Mitra. As in the surrounding pieces, interlinear Tibetan glosses have been copied into the running text, so many glosses stand apart from the examples they explain; the translation keeps the source order. Evident copyist slips read as follows: བསླུ as སྤུ "hair" (glossing loman); བསྲུབ as བསྲུང "protection"; གྲང་ as གླང "bull"; ཁྱེ as ཁྱི "dog"; རེ་བ and རབ as ར་བ "pen"; མདྨ as བརླ "thigh"; ངེའི as དེའི. Some glosses are obscure and are translated literally: "smeared all over", "the dust is pleasant", "foot and knee" (རྐང་པ་དང་རླང་མོང, the second word read as a word for knee), and "it is earth and it is damp". The compound type named ཕྱོགས་...པའི་བསྡུ་བ for the dvi examples is rendered "numeral compounds" (dvigu). Here ཀྲྀཥྞ and ནག་པོ mean "black" in grammatical examples, not the god Kṛṣṇa, and རྒྱལ་བ glosses jāta as "victor". As in the surrounding pieces, interlinear Tibetan glosses have been copied into the running text and stand apart from the examples they explain; the source order is kept. Evident copyist slips read as follows: ལང as ཡང; སྡོན་མ as སྔོན་མ; འདྲུ as འབྲུ (bahuvrīhi); བུལ as ཕུལ "outstanding"; ལམ་ཕྱིས as ལ་མ་ཕྱིས "here the m is dropped". The rule kimaḥ kṣepe is rendered in the Tibetan with ཕྲག་དོག ("envy"); it is translated "disparagement" to match the Sanskrit kṣepa. Some glosses are obscure and are translated literally ("one who smells everywhere", "it is indeed right", "each chest separately"). The phrase ལྤ་ངེ་ལ་བཟང་སོ་དེ་ལང་ཟང་པོ after māṃspāka is garbled; only its recognizable sense "good" is given. As in the surrounding pieces, interlinear Tibetan glosses have been copied into the running text and stand apart from the examples they explain; the source order is kept. Evident copyist slips read as follows: སྨིན as སྤྲིན "cloud"; ཡ་ངེ་ན as ཡང་ན "or else"; བུ་མ as བུམ "vase"; བྱིས as ཕྱིས "dropped"; བདེ་རྣམས as དེ་རྣམས. The gloss on grāmaṇī, ཕྲ་མ་མཁན, means "slanderer" and is translated as written. Some glosses are obscure and are translated literally ("one who abides in the water", "water thrown out", "sour water", "the kinsman of the stars"). The piece ends in the middle of a rule whose explanation follows in the next piece. This is a commentary on Sanskrit grammar, following the sequence of Pāṇini 6.3.85 to 6.3.99 on the replacement of samāna by sa and related changes. The block printing mixes the main commentary with interlinear Tibetan glosses that render each Sanskrit compound ("he whose X is equal, this one; one of equal X"), and these glosses often break into the middle of the commentary's sentences. The translation keeps them in the order they appear, gathered next to the examples they gloss where the placement makes this clear. The Sanskrit examples are given in standard romanization; the Tibetan spellings of them are often irregular. Some glosses do not clearly match their examples, notably those on worshipping a doorkeeper, a god or whatever, which probably belong to examples in the next section. They are translated as written. The opening line about a heavy garland carries over a gloss on mālābhārī from the previous piece. This piece continues a commentary on Sanskrit grammar following Pāṇini 6.3.99 to 6.3.117. As in the preceding pieces, the block print interweaves short Tibetan interlinear glosses with the main commentary, often in the middle of its sentences; they are translated in the order they appear. The Sanskrit examples are given in standard romanization, since the Tibetan spellings are frequently irregular. The list of calamities is said to number six, though seven are named; it is translated as written. Several glosses (for example "another parrot" and "a wild animal with a belly like a dog's") do not clearly fit the example they sit beside and are rendered literally. This piece continues the grammatical commentary (Pāṇini 6.3.117 to 6.3.122 and 8.4.4 to 8.4.10, with vārttikas), with short Tibetan interlinear glosses interwoven into the main text; these are translated in the order they appear, so some sit away from the example they explain. The Sanskrit examples are given in standard romanization because the Tibetan spellings are often irregular. Several glosses name plants that are hard to identify with certainty: "lac mountain" for the kiṃśuluka example, "fortress forest" for koṭara, "pine" (thang shing) and "aguru" (a ka ru) for sidhrakā and agra. They are rendered as the glosses give them. The opening words "quick to endure" and "fully flourishing, victorious" are stray interlinear glosses whose reference is unclear. This piece continues the grammatical commentary, following Pāṇini 8.4.10 to 8.4.38, 6.1.157, 8.3.47, 6.3.2 to 6.3.12 and 8.3.95, with vārttikas. As before, short Tibetan interlinear glosses are interwoven with the main text and are translated where they stand; a few have been moved beside the example they evidently explain. The Sanskrit examples are given in standard romanization, as the Tibetan spellings are often irregular. Some glosses are obscure, for example "the playing sun" and "the heart-stealer who has come of age," placed by the harikāmiṇī example, and "heavy in the middle," where the Tibetan gloss reads bla ma, guru, in its sense of "heavy" (a heavy syllable). This piece completes the section on compounds (Pāṇini 6.3.12 to 6.3.24 and 8.3.84 to 8.3.85, with vārttikas) and opens the section on taddhita suffixes (Pāṇini 4.1.83, 4.1.92 and 4.1.82). The colophon names the work as The Chariot That Draws the Jewel of Excellent Explanation, a set of notes on the Pāṇinivyākaraṇa. Short Tibetan interlinear glosses are interwoven with the main text; they are translated where they stand or beside the example they evidently explain. The Sanskrit examples are given in standard romanization, as the Tibetan spellings are often irregular. The gloss on nanāndṛpati is confused in the Tibetan (it speaks of a grandfather); the Sanskrit sense, the husband of one's husband's sister, is given. The Sanskrit closing line is reproduced as the Tibetan spells it. This is a grammatical commentary on the taddhita (secondary derivative) rules. The many short Tibetan phrases of the form "son of X" scattered through the passage are interlinear glosses on the Sanskrit examples, inserted into the running text by the copyist; they are rendered where they stand, in parentheses. The name glossed as "Bingnup" (an unclear bracketed reading) could not be identified and is given in phonetics; "the red one" and "the spotted one" are literal renderings of glosses whose referents are uncertain. The phrase rendered "when it is not ā" reads as written "when it is uttama," evidently a slip for "not ā," as the following explanation shows. The passage is a commentary on the taddhita rules for patronymics, and the short Tibetan phrases of the form "son of X" inside it are interlinear glosses translating the Sanskrit examples, carried into the running text by the copyist; they are rendered where they stand, in parentheses. Several glosses are unclear or corrupt (Gatumapo, dimī, Randhyāma, "sapebu," "son of the woman who composes," "to mahe"), and these are given literally or phonetically. The sentence on drimnatṛ belongs to the preceding mātṛ rule and appears displaced in the source. "Son of Kadrū" renders an unclear gloss. As in the preceding pieces, the parenthesized phrases are interlinear glosses and derivation notes that the copyist carried into the running text; they are rendered where they stand. Several of them are garbled or bracketed in the source (for example the gloss on parastrī, a fragment after śvasurlaḥ, and a garbled bracketed gloss after rājanyaḥ, both left untranslated as unreadable); they are rendered as far as they can be read. "Lizard" follows the reading rtsangs pa in the second gloss on godhā; the first gloss reads "bound one" (cings pa), evidently a slip. The commentary's "easterners" for the Sanskrit "udīcī" is kept as the Tibetan has it. As in the preceding pieces, the parenthesized phrases are interlinear glosses and derivation notes carried into the running text by the copyist; they are rendered where they stand. The glosses on the sages' names translate the Sanskrit names into Tibetan words; most are identifiable (Atri, Kutsa, Vasiṣṭha, Gotama, Aṅgiras), but "Danpong," apparently standing for Bhṛgu, could not be identified with confidence and is given in phonetics. The remark on what the ṅ and ṣ of ṣyaṅ serve is partly unclear in the Tibetan. As in the preceding pieces, the parenthesized phrases are interlinear glosses and derivation notes carried into the running text; they are rendered where they stand. The long glosses on the month names are partly garbled and bracketed in the source; they are rendered as far as they can be read (names of lunar mansions such as Maghā, Citrā, Viśākhā, Jyeṣṭhā, Śravaṇa, Aśvinī, Kṛttikā and Mṛgaśiras), and fragments that cannot be read are passed over. "Of the burning one" and "purified" render isolated glosses whose reference is unclear. This piece belongs to a Sanskrit grammar on the formation of collective nouns (the sense "its collection," tasya samūhaḥ). The Sanskrit sūtras and examples are given exactly as the Tibetan spells them, irregularities included. The many interlinear glosses, rendered here in parentheses, are badly transmitted in places; several (for instance "Indra and cause, view," "by Indra, pi, la," "blodmo," "khadmoma," "rdus," "gabu," "a collection of things given up") could not be matched with confidence to the words they gloss and are rendered literally or left in Tibetan spelling. In the gloss list after vṛddha, "a collection of fire" (མེ) has been read as "a collection of men" (མི), matching manuṣya in the sūtra. The glosses on uṣṭra and urabhra appear as "she-camels" and "the bellyless, that is, butchers." "Affix" renders the grammatical sense of the word otherwise glossed as "condition." In the sahāyatā example the word given in the name list as Mitra is here the common noun "friends," since it glosses sahāya. This piece of the grammar treats the taddhita affixes for "plays with this weapon," "studies or knows it," "a country containing it," "its abode," "nearness," "born there," "existing there" and "come from there." Sūtras and examples are given exactly as the Tibetan spells them. The interlinear glosses, shown in parentheses, are badly transmitted in many places; where they could not be construed they are rendered word for word or left in Tibetan spelling, and some words ("balanga," "rumaba," "brangspong," "Ngensel," "khuruba") remain unidentified. བཅོམ་བརླག is the standard Tibetan rendering of Mathurā, the city of the example māthuraḥ. "Sage" renders the Tibetan written དང་སྲོང in one place, read as དྲང་སྲོང. In śaibaḥ the Śivas are the people named in the example (the name is kept as Śiva for consistency with earlier pieces). The word given in the name list as Maghā is here the common noun "lips," glossing auṣṭhyaṃ, and has been translated as such. This piece of the grammar covers the taddhita affixes for "come from," "its abode," "proclaimed by," "composed by," "this is his," and the remainder (śeṣa) senses "born there, come from there, existing there," with the vṛddha designation and the pada designation before s-marked affixes. Sūtras and examples are given exactly as the Tibetan spells them. Many interlinear glosses are interleaved with the main text without marking; they are rendered in parentheses where they could be distinguished, and some are misplaced in the source (for example the glosses for the directions do not line up with prāc, avāc and pratīc); they are translated as they stand. A few gloss words (rab, rag, Śarga) are left as spelled. This piece of the grammar continues the remainder (śeṣa) affixes and then the time-words, before opening the rule on "its modification." Sūtras and examples are given exactly as the Tibetan spells them. The interlinear glosses are interleaved with the main text without marking; they are given in parentheses where they could be distinguished, and a few garbled stretches are left as spelled. In this piece the words listed for the moon, the sun and Vāyu are common nouns in the glosses ("month," "day," "wind"), and are translated as such. The family named in dākṣaḥ is that of Dakṣa. This piece of the grammar covers the affixes for "its modification" and "its part" (aṇ, mayaṭ, yat), the elision of these affixes in the sense of "fruit," and the affix for "one appointed there." Sūtras and examples are given exactly as the Tibetan spells them. The interlinear glosses are interleaved with the main text without marking; they are rendered in parentheses where they could be distinguished, and some garbled words (mingka, kunśa, rtagna, bhūrura) are left as spelled. In the gloss on gomaya the word སྦྱིན་པ is the common noun "giving," not the name Diti. Ṭhak is read for ཐག and ཐ་ཀ in the rule on "one appointed there," matching the sūtra form and the examples. This is a Sanskrit grammatical commentary following Pāṇinian sūtras (e.g. 7.3.5–9, 4.4.104, 6.4.135, 6.4.170–173, 4.4.1–2, 4.4.35), heavily overlaid with interlinear glosses that are often displaced or garbled; bracketed gloss material is rendered as "gloss" in parentheses as it stands. Sanskrit forms are romanized as the Tibetan spells them, even where they diverge from standard forms (e.g. bābreyaḥ for pātheyaḥ, śrābastiḥ for śvābhastriḥ). The gloss "foot of a dog" (khyi'i rkang pa) appears to arise from a misreading of janapada; rendered as written. The sentence on na mapūrvo... reads literally that the ṭi "is not left; it is elided," which seems to contradict the sūtra's intent (no elision); rendered as it stands. The name-list items Mitra, Puṣya, etc. do not occur here as names: གྲོགས here means "companion" and རྒྱལ "conquer." A Sanskrit grammatical commentary on Pāṇinian rules (4.4.35, 4.4.3, 4.4.34, 4.4.41, 4.4.60, 4.4.75–81, 8.2.77–79, 4.4.98, 4.4.105–109, 4.4.116–117, 5.1.5–9, 6.4.169, 5.1.37), heavily overlaid with displaced interlinear glosses; bracketed glosses are given in parentheses as "gloss," and Sanskrit forms are romanized as the Tibetan spells them, even where they diverge from the standard forms. "Being" for gdongs po reads it as dngos po (bhava). "The śima" (ཤི་མ) is unclear; the context (nābhya) suggests the navel. The name list's Puṣya, Brahmā, Hari, Śiva etc. do not occur here as names. A Sanskrit grammatical commentary on Pāṇinian rules (5.1.37, 5.1.21–24, 5.1.42, 5.1.115–117, 5.1.119, 8.3.101, 5.1.122, 6.4.155, 6.4.161, 5.1.123–124, and the vārttika on cāturvarṇya), heavily overlaid with displaced interlinear glosses; bracketed glosses are given in parentheses as "gloss," and Sanskrit forms are romanized as the Tibetan spells them, even where they diverge from the standard forms. The name list's Parvata and Kṛṣṇa occur here only as the ordinary words "mountain" and "black" (kṛṣṇa as a grammatical example). A Sanskrit grammatical commentary on Pāṇinian rules and vārttikas (cāturvarṇyādi, 5.1.125–132, sahāyād vā, 5.2.1–4, 5.2.7, 5.2.16, 5.2.24), heavily overlaid with displaced interlinear glosses, which are given in parentheses as "gloss." Sanskrit forms are romanized as the Tibetan spells them, even where they diverge from the standard forms; a few glosses are too fragmentary to render fully and are given with ellipses. The name-list Mitra here is only the ordinary word "friend" (sakhya). A Sanskrit grammatical commentary on Pāṇinian rules and vārttikas (5.2.24, 5.2.26, 5.2.29, the vārttikas on rajas, goṣṭha, saṃghāta, vistāra, dvitva, ṣaṭtva, sneha and bhavana, 5.2.36–40, 6.4.164), heavily overlaid with displaced interlinear glosses, given in parentheses as "gloss." Sanskrit forms are romanized as the Tibetan spells them. Rgyal pa in the vistāra rule is read as rgyas pa, "spreading," which fits the Sanskrit; it is not the name Puṣya. "Se'u" is a fruit name (pīlu) left as the Tibetan gives it. This piece belongs to a Sanskrit grammatical treatise on the taddhita suffixes (corresponding to Pāṇini 5.2.40–55 and attached vārttikas). The Tibetan text interleaves the sūtras, their glosses and dense interlinear notes, many of which are fragmentary or misspelled in the source; these interlinear notes are rendered as "gloss" and translated literally as they stand, and the Sanskrit sūtras and word forms are romanized as the Tibetan spells them. Some example glosses do not match their Sanskrit forms as written (for instance "a hundred and twenty" beside tiṃśaṃ śatam, and "a hundred and eleven" beside biṃśiśatram); they are translated as given. Tibetan khengs tshig (written khangs tshig once) is taken as "a word of contempt," rendering Sanskrit kṣepa. This piece covers taddhita rules corresponding to Pāṇini 5.2.56–59, 5.2.86–88, 5.2.94, 1.4.19, 8.2.9–10 and the opening of 5.2.96. As in the preceding pieces, the main text is interwoven with many fragmentary interlinear notes, rendered here as "gloss" and translated literally as they stand; the Sanskrit sūtras and word forms are romanized as the Tibetan spells them, irregularities included. Several glosses are too fragmentary to construe with certainty (for example "triṃ..., third" in the list of ordinals, and the scattered ritual phrases "Śrī wants a sacrifice," which appear to be misplaced interlinear examples). In "this one ate before" the gloss "fled from" (bros) is probably a slip for "eaten" (zos). This piece covers taddhita rules of the matup group, corresponding to Pāṇini 5.2.96–122 with their vārttikas. As in the preceding pieces, the main text is interwoven with many fragmentary interlinear notes (rendered as "gloss" and translated literally as they stand, including repeated words), and the Sanskrit sūtras and examples are romanized as the Tibetan spells them, irregularities included. The meanings given in the glosses often do not match the example beside them (for instance "having wood" beside sidhmala, which properly means "having a skin blemish"); they are translated as written. The repeated phrase "quoted in the commentary" appears twice in the source and is kept. The interlinear glosses of this grammatical work (Tibetan meanings of the example words and short grammatical remarks) have been copied into the running text, often in the middle of a rule or a word; they are given here as glosses, in places moved just past the word they split. Within them, evident slips are read as follows: གཟི་རྗེས as གཟི་བརྗིད "majestic", དགའ་ཐུབ as དཀའ་ཐུབ "ascetic", སྐྱུ་མ as སྒྱུ་མ "illusion", རྭ་ཅ་ན as རྭ་ཅན "horned", ཆོགས as ཚོགས "multitude", ཤིར་རྟ་བམ as ཤིང་རྟ་བའམ "or one with a chariot", གྲིང as གྲང "cold", ཚ་བེ as ཚ་བ "hot", སྟོབས་མ་བ་རྨོད་པ as སྟོབས་མི་བཟོད་པ "cannot bear strength", གྱིས as དབྱིས "is elided", དག as ངག "speech" and སྨ as སྨྲ "speaking", རྗོ་བོ as ཇོ་བོ "lord", སྐྲིན as སྤྲིན "cloudy", ཚད་འབྲུ as ཚད་འཁྲུ "dysentery", དེ་གེ as དགེ "virtue", and ཀས as ལས "from". The glosses དན་ཆོག and འཕྲང་རིང་ཅན ("having a long narrow passage"), and the designation named in the gloss on the formation of bāgmi, could not be identified with confidence. As written, the text gives the sense "cannot bear it" also for the rules on parvata and marutta and on vāgmin, which Pāṇini teaches in the possessive (matup) sense; this is translated as it stands. As in the preceding pieces, interlinear glosses (Tibetan meanings of the example words and brief grammatical remarks) have been copied into the running text, often splitting a rule or a word; they are given as glosses, in places moved just past the word they interrupt. Several are too corrupt to construe fully and are rendered word for word. Evident slips are read as follows: སང་བོ as མང་པོ "many", སུམ་ཟད as མ་ཟད "not only", ཡངས as ཡོངས "all around", མདོན as མདུན "in front", ཞིམ as ཀིམ, བར་རོ་ལ as ཕ་རོལ "follows", ཁོར་བ as བོར་བ "excluded", འགྲལ as འགྲེལ "commentary", ཡས as ལས "from", ནྡ་མ as ནངས་མ "tomorrow", and འདུང as འགྱུར "becomes". Conjectural: དུས་ཚོག་མ as "the first time" and དུས་རྩིམ་འམ་ཉི་མ་གྱིས as "the later time, or the following day". In these glosses ཉི་མ means "day", not the sun. This piece comments on a run of Sanskrit grammatical rules, with short interlinear glosses woven into the running text, often away from the word they explain; they are kept in place and marked as glosses, and Sanskrit forms follow the Tibetan spelling. Here several glossary words carry their grammatical senses: རྐྱེན is the grammarians' pratyaya, "suffix", not "condition"; མཐའ is "end, ending"; འགྲོ་བ renders "it", the dropped marker; མདོས is "by the sūtra", not a thread-cross. The recurring gloss དབྱངས་དོན is taken as "for the accent" (དབྱངས for svara), explaining markers such as the ca of bahuca and the r of jātīyar. ཁ་བསྒྱུར་བ in the rūpaya rule is rendered "disguise", following the commentary's own example of passing off the unlearned as learned. གྲངས་མེད་པ "the numberless" and མི་ཟད་པ "the indeclinables" both refer to indeclinable words. Evident slips in the glosses are read by sense: པ་བས་བ as པགས་པ "skin", ཆོས་པ and མུ་ཆོས་པ as ཚོས་པ and མ་ཚོས་པ "cooked, uncooked", འཆོད as འཚོད "cook", བརྗུ as བརྫུ "sham", ཐུ as མཐུ "might", བུན as ཕུན, པི as མི "not", འདིག as འཇིག. The gloss ཆེས་བྱེད་ཅན on srajiṣṭhaḥ is rendered literally. This piece closes the section on taddhita suffixes (དེ་ཕན་གྱི་རྐྱེན) with a Sanskrit and Tibetan section colophon naming the work, and then opens a section of miscellaneous rules on doubled forms. Several Tibetan terms are calques of Sanskrit technical terms: ཁྱབ་པར་འདོད་པ "the wish to pervade" is vīpsā; འབྲུ་མང་པོ "much grain" is bahuvrīhi; ཡང་དག་པར་མངོན་པར་འཕྲོག་པ "complete carrying-off" is samabhihāra, repetition or intensity of an action; གོ་བར་མི་བཟོད་པ "not bearing to understand" stands for asūyā; ཚིག་སྡུད is a compound (samāsa); in the last rule རྟགས is grammatical gender. Glossary words keep these senses here: ལས is "action", བཟོད་པ appears only in "not bearing", སེམས is "mind", and ཆོས in the gloss on bhadrākaroti (shaving the head) is the Dharma. The names flagged for this piece do not occur as names: རི་བོ is "the mountain" in the gloss on adhoñdhobarbataṃ (not Parvata), སྨད་པ is "contempt" (not Kutsa), མཁས་པ is "learned" (not Dakṣa), and ཙ་ར, ས་ག and མེ appear only inside other words or Sanskrit forms. Evident slips in the glosses are read by sense: སེ་འཐུ as སེ་འབྲུ "pomegranate", དཀའ་བ as དགའ་བ "pleasing", རྗེས་གུ as རྗེས་སུ, སྒྲ་བྲེགས as སྐྲ་བྲེགས "shaved the hair", ལྟ as ལྷ "god", ཤས་ཟིན as ཤེས་ཟིན "found out", ཕམ་ཚུན as ཕན་ཚུན "one another", མཇའ as མཐའ "end". This section is technical Pāṇinian grammar, and several words carry their grammatical senses. འགྲོ་བ ("going") renders it, an indicatory letter that drops away, translated here as "marker"; རྐྱེན, elsewhere "condition," here means pratyaya in its sense of suffix, and བར་རྐྱེན is the intermediate suffix (vikaraṇa); sup and tiṅ are the nominal and the verbal endings. The "first, middle and last" persons are the Sanskrit prathama, madhyama and uttama, which correspond to the English third, second and first persons; yuṣmad and asmad are the stems of the pronouns "you" and "I." The Tibetan verse calls nature "king" (here "sovereign"), which the author's gloss reads as the victors, the buddhas. A few evident scribal slips were read in context: the five from laṅ to lṛṅ are read as ṅ-marked (the text has པ for ང), "from ta up to ṅ" reads ཏ་ནས་དའི་ནར as ཏ་ནས་ངའི་བར in line with the later definition of tiṅ, and སྐད་གསང is read as སྐད་གདངས, "pitch," in the description of svarita; where the gloss writes ཏ་ད and དི་ཏ, the terms are taken as taṅ and ṅit, as the explanations that follow show. This piece interleaves the commentary with interlinear glosses and derivation notes that have entered the running text. The short Tibetan glosses ("exists," "you exist," "I exist," "obtains" and so on) give the meaning of each verb form; they often stand away from the form they gloss, and twice inside it, and are translated where they stand. The step-by-step derivations ("to bhū, laṭ, śap ...") are likewise rendered in place. These notes contain several evident scribal slips, rendered by their evident sense: laṭ written as aṭ or baṭ, liṅ written as laṅ, yāsuṭ as āsuṭ or lāsuṭ, the ṅ of "ṅ-marked" written as pa or ba, ṭ-marked written with ta, jha written as ja-ta, dhvam as dhāṃ, and "obtain" written as thog or thong; one stray syllable (ṇa) in the derivation note after the middle-person dual is unintelligible and is left aside. Technical terms keep their Pāṇinian senses: "marker" renders "going" (it), "suffix" renders rkyen (pratyaya), "pertaining to all roots" and "pertaining to half the roots" are sārvadhātuka and ārdhadhātuka, guṇa is the grammatical strengthening of a vowel, and su, au and jas are the nominative endings. As in the previous piece, the first, middle and last persons correspond to the English third, second and first persons. As in the preceding pieces, the commentary here is interleaved with step-by-step derivation notes (to bhava, liṅ; l becomes ta; and so on), which are translated where they stand. Many of them carry evident scribal slips, rendered by their evident sense: bhū written dhū, liṅ written miṅ, yāsuṭ written lāsuṭ or phāsuṭ, sīyuṭ written sīsuṭ or seuṭ, thas written zas, "iṭ becomes iṭ" for "iṭ becomes at," "previous" written lngama for sngama, "visarga" and "the sense of the action" miswritten, and "wish" written sman for smon. In the loṭ derivation one word after "the purpose of the p" (bod) is unintelligible and is left aside. A bracketed word, "lion" (seng ge), stands in the text after "These" near the end; it appears to be an intrusive marginal word and is left untranslated. The Kalāpa is the Kātantra grammar, in which the optative is called saptamī, "the seventh"; the Tibetan transcription of that term here is unclear. The rule quoted for the letter t is the Pāṇinian convention that a vowel followed by t denotes only a vowel of its own length. As in the preceding pieces, the commentary is interleaved with step-by-step derivation notes and with short Tibetan glosses of the verb forms, all translated where they stand. The wish-glosses "may I become supreme," "may I become other" and "may I become bad" render the forms with pra, antar and dur, though the last stands some way from its form; the gloss "the path exists" beside the form with srat is unclear. Several evident scribal slips are rendered by their evident sense, among them "ṅ" or "th" written for "p" in "p-marked," "self" (bdag) written for "s and v" (sa ba dag), dhvam written dhāṃ, āthām written ābhāṃ, a negation written ba'am for ba ma in the rule on dur, and the gloss of the rule after a ("elision of hi"), which is miswritten. One stretch, in the derivation after the middle-person dual of the ātmanepada, is badly garbled and is rendered by its evident gist. Upasarga, "preverb," is the Tibetan nyer bsgyur; "cause" renders rgyu mtshan, the conditioning factor (nimitta) for the change of n to ṇ. As in the preceding pieces, the commentary is interleaved with step-by-step derivation notes and short glosses ("may I obtain"), translated where they stand. These contain many evident scribal slips, rendered by their evident sense: the rule "luṅ, laṅ, lṛṅ" is variously miswritten (lṛṅ as gṛṅ, sṛd, phṛṅ or lṛd; laṅ as yaṅ), mip is written miṅ, iṭ is written aṭ, sic is written ca, ātmanepada is written ātyanepada, "past" is written 'angs for 'das, "obtain" is written thab, and "not of today" has mo for ma. Two fragments are unintelligible and are left aside: "ca'i rel ba" at the end of the first derivation, and a bracketed "o ra" in the derivation of the last-person forms of loṭ. The Kalāpa (Kātantra) names the imperative pañcamī, "the fifth," and the imperfect hyastanī, "yesterday's"; the Cāndra is the grammar of Candragomin, and the Sarasvatī grammar is the Sārasvata. The Tibetan rendering of the last rule ends with "of sic," leaving its operation, the elision of sic, unstated. The text uses the Indian order of persons: its first person (prathama) is the Western third person, its middle person the second, and its last person (uttama) the first. The derivations are very terse, and the Tibetan copy has many slips in the Sanskrit forms and in the names of the rules cited; the forms are given in their standard spelling, and the slips are read from the parallel derivations and the rules invoked. In particular, the bracketed yaṅ is read as laṅ, which with laṭ, liṅ and loṭ makes the four lakāras whose endings are sārvadhātuka; andra is read as ant; a phrase repeated in the abhūt derivation is translated once; and in the abhūtam derivation, where only "becomes s" stands, "la becomes thas" is supplied from the following step. The explanation of the gāti rule glosses pā as "to protect," although the line just before glosses it as "to drink," which is how the Pāṇinian tradition takes it here. In the derivation of abhaviṣātām, the closing "ṭ is brought in" does not fit the form and seems to be carried over from the derivation of abhaviṣṭa. As in the preceding derivations, the Sanskrit forms are given in their standard spelling, and the scribal slips in the steps are read from the parallel derivations and the rules invoked. For instance, the Tibetan rendering of the sūtra on s before dh reads "also before bha," taken as "also before dh," as the rule is cited a little later; the ending written thas in the derivation of abhaviṣṭhāḥ is taken as thās; and in the explanation of the māṅ rule, where the copy reads na yin, the evident ma yin, "does not," is translated, as the rule requires. The two forms that illustrate the option in which s becomes d are transcribed exactly as they stand. The derivation placed under the heading for the last person in fact repeats the case of dhvam, the middle person plural; the last person forms begin with abhaviṣi. The Tibetan glosses of the examples with mā read literally "did not become," although with the prohibitive mā the Sanskrit means "may not become." As in Indian grammar generally, the "first person" here is what Western grammar calls the third person, the "middle person" is the second, and the "last person" is the first; so babhūva in the first person singular means "he was," and in the last person singular "I was." The Tibetan of this piece has many scribal slips in its technical terms, which I have translated in their evident reading: laṭ for liṭ in the rule "for what is out of sight, liṭ"; arkus for atus; jñu for jhi; athas for thas; at for a; ā for ū; tha for pa or va; damaged spellings of abhyāsa, of thung ngu ("short"), of snga ma ("the former") and of phyed pa (in the term for ārdhadhātuka); yon for yod ("there is"); zad for med ("no"); and 'phrod, read as 'phros ("remaining"). In the first person dual the text says the v is joined to i; the form requires a, and I have read a. In the first derivation, after the remark on ṇ, the text says "the i is for distinction"; the parallel in the last person singular says this of the l of ṇal. I have kept the text's wording. "What has ṇ as marker" renders ṇa 'gro ba, where 'gro ba ("that which goes") calques the grammatical term it; it does not mean "being" here. In Indian grammar the "first person" corresponds to the English third person (he, she), the "middle person" to the second, and the "last person" to the English first person (I, we); the passage derives the forms of the liṅ of wishing (the benedictive) of bhū in the parasmaipada and the ātmanepada. As before, "first," "middle" and "last" person are the Indian grammatical persons (prathama, madhyama, uttama). Sūtras and forms are given as the Tibetan spells them, with compressed spellings and plain letter slips in the Tibetan transcription read as the evident forms (for example ནང་སེལ for "curing disease," ཙི་ཀིཏྶནྟནུ for cikitsantu, ཨ་ཅི་ཀིཏྶཧ for acikitsata, ཨང for "of a," ད་ཡིག for the letter ṅ). The three benedictive forms of cikitsa are garbled in the Tibetan (ཙིཀིཏྶཏཧ, ཙི་ཀི་ཏྶ་སྟཱཾ, ཙི་ཀི་ཏྶྟསུཿ) and are rendered as the forms the derivation describes. The phrase ནད་དོ་བར་བྱེད after "before the ārdhadhātuka affixes," and ཐི་ཚོམ་བྱེད ("making doubt") before "the letter ṅ of īyaṅ," are unintelligible in context and are left unrendered. "san and yaṅ" renders ཡང་དག, here the Sanskrit affix yaṅ, not the Tibetan word "genuine." The opening derivation of edhate is terse and partly garbled and is rendered step by step as it stands. This is a section of a Sanskrit grammatical commentary deriving the ātmanepada forms of the root edh ("to grow") in laṭ, the optative (liṅ), loṭ, laṅ, luṅ and liṭ. The Tibetan transcription of the Sanskrit forms and endings is heavily corrupted in this witness (for example ངྷ for dh, ཨེེ for ai, and many garbled syllables); the forms are given here in their evident standard Sanskrit shape, and the grammatical rules, which the Tibetan cites by translating their wording, are rendered according to the Pāṇinian sūtras they plainly reflect (for instance āto ṅitaḥ, lopo vyor vali, liṅaḥ salopo 'nantyasya, jho 'ntaḥ, ato guṇe, savābhyāṃ vāmau, eta ai, āḍ uttamasya pic ca, āḍ ajādīnām, āṭaś ca, ādeśapratyayayoḥ, ṣṭunā ṣṭuḥ, ātmanepadeṣv anataḥ, ijādeś ca gurumato 'nṛcchaḥ, āmaḥ). Where a step is garbled beyond certain recovery, the derivation required by the grammar has been followed. Here རྐྱེན renders the grammatical sense "suffix" (pratyaya). A continuation of the Sanskrit grammatical paradigms (ātmanepada of edh, then īkṣ, dad and ṣvaṣk). The Tibetan transcription of the Sanskrit forms is badly corrupted in this witness; forms are given in their evident standard shape, and rules cited in Tibetan translation are rendered after the Pāṇinian sūtras they reflect (e.g. liṭi dhātor anabhyāsasya, ur at, kuhoś cuḥ, liṭas tajhayor eśirec, iko yaṇ aci, tāsastyor lopaḥ, dhi ca, ha eti, syatāsī lṛluṭoḥ). The quoted Sanskrit sūtra iṇaḥ ṣīdhvaṃluṅliṭāṃ dho 'ṅgāt is given in its standard form. In the lṛṭ paradigm the text omits the dual edhiṣyete and, for the first-person singular, cites the rule replacing iṭ with at, which properly belongs to the optative; it is translated as it stands. In the dad section the heading reads lṛṭ, but the forms (dadade, dadadāte, dadadire) and the reference back to "apart from the section on liṭ" show it is liṭ, rendered so. In luṭ the form daditādhve is written twice and is given once. The "sūtra on śas, dad, roots beginning with v" is Pāṇini 6.4.126 (na śasadadavādiguṇānām); here མདོས is "by the sūtra," not a thread-cross. Continuation of the ātmanepada paradigms (ṣvaṣk, ṛj, tij in the desiderative titikṣ-, and ṣvañj). The Tibetan transcription of the Sanskrit forms is badly corrupted; forms are given in their evident standard shape, and rules cited in Tibetan translation are rendered after the Pāṇinian sūtras they reflect (e.g. ata ādeḥ and tasmān nuḍ dvihalaḥ, guptijkidbhyaḥ san, sanyaṅoḥ, halādiḥ śeṣaḥ, coḥ kuḥ, khari ca, kāspratyayād ām, dhātvādeḥ ṣaḥ saḥ, daṃśasañjasvañjāṃ śapi, jhalo jhali, aniditāṃ hala upadhāyāḥ kṅiti, parinivibhyaḥ). The luṭ paradigm of ṣvaṣk lacks the first form ṣvaṣkitā, and in tij's luṭ the form titikṣitā is written twice; both are translated as they stand. The words on śap and "a before guṇa" at the start of tij's luṅ seem displaced from the present-system derivation but are rendered as written. In the non-kit option of svañj the text writes sasvajire for the third plural, which contradicts its own statement that n is not deleted; the evident sasvañjire is given. The vārttika quoted from the commentary is given in its standard Sanskrit wording. Continuation of the ātmanepada paradigms (the ṣ-rules after upasargas, trap, jabh, stubh, paṇ, kam). The Tibetan transcription of the Sanskrit forms is badly corrupted; forms are given in their evident standard shape, and the quoted sūtras (sivādīnāṃ vāṭ vyavāye 'pi, sadisvañjyoḥ parasya liṭi, radhijabhor aci, kamer ṇiṅ) in their standard Sanskrit wording. ṣaha is glossed in this witness as "to show respect"; the usual dhātupāṭha meaning is "to bear," so the gloss may be a slip, but it is translated as written. In the paṇ section the headings read loṭ for luṭ (paṇāyitā) and leṭ for laṭ (paṇate), and the phrase "the option where āya is attached" before the second set must mean "is not attached"; these evident readings are followed. Some forms are written twice or are missing from a paradigm (trapsyete twice, stobhete twice, the first form of jabh's lṛṭ given as jambhiṣyete); they are translated as they stand. In "the sūtra on" (མདོས), the word is "by the sūtra," not a thread-cross. Continuation of the ātmanepada paradigms (kam with and without ṇiṅ, ay, day, sphāy). The Tibetan transcription of the Sanskrit forms is badly corrupted; forms are given in their evident standard shape, and the quoted sūtras (ṇau caṅy upadhāyā hrasvaḥ, sanval laghuni caṅpare 'nag lope, sanyataḥ, dīrgho laghoḥ, ṇer aniṭi, ayām antālv āyyetnviṣṇuṣu, dayāyāsaś ca, upasargasyāyatau, cāyasphāyapyāyām iḍ vā) are given in their standard wording. The glosses on the forms with pari, prati, nir and dur ("he makes go all around," "severally," "not," "badly") are scattered in this witness into the following section on daya; they have been placed with the forms they explain. The verb gloss for ās is garbled in the Tibetan and is given as "to sit," its standard meaning. Here མདོས is "by the sūtra," not a thread-cross. The Tibetan spellings of the Sanskrit forms in this piece are often garbled (for example sgāyiṣyate for sphāyiṣyate, and the root pyāy written alternately with bya and pya); as in the preceding pieces, the forms are given in their evident correct Sanskrit shape. The gloss on janī reads "to be wearied" (rab tu skyo ba), evidently a slip for "to be born" (rab tu skye ba), and tāyi's gloss rgyad is read as rgyud, "to extend," as the text itself gives it a few lines later. The phrase rendered "the root being one that takes the iṭ due before an affix beginning with val" (byings phyed pa) is uncertain in wording, though the grammatical point is clear. The gloss of ṣevṛ as "to wash" follows the Tibetan, though the Sanskrit root list gives it as "to serve." As in the preceding pieces, the Sanskrit forms, which the Tibetan often spells irregularly, are given in their evident correct shape; the Tibetan glosses inserted among them ("goes," "should go," "go!") are translated where they stand. The gloss of deṅ reads "to generate" (bskyed pa), evidently a slip for "to protect" (skyong ba), which the text itself gives for deṅ a few lines later. The phrase rendered "ta, the affix due at that time, being placed after it" is obscure in the Tibetan. In the liṭ of ḍīṅ the text explicitly turns the reduplicated ḍ into ṭ and writes ṭiḍye and so on, against the standard ḍiḍye; this is kept as the text has it. The text writes "liṭ" for the loṭ form jugupsatām, an evident slip. In this grammatical text "stem" renders the Tibetan word for the technical term aṅga. As in the preceding pieces, the Sanskrit forms, which the Tibetan often spells irregularly, are given in their evident correct shape. Several labels in the Tibetan are evident slips that are read here according to the forms they introduce: "liṅ" for the loṭ bībhatsatām and for the laṅ asyandata, "leṭ" for liṭ in the rules on dyut and vṛt, and "laṭ" for the liṭ of syand. The gloss of dyuta is partly illegible and is rendered "to shine," in line with the gloss "to blaze" the text gives it a few lines later. In the liṭ of syand, the remark on dropping sic and d, which properly concerns the forms of the aorist without iṭ, stands where the text places it. As in the preceding pieces, the Sanskrit forms, which the Tibetan often spells irregularly, are given in their evident correct shape. The Tibetan glosses "the chariot runs along" and "the elephant surely moves," which belong with the examples anuṣyandate rathaḥ and nisyandate hastī, stand displaced in the opening lines on kṛpū; they are translated where the text places them. In the aorist of kṛpū without iṭ, the text lists only two forms each for the middle and last persons, and only those are given. As in the preceding pieces, the Sanskrit forms, which the Tibetan often spells irregularly, are given in their evident correct shape. The gloss of ḍupacaṣ is written mtshed pa, evidently for 'tshed pa, "to cook." The gloss of patḷ contains a garbled word before "that is, to go"; only "to go" is rendered. At the end of the paragraphs on vam and bhram, the Tibetan scatters the bare labels of the liṭ endings ṇal, atus and us around the lṛṅ form; these stray labels are not rendered. This is a section of a Sanskrit grammatical commentary conjugating verbal roots through the ten tense-mood systems (laṭ, liṅ, loṭ, laṅ, luṅ, liṭ, luṭ, the benedictive liṅ, lṛṭ, lṛṅ); the Tibetan transliterates the Sanskrit forms, often irregularly, and they are given here in their intended standard IAST spelling. Short interlinear labels for verbal endings scattered through the text (tha va, atus, us, thal, ṇal, te, si) are marginal annotations, not running text, and are not rendered. Where the Tibetan has an evident slip (ལིང་ for laṅ before aphaṇat; ལུང་ for laṅ before asahata; the bracketed སྐྱེ་རབས་ where "are applied" is expected), the evident reading is translated. The gloss of ṣadḷ renders the Tibetan for viśaraṇa, gati and avasādana; the Tibetan word for the last literally suggests "making thoroughly pliant," here taken as "wearing down." The clause about "vada, vraja" in the rule for the seven roots is compressed in the Tibetan and its exact construal is uncertain. A Sanskrit grammatical commentary conjugating verbal roots; the Sanskrit forms, transliterated irregularly in the Tibetan, are given in their intended standard spelling, and a few evident slips are corrected silently (for example ལང for liṅ before gūhet, and the repeated root name where ṭubhlāśṛ is evidently meant). The opening bracketed syllable and a stray form rājiṣyanta among the lṛṭ parasmaipada forms are not rendered. Two short Tibetan glosses that appear misplaced in the khanu section, "makes eat flesh" and "the sound of the lute," evidently belong to the examples viṣvaṇati māṃsam and visvanati vīṇā just above and are reflected there rather than repeated. In the gloss of cāyṛ, the Tibetan for the second sense (niśāmana, "perceiving") reads oddly, with a repeated phrase, and is translated by its evident meaning. The Tibetan "ye vibhāṣā" rule's word for "optionally" is garbled but the sense is clear from the forms given. A Sanskrit grammatical commentary on the conjugation of guh and hṛ. The Sanskrit forms and rule citations are transliterated irregularly in the Tibetan; they are given in IAST according to their evident intent, keeping the forms this text itself gives (for instance jugūḍha, gūḍhā and ghukṣyati, where standard grammar has jugoḍha, goḍhā and ghokṣyati). The Tibetan gloss for duh reads "to place," evidently a slip for "to milk." The sentence placed at the head of the liṭ section, about sic being lost "after a short stem" before endings beginning with jhal, properly concerns the aorist forms just given; it is translated where it stands. A stray interlinear label (thal) among the luṭ forms is not rendered. A Sanskrit grammatical commentary conjugating verbal roots. Here the text calls the parasmaipada endings "non-taṅ" and the ātmanepada endings "taṅ," after the Pāṇinian abbreviation; this is kept, with the equivalence stated on first use. The Sanskrit forms, transliterated irregularly in the Tibetan, are given in their intended IAST spelling. In the ātmanepada aorist of bhaja the Tibetan writes long vowels (abhākṣa and so on) and inserts an unclear phrase before the second-person plural; the standard forms abhakta and so on are given, and the unclear phrase is not rendered. The Tibetan gloss for bhṛ reads "filling" and is translated as written. A Sanskrit grammatical commentary conjugating verbal roots; "non-taṅ" and "taṅ" denote the parasmaipada and ātmanepada endings. The Sanskrit forms, transliterated irregularly and sometimes repeated in the Tibetan, are given in their intended IAST spelling, with duplicated items merged as "X or Y." A garbled phrase inside the liṭ forms of tviṣa (apparently a misplaced reference to the deletion of k "before a vowel") and a few stray interlinear labels for endings (thal, ta, te, ātā) are not rendered. This is a Sanskrit grammatical paradigm section (the roots yaj, vap and vah). "First person" renders the Indian grammatical term prathama puruṣa, which corresponds to the English third person; "last person" is the English first person. The rules are quoted in Tibetan paraphrase and correspond to Pāṇinian sūtras such as jhalo jhali (loss of sic), vraścabhrasja... (j to ṣ), ṣṭunā ṣṭuḥ (retroflexion), ṣaḍhoḥ kaḥ si, liṭy abhyāsasyobhayeṣām and vacisvapiyajādīnāṃ kiti. The expression rendered "the rule of thorough change" is uncertain; it may refer to the substitution of ṣ for s. In the gloss on vac, the Tibetan reads "to hold," evidently a slip for "to explain"; this is translated. In "ṣ becoming ḍ ... ṣṭu with ṣṭu" the Tibetan writes ṣa cu for ṣa ṭu, a slip that has been read as ṣṭu. In lṛṭ of vap, "introducing the b" has been read as "introducing the s" (the future affix). Many of the paradigm forms are irregular as transmitted and are given exactly as written. A grammatical paradigm section (the roots vah and veñ), continuing the conventions of the previous pieces: "first person" is the Indian prathama puruṣa (English third person), "last person" the English first person. The quoted rules correspond to Pāṇinian sūtras such as ho ḍhaḥ, jhaṣas tathor dho 'dhaḥ, ḍho ḍhe lopaḥ, sahivahor od avarṇasya, ādeca upadeśe 'śiti, yamaramanamātāṃ sak ca, āto lopa iṭi ca, āta au ṇalaḥ, veñaḥ, veño vayiḥ, grahijyāvayivyadhi... ṅiti ca, liṭi vayo yaḥ and vaścāsyānyatarasyāṃ kiti. The clause "and before dh too sic is dropped" appears to be a stray fragment displaced into the sentence about veñ's exception; it is translated where it stands. Obvious scribal slips (ñṛd for ñid, ṅeña for veña, mi phyed for mi byed, byis for byas, va śad for bśad) are read in their evident sense. Here the glossary term "condition" (pratyaya) is used in its grammatical sense of "affix," and "the warp of threads" renders a phrase using the word that also means tantra, in its literal weaving sense. Paradigm forms are given exactly as transmitted, irregularities included. A grammatical paradigm section (the roots veñ, vyeñ and hveñ), with "first person" for the Indian prathama puruṣa (English third person) as before. In several places the source has short labels for the personal endings (such as atus, ṇal, va, ma, ta, ātāṃ, jha, thās, āthāṃ, dhvaṃ, iṭ, vahi, mahi), evidently headings from an interlinear or tabular layout, scattered through the lists of forms and occasionally splitting a form (in the middle and last persons of the taṅ liṭ of veñ, in luṭ, and at the start of the benedictive); these labels are not reproduced as forms, and the forms they split (ūvāthe, ūyimahi, ūvimahi) are given whole. A broken fragment at the head of the middle-person list (a ... ṣe) is not given as a separate form. A displaced remark about iṭ before thal (from the rule iḍ attyartivyayatīnām) interrupts the luṭ of vyeñ and is given in parentheses where it stands; a similar stray phrase about sic being dropped interrupts the derivation of vivyāya. The taṅ lṛṭ form of veñ is written twice in the source and is given once. Quoted rules correspond to Pāṇinian sūtras including veñaḥ / vaś cāsyānyatarasyāṃ kiti, na vyo liṭi, lipisicihvaś ca, ātmanepadeṣv anyatarasyām, abhyastasya ca, aci śnudhātubhruvām, akṛtsārvadhātukayor dīrghaḥ and vānyasya saṃyogādeḥ. Paradigm forms are given exactly as transmitted, irregularities included. A grammatical paradigm section (the roots vas, vad and śvi), closing the treatment of the bhū class and opening the ad class (adādi), where Pāṇini 2.4.72 deletes the class sign śap. "First person" is the Indian prathama puruṣa (English third person) as before. Several glosses from an interlinear layout are spliced into the running text: a remark on vṛddhi and the loss of sic interrupts the rule on śāsi, vasi and ghasi; a note on saṃprasāraṇa splits the laṭ form śvayati; and an explanation of the liṭ derivation splits the form śiśviyuḥ. These are translated in parentheses where they stand. The definition of vad is garbled in the Tibetan and is read as "speaking clearly" (vyaktāyāṃ vāci). The section headed lṛṭ before the benedictive of śvi gives the periphrastic future (luṭ) forms. In the closing statement the Tibetan writes bhrū for the root bhū, and ad as aṅ, read in their evident sense. Quoted rules correspond to Pāṇinian sūtras including saḥ syārdhadhātuke, śāsivasighasīnāṃ ca, jṝstambhumrucumlucu..., śvayater aḥ, ato guṇe, vibhāṣā dheṭśvyoḥ, vibhāṣā śveḥ and adiprabhṛtibhyaḥ śapaḥ. Paradigm forms are given exactly as transmitted, irregularities included. A grammatical paradigm section opening the ad class (the roots ad and psā), with "first person" for the Indian prathama puruṣa (English third person) as before. As in earlier pieces, glosses from an interlinear layout are spliced into the running text: a note on d becoming t breaks the liṅ list; a note on usy apadāntāt splits the quoted sūtra hujhalbhyo her dhiḥ; a long set of notes on the loṭ derivations (ser hy apic ca, mer niḥ, āḍ uttamasya pic ca) interrupts the rule adaḥ sarveṣām; a note on aṅ for ḷdit roots interrupts the liṭ derivation; and a note on the liṭ ending au interrupts the benedictive. These are translated in parentheses where they stand. In the liṭ of ad without ghasḷ, the Tibetan labels the second group "last person"; it is the middle person and is so rendered. In this passage the word sbyin pa means "giving" (hu, "to give"), not the name Diti. Śākaṭāyana is the early grammarian cited by Pāṇini; the Tibetan spells his name in several slightly different ways. Paradigm forms are given exactly as transmitted, irregularities included. This is a grammatical treatise conjugating the roots vaś and han through the ten tense-mood forms (lakāras). Following the Tibetan, "first person" is the Sanskrit prathama puruṣa (English third person) and "last person" is the uttama puruṣa (English first person). Sanskrit verb forms are transliterated as the Tibetan spells them, even where they deviate from the standard forms. Several rule names are abbreviated or garbled in the Tibetan (for example ཟ་ཤྩ for vraśca, and ས་ལ་ལྷ་དག་གི་སོ་གསོལ, taken here as the rule that ṣ and ḍh become k before s); these are rendered by their evident sense. A stray syllable ག before the optative forms uśyāta and so on, which appear to be the optative (vidhi liṅ) though unlabeled, has been left untranslated. An editorial bracket in the source (ཥབ་ཥ་ཊུ་འོས་ཏཊ་ཁྲ་ཧི་སོགས་ཀྱི་བྲ་སར) is incorporated into the running text. The heading of the second root reads ཏ་ན but the discussion is plainly of han ("harming and going"), so it is rendered "hana"; likewise ཧ་ན་འཚོ་བ ("living") is read as འཚེ་བ, "killing", and ཐ་མོ as བ་མོ ("v and m"). The phrase སྨི་པ་ར is taken as the parasmaipada endings. In this grammatical context ལུང is the aorist (luṅ), not "scripture", and སྦྱིན་པ is "giving" (adding an augment), not a name. The phrase རབ་ཏུ་མཚེ་བར་བྱེད, apparently an interlinear gloss on pra- with han, is rendered as "making the sense 'to harm intensely'". Following the Tibetan, "first person" is the Sanskrit prathama puruṣa (English third person) and "last person" the uttama puruṣa (English first person). Verb forms are transliterated as the Tibetan spells them, even where they deviate from the standard forms. Several tense labels in the Tibetan do not match the forms they introduce and have been rendered by the evident tense: ལེཊ (leṭ) at the opening for liṭ (jaghāna and so on), ལུཊ for laṭ with dyauti, ལིང for laṅ with ayota, ལྲིཊ for liṭ with yuyāva, and ལིང for lṛṅ with ayaviṣyata. ཙ་ར here is the grammatical letter-group car in a rule name, not the personal name Cara. The phrase ངྷཱ་ཕྲེས is unclear; ཕྲེས is read as ཕྱིས, "is elided". The words "with guṇa" after adyavaṃ and "vṛddhi before sic" among the liṭ forms of yu appear to be misplaced marginal glosses and are translated where they stand. Rule names cited in Tibetan translation are rendered by their sense in quotation marks. Following the Tibetan, "first person" is the Sanskrit prathama puruṣa (English third person) and "last person" the uttama puruṣa (English first person). Verb forms are transliterated as the Tibetan spells them, even where they deviate from the standard forms. Some tense labels have been rendered by the tense the forms show: ཝཊ for lṛṭ (kṣṇaviṣyati), ལུང for laṅ (asnauta and so on), and ལི་ར for liṅ. The root heading ཀྵུ is the root kṣṇu, whose forms follow. In the luṅ of iṇ, the words la, la, ḍbhaṃ (the last in brackets in the source) are unclear and are transliterated as they stand. In this grammatical context འགྲོ་བ means "going" and ཀ་འགྲོ་བ, ཉ་ཎ་འགྲོ་བ and the like mean "marked with k", "marked with ñ and ṇ" (the indicatory letters). Following the Tibetan, "first person" is the Sanskrit prathama puruṣa (English third person) and "last person" the uttama puruṣa (English first person). Verb forms and quoted Sanskrit are transliterated as the Tibetan spells them, even where they deviate from the standard forms. In this grammatical context དྲན་པ is "remembering" (the root ik), not the meditative term mindfulness; གཟུགས is the grammatical "form" of a word; and མེ in meyāta is part of a verb form, not the name Agni. The rule cited for liṭ of mā, spelled ཤཱ་ཀ་ཊཱལ་ཎས་ངས་བ, is garbled and is transliterated. In the passage on khyā, the word drāva and the sentence on the benedictive after the loṭ forms appear to be displaced from elsewhere and are translated where they stand. The final sūtra is spelled with liṭ in the Tibetan, but the next passage shows it concerns laṭ (vido laṭo vā), so the gloss reads laṭ. Following the Tibetan, "first person" is the Sanskrit prathama puruṣa (English third person) and "last person" the uttama puruṣa (English first person). Verb forms and quoted Sanskrit sūtras are transliterated as the Tibetan spells them, even where they deviate from the standard forms (for example the bracketed vatvra and asnustāta, which carry editorial brackets in the source). In this grammatical context ཀུ་རུ and བཱ་ཎི are syllables of the verb forms kurutāṃ and karavāṇi, not the Kurus or Pāṇini; མདོས is "by the sūtra", not a thread-cross; ཕིད is read as vid; and བྱིངས་བྱེད་པ is read as ārdhadhātuka (བྱིངས་ཕྱེད་པ). The phrase "bhū changed into aha" (བྷཱུ་ཨ་ཧ་ར་བསྒྱུར་བ) is unclear and is translated as it stands; the remark on elision of hi after vi in loṭ appears out of place but is translated where it stands. This is a Sanskrit grammatical text conjugating the roots as, mṛj and vac; the Sanskrit forms and sūtra quotations are given exactly as the Tibetan spells them, though many are irregularly written. "First person" renders the Indian prathamapuruṣa (Western third person), and "last person" the uttamapuruṣa (Western first person), following the earlier pieces. The list "luṭ, benedictive liṅ, liṭ, lṛṅ" is taken as lṛṭ for liṭ, since liṭ has just been excluded. The phrase rendered "the operations of the ad class apply" (Tibetan a tang rnams 'jug) is understood as the root belonging to the adādi class. In the loṭ paragraph the Tibetan "la i ba" is read as 'phel ba, "vṛddhi", and "ba ka" as ṣa to ka, as the evident readings; "lam" in the lṛṅ sentence is read as the particle "or". The Sanskrit forms and sūtra quotations are given exactly as the Tibetan spells them, though many are irregularly written, and the text itself repeats the last-person laṭ forms of rud. Gārgya is named once as "the son of Garga" and once in a slightly variant spelling; both are taken as Gārgya, and "drang grong" is read as drang srong, "sage." In the svap sūtra the Tibetan "bslu ti" is taken as the sūtra's sūti, explained as ṣūṅ. The Sanskrit forms and sūtra quotations are given exactly as the Tibetan spells them, though many are irregularly written. Several tense labels are evidently miswritten and are translated by their evident reading: "lriṭ" before the reduplicated forms of śvas as liṭ, "liṭ" before the present forms of an as laṭ, and "loṭ" before the reduplicated forms of jakṣ as liṭ; "gnyis sad pa" is read as gnyid sad pa, "waking." The gloss "rdan pa" for vevid is uncertain and is tentatively read as ldan pa, "possessing." The Sanskrit forms and sūtra quotations are given exactly as the Tibetan spells them, though many are irregularly written. A few slips are translated by their evident reading: "ming tshig" as mang tshig, "plural"; "zhag" as hal, "consonant"; "byongs" as byings, "root"; and "ling" before adaridriṣyata as lṛṅ. In the liṭ of daridrā the phrase "the āt is elided" is written three times over and is rendered once. In the rule on sip the Tibetan says the final letter "optionally becomes ru and optionally becomes ru"; the second is taken as the alternative in which ru does not apply, which the forms acakāḥ and acakād illustrate. The Sanskrit forms and sūtra quotations are given exactly as the Tibetan spells them, though many are irregularly written, and the text repeats the last-person loṭ forms of cakṣ. The term ataṅ is here explicitly paired with taṅ, so it denotes the parasmaipada endings as against the ātmanepada (taṅ). Some evident slips are translated by their intended reading: "laṅ" before the optative forms of śās and cakṣ as liṅ, "loṭ" before the reduplicated forms of śās as liṭ, "bzhi mnyam pa" as gzhi mnyam pa, "common basis," and "ta la" as ha la, "consonant." The rule cited as "without position" (gnas med pa) is left in its literal sense. This is a Sanskrit grammar treating the root cakṣiṅ ("to speak") and its substitutes khyāñ and ksāñ; the cited Sanskrit forms are romanized letter for letter as the Tibetan spells them, including evident misspellings. In this grammatical context several house-glossary words carry technical senses: rkyen is "suffix" (pratyaya), lung is the aorist tense luṅ (not "scripture"), sa is the letter s, mtha' is "final" or "ending," and dbang du byas na is "when used in the sense of." "Beginning with val" renders the Tibetan for valādi, the iṭ augment before ārdhadhātuka suffixes beginning with a val consonant; "yama, rama, nam" is the rule yamaramanamātāṃ sak ca (the Tibetan writes the augment simply as "ka"); "also of another, beginning with a conjunct" is the rule vā 'nyasya saṃyogādeḥ; "of a substitute" renders the rule ādeśapratyayayoḥ. The commentary's "'gyur bam yin" is read as "'gyur ba ma yin," "is not changed," which the following sentence requires. The bracket around "brāṃ" in the edition has been dropped; "khyāñu" in the luṭ section and "cakṣid" in the benedictive section are read as khyāñ and cakṣiṅ. This section of the Sanskrit grammar conjugates the middle-voice roots īḍ ("to praise"), īś ("to rule") and ās ("to sit"); the cited Sanskrit forms and rule-names are romanized letter for letter as the Tibetan spells them. The glossary words found here carry grammatical senses: lung is the aorist tense luṅ, sa is the letter s, mtha' is "final," las is "from," and 'gro ba in "ṭa 'gro ba" renders the rule-name ṭit ("marked with ṭ"). "Car" and "khar" are Pāṇinian sound-classes (pratyāhāras), not personal names; "khar" is once written "bar" in the laṅ section of īḍ, and "aliḍ" in the luṅ section, read as īḍ. The phrase "with the taṅ of la" (la taṅ) before "śap is elided" is obscure and rendered literally. In the īś section the words "by vraśca, bhrasja ... with ṣṭu, ṣṭu" stand inside the form īśīran, splitting it into "ī... śīran"; this looks like a misplaced gloss explaining īṣṭe, but it is translated where it stands. The first of the two "luṅ" headings in the ās section introduces imperfect forms (āsta, āsātāṃ, āsata) and is read as laṅ. The lṛṭ heading in the ās section survives only as "la" and is rendered as lṛṭ from the forms that follow. This section of the Sanskrit grammar conjugates the middle-voice roots vas ("to clothe"), ṇisi ("to kiss") and ṣūṅ ("to give birth"), and introduces śīṅ ("to lie down"); the cited Sanskrit forms and rule-names are romanized letter for letter as the Tibetan spells them, including evident misspellings. The glossary words found here carry grammatical senses: lung is the aorist tense luṅ, sa is the letter s, mtha' is "final," and 'gro ba in "i ta 'gro ba" and "ū ta 'gro ba" renders the rule-terms idit and ūdit ("marked with i," "marked with ū"). Yon tan here is the technical term guṇa (vowel strengthening), and "aniṭ" is the option without the iṭ augment. The lṛṭ heading in the vas section is written "ḷṭ" and is read as lṛṭ. This section of the Sanskrit grammar conjugates the roots śīṅ ("to lie down") and iṅ ("to study," always with the prefix adhi), then cites the rules on the substitute gāṅ, on ṅ-marked suffixes, and the opening of the rule on ghu and the other roots before consonant-initial endings, which continues in the next piece. The cited Sanskrit forms and sūtras are romanized letter for letter as the Tibetan spells them, including evident misspellings. The glossary words here carry grammatical senses: mdo is a grammatical sūtra (rule), rkyen is "suffix," lung is the aorist luṅ, sa is the letter s, mtha' is "final," don is "purpose," las is "from," and 'gro ba in "ña 'gro ba," "ṅa 'gro ba" renders the rule-terms ñit, ṅit ("marked with ñ," "marked with ṅ"). The second heading in the śīṅ section is written liṅ but introduces the imperfect forms aśeta and so on and is read as laṅ; in the laṅ of adhi-iṅ the augment written "mvaṭ" is read as āṭ. This section of the Sanskrit grammar treats the rule that turns the ā of ghu, mā, sthā, gā, pā, hā and sā into ī, the aorist, perfect and other forms of adhi-iṅ ("to study") with its substitute gāṅ, and the roots dīdhīṅ ("to shine"), vevī and dviṣ ("to hate"). The cited Sanskrit forms and sūtras are romanized letter for letter as the Tibetan spells them, including evident misspellings. The glossary words here carry grammatical senses: mdo is a grammatical sūtra, rkyen is "suffix," lung is the aorist luṅ, sa is the letter s, dbu ma is the "middle" person, mtha' is "final" or "ending," las is "from" or, in "ṣo mtha'i las," the Dhātupāṭha gloss "in the act of ending," and 'gro ba in "kaṅ 'gro ba," "ba 'gro ba" renders the rule-terms "kṅit" and "pit" ("marked with k or ṅ," "marked with p"); mi dga' ba is the Dhātupāṭha gloss "displeasure" (aprīti). The sentence "In the option where it is not changed into gāṅ, ac... iṅ is to be changed into gāṅ" is broken in the source and is rendered as it stands; it introduces the perfect, where iṅ becomes gāṅ. The augment written "vaṭ" is read as āṭ. The Tibetan gloss on vevī, "equal to a reward" (rngan pa mtshungs pa), is uncertain; it evidently renders the Dhātupāṭha's "like veti," and is given here simply as "in being alike." This is a section of a Sanskrit grammar giving verb paradigms of the roots dviṣ and duh; the quoted phrases are Tibetan renderings of grammatical rules (for example "before s, ṣ and ḍh become k" for ṣaḍhoḥ kaḥ si, "the rule on substitutes" for the ādeśa-pratyaya rule, "after hu and jhal, hi becomes dhi" for hujhalbhyo her dhiḥ). The Sanskrit word forms are transcribed as the Tibetan spells them, irregularities included. Evident slips read as intended: ན་ཌྷ in the first rule citation is read as ṣa ḍha, as the text itself gives it later; ཛུ་ཧ is read as hu jhal; བུ་ཀ as puk; the ending written ཥཱ་པ is given as dveṣāva. The phrase rendered "several changes are made" (མང) and the line "a, by reason of the s, d becomes dh, duhi" are unclear in the source and are translated as they stand. A section of a Sanskrit grammar giving paradigms of the roots duh, dih and lih; quoted phrases are Tibetan renderings of grammatical rules, and the Sanskrit forms are transcribed as the Tibetan spells them. Evident slips read as intended: ཡིན་ཏན as ཡོན་ཏན (guṇa); སྐུ་བས as སྐབས ("case"); གོར་མ as གོང་མ ("the preceding"); ཉའི་ཌྷ as ཧའི་ཌྷ ("ḍh for h"); the ending written ཧཱ་པ is given as lehāva, ཀྵྜ་ཏཱཾ as alikṣātāṃ, and ཀྵ་ཏྲ as alikṣata. A stray repeated "do, in the taṅ" (དོ་ཏང་ལ) after "in the ataṅ" in the lṛṭ paradigm of duh is a scribal repetition and is not rendered. A section of a Sanskrit grammar on the root ūrṇu; quoted Sanskrit phrases are rules of grammar, given as the Tibetan spells them and followed by the text's own Tibetan gloss, and the word forms are transcribed as spelled. Evident slips read as intended: ལང before the paradigm ūrṇuyāt and so on is read as liṅ; ལིཊ before the paradigm ūrṇuviṣyati is read as lṛṭ; སའི་ལུཊའི་ས is read as the s of sīyuṭ; མི་ངོ་འདིས as མདོ་འདིས ("by this sūtra"); ཨཱུ་མ as ām; དོའི as འདིའི ("this"). A stray "ṇal" inside the form ūrṇunuvāthe, and a stray repeated ཡིན་པ, are not rendered. The endings "mas" in ūrṇunavimas and ūrṇunuvimas stand in brackets in the source as an editorial reading. A section of a Sanskrit grammar on the roots ūrṇu, stu and kṣu; quoted Sanskrit phrases are grammatical rules, given as the Tibetan spells them with the text's own gloss, and the word forms are transcribed as spelled. Evident slips read as intended: ཏེར་ལའང at the opening as ཏང་ལའང ("in the taṅ too"); ཝྀང as lṛṅ; the first taṅ paradigm of stu, headed "middle person" (དབུས་མ) in the source, is read as the first person, since the middle person follows; the form written སྟ་སའ་མ་ཧཻ is given as stavāmahai; སྟའི་ཏཱ as stavitā. The sentence on kit in liṭ strings together several rule citations tersely and is rendered as it stands. ཞི་བ here is the verb "pacifying" in the root gloss of śam, not the name Śiva. A section of a Sanskrit grammar on the roots kṣu, ru, ṇu and brū; quoted Sanskrit phrases are grammatical rules, given as the Tibetan spells them with the text's own gloss, and the word forms are transcribed as spelled. Evident slips read as intended: སྲ་ཉྫ as svañj; ཀྲྀཏ་ལ་ཡིན་པ as "not kṛt" (ཀྲྀཏ་མ་ཡིན་པ), as elsewhere; ཨཱཊ as īṭ, the augment the rule nu-ru-stu prescribes; ཤྨུ and ཤྟ as śnu; ཟཱུ, མཱུ, བྲཱལ and བྲཱུལ as brū. The Tibetan glosses the "i" of vaci as "the letter a" being for pronunciation; this is rendered as it stands. This piece closes the section of the grammar on the adādi roots, with a Sanskrit colophon line and a Tibetan statement naming the work, and opens the section on the juhotyādi roots (hu, bhī). A section of a Sanskrit grammar on the reduplicating roots pṛ, hā and ṛ; quoted Sanskrit phrases are grammatical rules, given as the Tibetan spells them with the text's own gloss, and word forms are transcribed as spelled. Brief derivation notes stand among the forms in the source (after veviḍḍhi and after jajaniṣi) and are rendered in place. A section of a Sanskrit grammar on the roots dā and dhā; quoted Sanskrit phrases are grammatical rules, given as the Tibetan spells them with the text's own gloss, and word forms are transcribed as spelled. A section of a Sanskrit grammar on the roots dhā and bhṛ; quoted Sanskrit phrases are grammatical rules, given as the Tibetan spells them with the text's own gloss, and word forms are transcribed as spelled. Evident slips read as intended: བསྐྱ as བསྒྱུར ("changed"); ཨ་ཕྱས as ཨཱ་ཕྱིས ("ā dropped"); སི་ཙ་ཡ as "before sic"; ལས་སོས as ལས་འོས. This piece completes the juhotyādi roots (mā, hā), closes that section with a Sanskrit colophon line and a Tibetan statement naming the work, and begins the divādi roots with div. Quoted Sanskrit phrases are grammatical rules, given as the Tibetan spells them with the text's own gloss, and word forms are transcribed as spelled. Some rule notes stand displaced among the forms in the source and are rendered where they stand: "before dh too, sic is dropped" (explaining amādhvam) inside the liṭ of mā, and "after at, hi is dropped" (explaining the loṭ form dīvya) inside the laṅ of div. In the root gloss of div, སྡུ་གུ is taken as "delighting." A section of a Sanskrit grammar on divādi roots (div, siv, nṛt, tras, jṝ, śo); quoted Sanskrit phrases are grammatical rules, given as the Tibetan spells them with the text's own gloss, and word forms are transcribed as spelled. A section of a Sanskrit grammar on divādi roots (śo, cho, ṣo, do, rādh, sādh, vyadh); quoted Sanskrit phrases are grammatical rules, given as the Tibetan spells them with the text's own gloss. In the roots rādh, sādh and vyadh the Tibetan writes dh as ངྷ, and the forms are given with dh (rādhyati, rāddhā and so on); other forms are transcribed as spelled. The root of "in cutting" is supplied in brackets in the source (written རྡོ); the forms show the root do. A remark that in luṅ this root takes neither sak nor iṭ "although it ends in āt" is inserted in the source inside the liṭ paradigm, and is rendered where it stands. Evident slips read as intended: ཆོ་ག as cho; མ་ཏང as ataṅ; ལྲིཊ as liṭ in the remark on sādh; སཾ་པྲ་སཱ་ཏ་ཏ as samprasāraṇa. This is a section of a Pāṇinian verb-conjugation manual; the "first person" of the Sanskrit grammarians is the English third person. Sanskrit rule-citations and paradigm forms are given in romanized Sanskrit following the Tibetan transliteration (which writes dh as ṅh), keeping its convention of writing final consonants with an inherent a (e.g., avyātsīta, puṣyāta). A few evident copyist's slips in the forms have been given in their intended shape (e.g., abuṣatāṃ for apuṣatāṃ, aśīṣyata for aśliṣyata, piḍhyāsuḥ for vidhyāsuḥ, tṛbyati for tṛpyati, aśleṣyata for aślekṣyata). The reduplicated paradigm after "puṣa" is introduced in the Tibetan as lṛṭ, but the forms (pupoṣa and so on) and the parallel sections show it is liṭ; translated as liṭ. Likewise, for radha in luṅ the Tibetan cites "pug-anta" for the change of cli to aṅ, which is evidently a slip for "puṣādi"; translated accordingly. Here མདོས is the instrumental "by the sūtra," not the ritual thread-cross. This piece continues the conjugation of Pāṇinian fourth-class roots; rule citations and paradigm forms are given in romanized Sanskrit following the Tibetan transliteration, with evident copyist's slips in the forms given in their intended shape (e.g., atrābhaṃ for atrāptaṃ, tatrapatuḥ for tatṛpatuḥ, tarpriṣyati for tarpiṣyati, mumuhopa for mumuhiva, nāṃṣṭāsi for naṃṣṭāsi, anaraiṣyata for anaśiṣyata, ghramu for bhramu, maśeḥ for naśeḥ). For dṛpa the Tibetan glosses the meanings as "joy and releasing," whereas the Dhātupāṭha has harṣa and mohana ("delight and bewildering"); translated as the Tibetan reads. The commentary's rule for the optional e of naśi is written irregularly in the Tibetan and is given in its evident Sanskrit form. In the lṛṭ derivation of naśa the nuṃ rule is cited twice, the second time in a garbled form ("yarjinaśa"); both mentions are kept. Here ཉེ་བར་ཞི་བ is the root meaning "calming" (upaśama), not the god Śiva. Paradigm forms and rule citations are given in romanized Sanskrit following the Tibetan transliteration; evident copyist's slips in the forms are given in their intended shape (e.g., śamyāyuḥ for śamyāsuḥ, akalamīta for aklamīta, aklāmyati for aklāmyata, lulubhatuḍhaḥ for lulubhatuḥ, libhitasaṃ for lobhitāsi, mebyatu for medyatu, mimadathuḥ for mimidathuḥ, eṭ for iṭ, abdyāsa for abhyāsa). The lṛṅ form of śamu appears in the Tibetan as aśamyata, evidently for aśamiṣyata, and the last section of ñimidā is headed liṭ in the Tibetan though its forms (mediṣyati) are those of lṛṭ; both are translated by the evident reading. In the luṅ of yasu the Tibetan inserts a gloss, "strives hard," between two forms; it is kept where it stands. Here ཉི་མི་དཱ is the root ñimidā, not the sun.
