The luṅ of tṛmpa gives only two forms. The lṛṅ of spṛśa offers a second alternative ("or ...") whose form is missing in the Tibetan; the one form given is translated. This is a section of a Pāṇinian conjugation manual treating tudādi roots; "first person" here is the Sanskrit prathama puruṣa (English third person), and "last person" is the uttama (English first person), following the earlier pieces. Grammatical terms that coincide with house glossary entries (luṅ for ལུང, the letter s for ས, "going" for འགྲོ་བ, "affix" for རྐྱེན, "ending" for མཐའ) are used in their grammatical senses here. The Tibetan transliterations of the Sanskrit verb forms contain many scribal slips (for example བྲྀཙྪ for pṛccha, ལིང for liṭ, ཝྀཊ for lṛṭ, ཡང for laṅ, ཥ་ར་ལ for khari, and སྲང, read as s becoming d); the forms and sūtra names are given in their evident standard Sanskrit spelling. The term rendered "a-affixes" (ཨ་ཏང, once ཨ་རང) evidently refers to the tudādi thematic vowel; its exact form is uncertain. Some paradigms are incomplete in the text as it stands: the last-person plural of the aorist of masj is missing, the middle-person dual of the perfect of masj is missing, and the second loṭ form of vicch (vicchatu) is not written out; these gaps are kept. The benedictive of vicch lists an extra repeated dual form, reduced here to the standard three. A Pāṇinian conjugation manual on tudādi roots; "first person" is the Sanskrit prathama (English third person) and "last person" the uttama (English first person), as in earlier pieces. The text glosses mṛś as "forbearance" (བཟོད་པ), which properly belongs to the homophonous root mṛṣ; the Dhātupāṭha gives mṛś as "touching." The gloss is translated as written. The Tibetan transliterations of the verb forms and sūtra names contain many scribal slips (for example ལྲྀཊ for liṭ and lṛṅ, kuṭataṃ for kuṭati, kuṭatu for akuṭat, vicīt without the augment, iyeṣa paradigm forms, eṣitā written iṣitā). Forms are given in their evident standard spelling. A few paradigms are defective as transmitted: the middle-person aorist of mṛś with am lacks the dual, and the aorist of iṣ lists an extra variant of the dual. Glossary words occurring here in grammatical senses (ལུང as the aorist luṅ, ས as the letter s, ལས as "from," འགྲོ་བ in the it-marker terms, མཐའ as "-ending") are rendered in those senses. The terms ཏང and ཨ་ཏང are the Pāṇinian taṅ (the ātmanepada endings) and a-taṅ, "non-taṅ" (the parasmaipada endings), as this passage makes explicit; they are rendered "taṅ endings" and "non-taṅ endings." In the sūtra "mriyater luṅ-liṅoś ca" the Tibetan writes the syllable luṅ with the word for "wind" (རླུང), an evident slip; it is not the god Vāyu here. Likewise ཙ་ར in "abhyāse car ca" is the grammatical class car, not a name. Glossary words appear here in grammatical senses: རྐྱེན as "affix," མཐའ as "ending," གཟུགས as "stem" (aṅga), ལུང as the aorist luṅ, འགྲོ་བ in the it-marker designations, and འགོག་པ as "to block." The Tibetan transliterations of the verb forms contain many slips (for example mriyata for mriyeta, vijatvaṃ for vijatām, asphurata for asphuriṣyat), and forms are given in their evident standard spelling. Some paradigms are incomplete as transmitted, such as the missing second singular amṛthāḥ in the aorist of mṛ, and the last-person perfect of mṛ, which reads mamāra, mamāra, mamṛma, given here as mamāra, mamara, mamṛma. The opening sentence is the section colophon of this work, The Chariot That Draws the Jewel of Excellent Explanation, closing the tudādi roots; the rest begins the rudhādi class with rudh. The sūtras cited are Pāṇinian (rudhādibhyaḥ śnam, śnasor allopaḥ, naś cāpadāntasya jhali, jharo jhari savarṇe, irito vā, khari ca, and so on). The Tibetan transliterations of the verb forms contain many slips (ལུཊ for laṭ, རང for taṅ, repeated or misspelled forms such as rundhāte for rundhate and arāṃṇat for aruṇat), and the forms are given in their evident standard spelling. Some paradigms are incomplete as transmitted (the middle- and last-person plurals of the active present), and these gaps are kept. In the middle-person perfect active the text has an additional form that is too garbled to identify (རུ་ར་དདྟཱ); it is not rendered. The parenthetical explanation placed before the last-person taṅ forms of laṅ (d becoming ru, and so on) evidently concerns the second singular aruṇaḥ; it is translated where it stands. Glossary words appear in grammatical senses here: ཡུལ as "domain" (the place of a substituted affix), སྒྲིབ་པ as "obstructing" in the root gloss, མཐའ as "final" or "end," and ལུང as the aorist luṅ. This continues the rudhādi class (roots taking the infix śnam) with chṛd, tṛd and śiṣ, citing Pāṇinian sūtras (śnasor allopaḥ, jharo jhari savarṇe, se 'sici kṛtacṛtacchṛdatṛdanṛtaḥ, hujhalbhyo her dhiḥ, and so on). The Tibetan transliterations of the forms contain many slips (for example chṛṇadhi for chṛṇatti, ལྲྀང for liṭ, ཨ་ཏར for the non-taṅ endings, śeṣyāstām for śiṣyāstām), and the forms are given in their evident standard spelling, keeping the text's single ch where standard Sanskrit doubles it after a vowel. The bracketed forms in the Tibetan are translated. Two explanatory notes appear out of place: the remark on d becoming ru and visarga, placed under the aorist of chṛd, concerns the laṅ second singular; and the derivation of hi to dhi, placed under laṅ of śiṣ, belongs to the loṭ form śiṇḍhi. Both are translated where they stand. The benedictive of śiṣ lacks its third singular as transmitted. This continues the rudhādi class with tṛh, hiṃs and añj, citing Pāṇinian sūtras (tṛṇaha im, śnān na lopaḥ, añjeḥ sici, ho ḍhaḥ, hujhalbhyo her dhiḥ, and so on). The Tibetan transliterations of the forms are often corrupt (for example tṛḍhaḥ for tṛṇḍhaḥ, atrogma for atṛṃhma, hraṃhyāsuḥ for tṛhyāsuḥ), and the forms are given in their evident standard spelling. The first singular imperfect of hiṃs is written ahinaḥ, like the second singular; the standard form ahinat is given. In the perfect of hiṃs the text repeats the heading "in the three of the last person" with its first form, an evident dittography rendered once. The benedictive of tṛh gives only two forms, as transmitted. In the gloss of añj, "going" (འགྲོ་བ) is the root meaning gati, not the doctrinal term. This piece ends the rudhādi class with añj, indh and vid, gives the Sanskrit and Tibetan colophon of that class and the section colophon of The Chariot That Draws the Jewel of Excellent Explanation, and begins the tanādi class with tan. The Tibetan transliterations of the forms are often corrupt (for example ཋིནྟི for vinte, ལིཊ for laṭ in the vid paradigm, ལྀུཊ for lṛṭ, avintthāḥ and the like), and the forms are given in their evident standard spelling; for vid the benedictive and future are given with guṇa (vediṣīṣṭa, vediṣyate), where the text writes vidi-. The Sanskrit closing line of the rudhādi class is reproduced exactly as the Tibetan spells it. This continues the tanādi class with tan, san and kṣiṇ, citing Pāṇinian sūtras (tanādibhyas tathāsoḥ, anudāttopadeśavanatitanotyādīnām anunāsikalopo jhali kṅiti, janasanakhanāṃ sañjhaloḥ, ye vibhāṣā, and so on). The root gloss of ṣaṇu, སྦྱིན་པ, is the ordinary "giving" (dāna), not a name. The Tibetan transliterations of the forms contain many slips (for example ལིཊ for loṭ, ལཊ for loṭ in the kṣiṇ paradigm, sanotaṃ for sanoti, asanute for sanute), and forms are given in their evident standard spelling; the text's perfect second singulars tatanitha and sasanitha are kept as written, and the repeated atanvāthām is kept. In the gloss on the quoted rule about kṣiṇ, the Tibetan ཨུ་མངྷཱ་རཾ་ཡིག is obscure; it is read as "the penultimate is the letter ṛ," which is uncertain. This piece finishes kṣiṇ, treats ṛṇ, and begins kṛ in the tanādi class, citing Pāṇinian sūtras (tanādibhyas tathāsoḥ, halādiḥ śeṣaḥ, kuhoś cuḥ, ur at, ata ādeḥ, ata ut sārvadhātuke, nityaṃ karoteḥ, ye ca, and so on). The Tibetan transliterations contain many slips (for example ལིང for laṅ in the ṛṇ paradigm, kurvantaṃ for kurvanti, karemi for karomi, kuryāb for kuryāt), and forms are given in their evident standard spelling. The text's perfect of kṣiṇ (with guṇa in the dual and plural, and cikṣiṇitha in the second singular) is kept as transmitted. A few forms are repeated in the Tibetan (arṇathuḥ, arṇitā) and are given once. The rule cited for optional guṇa in ṛṇ refers back to the commentary's statement under kṣiṇ about ṛ as the penultimate, which supports the reading adopted there. This piece completes kṛ and the tanādi class (with the sūtras on the augment suṭ in saṃskṛ, pariṣkṛ and upaskṛ, Pāṇini 6.1.137 to 139), gives the class colophon and the section colophon of The Chariot That Draws the Jewel of Excellent Explanation, and opens the kryādi class. In the Tibetan, several interlinear glosses are displaced from the examples they explain: the gloss "adorns all over" stands before pariṣkaroti, the glosses on the three kanyā examples stand inside the next rule's statement, and the glosses on the three examples of the last rule ("brings a quality to the throat," "prepares the food," "furnishes the treatise with supplements") stand inside the Tibetan class colophon. They are translated here beside the examples they explain. The Tibetan transliterations contain many slips (for example kurvandu for kurvantu, akunāthām for akurvāthām, gaṇṭhaṃ for kaṇṭhaṃ, khūṃkte for bhuṅkte), and the forms are given in their evident standard spelling. The Tibetan gloss of krī, རྫས་ཚང་བ, is read as རྫས་ཚོང་བ, "exchanging goods" (dravyavinimaya). The repeated saṃcaskaruḥ is kept as in the text. This piece treats krī and skuñ in the kryādi class, citing Pāṇinian sūtras (ī halyaghoḥ, śnābhyastayor ātaḥ, stambhustumbhuskambhuskumbhuskuñbhyaḥ śnuś ca, śarpūrvāḥ khayaḥ, akṛtsārvadhātukayor dīrghaḥ, and so on). The text holds that in the perfect the reduplicated stems of krī and skuñ count as having a conjunct, so the endings are not kit and guṇa applies throughout (cikrayatuḥ, cuskavatuḥ); its forms are kept on that basis, though standard Pāṇinian grammar gives cikriyatuḥ and cuskuvatuḥ. The Tibetan transliterations contain many slips (for example krīṇātaḥ for krīṇītaḥ, cikrāyatuḥ, catrayuḥ, cuskavahuḥ, sūnātu for skunātu), and forms are given in their evident standard spelling. A few paradigms are incomplete as transmitted (the dual of the middle-person imperative of krī, the plural of the middle-person taṅ aorist of krī), and a repeated form in the aorist of skuñ is given once. The root gloss of skuñ, ཀུན་ཏུ་གྲོལ་བ, is translated literally as "setting free." This piece finishes skuñ and treats stambh, stumbh, skambh and skumbh (which take śnā or śnu, by Pāṇini 3.1.82) and begins mī, citing Pāṇinian sūtras (aniditāṃ hala upadhāyāḥ kṅiti, jṝstambhumrucumlucu..., veḥ skabhnāter nityam, mīnātiminotidīṅāṃ lyapi ca, yamaramanamātāṃ sak ca). The Tibetan transliterations contain many slips (for example stabhūtaḥ, stibhāna, སྦུ for sku, ལོང for liṅ, ལྲཊ for lṛṭ), and forms are given in their evident standard spelling; the aorist forms the text writes without the augment are given with it. Some forms are repeated in the Tibetan (astabhatām, and in the middle-person perfect of skambh, caskambhitha and a garbled dual each given twice) and the first are kept or given once; the aorist of skumbh lacks its third singular. The section on mī is disordered in the Tibetan: the label "luṅ" stands before the evidently present taṅ form mīnīte, the aorist derivation appears twice, and between the two stands only the tail of the imperfect (the end of a form ending in t, then the taṅ amīnīta). It is translated as it stands. This piece finishes mī and treats pū and kṝ in the kryādi class, citing Pāṇinian sūtras (er anekācaḥ, er liṅi, pvādīnāṃ hrasvaḥ, vṝto vā, ṛcchatyṝtām, ṝta id dhātoḥ, uraṇ raparaḥ). The root written ཀྲྀ་ཉ is the long-vowel root kṝñ, as its forms akārīt and kīryāt show. The quoted line written དྭཱ་དཱི་ནཱཾ་ཧྲ་སྭཿ ཀེ་ཙི་དྭཱ is read as pvādīnāṃ hrasvaḥ, kecid vā. The Tibetan transliterations contain many slips (for example བུ for pu in the perfect of pū, རིཊ for liṭ, apunīti, pavitāla, akaiṛīṣātām), and forms are given in their evident standard spelling. The doubled pupuviḍhve is kept as in the text. This piece treats dhū, grah and śṝ in the kryādi class, citing Pāṇinian sūtras (halaḥ śnaḥ śānaj jhau, graho 'liṭi dīrghaḥ, śṝdṝprāṃ hrasvo vā, vṝto vā, ṛcchatyṝtām, ṝta id dhātoḥ). In "in the ātmanepada" the Tibetan uses བདག, "self," as the short name of the ātmanepada endings, not the doctrinal self. The Tibetan transliterations contain many slips (for example bhunāti and hūnīte for dhunāti and dhunīte, རང for taṅ, ལཊ for loṭ, ལིཊ for luṭ, ལིང for lṛṅ, gṛhvāni for gṛhṇāni, dhavihā for dhavitā), and forms are given in their evident standard spelling. The Tibetan does not write out the long vowels of the roots śṝ and dhū consistently; they are given here as the forms require. This piece treats dṝ, pṝ, jyā, vrī, jñā and śranth in the kryādi class, citing Pāṇinian sūtras (śṝdṝprāṃ hrasvo vā, vṝto vā, ṛcchatyṝtām, ṝta id dhātoḥ, halaḥ, grahijyā..., jñājanor jā, vā 'nyasya saṃyogādeḥ). The root written བྲཱྀ, glossed "obstructing," is read as vrī (vrīñ varaṇe), as all its forms (avraiṣīt, vivrāya, vretā, vrīyāt) require; its present forms, written པྲྀ་ཎཱ་ཏི and the like, are given as vrīṇāti and so on. The benedictive of pṝ is given as the text has it, pīryāt; standard Pāṇinian grammar gives pūryāt. As before, the text keeps guṇa throughout the perfect of vrī. The Tibetan transliterations contain many slips (for example ལ་བ for laṅ, ཨ་ཥྟཱ་ས for abhyāsa, jijyītha, jijyaiva, abraiṣīt), and forms are given in their evident standard spelling. The last-person perfect of vrī lacks a dual in -iva as transmitted. This passage of a Tibetan commentary on Pāṇini's grammar quotes Sanskrit sūtras and verb forms in Tibetan script; they are romanized exactly as spelled, including evident irregularities. The Tibetan "first person" (skyes bu dang po) follows the Indian order, in which the first person corresponds to the Western third person and the "last person" to the Western first. The Pāṇinian rules cited by their Tibetan renderings are translated in English. "ka 'gro ba" is rendered as kit, a suffix having k as its indicatory letter; "bal" is the class val; and "dbyangs don" is taken as "for the sake of the accent." The Sanskrit forms and sūtras are romanized exactly as the Tibetan spells them, irregularities included. Pāṇinian rules cited by their Tibetan renderings are translated in English. "Becomes it" reads i ta for a ta, following the sense of the rule on the penultimate ṛ. The remark that "the operation as for san does not apply" refers to the reduplicated aorist of gaṇa, though here it stands after the benedictive forms. The person terms follow the Indian order, as before. Sanskrit forms are transliterated letter for letter as spelled, and several carry evident slips that are kept, for example akathayitā with a stray augment in luṭ, aṃkayate and arthayeta in the parasmaipada optative where aṃkayet and arthayet are expected, aṃkāpayiti for aṃkāpayati, arthapayati for arthāpayati, āṃchikana with ch for c, and arthayiṣīlāstrāṃ for arthayiṣīyāstāṃ. The bracketed syllable rtha in arthayate is an editorial supply in the source. The Tibetan a-taṅ and taṅ are the parasmaipada and ātmanepada endings respectively, and are rendered by those names. The sentence "since the a has been elided, the operation that applies as when ṇic follows is not carried out" renders a garbled line (literally "a-ka byis pa", read as "a ka phyis pa", "the a of ka elided"); its exact sense is uncertain. House glossary "being / destiny" for ’gro ba does not fit here: in the root gloss of aṃka it means "going," and in the phrase for the it-markers ñ and ṇ it renders the grammatical term it, literally "what goes away." In the gloss of the puk sūtra, rīṅ is rendered "to hear" after the Tibetan nyan pa, a translation of śravaṇa where the Dhātupāṭha has sravaṇa, "to ooze"; the gloss of krūyī ends in an unclear syllable, so its sense is left as uncertain; the phrase "roots of their own that end in ā" reads a corrupt rang byings sā ta mgra’ can as ā mtha’ can. "When ṇi follows aṃkā" reads the Tibetan i kā as aṃkā. "The rule cited as pracad" renders an unclear phrase in the aṃka luṅ derivation; its reference is uncertain. In the second artha commentary citation, ming dbyi is read as dbyi, "elided," matching the parallel aṃka citation. Tibetan slips read by sense: brtod for brjod, "reduplicate"; ma ba rjong for mi brjod, "is not reduplicated"; lring for lṛṅ. The closing Sanskrit line is a colophon to the section, evidently for iti pāṇinivyākaraṇasya sūtrāc curādayaḥ samāptāḥ; it is transliterated as spelled. Sanskrit forms are transliterated letter for letter as spelled; many carry evident slips that are kept, for example kāryiṃti, kāriṃyarta, kārayotu and akārayiṃte where kārayati, kārayet, kārayatu and akārayat are expected, corayimyati for corayiṣyati, and uḍḍhaukanatāṃ for aḍuḍhaukatāṃ. The sūtra cited as nāgopiśāspriditāṃ is evidently nāglopiśāsvṛditām; the Tibetan spelling ནཱ་གཱོ carries a stray ā-sign, which is dropped in the transliteration. The opening sūtra hetumaticāhetuḥ is given as spelled. "The eight and the eighty endings" renders brgyad dang brgyad cu literally; the intended count is unclear, perhaps the eighteen personal endings. House glossary "condition" for rkyen is set aside here: in this grammatical context it renders pratyaya in the sense of "suffix." Likewise ’gro ba in phrases such as "ṛ as their it" renders the grammatical term it, literally "what goes away," while in the root glosses of ḍhaukṛ and ṭuośvi it means "going." "By the rule that, where ak has not been elided, the treatment is as with san when caṅ follows" reads the garbled ya bal tsang pha rol las na bzhin as the rule sanvallaghuni caṅpare 'nag lope. "With r brought in" renders ra drangs pa; its exact sense is uncertain. In the cur section, ལེཊ (leṭ) is kept as written though laṭ is evidently meant; "the rule beginning with what ends in puk" renders bu ka mtha’ sogs, evidently the rule pugantalaghūpadhasya ca. In the ḍhaukṛ luṅ derivation a stray syllable group ḍhaḍa before ak is left untranslated, and the Tibetan reads tsa du for caṅ. "By giving in" in its lṛṭ line reads in as iṭ. Tibetan slips read by sense: sman pa for smon pa, "benedictive"; ’grel pa ra for ’grel par, "the commentary"; tsī for tsli, "cli"; ŚĀ su ri for śāsu ṛ in the repeated sūtra gloss; lit for lṛṭ before corayimyati; bzhun for bzhin. ṇaucasaṃśrāṅoḥ is evidently the sūtra ṇau ca saṃścaṅoḥ; its application follows in the next passage. Sanskrit forms are transliterated letter for letter as spelled, with b or v for the Tibetan letter ba according to the evident word; many carry evident slips that are kept, for example śvūyeyitā for śvāyayitā, śrāyayiṣyati for śvāyayiṣyati, astamhayata for astambhayat, baryasīṣivatāṃ for paryasīṣivatām, sevayiṅhuti for sevayiṣyati, vyasīṣatata for vyasīṣahat and cakīsayatu for cakāsayatu. The root heads stamvū and the stems savi and unī are likewise given as spelled, for stambhu, sevi and undi. The sūtra stambhusibusahāṃcadi is evidently stambhusivusahāṃ caṅi; the commentary citation subhātoranikācaścasanātkacidvā is evidently subdhātor anekācaś ca sanvat kvacid vā. Glosses of roots are rendered from the Tibetan: skri ba pa in the stambhu heading is read as sgrib pa, "obstructing," matching the gloss that follows; for ṣivu, thags kyi rgyu is "the warp of a weave," setting aside the house rendering "cause" for rgyu; for cakāsṛ the Tibetan gives sgra smad pa, "a contemptible sound," a common noun here, so the name Kutsa used elsewhere for smad pa does not apply. "Even though a prefix, the reason for changing s to ṣ, comes before" reads nyer bsgyur as upasarga, prefix; the stray syllables tsa na after it are left untranslated. Tibetan slips read by sense: sa pra sār nar for samprasāraṇar; ’dies for ’dis; satsli and tsī for tsli, "cli"; ’os ngos for ’os; ni bcar for ṇi tsang; zung du for thung ngu, "shortened"; ṇi tsha for ṇi tsa, "ṇic"; lit, lring and līṭ for lṛṭ; u bangdhā for upadhā; and a repeated "on a light syllable" in the ṣaha derivation is given once. In the ṣaha derivation the Tibetan cites the sūtra as "stambhu, śāsu, saha," which is translated as written though sivu is meant. In the undi derivation, "āṭ for an initial ac" reads a tsa dang po’i wa ṭa, and "by giving iṭ" reads in as iṭ. This is a section of a Sanskrit grammatical manual giving causative (ṇic) paradigms. ལུང here is the aorist tense luṅ, not "scripture"; རྐྱེན is a grammatical affix (pratyaya); མཐའ་ཅན means "ending in"; འགྲོ་བ glosses the root meaning "going" (gati). The Tibetan spells the root ubja as ubṅa and ubṅi, read here as ubja and ubji (Dhātupāṭha "ubja ārjave", hence "propriety"). Evident scribal slips corrected: ལ་སོགས་སྦྱང for ལཊ་སོགས་སྦྱར ("laṭ and the rest attached"); སྨོན་པའི་ལང for ལིང (benedictive liṅ); ཤ་ལམྦྷ་ཏ for alambhata; ཨཱ་ཧཱ་ལ་ཡི་ཥྱ་ཏ for ahāyayiṣyata; ཨཽ་བ་ཡཱི་ཏ for aunayīta. Other irregular forms are kept as written. The tense labels inserted among the forms in the drai, ḍulabhaṣ and hi paradigms look like interlinear glosses and are not always correct (for example "laṭ" before the imperative drāyayatu, "loṭ" before the optative lambhayeta); they are kept where they stand. The remarks on shortening the penultimate before caṅ (Pāṇini 7.4.1) stand after the benedictive forms in the Tibetan, though they bear on the aorist. The quoted sūtra on ūna and the others (Pāṇini 3.1.51) is badly spelled in the Tibetan and is given in its intelligible form; the syllable after dhvan, presumably its meaning "to sound," is unclear and is left out. A section of a Sanskrit grammatical manual giving causative (ṇic) paradigms; ལུང here is the aorist luṅ, not "scripture," and མདོ is a grammatical sūtra. The Tibetan spelling of the Sanskrit forms is often faulty; where a single letter is plainly a copyist's slip and the intended form is clear from the rest of the paradigm, the form is given as intended (for example dhvani for dhrani, the many ṅh for dh in the dhvana paradigm, dhvaniyati for dhvanilati, elayati for elayaṇi, ārdayiṣuḥ for ārdayimuḥ, ardyāta for ardyāha, smārayati for smārayataṃ, caṅ for caḍ, atatvaratāṃ for atadāratāṃ, and luṅ for the ལྲྀང that heads the tvara aorist). Other irregular forms are kept as written. The tense labels among the forms (such as "laṅ" before the imperative dārayatu) appear to be interlinear glosses and are kept where they stand. The rule on the reduplicate taking a (Pāṇini 7.4.95) is given in its intelligible form; the root glosses follow the Tibetan, which here renders the Dhātupāṭha meanings somewhat freely. A section of a Sanskrit grammatical manual giving causative (ṇic) paradigms; ལུང here is the aorist luṅ, not "scripture," and མདོ is a grammatical sūtra (in མདོས the ས is the instrumental "by the sūtra," not a thread-cross). "L-affixes" renders ལ་ཡིག, the tense and mood affixes beginning with l. The Tibetan spelling of the Sanskrit forms is often faulty; where a single letter is plainly a copyist's slip and the intended form is clear from the rest of the paradigm, the form is given as intended (for example mradayati for mradayañi, mradayiṣyati for mradayibyati, stārayitā for sarayitā, atastaratāṃ for atestaratāṃ, laṭ for the ལིཊ that introduces the stṛ paradigm, veṣṭayeta for veṣṭuyete, avaveṣṭatāṃ and avaveṣṭana for a repeated avaveṣṭata and aveṣṭana, veṣṭayiṣyati for veṣṭayiṣṭyati, bhāṣayati for bhrāṣayiti). Other irregular forms are kept as written, as are the tense labels placed among the forms, some of which are wrong (for example "liṅ" before the imperfect aspāśayata and "liṭ" before the future bhrājayiṣyati). The sūtras quoted in Sanskrit (Pāṇini 7.4.96 and 7.4.3) are given in their intelligible forms; the quoted lists follow the Tibetan in reading bhrāsa and pīṭa. The root glosses follow the Tibetan renderings. The stem བཱ་ཎི here is the causative stem bāṇi of the root baṇa, not the name Pāṇini. The Tibetan spelling of the Sanskrit forms is often faulty; where a letter is plainly a copyist's slip and the intended form is clear from the paradigm, the form is given as intended (for example amimīlata for a repeated amimilata, pīḍi for pīdri, apipiḍata for abibiḍata, loṭ for ལེཊ, bāṇayatu for a repeated bāṇayata, aluloṭhata for the garbled ཨ་ལིའོ་ཋ་ཏ, "sound" for སྦྲ, luṭha for ལུཊ). A duplicated benedictive entry (pīḍyāta) is given once. Other irregular forms and the misplaced tense labels (for example "liṭ" before pīḍayeta, "laṭ" before akāṇayata) are kept as they stand. For paṇa the Tibetan gives the meaning as the unclear syllable སྠ, evidently for "sound" as with dhvan earlier and as the list says of baṇa; the forms are of baṇa. The quoted rule extending 7.4.3 to kaṇa and the rest is given close to the Tibetan spelling; the root glosses follow the Tibetan renderings. A section of a Sanskrit grammatical manual giving causative (ṇic) paradigms. ལུང here is the aorist luṅ, not "scripture"; མདོ is a grammatical sūtra; ཉེ་བའི་ཡུལ renders upadeśa, the original enunciation of a root (Pāṇini 6.1.45), not a sense-object; ལས in ཥོ་མཐའི་ལས is "action" in the plain sense ("to end"); མཐའ is "end" in "ending in puk"; ཐགས་ཀྱི་རྒྱུ is the weaving of thread, not a cause. Evident copyists' slips are read as intended where the paradigm makes the form plain, for example hāpayatu for tāvayatu, ajahāpata for ajatāpata, mārjayati for mārjasayati, sāyayāṃcakāra for svayayāṃcakāra, ṇic for ཆི་ཙ, and སན ("as before san") for ལས་ན. In the ṣo paragraph the Tibetan reads "yuk not given," which contradicts the form sāyi and the parallel paragraphs; it is read as "the augment yuk is given." The gloss for pā, written བ་ཏྱང་བ, is read as བཏུང་བ "to drink." The sūtras quoted in Sanskrit (Pāṇini 7.4.7, 6.1.18, 7.3.37, 6.1.32) are given in intelligible form where the Tibetan spelling is garbled. Misplaced tense labels (for example "lṛṭ" before the imperative vartayatu, "liṅ" introducing the hvā aorist) are kept as they stand. A section of a Sanskrit grammatical manual giving causative (ṇic) paradigms. ལུང here is the aorist luṅ, not "scripture"; མདོ is a grammatical sūtra; མཐའ is "end" in "ending in puk"; སྒྲིབ་པ is the root meaning "to cover," not an obscuration. The Tibetan writes the root vlī and its forms with ཙླ (c), and knūy and its forms with ཀྲ (kr); these are read as vlī and knū, the roots of the Pāṇinian list "arti, hrī, vlī, rī, knūy, kṣmāy" (7.3.36). Other evident copyists' slips are read as intended where the paradigm makes the form plain (for example laṭ for ལྲཊ, vāyayati for vāyayihi, pāyi for bāyi, āṭ for ཨུཊ, "cease" for དོག, sthāpayiṣyati and asthāpayiṣyata for sthāpayaṣyati and asthābaṣyata, lṛṭ hvāyayiṣyati for hvāyayiṣyata); a duplicated lṛṭ entry for arpayiṣyati is given once. Other irregular forms (such as ārpata and acakṣmāpata) and misplaced tense labels (such as "lṛṅ" before hrepayeta) are kept as they stand. For rīṅ the Tibetan gloss is "hearing," apparently taking the Dhātupāṭha's śravaṇa ("oozing") in its other sense; for ghrā it gives only "taking up," the Dhātupāṭha having "taking up a smell." The sūtras quoted in Sanskrit (Pāṇini 7.4.4, 7.4.5, 7.4.6) are given in intelligible form. A section of a Sanskrit grammatical manual giving causative (ṇic) paradigms and the rules for special causative stems (Pāṇini 7.3.37 to 7.3.40, 6.1.51 to 6.1.57, 1.3.68 and 1.3.70, with vārttikas). ལུང here is the aorist luṅ, and ལུང་དྲངས་པ "cites" a quotation; རྐྱེན is a grammatical affix; གཟུགས is the grammatical form; ཏང are the taṅ (ātmanepada) endings. The root of pāli is glossed སྦྱོང་བ, read as སྐྱོང་བ "to protect" (pā rakṣaṇe); the root of vāji is written པཱ but the rule quoted (vo vidhūnane juk) shows it is vā. Evident copyists' slips in the forms are read as intended where the paradigm makes them plain (for example ajaghrapata for ajagrapata, vāpayati for vāvayati, prīṇayatu for prīṇayitu, dhāvayāṃcakāra for dhāpayīcakāra, bhāpayate for bapayate). Other irregular forms (such as aprīṇata, abhiṣata) and misplaced tense labels (such as "lṛṭ" before vājayāṃcakāra, "luṭ" before aorist forms) are kept as they stand. The Sanskrit sūtras and vārttikas are given in intelligible form where the Tibetan spelling is garbled. The Tibetan glosses of the vārttika on lī render pralambhana ("deceiving"), abhibhava ("overpowering") and pūjā as "destruction, prior occurrence, and worship"; the translation follows the Tibetan. Its gloss of the first lī as "to become small" likewise follows the Tibetan. The Tibetan sentences explaining the three ātmanepada examples (honor by matted locks, the hawk and the quail, "who wishes to obtain you") stand after the bhī rule in the source and are translated where they stand. A section of a Sanskrit grammatical manual on special causative stems (Pāṇini 7.3.41 to 7.3.43, 6.1.48 to 6.1.54, 2.4.51). ལུང here is the aorist luṅ; མདོ is a grammatical sūtra; མཐའ is "end"; དཔེར་བརྗོད is a grammatical illustration; རྒྱལ་བ in "ji, to conquer" and རྒྱལ་པོ "king" are ordinary words, not the epithet Jina; ཀུ་རུ in the example "guruḥ sedhayati" is the word guru, as the Tibetan gloss བླ་མ "teacher" shows, not the Kurus. The Tibetan glosses of the two śad examples ("he makes the fruits fall," "the cowherd drives the cows") are displaced in the source into the middle of the form ropayatu; they are given here after the examples they translate. The gloss for the fruits reads literally "makes the fruits cover [the ground]." The root meaning of śadḷ is written འཇིགས་པ "fearing," read as འཇིག་པ "perishing" (śātana). A section of a Sanskrit grammatical manual on special causative stems (Pāṇini 6.1.55, 7.4.80, 7.4.81, 6.4.89, 6.4.90). ལུང here is the aorist luṅ; ཉེ་བའི་ཡུལ renders upadeśa, the original enunciation of a root, not a sense-object; སྒྲིབ་པ is the root meaning "to cover," not an obscuration; ཉོན་མོངས་པ glosses duṣ, "to become corrupt." Root names are read from the forms where the Tibetan headword is miswritten: ṣṭuñ "to praise" for ཥཱུ་ཉ་བ, ju for ཛི, and cyuṅ for བྱུང (as with vlī earlier, this scribe confuses ཙ and བ; the forms are written byāvayati and so on). A section of a Sanskrit grammatical manual on special causative stems (Pāṇini 6.4.90 to 6.4.92, the Dhātupāṭha's notes on "mit" roots, and related vārttikas). ལུང here is the aorist luṅ, and ལུང་དྲངས་པ "cites"; མདོ is a grammatical sūtra; མཐའ is "end, ending in"; དཔེར་བརྗོད is a grammatical illustration. The Tibetan མ་འགྲོ་བ renders "mit," a root marked with m, rendering the marker term "it" literally as "going." The Tibetan glosses of the three jña examples ("he wishes his foes to die," "he wishes the kings to be pleased," "he wishes to make the weapon very sharp") are displaced in the source into the middle of the gloss on the jvala rule; they are given here after the examples they translate. In them ཟླ་བོ is "foes, rivals," not the moon, and མྱེ་ལ་པོ is read as རྒྱལ་པོ "kings." The rañja vārttika's mṛgaramaṇa ("sport with deer") is glossed in the Tibetan as "the color of deer," which the translation follows. Evident copyists' slips are read as intended where the paradigm makes them plain (for example ghaṭa for dhaṭa, ghaṭyāta for ghanyāta, dūṣayati for dūṣayiti, "trembling" for the stray དགའ in the vyatha headword, "dyeing" for ཆིས, ajījanata and ajanayiṣyata for ajījanate and ajaniṣyata, jaryāta for jarlāta, knasayitā for knanasayitā, jñapi and jñapayeta for jhavi and jñipayeta, jvalayeta and ajījvalata for jālayeta and ajījvayata, glapayati for glāvayati, luṅ for ཕུད, ṭuvama for thuvama); a repeated clause "ṇic is attached to knasi" is given once. Other irregular forms and the misplaced tense labels (such as "luṅ" before ajñapayata) are kept as they stand. The Sanskrit rules are given in intelligible form where the Tibetan spelling is garbled. A section of a Sanskrit grammatical manual on special causative stems (the Dhātupāṭha's notes on "mit" roots, Pāṇini 2.4.46, 7.3.32, 7.3.54, and a vārttika on īrṣya). ལུང here is the aorist luṅ, and ལུང་དྲངས་པ / ལུང་འདྲེན "cites, citation"; རྐྱེན is a grammatical affix; མཐའ is "end, ending in"; མདོ is a grammatical sūtra. ཉེ་བར་ཞི་བ glosses śamu, "to become calm," and is not the name Śiva. The designation "marked with m" (mit) is written in several slipped forms (ལམ་འགྲོ་བ, ནམ་འགྲོ་བ, འམ་འགྲོ་བ, and simply འགྲོ་བའི་མིང་ཅན); all are read as "marked with m," and ལམ there is not "the path." Evident copyists' slips are read as intended where the paradigm makes them plain (for example kāmayitā for kāmalitā, akāmayiṣyata for akāmayisyati, aśamayata for aśamayatu, apīphaṇata for abīphaṇata, praphāṇayati for a repeated praphaṇayati, ghātayati for ghātayata, gami's ga for ནག་རུ, āyi formed for ཁྲུ་བ་པ, īrṣyayatu for īrṣyāyatu). The glosses ཉེ་བར་ནི་བ for yamu and the unclear སྑ for phaṇa are read as "to cease" and "sound." Other irregular forms (such as ayāṃyamata, acīskhadata, āyayata, airṣiṣyata) and misplaced tense labels (such as "laṅ" before kāmayeta and īrṣyayati, "liṅ" before aśīśamata) are kept as they stand. The Sanskrit rules are given in intelligible form where the Tibetan spelling is garbled. This piece closes the manual's section on causatives (ṇic) with a Sanskrit colophon line and its Tibetan rendering, then opens the section on desideratives (san), Pāṇini 3.1.7. The Sanskrit colophon is garbled in the Tibetan script and is given in intelligible form. The title of the notes, ལེགས་བཤད་ནོར་བུའི་དྲན་པའི་ཤིང་རྟ, is translated; དྲན་པ here is recollection, rendered with the house term "mindful." A stray grammatical remark (ཧ་ལ་ལས་ཡས་རྣམས་ཀྱི་ཡམ་ལང་དྱྀ་འོས་ཡ་གོང་མ་ཕྱིས, the rule "halo yamāṃ yami lopaḥ") stands inside the closing sentence in the source; it is translated after it. ཙ་ར here is the grammatical class car, not a name; ལུང is the aorist luṅ; རྐྱེན is a grammatical affix; གཟུགས is the grammatical form; ཡུལ is the domain of application; "marked with k" renders ཀ་འགྲོ་བ (kit). A stray fragment བར་འདོད ("wishes to") interrupts the liṭ forms of ad and is left out of the body. Evident copyists' slips are read as intended where the paradigm makes them plain (for example san for རྣ, didīṣate for didaṣete, didāsatāṃ for didāsatī, ucicchiṣa for ucicchaṣa, aucicchiṣīta for aucicchitīta, "to recite" for གློག, didyotiṣate for dodyotiṣate, adhijigāpayiṣati for adhyajigāpayiṣati in the present). Duplicated forms (a second adidāsiṣyata) are given once, and the paired kit and guṇa forms of dyut are set side by side. Other irregular forms are kept as written. The Sanskrit rules are given in intelligible form where the Tibetan spelling is garbled. A section of a Sanskrit grammatical manual on desiderative (san) stems (Pāṇini 6.1.31, 8.4.21, 1.2.9 and 1.2.10, 7.2.41, 7.2.57 and 7.2.59, 6.4.16, 7.1.100 to 7.1.102). ལུང here is the aorist luṅ; ཉེ་བའི་ཡུལ is upadeśa, the original enunciation; ཏང are the taṅ (ātmanepada) endings and ཨ་ཏང the non-taṅ (parasmaipada) endings; "marked with k" renders ཀ་འགྲོ་བ (kit). In བྲྀ་ཏ་རྣམས་ལས་བཞི the phrase ལས་བཞི is "from the four" (the rule "na vṛdbhyaś caturbhyaḥ"), not the four ritual activities; རྒྱུ་མཚན is the cause (nimitta) of the change to ṇ, not a major mark. The illustration of the ṇ rule is written སྭཱ་ནི་ནི་ཥ་ཏི in the Tibetan and is read as prāṇiṇiṣati, the form the rule produces. Evident copyists' slips are read as intended where the paradigm makes them plain (for example aśiśvayayiṣīta for aśiśvalayiṣīta, juhāvayiṣa for jusāvayiṣa, juhāvayiṣiṣyati for juhāvayiṣiṣyatu, vivṛtseta for vivṛtsita, vivartiṣeta and vivartiṣatāṃ for the garbled forms, titīrṣitā and titīrṣyāta for titīrṣītrā and titīrṣaṣyata, bubūrṣa and bubūrṣati for budūrṣa and bubūbūrṣata, vivariṣati for vivirṣata, san for ན and ས་ནས, ninṛtsiṣyati for the first lṛṭ form written ninartiṣyati). The paired forms without and with iṭ for nṛt are set side by side. Other irregular forms (such as śiśvayayiṣati, aśuśavayiṣīta, vivartiṣīṣṭa) are kept as written. The Sanskrit rules are given in intelligible form where the Tibetan spelling is garbled. Evident scribal slips in the Sanskrit forms have been normalized (for example saṃciskīrṣati for "saṃciskerṣati," jigīṣati for "jigaṃti," jighāṃsati for "jibhānsati," īrṣyiṣiṣati for "īrṣyimati," bubhūṣa for "bughāṣa"), and the long ī of the desideratives of ji and ci is restored. The text writes the desiderative of dhṛ with iṭ as didhāriṣati and that of iṇ as jigāmiṣati with a long ā; the latter is kept as written. The note "by abhyāsāc ca, gh," which stands after the laṭ form of han, has been moved into the derivation it explains. The text labels the second form of iṇ (jigāmiṣeta, the optative) as liṭ and omits the lṛṅ label before ajigāmiṣiṣyata; these are left as they stand. The laṅ and luṅ forms of prati with iṇ, written aprataiṣiṣata and apratiṣiṣīta, are given in their regular forms. In the rule for dhṛ the Tibetan reads "not preceded by a labial"; the standard rule (ud oṣṭhyapūrvasya) concerns a ṛ preceded by a labial. Glossary terms are adjusted to the grammatical context: the verb glossed as "Victor" here means "to conquer" (ji), "mindfulness" here means "to remember" (ik), "obscuration" here means "to cover" (guhū), and the glossary's "thread-cross" here is simply "sūtra." The root dhṛ is written in the Tibetan in a garbled form; its identification rests on the derived forms. Evident scribal slips in the Sanskrit forms have been normalized (for example suṣupsāṃcakāra for "asuṣupsāṃcakāra," pipaviṣa for "popaviṣa," añjijiṣati for the laṭ form written with the luṅ ending, adidariṣiṣṭa for "adidariṣiṣū," pipṛcchiṣa for "pipṛcchaṣa," ardidhiṣa for "ajidhiṣa," laṭ for "phaṭ," and īrtsīta, īrtsitā, and īrtsyāta for forms written with the vowels confused). In the last paradigm the text labels the loṭ form īrtsatu as laṭ and gives īrtsāṃcakāra without its liṭ label; these are left as they stand. The second of the five roots in the rule "kiraś ca pañcabhyaḥ" is written in a garbled form in the Tibetan; it is given here as dhṛṅ on the strength of the forms didhariṣate and so on that follow. In the gloss on "āpjñapyṛdhām īt," the Tibetan gloss of jñā is garbled; "to make known" follows the causative jñapi named in the rule. The Tibetan word that the name list renders as Diti here means "to give" (ṣaṇa), and the syllables rendered elsewhere as Cara here name the substitute car; neither is a proper name in this passage. Likewise the glossary's "thread-cross" here is simply "sūtra." This is a section of a Tibetan manual of Sanskrit grammar deriving desiderative (san) stems with and without the augment iṭ; the Sanskrit forms are given as the Tibetan spells them, including evident miswritings (for example the labels laṭ and liṅ placed before forms of other tenses). The rule cited as "ut where a labial precedes" reads in the Tibetan as "not preceded by a labial," which contradicts both the Pāṇinian rule (udoṣṭhyapūrvasya) and the forms derived from it; the evident sense is translated. The Tibetan glosses of some roots are unusual: "to perish" for śṛ and "to bestow" for ṣaṇa are tentative. Several copyist slips are read by their evident sense: ལས་ན for ལ་སན ("san is attached"), ན་པ for སན་ལ, ཌུབྷཱ་ཏ for ḍudhāñ, ར་བ and བ་ཏླྀ for rabh and patḷ, དཱ་དྷ for rādh, གྲོ་བ for གྲོལ་བ ("to release"), and ཨུ་ར for ཨུ་ཨིར ("u to i"). The tense labels ལོཊ (under dhā), ལཊ (the third form under śak) and ལུཊ (under pū) are rendered as liṭ, liṭ and luṅ to match the forms. The Tibetan gloss on the muc rule (མུ་ཙའི་ལ་སམ། སོ་སོར་འཚེ་བར་འདོད།) is garbled and is rendered by its evident sense, "when it takes no object." A few copyist slips are read by their evident sense: ཨཊ for iṭ (under ṇu), the label ལིང for luṅ (under sru, where the form has the augment a), ཏཾ་ཏི for stauti, ཉི་ཥྭ་ད for ñiṣvid, སྭ་དིས་ཧ for svadi and sah, and the rule ཨ་ཏི་དུ for "changed to i" (under svad), matching the parallel wording under sah. The root under svad's reduplication reads གཉིས་བརྗོད་པ་ཕྱིས, taken as "reduplicated, and v is dropped," as with svid. In "the abhyāsa iṇ," ཨིན is read as the pratyāhāra iṇ. Here སྨད་པ is the grammatical sense "contempt" (garhā), not a personal name. Several copyist slips are read by their evident sense: སྭུ་ཙ for sūc; the label ལིཊ for loṭ (under sūc), ལིང for laṅ (under mūtr and aś), and the first ལང for liṅ (under ūrṇu); ཡང་ཕྱིས for "yaṅ is attached" (under aś); ཨཊ for at (under ūrṇu); and གྷུ་བུ་ཉ and ཌུ་རྷཱ་ཉ for ḍudāñ and ḍudhāñ. A few copyist slips are read by their evident sense: ཐ་ཐར as "th to ṭh" (under ṣṭhā), ཨཱ་ཨཱཾ as "ā to ī" (under ohāk), ཀྱི་སར as "r is dropped" (under vraj), མཉྩུ as vañcu and ལ་དླྀ as patḷ (under the nīk rule). In this grammar ནང (literally "inner") names the anusvāra. This is a Sanskrit grammatical treatise on intensive (yaṅ) formations; the paradigm forms are given as the Tibetan spells them, including evident slips (for example bābhūmitā, didahyato, jikhanīcakre). In the bhāma section the Tibetan reads that nuk does not occur "if the penultimate is at (short a)"; the sense and the forms require long ā, so long ā is translated. In the jana section the change is written as "at" but the forms and the parallel ṣana section show ā. The root written "cola" is evidently cala (the forms are cañcal-), "btvañju" is evidently bhañju, and in the list of roots paśa is glossed "to explain" where the following paradigm reads "to bind," which is evidently intended. The quoted rule says "ending in the letter cha" where ca is evidently meant. The phrase translated "before san and yaṅ" reads the obscure Tibetan as Pāṇini's sanyaṅoḥ (reduplication before san and yaṅ). This section of the grammatical notes closes the treatment of intensive (yaṅ) stems and opens that of the elided intensive (yaṅluk). Paradigm forms and roots are given as the Tibetan spells them, including evident scribal slips; in the byeña paradigm the last form is labeled laṭ in the Tibetan but is plainly the liṭ, and is so labeled here. The root written ghādri is evidently ghrā, and dhyā in the following section is evidently dhmā, as the glosses on the quoted sūtra show. The persons follow Indian grammatical usage: the "first person" (prathama puruṣa) corresponds to the English third person, and the "last person" (uttama) to the English first. Paradigm forms are given as the Tibetan spells them, including evident slips. The clauses about jhi becoming jus (and guṇa before jus) in the liṭ discussions appear to be displaced glosses and are translated where they stand, in parentheses. The vañcu paradigm labeled liṭ in the Tibetan has optative forms and is given as liṅ. "Vṛddhi in the two singular endings" interprets an unclear phrase (literally "the two ca pa"). After the gamḷ dual rule the edition shows an empty bracket where the dual form would stand; no form is supplied. Paradigm forms are given as the Tibetan spells them, including evident scribal slips. In the hana section the rule changing h to gh is written as "at after a reduplicated stem," evidently a slip for the rule "also after the abhyāsa," which is translated. Paradigm forms are given as the Tibetan spells them, including evident scribal slips. The Tibetan introduces the second cited rule with a word that is evidently "scripture" (that is, a quotation from the commentary) miswritten. Paradigm forms are given as the Tibetan spells them, including evident scribal slips. In the loṭ of yoyu the heading for the three forms of the last person is absent in the Tibetan, and the forms simply follow. Paradigm forms are given as the Tibetan spells them, including evident scribal slips. The note "jhi becoming jus" appears out of place in two sentences, apparently a displaced gloss, and is kept in parentheses where it stands. The Tibetan renders ārdhadhātuka literally as "half-root." This passage closes the section on the elided intensive and opens the section on denominative verbs formed with kyac. Paradigm forms are given as the Tibetan spells them, including evident slips (for example ṅ where d is expected in tvaṅya, maṅyati, yuṣmaṅyati and samiṅgha). The Sanskrit closing line of the yaṅluk section is broken up by interpolated Tibetan grammatical notes, which are kept in parentheses where they stand. Short Tibetan glosses on the meanings of the denominatives (such as "one wishes for a son") are interspersed in the paradigms, sometimes displaced from the form they explain; they are likewise kept in parentheses where they stand. This passage treats denominative suffixes (kyac, kāmyac, kyaṅ, kvip). Paradigm forms and the Sanskrit examples are given as the Tibetan spells them, including evident slips. Many short Tibetan glosses on the meanings of the examples ("one wishes for curd," "the she-camel desires salt," "the weakling fancies himself strong," and so on) are interspersed in the text, often displaced from the example they explain; they are kept in parentheses where they stand. The gloss after udanya reads literally "wishes for tho," taken here as a slip for drinking; the gloss "one wishes for asu" is left as written. Denominative suffixes (kyaṅ, kyaṣ, kyac) in their special senses. Sanskrit examples and forms are given as the Tibetan spells them, including evident slips. The short Tibetan glosses on the examples are kept in parentheses. In the lists of the bhṛśa and sukha groups several Tibetan glosses are obscure; "excrement" appears between phena and harita without a Sanskrit headword, and the glosses for tṛpra and kṛpaṇa (including the unclear "seng sna") are rendered as literally as possible. The gloss on satrāyate is read as "in deceit," and that on kaṇṭhāyate as "makes it thin," both tentatively. This passage treats kyaṅ in special senses and then the denominative causal suffix ṇic. Forms are given as the Tibetan spells them, including evident slips; several tense labels are miswritten in the Tibetan (for example leṭ for liṭ) and are given as the intended tenses. The Tibetan glosses on the meanings of the examples are kept in parentheses. Some glosses are obscure: those on vrata, kṛta and tūsta in the list of the muṇḍa group are rendered tentatively; the gloss on pāśayati is read as "snare" and that on senā as "army," each correcting a one-letter slip; the gloss on tvaca ("eight hands") is left literal. The remark about artha refers back to an earlier citation that is not identifiable from this piece. This passage treats denominative causatives with ṇic (with the substitutions of the iṣṭhan section) and the yak denominatives of the kaṇḍū group. Forms are given as the Tibetan spells them, including evident slips; in the bandha paradigm, where the Tibetan writes ṅ for d, the forms are given in their evident reading. Many short Tibetan glosses on the meanings of the stems are interspersed, often displaced from the word they explain; they are kept in parentheses where they stand. Several glosses in the kaṇḍū list are obscure and rendered tentatively. This passage closes the section on nominal roots and opens the section on the voice (parasmaipada or ātmanepada) taken by roots with particular prefixes. Forms are given as the Tibetan spells them, including evident slips. The many short Tibetan glosses on the meanings of words are interspersed in the text, often displaced from the words they explain (for example, glosses on the kaṇḍū list and on the causatives of pā, dam and the rest appear before or after the wrong items); they are kept in parentheses where they stand. This passage continues the rules on which voice (parasmaipada or ātmanepada) roots take with particular prefixes. The opening sentence says the parasmaipada endings do not occur, although its examples show parasmaipada forms and the rule concerned denies the ātmanepada; the Tibetan is translated as written. Forms and Sanskrit examples are given as the Tibetan spells them, including evident slips. Many short Tibetan glosses on the meanings of the examples are interspersed, often displaced from the words they explain; they are kept in parentheses where they stand. Displaced interlinear glosses are kept in parentheses where they stand in the block print; several belong to examples given elsewhere (for instance "a wrestler challenges a wrestler" belongs to mallo mallamāhvayate, "Viṣṇu's might over you asuras" to daiṅyān abhikurute biṣṇuḥ, "the brahmin chants the notes" to svarān bikurute bipraḥ, "Vāyu acts in various ways" to bāyurbakurute, and "one subdues anger" to kroṅhaṃ binayate). The Sanskrit examples are badly garbled and are given as spelled. "Acting together" reflects the Tibetan reading of sāhasikya, and "capability" its rendering of prahasana. "Śaṅ is lost" probably means the loss of the vikaraṇa śap in the hu class. Here མཁས་པ is the ordinary word "learned one" (glossing prajñe), not the name Dakṣa. This is a Tibetan commentary on the Kalāpa rules for the ātmanepada (taṅ) endings. The Tibetan text interleaves short interlinear glosses (Tibetan renderings of the Sanskrit examples) at points that often do not match the example they explain; these are given in parentheses where they stand in the Tibetan, moved only to the nearest phrase boundary. The Sanskrit rule headings and examples are romanized as the Tibetan spells them, without correction. In the vipralāpa rule, the phrase rendered "taṅ and e-taṅ are made optional" is obscure as written; the examples show that the taṅ endings are optional there. In the upayam rule, "the m is deleted" reads the Tibetan ma phyis as the letter m being elided (yam becoming ya in upāyata); "simply carried through" for the non-kit alternative is a tentative rendering. The isolated note "of that which is not preceded by a labial" appears to be a marginal grammatical remark, probably connected with the labial rule behind susmūrṣate. As in the preceding pieces, short interlinear glosses translating the Sanskrit examples are interleaved in the Tibetan, often away from the examples they explain; they are given in parentheses where they stand. The Sanskrit rules and examples are romanized as the Tibetan spells them. Some evident slips are read in their obvious sense: ཏ་པ་རྣམས as the taṅ endings; the gloss འཆོད་པར་བྱེད as འཚོད, "one cooks" (for pacate); སྲུ་བར་བྱེད as སླུ, "deceives"; མཆོག་སྦྱིན as མཆོད་སྦྱིན, "sacrifice"; and ཕྱིན་པས as བྱིན་པས, "given". The Tibetan renders pralambhana (deceiving) literally as "thorough obtaining," and this is kept. "First person" follows the Indian convention, in which the first person (prathamapuruṣa) is the Western third person. The particle འོས after a quoted rule is read as "by the rule ...". The statement that the dual and plural liṭ forms occur "if a preverb is not placed before" stands as written, though the surrounding argument would lead one to expect "if a preverb is placed before." This piece gives the impersonal and passive (bhāva and karman) paradigms of a series of roots, with the Sanskrit forms romanized as the Tibetan spells them; tense labels are kept as written even where a label and its form do not match (for example "liṭ janyeta," "lṛṅ taniṣyate"). The quoted rule names are given by their opening words, as the text cites them. A few evident slips are read in their obvious sense: སྤྱང as སྦྱར ("add"), སི་པྲ་སཱར་ཎ as saṃprasāraṇa, and ཥཊུ་ལ་བཅུ as the rule "ṣṭu with ṣṭu" (ṣṭunā ṣṭuḥ). The paradigm forms and tense labels are romanized and kept as the Tibetan writes them, even where a label does not match its form (for example "laṭ hanyatā" where loṭ is meant, and "benedictive" written as སྨོན་ལུང). Obvious slips such as ལག་མ for ལྷག་མ ("the remaining ones"), སྨིན for སྨོན ("benedictive") and ལྲིང for ལིང are read in their evident sense. In the rule for labha, the Tibetan ལ་བྷ་ལ is read as "for labha." The Sanskrit rules, examples and the Sanskrit verse are romanized as the Tibetan spells them. In the Tibetan rendering of the verse, the second line reads "growth, excellence, perishing, and living," which does not match the Sanskrit list (growth, decline, fear, living, death) item for item; it is translated as it stands. The words "one adorns" inside the verse are an interlinear gloss (on taṃsate), left where they stand. In the rule "not with yat," the Tibetan reads "happened today" (དེ་རིང་བ་ཡིན་པ); this is read as "not today" (དེ་རིང་མ་ཡིན་པ), as in the preceding rule, since the rule concerns the non-today past. The "twelve categories" are as the text counts them. This piece treats the uses of the tense affixes. As before, many short interlinear glosses (Tibetan renderings of the Sanskrit examples, or brief grammatical remarks) are interleaved in the Tibetan, often away from the example they explain; they are given in parentheses where they stand. Sanskrit rules and examples are romanized as the Tibetan spells them, and the text's tense labels are kept even where they seem displaced (for example lṛṭ for liṭ in the sma rule, and liṅ for laṅ in the ha and śaśvat rule). The gloss "I do not go to the Kali age" reflects the Tibetan translator's rendering of Kaliṅga as rtsod ldan, the Age of Strife. The phrase rendered "the separate particles na and nu" is literally "the unexhausted na and nu." The gloss "done in the former time of Viṣṇu" (khyab bdag) and the gloss "I did it by turns" are uncertain in sense. Evident slips read in their obvious sense: མ་ཕྱོགས་པ as མགྱོགས་པ ("quickly"), རྵཱ་ཏུ as jātu, and ཀ་ཐི as katham. As in the preceding pieces, short interlinear glosses translating the Sanskrit examples are interleaved in the Tibetan, often away from the example they explain; they are given in parentheses where they stand. Sanskrit rules and examples are romanized as the Tibetan spells them. In the alam rule, the Tibetan explanation says that liṅ "does not occur" (ལིང་མི་འགྱུར), although the rule as usually understood prescribes liṅ there; the negation is kept as written. The gloss མ་གོས is read as མགོས, "with his head," and ཀྲཾཏ as kṛt. The glosses "Please protect my work" and "Come as you wish" (ཁྱོད་འདོད་པ་འབྱོད) are uncertain in sense. "Śūdra" renders དམངས་རིགས, the lowest of the four classes. This piece closes the section on verbal conjugation (ākhyāta, Tibetan ཀུན་བཤད) and opens the section on the kṛt affixes that form nouns from roots. The Sanskrit verse, rules and examples are romanized as the Tibetan spells them. The commentary named here is that of Rāmacandra, presumably the Prakriyākaumudī. "The ten groups, laṭ and the rest, or the hundred and eighty, ti and the rest" refers to the ten tense-mood sets and their eighteen endings each. As before, a few interlinear glosses stand in parentheses where they occur. བྱེད་ས in the first rule is read as "a root," and ཉེད་བསྒྱུར as ཉེར་བསྒྱུར, "preverb." This piece continues the kṛt affixes, chiefly the gerundives in anīyar, yat and ṇyat. As before, short interlinear glosses translating the Sanskrit examples are interleaved in the Tibetan and given in parentheses where they stand; the Sanskrit rules and forms are romanized as the Tibetan spells them. ཚིག་ཕྲད is rendered "set form (nipāta)," for forms the grammar gives as fixed. ཨ་ནའི་ཡར is read as anīyar, ཨིཏ་འགོ་བ as "having i as its marker," and བཅོད་བྱ as བཙོང་བྱ, "to be sold." The gloss "a line, that is, without prose" is uncertain in sense. This piece continues the gerundive affixes ṇyat, yat and kyap. As in the preceding pieces, short interlinear glosses translating the Sanskrit examples are interleaved in the Tibetan and are given in parentheses where they stand; the Sanskrit rules and forms are romanized as the Tibetan spells them. In the āvaśyaka rule the Tibetan uses ལྷག་པར ("especially") for "necessity." ཚིག་ཕྲད is rendered "set form," and ཡམ་ཤིང "kindling sticks" (sāmidhenī). The gloss ཙོར་ appears to be the Sanskrit cora, "thief," which the next gloss translates. Some glosses are uncertain in sense, notably "mad," "illness" (ན་དབ), and "Śiva drinks" (ཞི་བ་འཐུང), given as written. རྟྱཏ is read as ṇyat. This piece continues the gerundive affix kyap. As in the preceding pieces, short interlinear glosses translating the Sanskrit examples are interleaved in the Tibetan and are given in parentheses where they stand; the Sanskrit rules and forms are romanized as the Tibetan spells them. ཚིག་ཕྲད is rendered "set form." In the bhṛñ rule, both clauses read "when it is not a name," although the form bhāryā is the one used as a name; the negation is kept as written, and an obscure word (ཟག་གི) before "name" is not rendered. The gloss རྒྱལ is the Tibetan name of the lunar mansion Puṣya. "Metrical language" renders སྡེབ་སྦྱོར (chandas, the Vedic idiom). This piece ends the section on the kṛt affixes in the sense of the state and the object and begins the affixes in the sense of the agent (ṇvul, tṛc, lyu, ṇini, ac, ka). As in the preceding pieces, short interlinear glosses translating the Sanskrit examples are interleaved in the Tibetan and are given in parentheses where they stand; the Sanskrit rules and forms are romanized as the Tibetan spells them. In the quoted rule on praiṣa and the rest, the Tibetan renders atisarga as "birth" (སྐྱེ་བ), and this is kept. ཚིག་ཕྲད is rendered "set form." The gloss ཀྱུ་བྱེད and the phrase "the c serves for distinction" (ཙ་ཁྱད་དོན) are uncertain. The gloss "god" renders ལྷ, glossing devaḥ. Throughout the passage short glosses are interleaved with the running text, mostly giving the meaning of the forms just cited or about to be cited. They are kept in parentheses where they stand. The glosses "one who goes about at night" and "growth" in the first section seem to have strayed from the preceding discussion of rātri and from a word for vṛddhi. The glosses "a measure; good giver; wisdom; direct knowledge" match prastha (a measure), suda, prajña and abhijña. The glosses after the dadāti rule match limpa, vinda, dhāraya, pāraya, vedaya, udejaya, cetaya, sātaya and sāhaya. The glosses in the dunyor section match the ṇa forms listed just before them, with "frost" for avaśyāya. The glosses in the śilpini section belong to grāha and graha, and those in the prusṛlvaḥ section belong to hāyana. The one obscure gloss after the first grahaḥ could not be construed. Evident slips in the forms, kept as written: in the limpa list, pedayaḥ stands for vedayaḥ and catayaḥ for cetayaḥ, and dhārayaḥ is missing. Jalaḥ stands for jvalaḥ, and pyādhaḥ for vyādhaḥ. Āśvābaḥ stands for āśrāvaḥ, and tajakaḥ for rajakaḥ. The first grahaḥ under vibhāṣā grahaḥ should be grāhaḥ, and bhūhiḥ stands for bhūtiḥ. The Tibetan writes ṇyut once for ṇyuṭ. In the jvalādi section the end of the list is written kab; Pāṇini's list ends at kas. In the samabhihāra rule the text glosses samabhihāra as "equal doing," and this is rendered here as "repeated action." The rule cited as "not in the domain near where ś goes" is a literal rendering of the Tibetan for the rule that changes ec to ā in the root list, but not before a śit affix. The root khanu is glossed "destroying" in the text, and hṛñ "harming"; both are kept as written. Where the text says an affix's n "serves the vowel," the wording is kept; it seems to refer to the accent purpose of the marker. As in the preceding passages, many short Tibetan glosses are interleaved with the running text. They are kept in parentheses where they stand. Most of them give the meaning of forms cited just before or just after them. "Prosperity" and "birth" refer to bhūti and sūta. The long list of "dwelling in..." glosses refers to the ṣṭha forms: the peg is śaṅku, the thumb aṅgu, madder mañji, the peacock barhi, and the gods divi. The holder list refers to śaktigraha and the rest. "Lies in the sky" and "lies on the chest" refer to khaśaya and udaraśaya. The fragment "spoken from the mouth; the supreme ear's ..." is garbled and its reference is unclear. Several slips are kept as written. Yaṃtiḥ, baṃtiḥ and taṃtiḥ are written with anusvāra and b for yantiḥ, vantiḥ and tantiḥ. Sayiḥ stands for satiḥ, kanpaladaḥ for kambaladaḥ, daṭigrahaḥ for ghaṭīgrahaḥ, and baktragaḥ probably for vaktragaḥ. Samagaḥ stands for sāmagaḥ, sūrapaḥ for surāpaḥ, śidhupaḥ for śīdhupaḥ, and bidyāśaskaraḥ for vidyā yaśaskaraḥ. In the ṣṭha list, śaṅku and mañji have no form; amāṣṭhaḥ and āmāṣṭhaḥ stand for ambaṣṭhaḥ and āmbaṣṭhaḥ; and dvi and tri appear where the sūtra list has them. The sūtra under puraḥ and the rest gives the affix as "laṭ," a slip for ṭa. "Ngan ngag" is read as "ngan dag," "grief." The rule label "prade jñaḥ" follows the Tibetan spelling, which is corrupt. The gloss "giver of curds" does not match kambalada, a blanket giver. In "plough holder" the Tibetan has an evident slip. Hṛñ is glossed "harming," as elsewhere in this text. This is a Tibetan explanation of Pāṇinian sūtras on kṛt affixes and the mum augment. Short Tibetan glosses on the example words (for instance "one who makes faith", "breast-drinker", "vein-breaker") have been copied into the running text, often away from the words they explain and sometimes in the middle of a sūtra (between hara and teḥ, between bahā and bhrilihaḥ, between la and lāṭa); they are translated where they stand, in parentheses, and the split words kūla and lalāṭa are given whole. Some spellings are evident slips and are translated as the intended words: རྣམ་ན for karman, ཀྡུ་ལ and དུ་ཛི for kūla and ruji, པརླ for བརླ "thigh". A few glosses are obscure and rendered literally: བུས་པ (taken as "portion", for bhakti), བེའུའམ་མ་ཧེས་གཤིན་པ ("a calf, or what a buffalo has left"), བགས་ལྡན་གྱི་རི་དགས ("the wild animal with a hide"), འདམ་སེང ("marsh lion"), ལྷང་ཚེར ("thistle"), and རིགས་ཤིན་ཏུ་ནད་ཅན / རིགས་མཐོ་ཐོབ་པ. As in the preceding pieces, short Tibetan glosses on example words have been copied into the running text, often away from the words they explain and sometimes inside a sūtra or a word (between lakṣaṇejā and yāpatyoṣṭaka, inside bhayaṃkaraḥ, madruṃkaraḥ and the Tibetan for "state"); they are translated in parentheses where they stand. Evident slips are translated as intended: པ་པ for para, པ་ཡི for pati, སརྦ་ལས་ཧ for sarba with saha, འགྲེལ་བ་ར for "in the commentary". A few glosses are obscure and given literally: ཕྱེད་བསྟེ་ཁག་བ ("halved and divided"), ལག་པ་ཞིབ ("hand-scrutinizer"), སྔོན་བཟོད ("forbearing first"), and the two glosses with "eighty". The text says "these three" for the four stems sarba, kūla, abhra and kariṣa; this is kept as written. This is a Sanskrit grammatical commentary built around Pāṇinian sūtras (Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.2.53 to 3.2.76 and related rules, plus Uṇādi rules). The Sanskrit sūtras, affixes and example words are given romanized letter for letter as the Tibetan spells them, including evident misspellings (e.g. pittabhnaṃ, sughagaṃkarṇaṃ, rājaga, tāvanin, kanīp). Short Tibetan interlinear glosses are scattered through the text, often displaced from the words they explain (e.g. "phlegm-destroying, the three pungents" belongs with śleṣmaghnaṃ trikaṭukaṃ; "unborn, cow-giver, well-digger" with ajāḥ, goṣāḥ, kūpakhāḥ; "worship, pure, blazing" with arciḥ etc.); they are translated where they stand and marked "gloss." The phrase rendered "the affixes ḍava" and the reference "the rule beginning 'for all that is not saṃbuddhi, standing...'" are obscure as written and are rendered literally. ཚིག་ཕྲད here renders the grammatical term nipātana, "set (irregularly formed) word." Here རྒྱལ་བ is the root meaning "conquering" and རླུང is the bodily humour "wind," not the epithet Jina or the god Vāyu. This is a Sanskrit grammatical commentary on Pāṇinian rules (chiefly Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.4.19 to 6.4.41 and 3.2.78 to 3.2.103, with 1.1.26). Sūtras, affixes and examples are romanized as the Tibetan spells them, including evident misspellings. Short Tibetan interlinear glosses are scattered through the text, often displaced from the words they explain (for example "slayer of a brahmin, embryo, the obstructer" belong with brahmahā, bhruṇahā, vṛtahā; "father-killer" with pitṛghātī; "born from a lotus" with padmajaḥ); they are translated where they stand and marked "gloss." The glosses rendered "embryo" (Tibetan khru ba) and "the obstructer" (sgang yol) are uncertain readings, taken as explaining bhruṇa and vṛtra. Here ལས is the grammatical "object" (karman), མདོ is a grammatical sūtra, and མཁས་པ is "skilled," not the name Dakṣa. A Sanskrit grammatical commentary on Pāṇinian rules (chiefly Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.2.11 and 8.2.42 to 8.2.57, with 6.1.22 to 6.1.26, 7.2.14 to 7.2.16 and 7.4.89). Sūtras, affixes and examples are romanized as the Tibetan spells them, including evident misspellings. Short Tibetan interlinear glosses are scattered through the text, often displaced from the words they explain (for example "fire" belongs with nirvāṇa, "wind" with vāta, "dried" with śuṣka, "ashamed" with hrīṇa); they are translated where they stand and marked "gloss." Two glosses (Tibetan klas and glas) could not be identified and are given in phonetics. In the dyūta example the Tibetan says "t is changed to n," although the rule and the example require "t is not changed"; it is translated as written. Here རླུང is "wind" and མེ "fire," not the gods Vāyu and Agni, and རྒྱལ་བ is "victory" (vijigīṣā), not the epithet Jina. A Sanskrit grammatical commentary on Pāṇinian rules (chiefly Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.2.57 to 8.2.60, 7.2.17 to 7.2.27, 7.2.47 to 7.2.53, 1.2.19 to 1.2.23, 3.4.71 and 6.4.52). Sūtras, affixes and examples are romanized as the Tibetan spells them, including evident misspellings. Short Tibetan interlinear glosses are scattered through the text, often displaced from the words they explain (for example "the god worshipped" belongs with añcitaḥ devaḥ, "fire; mountain" with kaṣṭo'gniḥ and kaṣṭaḥ parvataḥ, "disobedient; harmed" with dhṛṣṭa and viśasta); they are translated where they stand and marked "gloss." One gloss (Tibetan da shad) is unidentified and given in phonetics. In the dṛḍha rule the Tibetan writes sdom pa ("vow") where the sūtra requires sbom pa ("stout"); "stout" is translated. Under the dānta rule, tshil pa ("fat") is read as tshim pa ("being satisfied") for pūrī; the glosses there for dasu and spaśa ("placing near," "vessel") are uncertain. Here ཞི་བ is "being calm" (śamu), not the god Śiva; མེ is "fire," not Agni; ཡིད renders manas, "mind." A Sanskrit grammatical commentary on Pāṇinian rules (chiefly Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.2.28 to 7.2.30, 6.1.28 to 6.1.29, 7.4.40 to 7.4.47, 6.3.124, 2.4.36, 6.4.61, 8.3.89, 3.4.72 to 3.4.76, 3.2.187 to 3.2.188, 3.3.114 and 3.2.106).
