A Sanskrit grammatical commentary on Pāṇinian rules (chiefly Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.2.107 to 3.2.148, with 7.2.67 to 7.2.68, 6.1.12, 7.2.82 to 7.2.83, 7.1.36 and 3.3.14). Sūtras, affixes and examples are romanized as the Tibetan spells them, including evident misspellings (e.g. pacamdanaḥ for pacamānaḥ, ṅharan for dhārayan). Short Tibetan interlinear glosses are scattered through the text, often displaced from the words they explain (for example "adorns, disparages, born forth ... moving about" belong with alaṃkariṣṇu through cariṣṇu, and "frightened; desiring" with trasnu and gṛdhnu); they are translated where they stand and marked "gloss." The clause "for those ending in prāyat, laṭ is changed to śatṛ and śānac" under videḥ śatur vasuḥ appears displaced and is translated where it stands. Here མཉམ་པའི་ལྷག་པར་བྱེད་པ renders samānādhikaraṇa, "co-reference"; ཆོས in the ā kveḥ rule is "custom" (dharma) in the grammatical sense; and རྒྱལ་བ in the glosses is "conquering" (for jiṣṇu), not the epithet Jina. A Sanskrit grammatical commentary on Pāṇinian rules (chiefly Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.2.148 to 3.2.179 with related vārttikas). Sūtras, affixes and examples are romanized as the Tibetan spells them, including evident misspellings. Short Tibetan interlinear glosses are scattered through the text, often displaced from the words they explain (for example "wise; destroyer, or vajra; cutter" belong with vidura, bhidura, chidura; "abiding; the Lord; clear; flour" with sthāvara, īśvara, bhāsvara, peṣvara; "a monk" with bhikṣu); they are translated where they stand and marked "gloss." Three gloss fragments (Tibetan 'dre ldog, rtsā lhas, so pa) could not be identified and are given in phonetics. The rendering "for a name and for what comes after it" for the last sūtra (saṃjñāntarayoḥ) follows the Tibetan, whose wording is broken by a gloss, and is uncertain. In the glosses སྦྱིན་པ is "giving," not the name Diti; མཁས་པ is "wise," not Dakṣa; and ཀླུ in kluk is part of an affix, not "nāga." A Sanskrit grammatical commentary on Pāṇinian rules (Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.2.179 to 3.2.185, then Uṇādi sūtras, then 3.3.1, 3.3.10 and 3.3.158), with two section-closing colophons. Sūtras, affixes, examples and the two Sanskrit closing lines are romanized as the Tibetan spells them, including evident misspellings. Short Tibetan interlinear glosses are scattered through the text, often displaced from the words they explain (for example "craftsman; wind; anus; conquering ..." belong with kāru, vāyu, pāyu, jāyu and the rest, and "the moon; a boat" with glau and nau); they are translated where they stand and marked "gloss." In the gloss read as "anus," the Tibetan writes bshad lam ("path of explanation") for bshang lam, which pāyu requires; and in "a vessel, or a leaf" 'dam ma is read as 'dab ma. One gloss (Tibetan mtsha') is unidentified and given in phonetics. The phrase "affixes to be examined" (brtag pa'i rkyen) for the Uṇādi affixes is rendered literally. Here རྐྱེན is the grammatical "affix" (pratyaya); རྒྱུད in the glosses is "thread" (tantu), not tantra; and མཁས་པ is "skilled," not the name Dakṣa. A Sanskrit grammatical commentary on Pāṇinian rules (chiefly Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.4.65, 3.3.10 to 3.3.92, 6.3.123, 2.4.38, 5.4.14 to 5.4.15, 7.1.67 to 7.1.68, 6.1.47, 6.4.27 to 6.4.28 and 4.4.20). Sūtras, affixes and examples are romanized as the Tibetan spells them, including evident misspellings (e.g. pajñaḥ for yajñaḥ, vepadruḥ for vepathuḥ). Short Tibetan interlinear glosses are scattered through the text, often displaced from the words they explain (for example "compounded poison; barley; purifier" belong with garaḥ, yavaḥ, pavaḥ, and "obtained good; obtained bad" with sulabha, durlabha); they are translated where they stand and marked "gloss." A stray syllable "ha" is kept as it stands. Evident copyists' slips read in the translation: skras ("by hair") as sgras ("by sound"), ngag rgyas pa ("speech expanded") for dag rgyas pa, tshos pa ("cooked") for tshes pa, 'dar ba ("trembling") for 'dang ba, and kar ("into k") for dkar. The last sūtra and its gloss are repeated in the Tibetan and are translated as they stand. Here མེ is "fire" (the fire-altar, citi), not the god Agni; ཕུང་པོ is a "heap," not an aggregate; and རྒྱལ་བ is "victory" (jaya), not the epithet Jina. A Sanskrit grammatical commentary on Pāṇinian rules (chiefly Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.3.91 to 3.3.118 with related vārttikas and 2.4.57). Sūtras, affixes and examples are romanized as the Tibetan spells them, including evident misspellings. Short Tibetan interlinear glosses are scattered through the text, often displaced from the words they explain (for example "skilled; intelligence; mindfulness" belong with kṛti, buddhi, smṛti, and "wisdom; respect; great respect; going; food" with jñāna, māna, pramāṇa, gamana, bhojana); they are translated where they stand and marked "gloss." The repeated gloss "what work did you do, making the words into chapters?" renders the example kāṃ tvaṃ kārim akārṣīḥ. One gloss (Tibetan kla rna) is unidentified and given in phonetics; the gloss "cut" reads ཚད་མ as ཆད་མ (not "valid cognition"); the gloss "teaching" for sīvana/sevana stands as written, though the sense required is "sewing." The derivation of kriyā ("by the rules giving a and īya") is obscure in the Tibetan and rendered loosely. Here ལྟ་བ in a gloss is "looking" (īkṣā), not "view" as a doctrinal term. This piece continues the commentary on Pāṇini's third book (3.3.119 to 3.3.128 and vārttikas, then 3.4.18 and 3.4.21), followed by the rules on ktvā and lyap from books one, six and seven (1.2.7, 1.2.23 to 25, 6.4.31 and 32, 6.4.18, 6.4.38, 7.1.37, 7.2.51, 7.2.55 and 56, 7.4.43). Sūtras and example words are romanized exactly as the Tibetan spells them, including copyists' errors. Thus bracharaḥ and samubrachadaḥ stand for pracchadaḥ and samupacchādaḥ (the second should be long), ghukhābrājati for bhuktvā vrajati, alikhalāoḥpratiṣedhegdā for alaṃkhalvoḥ pratiṣedhe ktvā, kṣīskandasyandoḥ for na ktvi skandisyandoḥ, pūdaśca for pūṅaś ca, pālyapi for vā lyapi, and īkhatkaraḥ, īṣatvānaḥ and naṃṣṭrā for īṣatkaraḥ, īṣatpānaḥ and naṃṣṭvā. "Khvā," "khyā," "gtvā," "ghā" and "ktā" in the running text are scribal forms of the affix ktvā. "Niśa" stands for the root naś.

Interlinear glosses displaced from their words are given inline as "(gloss: ...)". Several sit far from the word they explain: "obtaining; going; debt; pervading" repeats the root meanings of vaha, vraja, vyaja and apa; "becomes slightly rich" and the like explain the āḍhyaṃbhava examples; "drinks a little; hard to drink; easy to drink" belong to īṣatpāna and the rest; "endured well" belongs to sumarṣaṇa; "makes ornament; makes certain" belong to alaṃkṛtvā and khalukṛtvā; "thirst," "patience" and "subtle" belong to tṛṣ, mṛṣ and kṛś; "having been cleansed; pure" and "Śiva" belong to pū. "Rich with joy" renders dga' ba as written; dka' ba, "with difficulty," is probably meant. "Drinks well" for sudharṣaṇa may be a slip for 'thub, "overcomes." Some glosses could not be identified and are given in phonetics: tserpa ('tsher pa), tsepa (tshes pa, said to be "from the sūtra"), nyepa (nyed pa) and tulga (tul ga).

Grammatical senses of glossary terms: ལས here is mostly the ablative "from," and in "agent and object" it means the grammatical object (karman), not karma. Glossed as "to go" or "going," འགྲོ་བ is a verb meaning. In "one whose k goes" (kit), "whose ū goes," "whose u goes" and "whose ut goes," it means an indicatory letter that drops away. དོན means "sense," as in "in the sense of an action." མཐའ means "final" or "end," not an extreme. ཡུལ appears only within spyod yul, "domain of activity," the gloss on gocara. དགའ་བ ("joy") and བཟོད་པ ("patience," "endured") appear in glosses. མདོ ("sūtra") appears in one gloss. དྲང་སྲོང is the sage Kāśyapa. Kāśyapa is cited in sūtra 1.2.25 as the authority for the optional rule. Rendered literally, the gloss says this is the name of the sun's father. The words "bears the name of one whose k goes" render the technical term kit. "Set form" renders nipātana. "Preverb" renders upasarga. This piece completes the commentary on the kṛt section of the Pāṇinivyākaraṇa. It covers the rules on lyap (6.4.69, 6.4.56 and 57, 6.4.70, 6.1.41, 6.1.44) and on ṇamul and khamuñ (3.4.22 to 3.4.59, with Kāśikā-type supplements). It closes with a Sanskrit colophon and a verse, followed by a Tibetan rendering of the verse. As before, sūtras and examples are romanized exactly as spelled, errors included. For example, bhuktvābhuktvāprajati stands for bhuktvā bhuktvā vrajati, cauraṃkāri for cauraṃkāram, svādukṛtvāphukte for svādu kṛtvā bhuṅkte, samūlabhātaṃ for samūlaghātaṃ, ratvānidhāyaṃ for ratnanidhāyaṃ, jībagrāhaṃ for jīvagrāhaṃ, and urcaicakṛtya for uccaiḥkṛtya. "Sra" stands for sva, and "ktrā" in the sūtra for ktvā. "Samprasāraṇa" is spelled samprasūraṇa once in the Tibetan. At sūtra 6.1.44 the explanation omits "optionally," which the sūtra requires. The text says "to rim pa ṣa," a slip for piṣa, and is rendered "to piṣa." Sūtra 3.4.59 actually concerns an unpleasant statement (ayathābhipreta), but the Tibetan explains it as "expressing delight," and it is translated as written. "Mēṅ, to harm" is the text's own gloss on the root of mayati.

Interlinear glosses are given inline as "(gloss: ...)". Many are displaced from the words they explain. "Goes having eaten and eaten" explains bhuktvā bhuktvā vrajati. "Does the act of a thief" explains cauraṃkāram. "Having said 'Well done!', he praises" explains sādhu kṛtvā stauti. "He eats having done it otherwise," and the three like it, explain anyathākāraṃ and the rest. "He eats having obtained a living" explains jīvavedaṃ. "Grinds dry, fine, coarse" explains śuṣkapeṣaṃ and the rest; the verb theg is read as btags, "ground." "Seized with the hand" explains hastagrāhaṃ. "Holds firmly like a jewel" explains ratnanidhāyaṃ. "Having seized the staff" explains yaṣṭiṃgrāhaṃ. "Expressing delight, he raised it high" explains uccaiḥkṛtya. "Natural form; not made" goes with prakṛtya (prakṛti). "Self-victor" (rang rgyal ba, the usual word for a pratyekabuddha) is unplaced and is translated literally. One gloss could not be identified and is given in phonetics: rabtu jabpa (rab tu byab pa).

The Sanskrit colophon is corrupt. It would read iti pāṇinivyākaraṇasya sūtrāt kṛtādayaḥ samāptāḥ. The final verse is the closing verse of Rāmacandra's Prakriyākaumudī, roughly prakriyākaumudī seyaṃ rāmacandraprakāśitā, asadvacastamovṛttād ... ciram. Both are transliterated exactly as written. In the Tibetan verse, "the Very Clear" (rab byed shin tu gsal ba) renders the title Prakriyākaumudī, and "binds the last of untrue speech" translates the Tibetan literally; the Sanskrit speaks of the darkness of false speech.

Grammatical senses of glossary terms: རང་བཞིན here means a word's natural form (prakṛti), not inherent existence. ལས is mostly the ablative "from"; it means the grammatical object (karman) in "object word," and "act" or "deed" in the thief gloss. འགྲོ་བ means "going." དོན means "sense." མཐའ means "ending" in "ending in the third case." In the verse, mtha' ma means "the last." རྒྱུད appears in rab tu rgyud, "continuing on," and is not tantra. རྒྱལ་བ appears only within the gloss "self-victor." དགའ་བ means delight. དཔེ appears in dper brjod, "illustrative examples." མདོ is Pāṇini's sūtra text. བསྟན་བཅོས is "treatise." ཚིགས་སུ་བཅད་པ is "verses." ལེགས་སོ is "Well done!" This is the closing piece of the text: two benedictory Sanskrit verses with their Tibetan renderings, then the translator's colophon and his dedicatory verses. Both Sanskrit verses are corrupt, and they are transliterated exactly as written. They would read: ācāryaṃ pātu bhagavān śiṣyaṃ pātu vināyakaḥ, nirvighnaṃ syāc ca sarvatra pāṇinīyaprasādataḥ; and maṅgalaṃ lekhakānāṃ ca pāṭhakānāṃ ca maṅgalaṃ, maṅgalaṃ sarvabhūtānāṃ bhūmibhūpatimaṅgalaṃ. "The Guide" renders rnam par 'dren pa, the Tibetan for vināyaka. "Writers" reads 'dri pa as 'bri pa. In "the land and the lord of the land," ས means "earth" or "land," not a bodhisattva ground.

The colophon names the patron as the Fifth Dalai Lama, by his full religious name, and presents him as Padmapāṇi, that is, Avalokiteśvara. The epithet ཉིད་གསུམ་ལྡན is read as the usual "endowed with the three vows." The Tibetan spells the opening syllables of his name dag dbang, a slip for ngag dbang. In personal names, རྒྱ་མཚོ is given in phonetics (Gyatso), not as "ocean." The translator, Ngawang Phuntsok Lhundrub (also called Tsewang Rabten Dorje), worked under the paṇḍitas Balabhadra (spelled Palabhadra) and Gokulanātha Miśra, and based his notes on Rāmacandra's Prakriyākaumudī. "The Complete Explanation" (kun bshad) is an unidentified work. A zho is a Tibetan unit of weight for precious metals.

The dating uses Tibetan conventions. "Fire, sky, ocean" are symbolic numerals (3, 0 and 4), and the clause about ten sixty-year cycles appears garbled in the Tibetan. "Nachang" (rna 'phyang) appears to be the year named rnam 'phyang (Vilambin, the thirty-second year of the cycle), and "Kündén" (kun ldan) is a later cycle year, here an iron rat year. "Chutö" reads chu stong as chu stod, the month named after the lunar mansion Pūrvāṣāḍhā. "The third victory day" (rgyal ba, the Jayā lunar days) is the thirteenth day of the fortnight. "Bashé" (ba she) is an unidentified lunar mansion or yoga, given in phonetics. "Completed" renders sbyang ba, probably a slip for sbyar ba, "composed." The parenthetical note on detailed annotations interrupts the dating sentence in the Tibetan, and is kept where it stands.

The dedicatory verses embed the patron's name: Lord of Speech (Ngag dbang), excellent intelligence (blo bzang), ocean (rgya mtsho). "Twofold law" is the joint religious and secular system. "Sole father of the Ganges" is a poetic image for the Himalaya. The folio marker at the end of the input is omitted.

Glossary terms: ཆོས here means Dharma, as in "Dharma college." རྒྱལ་བ appears in "Victorious Lord" (rgyal dbang) and as the name of a lunar day. ལུང་བསྟན is a prophecy. ཟླ་བ means "month" or "moon" in the dates. Within the name of Caitra, ནག་པ་ཟླ་བ is kept as Caitra. མཁས་པ is the adjective "learned" here, not the example name Dakṣa used earlier in the text. བཟོད་པ means "bear patiently." དཔེ appears in dper brjod, "illustrative examples." ས is "land." The verses render དགེ་བ as "virtue," སེམས་ཅན as "sentient beings" and འགྲོ་བ as "beings."
